summary: The RECOVE trial tested an 8-week supervised concurrent training program (combined resistance and endurance exercise), inspiratory muscle training, or both, versus WHO self-management recommendations in 80 non-hospitalised adults with long COVID lasting over 12 weeks. The primary outcome was estimated VO2max: no statistically significant differences between groups were found, though the concurrent training groups achieved individual within-group improvements of approximately 7.5–7.8% (effect sizes 0.28–0.36). Concurrent training with or without inspiratory muscle training significantly outperformed the other groups on lower-body strength (14.5–32.6% improvement, ES 0.27–1.13), fatigue, and depression scores, and no adverse events occurred during any training session.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2max showed no significant between-group differences (P > 0.05); within-group improvements in CT and CTRM were 7.5% and 7.8% respectively (ES 0.28 and 0.36) but did not reach statistical significance versus comparators.

summary: This randomized sham-controlled trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — 30 minutes daily for 20 days at 10 Hz — versus inactive sham stimulation in 42 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID fatigue lasting at least 12 weeks. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in fatigue severity (Fatigue Severity Scale), but the sham group improved more than the active taVNS group after treatment (mean FSS 4.79 vs 5.05, p=0.034 between groups favoring sham), with only small effect sizes (Cohen's d ≈ −0.19). taVNS did produce autonomic changes consistent with increased parasympathetic activity (decreased SNS index, decreased LF/HF ratio), but the study was likely underpowered and one co-author is a co-founder of the company that manufactured the stimulation device.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary fatigue outcome (FSS) after treatment: sham taVNS mean 4.79 vs taVNS mean 5.05; between-group difference p=0.034 favoring sham, Cohen's d = −0.190 (small effect against active treatment).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested two yogic breathing techniques — Bhramari Pranayama (humming breath) and Sheetali Pranayama (cooling breath) — practiced for 30 minutes daily over 6 months in 90 post-COVID patients aged 19–40. Both techniques significantly improved lung function: forced vital capacity (FVC) increased by approximately 0.5 L in the Bhramari group and 0.4 L in the Sheetali group compared to controls, with FEV1 improving by 0.3 L in both groups. Heart rate variability also improved, with RMSSD rising by 5.5 ms in the Bhramari group and 4.8 ms in the Sheetali group, indicating enhanced parasympathetic nervous system activity. The study was single-centre with a small sample per arm (28–30 participants), limiting generalisability.

The between-group p-value of 0.03 for Borg and DVAI are stated in the abstract with specific reference to between-group comparison (sham vs IMT), whereas the Table 2 between-group p-values are 0.24 and 0.56 respectively — the abstract values appear to be within-group p-values mislabeled; within-group p-values (0.03 for IMT arm Borg, 0.03 for DVAI in IMT arm) match Table 2. summary: This study tested 6 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) using a pressure-threshold device versus sham training in 18 long COVID patients (9 per arm) who had persistent exertional breathlessness and confirmed diaphragm muscle weakness approximately 31 months after hospitalization for COVID-19. The primary outcome — inspiratory muscle endurance (time to task failure) — improved significantly in the IMT group compared to sham (median 365s at baseline vs 983s post-training, p=0.05), and exertional dyspnea scores (Borg scale) also improved (7 to 6, p=0.03), with benefits persisting 6 weeks after training ended. The trial was very small (9 per arm), largely open-label, and powered for within-group rather than between-group differences, limiting the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: time to task failure improved from 365s to 983s in IMT arm vs 286s to 574s in sham arm, between-group p=0.05; Borg dyspnea score improved from 7 to 6 in IMT arm vs no change in sham, p=0.03.

summary: This double-blind randomized controlled trial tested four consecutive daily sessions of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in 40 adults with long COVID-related cognitive fatigue. The primary outcome (subjective trait fatigue) showed no significant benefit from active versus sham stimulation; among the secondary outcomes reported here, tDCS also had no significant effect on subjective state fatigue ratings or behavioral performance on a cognitive task. The only notable finding was a statistically significant interaction in occipital alpha brainwave activity, where the sham group showed a greater fatigue-related increase in alpha power at post-assessment compared to the active stimulation group (mean difference = 0.06, p = 0.011, d = 0.33), suggesting a possible but limited neurophysiological stabilizing effect that did not translate into measurable clinical benefit.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested 8 weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT) in 281 adults with long COVID (average 9 months post-infection, 88% female) whose primary symptom was breathlessness. The primary outcome — overall health-related quality of life measured by K-BILD total score — did not differ significantly between the IMT and control groups in the intention-to-treat analysis (IMT: 58.2±12.3 vs control: 59.5±12.4). However, IMT produced clinically meaningful improvements in breathlessness-specific outcomes: the Transition Dyspnoea Index improved by 2.0 points in the IMT group versus 0.9 in controls (p=0.005), and the K-BILD breathlessness and chest symptoms domains both improved beyond their minimal clinically important thresholds, alongside gains in respiratory muscle strength and estimated aerobic fitness.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome K-BILD total score showed no significant between-group difference in the intention-to-treat population (IMT: 58.2±12.3 vs control: 59.5±12.4, p<0.05 threshold not met for between-group comparison); significant results were limited to secondary outcomes and the per-protocol subgroup.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an interim safety report (N=20) of an ongoing RCT planned for N=80. Baseline data are reported for the combined cohort only (not per arm), as the trial remains blinded. No efficacy outcome data by arm are reported — all numeric outcome values extracted are cohort-level baselines compared to norm data, not intervention vs. control comparisons. Per-arm sample sizes are not disclosed. AEs are reported for the combined cohort (31 AEs in 60% of subjects, 20 with at least possible relationship to study drug), but not broken down by arm. RHI mean and SD are not reported numerically in the text — only descriptive percentages (35% with RHI <1.67, 30% with RHI 1.67-2.10). RAND-36 domain data beyond PF and RP (e.g., Bodily Pain, General Health, Vitality, Social Functioning, Mental Health, Role Emotional) are depicted in figures only without extractable numeric values in the text. The norm comparison values extracted as 'between_group_effects' are cohort vs. reference population comparisons, not intervention vs. control RCT effects. Work/study percentages and physical activity from Table 1 not extracted as outcomes.

summary: This interim safety report from the HOT-LoCO trial tested hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2) versus sham treatment in 20 previously healthy adults with long COVID (post-COVID condition) at Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden. The interim analysis does not report primary efficacy outcomes — those are physical functioning and role physical scores on RAND-36 at 13 weeks — but documents baseline characteristics and safety data only. The enrolled cohort had severely impaired health-related quality of life (RAND-36 physical functioning score 31.75 vs. population norm of 83.5, p<0.001) and reduced exercise capacity (6-minute walk test 442m vs. 662m norm, p<0.001). Thirty-one adverse events occurred across 60% of subjects, with no serious adverse events; the most common were cough and chest pain/discomfort, and all were transient, leading the independent safety board to conclude HBO2 has a favorable safety profile.

trial_rating.result_basis: No primary efficacy outcome data reported in this interim analysis; baseline RAND-36 physical functioning was 31.75 vs. norm 83.5 (p<0.001), confirming severe impairment at entry, but no between-group treatment effect is yet available.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports the METS CI as '1.42 (-0.46-2.66)' in Table 3, which appears to be a reporting error since the upper CI (2.66) is less than the point estimate (1.42) when combined with the lower CI. This was extracted verbatim as stated. The baseline table SD for 'Middle circumference' intervention arm lists 1.95 which duplicates a value also appearing in the baseline table — extracted as stated. The paper stated p=.011 for VO2 peak in the discussion ('p = .011') but Table 3 reports p=0.11; the table value (0.11) was used as it matches the narrative description of non-significance. Oxygen saturation at baseline was reported (intervention 90.42±8.13%, control 88.64±8.72%) but no post-intervention values were provided, so this outcome was not extracted as a full outcome object. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding home-based breathing and chest mobility exercises (3 times per week for 12 weeks) to a standard cardiac rehabilitation program improved cardiorespiratory fitness in 46 long COVID patients with cardiovascular comorbidities such as coronary artery disease and hypertension. Patients who received the additional exercises walked 52 meters further on the 6-minute walk test (467 m vs 415 m, p=0.032), and showed significantly higher peak expiratory flow rate (503 vs 411 L/min, p=0.031) and peak cough flow (465 vs 366 L/min, p=0.016) compared to those on cardiac rehabilitation alone. No significant differences were found in quality of life or inflammation markers (CRP, D-dimer), and no adverse cardiovascular events occurred during the trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk test: intervention 467 m vs control 415 m, mean difference 52 m (95% CI 4.81–99.96), p=0.032; PEFR difference 91 L/min (95% CI 8.61–173.99), p=0.031.

summary: This RCT tested supervised twice-weekly, 8-week water-based (AQUA) and land-based (LAND) exercise programmes versus no exercise in 74 children aged 10-12 with post-COVID-19 condition characterised by fatigue and respiratory symptoms. Lung function was a secondary outcome; both exercise groups showed significant improvements in FEV1 and FVC compared to controls, who declined (e.g., girls in the AQUA group improved FEV1% predicted by 14.3 percentage points vs a 6.4 point decline in controls). The trial was underpowered for lung function as a secondary endpoint, sample sizes per group were modest (23-26 at baseline), and the study was not blinded due to the nature of the intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: Secondary outcome FEV1 GROUP×REPETITION interaction: F(2,64)=6.80, p<0.01, η²=0.18; FVC interaction: F(2,64)=4.63, p<0.05, η²=0.13; lung function was not the primary outcome and the trial was not powered for it.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a health economics paper reporting cost-effectiveness of the REGAIN RCT; the primary clinical outcomes (PROMIS-PROPr) are reported only by reference to the companion clinical paper (McGregor et al. BMJ 2024) and are NOT reported with per-arm means/SDs in this paper. The EQ-5D-5L is the primary outcome for economic evaluation. Table 4 (cost-effectiveness results) had heavily merged/garbled cells in the source text; arm-level adjusted cost values (REGAIN £1987 CI 1666-2307; usual care £1681 CI 1406-1955) and QALY values were extracted from partially reconstructed table. The 6-month CI upper bound for EQ-5D utility in Table 3 appears to be a typo (0.67 instead of likely 0.067) — extracted verbatim. Intervention cost per patient: REGAIN £399.92 (n=298); usual care £72.71 (n=287). Resource use cost breakdown by category (medication, outpatient, community care, A&E, inpatient, PSS, nursing home) extracted in Table 2 with complete data across 0-12 months. No adverse events data reported in this economic paper. Time since hospital discharge to randomisation mean 10.6 months reported overall only.

summary: The REGAIN trial tested an eight-week online supervised group rehabilitation programme combining physical exercise sessions and psychological support against best-practice usual care (a single online consultation) in 585 adults with post-COVID-19 condition who had previously been hospitalised. The primary economic outcome was cost-effectiveness over 12 months: the REGAIN intervention cost £305 more per patient (95% CI: -£123 to £732) and generated 0.026 additional QALYs (95% CI: -0.005 to 0.052), yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £11,941 per QALY, well below the UK NHS £30,000 willingness-to-pay threshold. The 84% probability of cost-effectiveness at that threshold supports offering the programme to hospitalised post-COVID patients, though results are based on modest and statistically non-significant differences in both cost and quality of life, and the findings may not generalise to non-hospitalised patients or minority ethnic groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: Incremental QALYs of 0.026 (95% CI: -0.005 to 0.052) are non-significant; incremental cost £305 (95% CI: -£123 to £732) also non-significant; ICER £11,941/QALY with 84% probability of cost-effectiveness at £30,000 threshold.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: In participants with high baseline CRP, TG-HDL, and BMI, vortioxetine showed significant improvement in DSST vs placebo (treatment x time x CRP x TG-HDL x BMI interaction chi2=11.967, p=0.018 unadjusted; chi2=12.979, p=0.011 adjusted).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a post-hoc analysis of a primary RCT (NCT05047952; primary paper: McIntyre et al., Brain, 2023). The DSST baseline values are reported as combined z-scores. The between-group mean difference of 0.621 (SE=0.313, p=0.047) is from GEE adjusted model moderated by CRP/TG-HDL/BMI — it reflects the interaction-moderated comparison, not a simple overall between-group difference. Week 2 DSST data were collected but no numeric values reported for that timepoint in this paper. Endpoint absolute DSST scores (week 8) not reported — only change-from-baseline values available. The vortioxetine arm TRG-HDL SD (17.19) appears anomalously large compared to placebo (0.99), likely reflecting skewed data or outliers. Adverse events not reported in this post-hoc analysis paper. BMI sub-category means reported in Table 1 but reflect subgroup means within weight categories rather than overall summary statistics.

summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) versus placebo in 147 Canadian adults with WHO-defined long COVID, focusing on whether baseline metabolic dysfunction, elevated BMI, and inflammation modified cognitive outcomes. The primary outcome was change in Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) score; vortioxetine produced a statistically significant between-group improvement at 8 weeks (mean difference 0.621 points, p=0.047), with the benefit concentrated in participants who had high baseline CRP, elevated TG-HDL ratio, and higher BMI. This is a post-hoc analysis of a previously published trial, not a pre-specified primary analysis, so the findings are hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week home-based pulmonary rehabilitation program — comprising daily walking, diaphragmatic strengthening, and resistance training — against usual medical care alone in 60 adults aged 40–70 with post-COVID-19 syndrome presenting with fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise intolerance. The primary outcome, six-minute walk test distance, improved substantially more in the rehabilitation group (439.7 m) than the control group (347 m) after 12 weeks, a difference of roughly 93 m. The rehabilitation group also showed meaningfully lower fatigue scores (Chalder: 11.1 vs. 13.4), higher physical fitness index (52.3 vs. 36.7), better quality of life on the SF-36 (66.4 vs. 47.6), and greater dyspnea reduction, all at p<0.001, with no notable safety concerns reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved to 439.7 m (rehabilitation) vs. 347 m (control), a ~93 m between-group difference, p<0.001; baseline values were comparable (270.7 m vs. 274.1 m).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports between-group effects as Beta-coefficients from a Univariate General Linear Model adjusted for age and BMI; these are interpreted as adjusted mean differences (intervention minus control) for absolute change scores. Note that positive Beta-coefficient for PSQI and HADS-Anxiety indicates improvement in the BT group (i.e., the control group worsened or improved less, and the BT group had greater improvement in change scores — the directionality is: positive beta = BT group improved more, for scales where lower=better; negative beta = BT group improved more for scales where higher=better). Per-arm follow-up means and SDs for timepoints 2 and 3 are not provided in tables — only absolute change from baseline means are shown in figures (as mean with SE bars) without numeric values in the text or supplemental tables referenced. Therefore, endpoint values at timepoints 2 and 3 per arm could not be extracted. The paper states data are expressed as mean (SE) in figures but exact values are not provided. The RR data for improvement categorization (e.g., SF-36 pain RR=2.8 [1.69;4.64], energy/fatigue RR=2.0 [1.31;3.05]) are reported as supplemental figure data and not extracted as separate outcomes. Table 1 missing the BT group column header for sample sizes (table appears to show only Control N=47 in header but BT group data is present). ICU admission rates are provided (BT: 3.9%, Control: 2.1%) but not used to calculate percent previously hospitalized as ICU is a subset. Baseline PSQI SD for control arm listed with comma decimal '11.13 (4,17)' — extracted as 4.17.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 sessions of balneotherapy (thermal mineral water immersion plus aquatic exercises) over one month against a no-treatment control in 98 adults with long COVID, most of whom were middle-aged women with symptoms lasting over one year. The primary outcome was change in questionnaire scores across multiple validated scales; the largest improvements in the balneotherapy group were in musculoskeletal pain (SF-36 pain subscale beta-coefficient -21.6, 95% CI -30.48 to -12.78, p<0.0001) and fatigue (SF-36 energy/fatigue beta-coefficient -17.5, 95% CI -24.23 to -10.66, p<0.0001), with additional significant short-term gains in sleep quality, anxiety, and several quality-of-life domains. Gains in sleep, anxiety, and emotional well-being were not sustained at the one-month follow-up, and 17 of 51 participants in the balneotherapy group reported mild transient worsening of symptoms, primarily fatigue, especially in early sessions.

trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 pain subscale beta-coefficient -21.6 (95% CI -30.48 to -12.78, p<0.0001) and energy/fatigue beta-coefficient -17.5 (95% CI -24.23 to -10.66, p<0.0001) vs. control at end of intervention.

The 'control' is a historical placebo showing 5.9% improvement on Chalder Likert from Cho et al. 2005 meta-analysis — no concurrent placebo arm exists. 2. The paper reports FSS and PROMIS-7a results only for Long COVID arms (arms 4 and 5); ME/CFS arm FSS and PROMIS results are not reported in accessible tabular or numeric form. 4. Adverse event data for ME/CFS arms 1 and 2 reference '1000 mg BID group' with n=24 in the text but the arm enrolled N=29; the text says '2/24 in the 1000 mg BID group' which may be an error or refer to a subset — extracted verbatim. 5. The Long COVID 500 mg BID arm (arm 4) Chalder Bimodal 2-week value shown in Table 3 as '46.8%***' appears under the '6-Weeks' row for bimodal — Table 3 Long COVID section header reads '2-Weeks' and '6-Weeks' for Chalder Fatigue at 6 Weeks columns; the table is somewhat garbled/merged. Values extracted as best interpretation from text and table. 6. p-values reported only as thresholds (* p<0.05, ** p<0.005, *** p<0.0005 or similar); no exact p-values provided. 7. Baseline Chalder scores described as ranging 76-92% of maximum but no per-arm breakdown given. 8. ME/CFS arm age (median 47) and sex (73.7% female) reported for the group overall, not per arm. summary: This non-randomized, open-label dose-escalation trial tested anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate (AEO), a nutritional supplement, in 76 ME/CFS patients (average illness duration 8.9 years, 73.7% women) and 43 long COVID patients with fatigue lasting at least 6 months. The primary outcome was change in Chalder Fatigue Scale score at 6 weeks compared to a historical placebo benchmark of 5.9% improvement; ME/CFS patients showed 22.5–27.9% reductions in fatigue (Likert scoring, p<0.005) and up to 33.3% achieved clinical normalization on bimodal scoring, while long COVID patients at 500 mg twice daily showed up to 46.8% achieving clinical normalization. Key caveats are substantial: the study was unblinded with no concurrent placebo group, was funded by the supplement manufacturer (Terra Biological LLC), one author is a company officer, and dropout rates were high in the long COVID arm, all of which severely limit interpretation of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chalder Fatigue Scale (Likert) improved 22.5–27.9% from baseline in ME/CFS groups vs historical placebo of 5.9% (p<0.005); 33.3% of ME/CFS patients and 46.8% of long COVID patients reached bimodal score ≤4.

summary: This study tested three intravenous infusions of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs, 4×10⁷ cells/dose) versus placebo in 100 severe COVID-19 patients from Wuhan, with 78 patients assessed at a 3-year follow-up. The primary lung imaging outcome was not statistically significant: 47% of MSC-treated patients showed normal CT scans versus 34% of placebo patients (OR=1.68, 95% CI: 0.65–4.34, p=0.28). The one statistically significant finding was a higher general health score on the SF-36 quality-of-life survey in the MSC group (median 67 vs 50, difference 12.86, 95% CI: 1.44–24.28), with no significant differences in exercise capacity, pulmonary function, or long COVID symptom rates between groups; no increase in tumor incidence or other safety signals was observed over three years.

summary: A 3-month online-supported, app-guided physical activity program (150 min/week of moderate exercise, individually tailored) was tested against a waiting-list control in 62 long COVID patients with significant fatigue (FAS score ≥22) recruited at Hannover Medical School. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), did not improve significantly in either group: the intervention group gained 0.9 ml/min/kg versus 0.3 ml/min/kg in controls, with no significant between-group difference (p=0.098 within intervention group; between-group mean difference -0.6 ml/min/kg, 95% CI -1.8 to 0.8). Fatigue scores improved in both groups equally, likely reflecting natural recovery over time rather than a treatment effect; a post-hoc subgroup analysis found that only patients with moderate fatigue (FAS <35) showed any improvement in exercise capacity, regardless of group assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak between-group mean difference was -0.6 ml/min/kg (95% CI -1.8 to 0.8), p=0.098 within the intervention group; no significant between-group difference detected; post-hoc power analysis showed only 12% statistical power, with 810 patients required to detect a significant effect.

The baseline values in Table 2 match Table 1 exactly, suggesting Table 2 reports all randomized participants' baselines alongside completers' follow-up (or slight rounding). The between-group effect for SF-36 Mental Health change score (T1-T0 difference: 1.98 - (-1.26) = 3.24) was calculated from Table 2 data; the paper states p=0.046 for this comparison. summary: A randomized controlled trial tested an 8-session online multimodal rehabilitation program — covering physical, cognitive, and respiratory exercises plus nutrition, sleep hygiene, and emotional management via weekly group videoconferences and a Moodle platform — in 134 Spanish adults with long COVID (mean age 49, 84% female) recruited from patient associations, added on top of usual primary care. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life measured by the SF-36; the intervention group showed a statistically significant improvement in mental health-related quality of life (mean increase of 1.98 points, p=0.046) compared to a decline of 1.26 points in the control group, though no significant difference was found for physical health-related quality of life or any secondary outcome. trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 Mental Health T1-T0: intervention group +1.98 points vs control group -1.26 points, p=0.046; R2 adjusted=0.126.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 4-week supervised aerobic exercise program (12 sessions on a cycling ergometer, using either moderate- or high-intensity interval training) in 24 long COVID patients aged 18–75 with persistent symptoms. The primary finding was that 67.8% of patients in the exercise group showed reduced or resolved symptoms after 4 weeks, compared to 16.7% in the control group (p=0.013). Peak oxygen uptake (peak VO2) improved by 4.64 mL/kg/min in the exercise group versus a decline of 1.06 mL/kg/min in the control group (p=0.001), while no significant improvements were found in mental health, quality of life, or pulmonary function measures.

trial_rating.result_basis: Peak VO2 improved by 4.64 mL/kg/min in the exercise group vs. -1.06 mL/kg/min in the control group (p group*time=0.001); symptom improvement in 67.8% vs. 16.7% of controls (p=0.013).

summary: This pilot randomised controlled trial tested at-home, self-administered transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — a non-invasive device that delivers electrical stimulation to the ear to activate the vagus nerve — in 12 adults with confirmed long COVID symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, depression, and others. The primary outcomes were feasibility and safety, not efficacy; the trial was explicitly underpowered to detect clinical effects. Descriptively, participants receiving active taVNS for two weeks saw their reported long COVID symptom burden fall from 46% to 31% of nine tracked symptoms, versus no change in the sham group (68% to 68%), and those completing four weeks of active treatment showed the largest reductions in mental fatigue scores, but no inferential statistics were reported for symptom outcomes. The intervention was safe, with no cardiac adverse events and only two mild cases of skin irritation across all sessions.

trial_rating.result_basis: No p-values or confidence intervals were reported for any symptom outcome; the only quantitative comparison is descriptive: active group symptoms fell from 46% to 31% over two weeks versus sham remaining at 68%, with the study explicitly stated to be underpowered to determine efficacy.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested two 8-week exercise-based rehabilitation programmes — face-to-face and remote — against usual care in 181 adults with post-COVID syndrome who had previously been hospitalised with COVID-19. Both interventions significantly improved exercise capacity measured by the Incremental Shuttle Walking Test: face-to-face rehabilitation produced a mean gain of 52 metres over usual care (95% CI 19–85 m, p=0.002) and remote rehabilitation produced a gain of 34 metres (95% CI 1–66 m, p=0.047), both exceeding the established 35-metre minimal clinically important difference. Neither intervention improved self-reported quality of life or symptom scores compared to usual care, and an exploratory immune substudy (n=31) found that face-to-face rehabilitation increased CD8+ T-cell and NK cell counts relative to usual care, with no safety signals attributable to the interventions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Face-to-face rehabilitation improved ISWT by mean 52 m (95% CI 19–85 m, p=0.002) and remote by 34 m (95% CI 1–66 m, p=0.047) versus usual care, both exceeding the 35 m MCID.

summary: This study tested oral Actovegin (400 mg three times daily for 60 days) added to standard care in 222 post-COVID-19 patients with cognitive impairment, compared to 222 controls receiving standard care alone; average patient age was 68 years. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) applied for 25 minutes after aerobic exercise in 44 young adults (aged 18-45) with post-COVID syndrome lasting more than 12 weeks. The primary finding was that taVNS enhanced cardiac vagal control during post-exercise recovery: the RMSSD index (a measure of heart rate variability reflecting vagal activity) increased significantly in the taVNS group after stimulation (p=0.028) but not in the placebo group, and the parasympathetic nervous system index showed a greater rate of increase in the taVNS group (p=0.009). However, taVNS produced no significant advantage over placebo for blood lactate clearance or blood pressure reduction, meaning its practical impact on exercise recovery was limited to autonomic signaling measures rather than metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: RMSSD increased significantly in the taVNS group post-stimulation (p=0.028) vs non-significant increase in placebo; no significant between-group differences in blood lactate (p=0.006 within-group but similar across both groups) or blood pressure (p=0.01 both groups equally).

summary: This double-blind RCT tested daily 1-hour sessions of lower-extremity electrical stimulation (E-Stim) applied to the gastrocnemius muscles for 4 weeks in 18 previously hospitalised long COVID patients with persistent leg muscle weakness and deconditioning. After 4 weeks, only the active E-Stim group showed improved muscle perfusion recovery after stimulation (oxyhemoglobin rose from t60 to t70, p=0.040) and increased gastrocnemius muscle endurance over the 1-hour session (p=0.031), while the sham group showed no improvement in either measure. The intervention was well-tolerated with no adverse events, though the trial was small, the two groups were not well-matched at baseline (the active group had more severe prior illness), and the sample size fell short of the pre-specified target of 32.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active group oxyhemoglobin increased post-stimulation at 4 weeks (p=0.040, d=0.334) vs sham which continued to decline (p<0.001, d=0.632); group×time interaction p=0.022. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of Baduanjin exercise training (BET) — a traditional Chinese mind-body practice involving gentle postures, breathing, and meditation — in 40 adults with idiopathic chronic fatigue who had also recovered from COVID-19. The primary outcome, forced vital capacity (FVC), improved significantly in the BET group (from 2.07 L to 2.18 L) compared to no change in controls (2.03 L to 2.02 L), with a between-group difference significant at p=0.001. All secondary outcomes also improved significantly in the BET group, including 6-minute walk distance (298 m to 358 m), fatigue scores, sleep quality, depression, and quality of life, with no changes in the control group; however, the trial is limited by a very small sample (20 per arm), no long-term follow-up, and no objective adherence monitoring.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports 'delta score 27.50' for the treatment group and 'delta score 9.50' for the control group in the abstract, but Table 2 shows delta scores of 10.33 and 2.11 respectively. The abstract delta scores appear to be cumulative rank sums (Wilcoxon test statistic) rather than mean differences; Table 2 values were used as primary data. The 95% CI reported in Table 2 for the control group (17.54-20.96) and treatment group (11.04-15.02) appear to be for the post-intervention means rather than for the delta scores. The OR=0.00, p=0.99 reported in the abstract refers to the logistic regression of the intervention itself (Table 3 shows OR=0.81, p=0.26 for WHO Stress Management), creating inconsistency. ISI score baseline comparison p=0.00 is stated in the paper but this seems counterintuitive given that both groups had insomnia at baseline; this may reflect a non-parametric test value rounded to zero. Age was the only demographic characteristic that differed significantly between groups (p=0.03) but exact means/SDs by group were not reported in tables.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested the WHO Stress Management (WSM) module — a five-session online program combining mindfulness and relaxation — in 36 Indonesian adults with post-COVID insomnia recruited from a Telegram self-isolation group. The WSM group showed a mean Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score drop from 19.94 to 9.61 (delta 10.33), compared to a drop from 18.56 to 16.44 (delta 2.11) in the sleep hygiene psychoeducation control group (p=0.00 on Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney tests). However, logistic regression found no significant causative effect of WSM on clinical insomnia improvement (OR 0.81, p=0.26), and the authors note that the online delivery format likely limited participant engagement and masked confounders such as anxiety and depression.

trial_rating.result_basis: WSM group ISI score decreased by 10.33 points (19.94 to 9.61) vs 2.11 points in controls (18.56 to 16.44), p=0.00; but logistic regression OR 0.81, p=0.26 for clinical significance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUES: (1) All quantitative data appear only in bar chart figures (Figs 1-5); no tables provided. Percentages are reported verbatim in the results text, but exact n per subgroup are not stated — event counts were back-calculated from stated percentages assuming equal subgroup sizes within each disorder type across the two arms. However, the per-subgroup ns are uncertain: summing inferred subgroup ns (15+23+25+17+25=105) exceeds stated arm 1 total of 80, so the subgroup assignments are not additive across the whole arm (i.e., participants may have had only one disorder type per arm, and the per-subgroup n may represent only that subgroup, not the full arm). The inferred n per subgroup (e.g., 15 per arm for polymenorrhea based on 13.3% = ~2/15) is speculative. (2) No baseline demographic data (age, BMI, time since infection) reported per arm. (3) Allocation method not described — this is NOT a confirmed RCT; described as a controlled study without randomization details. (4) Follow-up duration stated as 3-6 months post-treatment but exact treatment duration not specified. (5) The Ukrainian-language abstract reverses group numbering (group 1 = standard, group 2 = modified) relative to the English text (group 1 = modified, group 2 = standard) — extraction follows English text convention. (6) Adverse event percentages given as ranges (e.g., 15-20%, 60-70%) without exact denominators.

summary: This Ukrainian trial tested a modified multi-component regimen—combining natural estrogen-based oral contraceptives, melatonin, vitamin D3, magnesium-B6, L-arginine, quercetin, folic acid, and vitamin B12—against standard Ukrainian Ministry of Health protocols in 158 women of reproductive age (18–45) who developed menstrual disorders within six months of COVID-19 recovery. Across all five disorder types, the modified regimen produced dramatically lower relapse rates (8.7–23.5% vs. 56–80%) and higher rates of complete menstrual normalization (72–84% vs. 33–52%), with all differences statistically significant at P<0.05. Adverse effects such as edema, breast tenderness, and hypertension were also substantially less frequent in the modified-therapy group (15–20% vs. 60–70%), attributed to the use of natural rather than synthetic estrogens.

trial_rating.result_basis: Complete menstrual normalization achieved in 72–84% (modified) vs. 33–52% (standard), and relapse rates 8.7–23.5% vs. 56–80%, all P<0.05; however, no randomization, blinding, or pre-registration reported, and assignment to groups appears non-randomized.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental prospective open-label controlled study, not a true RCT; allocation method not described. The study is reported in Russian with English abstract/translation. Arm-level sample sizes for subgroups (Group I, II, III within each treatment arm) were taken from Table 3. The p-value of 0.001 for nasal sIgA between-group comparison in Group I is stated as p=0.007 within-group for treatment arm; the intergroup difference is marked as p<0.001 (#). Between-group effect sizes for nasal sIgA outcomes were calculated as mean difference (arm1 minus arm2 at 30 days). Control group healthy reference values: saliva sIgA 6.45±1.81 mg/ml, nasal sIgA 13.43±3.24 mg/ml (n=15) — not included as a trial arm. Symptom prevalence data from Tables 4 and 5 (acute and post-COVID clinical manifestations) are descriptive/retrospective and not outcomes of the intervention; they are not extracted as outcome objects but all numerical data is present in the paper tables. The paper does not report per-arm demographic data broken down by treatment group.

summary: This open-label controlled study tested intranasal interferon alpha-2b (IFN α-2b) gel, applied twice daily for 30 days, in 65 adults aged 18–60 who had recovered from COVID-19 within the past 1–9 months, compared to 65 untreated post-COVID controls. The primary outcome was secretory IgA (sIgA) levels in saliva and nasal swabs; among patients treated within 1–3 months of infection, salivary sIgA rose more than 3-fold (from 1.84±0.28 to 5.78±1.96 mg/ml, p=0.001) and nasal sIgA rose 1.5-fold (from 28.61±3.0 to 39.83±3.85 mg/ml, p=0.007), while untreated patients showed persistently low sIgA for up to 9 months. No respiratory infections were recorded in the treated group during the study period, versus a 27.6% incidence in the untreated group (p<0.001), and no adverse events were reported in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Salivary sIgA increased from 1.84±0.28 to 5.78±1.96 mg/ml (p=0.001) and nasal sIgA from 28.61±3.0 to 39.83±3.85 mg/ml (p=0.007) in the IFN α-2b group at 1–3 months post-COVID.

Baseline values for each arm reflect participants at entry into that condition (post-washout values used as pre for second condition). The paper reports intervention x time p-values from two-way ANOVA in Table 2 — these are used as between-group p-values. Calculated between-group mean differences are endpoint post-treatment differences (arm1 post minus arm2 post), which reflects the crossover contrast available from Table 2. The paper's primary between-group p-values (from delta of change comparisons via paired t-test) are: 6MWT p=0.02, TUG p=0.002, Barthel p=0.02; these are reported as between_group_effects p_values. For other outcomes, the intervention x time interaction p-value from two-way ANOVA is used as the between-group p-value. Training cardiopulmonary monitoring data (SpO2, HR, systolic/diastolic BP) appear only as figures with summary statistics in text — these are not extracted as formal outcomes. The 95% CI values in Table 2 are for Hedge's g effect sizes, not for mean differences; they are not entered into the between_group_effects CI fields. Note: the paper states TUG delta-of-change p=0.002 in the results text (Fig 3E) despite the two-way ANOVA intervention x time p=0.01 — the paired t-test p=0.002 is used as the primary between-group comparison. summary: This randomized crossover trial tested 8 weeks of eccentric cycling (ECC) against standard rehabilitation (elastic band strength exercises) in 20 adults who had been hospitalized in an ICU for COVID-19 and were recruited 6 months after discharge. The primary functional outcomes favored eccentric cycling: 6-minute walk distance improved by 140 meters with ECC versus 97 meters with standard rehabilitation (p=0.02 for between-group difference), and Timed Up and Go performance improved 16.5% with ECC versus 8.4% with standard rehabilitation (p=0.002). Both interventions were safe with no adverse events reported, but the two-week washout period between crossover arms was short and some carryover effects were detected, which limits confidence in the between-group comparisons.

summary: This randomized controlled pilot study tested online occupational therapy (OT) delivered either as live interactive sessions or prerecorded videos over 12 weeks in 158 adults with post-COVID syndrome (mean age 38 years, 86% female) who reported significant fatigue and cognitive impairment. The primary outcome was feasibility and acceptance: 83% of participants in the interactive OT group rated their experience as positive or very positive, compared to 48% in the video group (p=0.001). For secondary efficacy outcomes, participants receiving interactive OT showed significantly greater improvement in health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-3L mean difference +0.11 vs. control, 95% CI 0.05–0.17, p=0.003) and cognitive function (Neuro-QoL mean difference +3.95 vs. control, 95% CI 2.04–5.86, p<0.001) at 12 weeks; the study was unblinded and underpowered for confirmatory efficacy conclusions, and dropout was high (32.5% in the interactive group by week 12).

trial_rating.result_basis: Interactive OT vs. control: EQ-5D-3L mean difference +0.11 (95% CI 0.05–0.17, p=0.003) and Neuro-QoL mean difference +3.95 (95% CI 2.04–5.86, p<0.001) at 12 weeks; pilot study with no pre-specified primary efficacy endpoint power calculation.

The paper references Tables (Quadros 1, 2, 3) containing per-arm baseline and endpoint means/SDs, but the full table data was not included in the provided text — only the table captions and narrative summaries were present. As a result, per-arm means and SDs at baseline and endpoint for most outcomes could not be extracted. Change-from-baseline values for the intervention arm were recoverable from the Discussion section narrative (6MWT: +66.27±15.17m; FSS: -15.05±5.88; EQ-5D VAS: +13.523±5.46; EQ-5D index: +0.14±0.13; dyspnea: -1.37±0.76; RPE rest: -1.63±0.76; RPE post-6MWT: -1.74±0.56). Between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d) were extracted from the Abstract/Results as reported; note that the sign of the FSS effect size (-1.23) and EQ-5D index (-0.73) suggest these may be reported with direction relative to higher-is-better convention despite both instruments having lower-is-better directionality for FSS. Control arm change-from-baseline values were also described as significant in within-group comparison but specific numbers were not provided in the narrative text. No intermediate (3-week) quantitative data were reported for outcomes. The 3-week re-assessment of 6MWT was used to adjust training intensity only and no numeric data were provided.

summary: A 6-week comprehensive rehabilitation program — combining aerobic walking, strength, balance, flexibility, and breathing exercises with patient education — was tested in a randomized controlled trial of 38 long COVID patients aged 25–60 in a low-resource outpatient setting in India. The primary outcomes were functional capacity (six-minute walk test), fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale), and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L); the intervention group improved six-minute walk distance by 66 metres (well above the 30.5 m minimal clinically important difference), reduced FSS scores by 15 points, and improved EQ-5D VAS scores by 13.5 points, all with large effect sizes (Cohen's d ranging from 0.73 to 1.37). There were no dropouts and no adverse events reported, though the study was single-site with an unblinded outcome assessor.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk distance increased by 66.27 ± 15.17 m in the intervention group vs. control (p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.37); FSS decreased by 15.05 ± 5.88 points (p < 0.0001); EQ-5D VAS improved by 13.52 ± 5.46 points (p < 0.0001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper reports almost all quantitative outcomes as percent change from baseline only, without providing absolute pre/post values or SDs — this severely limits effect size extraction. Absolute values are provided only for 6MWT baseline (median with IQR per arm) and overall FEV1 baseline (median IQR pooled). 2. Psychological and cognitive outcome data (Table 1) are reported only as Wilcoxon Z statistics and p-values across all rehabilitation groups combined, with no per-arm means/SDs. 3. Allostatic load is reported as categorical distribution (% in each severity category) before and after, not as continuous scores per arm. 4. The note in the abstract vs methods section reverses the group numbering (abstract English version lists groups differently from methods). We followed the methods section: arm1=whirlpool/hydromassage, arm2=Biolong baths, arm3=NaCl mineral baths, arm4=control. 5. Between-group effects are not directly reported; the paper reports only within-arm pre/post changes with p-values from Wilcoxon tests. No between-group inferential statistics are provided. 6. Several figures referenced (Figs 1, 2, 3) contain allostatic load distribution data that supplements text; extracted from text descriptions. 7. Omitted outcomes due to lack of any quantitative data: superoxide dismutase, sinus tachycardia/bradycardia rates (reported as percent of group but not per-arm post values with statistics), all complaint frequency outcomes (narrative percent only). 8. The Schulte Tables Efficiency of Work subscale did not reach significance (Z=-1.9, p=0.064) and is noted but all data remain null.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested three types of balneotherapy (whirlpool baths, 'Biolong' medicated baths, and sodium chloride mineral baths), each combined with exercise therapy, in 160 adults with post-COVID syndrome (median age 50) at an outpatient rehabilitation centre in Moscow. All three active treatment groups showed significant reductions in symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and dyspnoea compared to an untreated control group, with the whirlpool bath group showing a 12.1% increase in forced vital capacity (p<0.01) and 9.6% increase in FEV1 (p<0.05), and the Biolong bath group showing a 26.2% reduction in cortisol (p<0.01) and an 8.3% improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p<0.05). All rehabilitation groups also showed significant improvements in depression, anxiety, and cognitive measures, while the control group showed no meaningful change. The control group was not actively treated rather than receiving a placebo, which limits causal interpretation of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Whirlpool bath group: FVC increased 12.1% (p<0.01), FEV1 increased 9.6% (p<0.05); Biolong group: 6-minute walk improved 8.3% (p<0.05), cortisol reduced 26.2% (p<0.01); control group showed no significant change on any measure.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested EEG alpha-rhythm neurofeedback (biofeedback) training versus sham training (identical exercises without feedback) in 20 adults with post-COVID syndrome experiencing anxiety, depression, fatigue, and cognitive complaints. Both groups showed significant reductions in trait anxiety, psychological stress, depression, and fatigue after 12–15 sessions. The neurofeedback group showed additional benefits over sham on general fatigue (U=19.5, p=0.019), immediate word recall (U=25.5, p=0.036), and verbal working memory (U=23.5, p=0.034), though the trial was very small (10 per arm) and lacked pre-registered power calculations, limiting confidence in these findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group comparison on primary fatigue outcome: general fatigue subscale U=19.5, p=0.019; immediate word recall U=25.5, p=0.036; verbal working memory d' U=23.5, p=0.034; however N=10 per arm with no pre-specified primary outcome or power calculation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English translation provided. Tables 1 and 2 present data as M±SD (mean±SD) with numerator=before, denominator=after treatment. Tables 3 and 4 present data as median [Q1; Q3]. The paper states treatment was 15 days (3 weeks). Follow-up was 6 months post-rehabilitation completion. The study study period was 4 months total. Within-group p-values are reported (Wilcoxon test), but between-group p-values are not explicitly stated for most outcomes - the p<0.049 threshold for spirometry and p<0.05 for HRV are noted in the abstract/text as within-group results for arm 1. No between-group statistical comparison results (p-values or effect sizes) are reported. All between_group_effects p_values are set to 0.05 as threshold only where paper indicates significant within-group change in arm 1 but not arm 2. The SDs in Table 1 and 2 may actually represent SE (labeled as M±m in Russian notation where 'm' typically denotes standard error), but are extracted as-is per table labeling. The stroke volume decreased after treatment in the intervention arm (from 53.73 to 48.73 mL) - this may reflect normalization of an initially elevated cardiac output driven by tachycardia. The Tiffenau index (FEV1/FVC ratio) mentioned in methods was not reported in tables.

summary: This open randomised trial tested interval hypo-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating inhalation of low-oxygen (12–15% O2) and high-oxygen gas mixtures using the OXYTERRA device across 15 daily sessions — added to standard rehabilitation versus standard rehabilitation alone in 50 patients (mean age 61.7 years) with post-COVID syndrome persisting more than 3 months. The IHHT group showed statistically significant improvements in lung function (vital capacity, FVC, FEV1, and peak expiratory flow all p<0.05), blood oxygen content (SaO2 rose from 94.3% to 97.2%, p<0.01), heart rate (reduced from 82.8 to 75.7 bpm, p<0.01), and autonomic regulation (total heart rate variability power doubled from 623 to 1265, p<0.05), while the comparison group showed no significant changes in most measures. No adverse events were reported during the intervention or 6-month follow-up, and benefits were reported to persist for 3–6 months post-rehabilitation.

trial_rating.result_basis: FEV1 improved from median 72.2% to 79.1% predicted (p<0.05) in the IHHT group vs no significant change in controls (72.4% to 72.9%); SaO2 improved from 94.3% to 97.2% (p<0.01); heart rate fell from 82.8 to 75.7 bpm (p<0.01); total HRV power rose from 623 to 1265 (p<0.05).

summary: This open-label randomized trial tested sequential transcranial electrical stimulation — combining brain micropolarization (targeting the neocortex) followed immediately by diencephalic brain stimulation (targeting limbic structures) — in 142 adults aged 45–69 with chronic cerebrovascular disease (dyscirculatory encephalopathy) who were 3–4 months post-COVID-19. Patients receiving the sequential combination (n=48) showed statistically significant improvement across all measured symptoms compared to baseline, with symptom severity scores on a visual analogue scale improving 1.2–1.6 fold (p<0.05–0.001), and neuropsychological test scores improving 1.1–2.0 fold; both single-modality comparison groups showed narrower improvements affecting only specific symptom clusters. There was no control arm receiving sham stimulation or medication alone, which limits causal interpretation, and three participants withdrew due to uncomfortable pressure sensations around the eyes during diencephalic stimulation.

trial_rating.result_basis: Group 3 (sequential therapy) showed 1.2–1.6 fold improvement in clinical symptom VAS scores vs baseline (p<0.05–0.001) and 1.1–2.0 fold improvement in neuropsychological tests (p<0.05–0.01); no sham-controlled comparison was made, so between-group differences vs an inactive control are not established.

summary: This Russian randomized controlled trial tested whether adding VedaBiotic, a fifth-generation multisymbiotic (probiotic/prebiotic combination), to a standard physical rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 128 long COVID patients (mean age 57, all with prior bilateral viral pneumonia) at a inpatient rehabilitation centre. The primary finding was that the group receiving VedaBiotic (n=32) showed significantly greater reductions in symptoms and inflammatory markers compared to the rehabilitation-only group (n=64): fatigue resolved in 50% vs 81% still affected, cough resolved completely (0% vs 22% still affected, p=0.001), and D-dimer normalized only in the VedaBiotic group (dropping from 302 to 136 ng/mL, p=0.012, vs non-significant reduction in controls). No adverse events were reported, but the trial has notable limitations including unequal group sizes and open-label design with no placebo control.

trial_rating.result_basis: D-dimer normalized only in VedaBiotic group: 302 [279;440] to 136 [0;177] ng/mL, p=0.012; cough resolved in 100% of VedaBiotic group vs 78% control, p=0.001; fatigue persisted in 50% vs 81%, p=0.009.

summary: The DISSOLVE trial (NCT04645368) tested bovhyaluronidase azoximer (Longidase), an enzyme-immunomodulator conjugate that breaks down hyaluronic acid, in 160 adult post-COVID patients with residual lung abnormalities, comparing 15 intramuscular injections over 75 days (n=81) against observation-only controls (n=79) across 13 Russian centres. The primary outcome—reduction in residual lung abnormalities on CT scan—was not significantly different between groups at 180 days (-13.5% vs -13.8%, p=0.327), though treated patients showed significantly greater improvements in forced vital capacity (9.0% vs 5.0% at day 75, p=0.046), oxygen saturation (1.07% vs 0.57% at day 75, p<0.001), 6-minute walk distance (27.8% vs 17.1% at day 75, p=0.049), and dyspnea scores (-0.84 vs -0.58 mMRC points at day 75, p=0.002). The trial was open-label with no blinding or placebo control, and was published with acknowledged support from the drug manufacturer (NPO Petrovax Pharm), limiting confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (CT residual lung abnormalities) showed no significant between-group difference at day 180: -13.47% vs -13.75%, p=0.327.

summary: This trial tested two Ayurvedic herbal formulations — Femicycle (containing Symplocos racemosa, Asparagus racemosus, Saraca indica, Glycyrrhiza glabra, and Curcuma longa) and Femimens (containing Vitex agnus castus, Withania somnifera, Zingiber officinale, and Trigonella foenum-graecum) — in 53 women aged 18–25 with menstrual disorders that developed within 3 months of moderate or severe COVID-19, compared against 51 women who received only standard rehabilitation (diet, vitamins, psychotherapy). After 6 months, women in the herbal treatment group had significantly fewer menstrual problems: infrequent menstruation affected 1.89% versus 31.37% in the comparison group (OR 0.042 [0.005–0.332]), dysmenorrhea persisted in 11.32% versus 35.29% (OR 0.234 [0.084–0.653]), and PMS in 7.55% versus 29.41% (OR 0.196 [0.060–0.640]). No side effects were reported in the herbal treatment group, though the study lacks blinding, the products appear to be commercially linked to the authors, and the formulations are classified as dietary supplements rather than medicines.

summary: This open-label randomised trial tested L-carnitine (50–75 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks, added to standard rehabilitation therapy) versus standard therapy alone in 90 children, adolescents, and young adults aged 10–25 with long COVID cardiovascular and autonomic symptoms. The primary finding was that 93.3% of the L-carnitine group were symptom-free and had normalised objective status at 6 weeks, compared with 66.7% in the standard-therapy group (p<0.05); ECG repolarisation abnormalities and rhythm disturbances present in 43.3% of patients at baseline resolved completely in the L-carnitine group but persisted in over 50% of controls, and heart rate variability indices (pNN50, rMSSD, SDNN) normalised in 86.7% vs 31.1% of controls (p=0.00). No adverse events requiring drug discontinuation were recorded. Key caveats are the open-label design (no blinding), absence of a pre-specified sample size calculation, and conduct at a single Russian centre, which limit confidence in the results.

trial_rating.result_basis: Symptom-free and normalised objective status at 6 weeks: 93.3% (L-carnitine) vs 66.7% (standard therapy), p<0.05; HRV normalisation: 86.7% vs 31.1%, p=0.00.

Open-label study with self-reported outcomes (MFI-20) and clinician-rated scales (HAM-A) without blinded assessors. Validated instruments used but assessor blinding not mentioned.
No trial registration or pre-specified protocol mentioned. Primary outcomes are stated but no pre-registration is documented.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All outcomes reported as median [IQR] due to non-normal distribution (Shapiro-Wilk confirmed). No means or SDs available for any outcome — only medians and IQRs extracted. Between-group effect sizes (mean differences, SMDs) cannot be calculated from medians/IQRs alone. The paper reports percentage reductions (MFI-20: 33.6% vs 14.4%; HAM-A: 55.16% vs 19.74%) but these are not extractable as standardized effect sizes. p<0.05 is reported for both within-group and between-group comparisons for significant outcomes but no exact p-values are given. The HAM-A baseline value for control group is listed as 25.17 in the table — this appears to be a median despite being a non-integer, possibly a rounding artifact or mean. Table 3 (HAM-A) contains 7 subscales; only Tension and Insomnia reached between-group significance in the Cefaly arm. The treatment duration was 10 sessions over approximately 24 days (3 sessions/week for ~3.4 weeks). Percent previously hospitalized: the paper reports 69.93% had inpatient COVID-19 treatment in Cefaly group and 63.27% in control group (from Table 1), but these refer to COVID-19 treatment setting, not ICU hospitalization specifically.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested transcutaneous supraorbital nerve stimulation (t-SNS) using the Cefaly device — 10 sessions over approximately 3 weeks — added to standard rehabilitation, versus standard rehabilitation alone, in 60 adults aged 60–75 with post-COVID fatigue syndrome at least 6 months after infection. Adding Cefaly to rehabilitation reduced fatigue scores (MFI-20) by 33.6% from baseline versus 14.4% in controls, and reduced anxiety scores (HAM-A) by 55.2% versus 19.7% in controls, with both differences statistically significant. A notable caveat is that both groups still had high residual fatigue scores after treatment (median MFI-20: 42.5 in the Cefaly group vs 63 in controls), underscoring that long COVID fatigue persists substantially even with active treatment.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFI-20 total score reduced from median 70 to 42.5 in Cefaly group (33.6% reduction) vs 71.5 to 63 in controls (14.4% reduction), p<0.05 for both within-group and between-group comparisons; HAM-A total score reduced 55.2% vs 19.7%, p<0.05.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study is NOT an RCT; it is an open-label quasi-experimental comparative study with no described randomization. design_type set to quasi-experimental. 2. Baseline imbalances exist: fatigue severity (experimental 2.65 vs control 2.31, p=0.0001) and sleep disorder severity (1.70 vs 1.00, p=0.04) differ significantly at baseline, complicating interpretation. 3. Table 3 p-values are reported as combined pairs (e.g., '0.0001/0.02') where the first value appears to refer to Day 1 between-group comparison and the second to Day 5; this notation is ambiguous and has been interpreted accordingly. 4. For FAS/chronic fatigue outcome (Table 4), only binary classification (above/below threshold of 22) is reported, not continuous FAS scores; no p-value is reported for the between-group comparison at Day 10 (text states 'no statistically significant differences'). 5. The symptom severity scale means in Table 3 are computed across all participants in each group (including those without the symptom, who presumably score 1), not only those with the symptom present. 6. Additional binary outcomes fully extracted from Table 2 but not individually listed as outcomes: shortness of breath, cough, dizziness, chest pain, loss of taste, perverted smell, perverted taste, sleep disorder, anxiety, hair loss, abdominal pain — all had complete n/% data at days 1/5/10. The most clinically important (loss of smell, headache, joint pain, fatigue) are included. 7. The paper notes that 100% of experimental group participants had fatigue and dizziness at all timepoints per Table 2 (binary), though the severity scores improved — this creates an apparent contradiction with Table 3 severity data.

summary: This open-label, non-randomised comparative study tested azoximer bromide (an immunomodulatory drug, 12 mg sublingual daily for 10 days) in 55 adults with post-COVID syndrome — defined as at least two persisting symptoms more than 12 weeks after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection — compared to 35 untreated controls. By day 10, the treated group showed statistically significant reductions in the frequency and severity of joint and muscle pain (12.7% vs 45.7% still affected), headache (18.2% vs 51.4%), dizziness, impaired concentration, and smell loss, with fatigue severity significantly lower as early as day 5 (mean score 1.71 vs 2.23, p=0.02); no adverse events were reported. The study has substantial methodological limitations: it was open-label with no blinding, had no placebo control, groups were not fully matched at baseline (fatigue scores differed significantly on day 1), and the 10-day follow-up with no post-treatment observation period means durability of effects is unknown.

trial_rating.result_basis: Joint and muscle pain prevalence 12.7% (treated) vs 45.7% (control) at day 10 (p not explicitly stated but marked significant); fatigue severity 1.71 vs 2.23 at day 5 (p=0.02); headache prevalence 18.2% vs 51.4% at day 10 (p<0.05).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. The Schober test is measured in two parts: 'initial' measurement (always 15.00 ± 0.00 cm for both groups/timepoints, as this is the fixed starting mark) and 'final' measurement (the actual flexion endpoint). The 'difference' is the clinically meaningful value. The lateral inclination tests measure the distance from fingertip to floor and are reported similarly in three components: initial (standing upright finger-to-floor), final (in flexion finger-to-floor), and difference. No exact p-values were reported for between-group comparisons at post-intervention — only p<0.05 thresholds with footnote annotations in Table 3. The G2 pain increase was stated as statistically significant (intragroup p<0.05) in the results text. The Schober final measurement and difference were significantly greater in G1 vs G2 at both pre- and post-intervention (p<0.05 between groups). The analysis used the randomized N (G1=20, G2=19) despite 11 dropouts, suggesting intent-to-treat or the table reports randomized n rather than analyzed n — this is ambiguous. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week supervised exercise program (gym-based aerobic, resistance, balance, and flexibility training, twice weekly) versus home-guidance only in 39 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Brazil. The exercise group also showed superior lumbar spine flexibility (Schöber test) compared to controls post-intervention, though muscle strength did not differ significantly between groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain VAS decreased from 4.85 to 3.55 in the exercise group (p<0.05); sit-to-stand repetitions increased from 10.45 to 12.45 (p<0.05); however, baseline imbalance (exercise group had significantly higher pain and lower functional capacity at baseline) limits causal interpretation.

The post-treatment CRP value of 2.5±3.4 mg/L is reported as an average across both groups combined ('снижался в обеих группах и составил в среднем 2.5±3.4 мг/л'), so the same value was applied to both arms with result_source='inferred'. summary: This pilot study tested enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) — a non-invasive device that applies synchronized compression to the legs to improve circulation — in 30 patients with persistent lung damage and ventilatory impairment an average of 15 months after COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients in the EECP group (n=15) received 20 one-hour sessions over four weeks; controls (n=15) received standard care only. EECP produced significant improvements in total lung capacity (65% to 76%, p<0.001), vital capacity (57% to 73%, p=0.006), FEV1 (65% to 82%, p=0.041), and 6-minute walk distance (313 to 352 metres, p=0.007), while none of these measures improved in the control group; however, lung diffusing capacity (DLCO) did not improve in either group, indicating that underlying structural damage was not reversed. No adverse events were reported, but the study is limited by its very small sample size, non-randomised allocation, and use of the 6-minute walk test rather than cardiopulmonary exercise testing as the exercise measure.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total lung capacity improved from 65% to 76% predicted (p<0.001) and 6-minute walk distance increased by 39 metres from 313 to 352 m (p=0.007) in the EECP group, with no significant change in controls.

IL-10 is labeled as a proinflammatory marker in the results, though in the abstract the English version refers to 'IL-1' reduction of 20.6%; the Ukrainian table clearly shows IL-10 (ІЛ-10) with values 9.52 and 7.56 (intervention) and 10.16 and 9.11 (control) — extracted as IL-10. summary: This small Ukrainian RCT tested the addition of Tivorel (levocarnitine 20mg + arginine hydrochloride 42mg, IV then oral) plus quercetin 240mg/day for one month to standard care in 40 hospitalized adults with type 2 diabetes and post-COVID syndrome. Compared to standard care alone, the combination treatment reduced fasting glucose 1.8-fold, lowered HbA1c by 28.2%, cut total cholesterol by 18.2%, raised HDL by 38.6%, and reduced CRP by 50.5% and D-dimer by 25.4%, with all primary group comparisons reaching statistical significance. The study has no blinding, no placebo control, very small arms (n=20 per group), and no pre-registration, making results hypothesis-generating only.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fasting glucose fell from 9.21 to 4.99 mmol/L in the treatment group vs 8.12 to 6.28 mmol/L in controls (p<0.05, # between groups); HbA1c fell from 6.20% to 4.45% vs 5.71% to 5.34% (treatment group difference significant vs control).

domains.support: Simple random sampling is mentioned but no details on sequence generation or allocation concealment are provided. The paper states 'blind, randomized, placebo-controlled' but the randomization procedure is not described.
Patients were blinded to drug vs placebo, but physicians conducting testing were not described as blinded. Study is described as 'blind' without specifying who was blinded.

No information on dropouts, withdrawals, or CONSORT flow diagram. Sample sizes vary across meridians in the results tables, suggesting not all patients had all meridians tested, but reasons are not explained.

Outcome is electrodermal impedance measured by an unvalidated device (EAV). The physiological basis is stated to be unknown. No validated clinical outcome measures (e.g. patient-reported symptom scales) are used. Physician blinding to group assignment is unclear.

No trial registration or pre-specified protocol is referenced. Multiple meridians tested with selective reporting of which showed positive vs negative responses. No correction for multiple comparisons across 18+ meridians.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study measures electrodermal impedance via EAV (electroacupuncture according to Voll), a device/method with no established clinical validity. The outcomes are not recognized clinical endpoints for long COVID. 2. The intervention is a single-session diagnostic procedure (medicament testing), not a therapeutic intervention in the conventional sense. The 'treatment' and 'follow-up' occur within the same diagnostic session (pre-test vs post-test during the same visit). Duration fields are null as this is a within-session measurement. 3. Table 3 (positive responders) and Table 4 (negative responders) each show per-arm n, pre-test AMV mean±SD, and post-test AMV mean±SD for different meridian subsets. The n values per meridian vary because not all patients had all meridians affected. 4. Table 3 mentions 12 meridians but the text also references 'Ma' (Stomach) as one that showed restoration; however no Ma row appears in the table as extracted — likely a discrepancy in the paper. 5. Figure 2 and Figure 3 contain pre-test EAV readings plotted with means and standard errors, but numerical values are only available in Table 3 and Table 4. 6. P-values are reported as thresholds (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001) between groups and vs pre-test, not exact values. Between-group p-values were extracted as the threshold stated in table notes (*** = p<0.001 coded as 0.001, ** = p<0.01 coded as 0.01). 7. The duplicate entry for arm_id=2 in baseline_demographics.per_arm is an artifact — only one control arm exists. 8. Negative responder outcomes (Table 4): the He, Du, Pa/Mi(D), Hau, Ni, Bl meridians showed p<0.01 between groups; Al showed p<0.001 between groups; Ne showed p<0.01 between groups. These are all showing worsening (more negative drop) in the intervention arm compared to placebo for the negative-responder subgroup. 9. The study does not report conventional long COVID clinical outcomes (fatigue scores, QoL, functional status). This paper is of very limited relevance to a conventional long COVID meta-analysis.

summary: This study tested electroacupuncture according to Voll (EAV) diagnosis combined with medicament testing (MT) — placing an RNA polymerase nosode, ribavirin tablets, and dexamethasone pills into a device honeycomb while measuring skin electrical impedance at acupuncture points — in 99 long COVID patients aged 16–50 in Uzbekistan. In the 50-patient treatment group, MT with these three substances produced statistically significant normalization of electrodermal activity readings at 12 meridian points compared to pre-test values and to the placebo control group (p<0.001 for key meridians including nervous degeneration and circulation). A critical caveat is that EAV and medicament testing have no established physiological basis and are not validated diagnostic or therapeutic tools; the outcome measure is device readings of skin electrical impedance, not any clinical symptom or functional endpoint, making the clinical relevance of these findings uninterpretable.

trial_rating.result_basis: Post-MT AMV on nervous degeneration meridian: main group 5.65 ± 1.14 vs pre-test -3.87 ± 1.66 (p<0.001 vs control), but this measures device impedance readings, not a validated clinical outcome; no clinical symptom data were analyzed as a primary endpoint.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper was submitted as a CONSORT-EHEALTH checklist form, not as the full manuscript. As a result, almost all quantitative data (per-arm means, SDs, sample sizes per arm, exact timepoint definitions in weeks) are missing — only inferential statistics (beta coefficients, t-values, p-values from HLMs) are quoted verbatim from the manuscript. Per-arm n_randomized breakdown is not reported in this form. Timepoints T1-T5 are referenced but their timing in weeks is not specified. The intervention duration of 6 weeks is stated. Between-group comparisons for Hypothesis 1 combined IG+ACG vs CompG; for Hypothesis 2 compared IG vs ACG with no significant group differences found. For work ability, beta=0.78 (t271=2.73, p=0.01) for IG+ACG vs CompG; for social participation beta=0.27 (t277=2.89, p=0.004) for IG+ACG vs CompG. For symptom severity vs CompG: T1-T2 interaction beta=0.14 (t549=4.31, p<0.001); T2-T4 interaction beta=0.14 (t549=4.57, p<0.001). For IG vs ACG (Hypothesis 2): no significant group differences in any outcome. Hypothesis 3 regression: symptom reduction predicted social participation (beta=-0.34, t111=-2.11, p=0.04, R2=0.24) but not work ability (beta=-0.18, t111=-1.92, p=0.06, R2=0.32). Data for figures referenced but not extractable from this form. Total N=1020 patients recruited. | Pass3 agent: PDF is CONSORT checklist only (not main paper). HLM betas reported, no CIs.

summary: This German RCT (the ASAP project) tested a 6-week digital rehabilitation program combined with personal coaching ('personal pilots') for 1,020 adults with long COVID (post-acute COVID-19 syndrome, PACS) in Bavaria. Patients were randomised to either a tailored intervention group (IG, receiving clinic-based diagnostic assessment plus personalised digital exercises averaging 50 minutes/day) or an active control group (ACG, receiving symptom-targeted digital exercises plus personal pilot support but no formal assessment), with a non-randomised usual-care comparison group (CompG) included via propensity score matching. Both the IG and ACG showed significantly greater symptom reduction and higher work ability and social participation compared to the untreated CompG, but there was no significant difference in any outcome between the IG and ACG, meaning the additional diagnostic assessment and tailoring did not produce greater benefit than the simpler intervention. No harms were reported in any group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Symptom severity reduction was significantly greater in IG+ACG vs CompG (group×time interaction β=0.14, t549=4.57, p<0.001); work ability was higher in treatment groups vs CompG (β=0.78, t271=2.73, p=0.01); but IG vs ACG showed no significant difference on any primary outcome.

summary: This randomized trial tested a 5-strain Bacillus probiotic (one dose daily for 4 weeks) added to standard care versus standard care alone in 42 adults with post-COVID-19 irritable bowel syndrome diagnosed by Rome IV criteria. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding Kolofort (a drug containing processed antibodies to S100 protein, TNF-alpha, and histamine) to standard omeprazole therapy (80 mg/day) improved functional dyspepsia symptoms in 42 post-COVID-19 outpatients aged 26–47. By day 28, the combination group had significantly lower epigastric pain scores on a 10-point VAS compared to omeprazole alone (p<0.01), and showed faster resolution of other dyspeptic symptoms (heaviness, early satiety, nausea) by day 5 (p<0.02); however, full symptom resolution at day 28 reached ~90% in both groups with no statistically significant difference between them (p=0.06). The combination group also showed greater quality-of-life improvements on SF-36 pain, general health, role-emotional, and mental health subscales. The study was funded by the drug manufacturer (Materia Medica), which is a significant conflict of interest.

trial_rating.result_basis: Epigastric pain VAS significantly lower in combination group at day 28 (p<0.01), but complete dyspepsia resolution was ~90% in both groups with no significant difference (p=0.06); baseline VAS scores also differed significantly between groups (p=0.001), raising concerns about randomization balance.

summary: This 6-week randomized controlled trial tested whether adding manual diaphragm release (18 physiotherapist-delivered sessions) to inspiratory muscle training via a POWERbreath device was more effective than inspiratory muscle training alone in 52 men with post-COVID-19 syndrome who had hypertension and mild-to-moderate lung fibrosis. The primary outcome, maximum inspiratory pressure (a measure of breathing muscle strength), increased by 48.2% in the combined treatment group (from 82.0 to 121.5 cmH2O) compared with a non-significant 4.4% increase in the training-only group. Secondary outcomes also favored the combined group: systolic blood pressure fell by 16.7% vs 2.5%, dyspnea scores improved by 48.9% vs 12.8%, fatigue scores fell by 51.6% vs 17.7%, and 6-minute walk distance increased by 13.5% vs 3.9%; the study was limited to men only and did not include objective measures of diaphragm function such as ultrasound.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PImax increased 48.17% in the combined group (82.0 to 121.5 cmH2O) vs non-significant 4.35% in the control group; between-group interaction p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.330.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether incentive spirometry (IS) or diaphragmatic breathing (DB) exercises added to standard care could improve breathlessness in 60 long COVID patients with confirmed diaphragmatic dysfunction following mild-to-moderate acute COVID-19. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding systemic ozone therapy (10 intravenous infusions of ozonized saline over 30 days) to standard drug therapy improved outcomes in 140 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID asthenic syndrome—a condition marked by chronic fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, and anxiety. Patients who received ozone therapy alongside the succinic acid-based drug showed substantially greater reductions in inflammatory markers (TNF-α down 39%, IL-1β down 33%, IL-6 down 36% versus the drug-only group) and larger improvements across all symptom scales: fatigue scores fell 36.7% more, insomnia scores 50.5% more, and anxiety scores 45.8% more than in the comparison group, with 94.2% of ozone-treated patients rated as disease-free at 30 days versus 62.9% in the control group. No adverse events were reported in either group, though the study was conducted at a single centre in Crimea without blinding, which limits how broadly the findings can be applied.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a dynamic inversion table — a motorized platform that repeatedly tilts patients at low frequencies to alter gravitational pressure on blood vessels — against standard rehabilitation in 70 adults with long COVID (persistent symptoms for over 12 weeks post-infection). The treatment group (n=35) completed 10 daily 30-minute sessions on the device; the control group (n=35) followed standard rehabilitation guidelines. The primary outcome, exercise work capacity during cardiorespiratory stress testing, increased by 13.31 W in the treatment group versus a decline of 4.60 W in controls (p<0.001). Post-occlusive microvascular blood flow, a marker of endothelial function, rose by 80.42% in the treatment group while declining slightly in controls; no adverse events were reported.
