summary: This double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial tested EchA Marine, a dietary supplement derived from sea urchin eggs and rich in Echinochrome A, in 46 long COVID patients (18–60 years) across three Argentine hospitals over 90 days. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life measured by the EQ-5D-3L questionnaire: after three months, the treatment group showed statistically significant improvements in mobility (p=0.013) and pain/discomfort (p=0.005), as well as in overall health perception by VAS (p=0.022) and time trade-off scores (p=0.003), while the placebo group showed no improvement in these dimensions. Secondary inflammatory biomarkers also shifted favourably, with IL-2 falling (84 vs 90 pg/ml, p=0.038) and anti-inflammatory IL-10 rising (15.5 vs 12.4 pg/ml, p=0.038) in the treatment group; however, the trial is small (24 treated, 22 placebo), and two of the study authors are founders or employees of the company that supplied the supplement.

summary: A 63-day remote medical and psychological rehabilitation program—incorporating cognitive-behavioural therapy, mindfulness, art therapy, and body-oriented practices—was tested in 240 Ukrainian adults with anxiety and depressive post-COVID syndrome during the ongoing war. At 3-month follow-up, 92.6% of the treatment group (n=122) had minimal anxiety on the GAD-7 versus 51.7% with severe anxiety in the comparison group, and 84.3% of the treatment group had minimal depression on the PHQ-9 versus 37.3% with severe depression in controls (all p<0.001). No participants in the treatment group had clinically significant PTSD symptoms at follow-up, while the comparison group's PTSD case count grew from 44 to 47; 73.8% of the treatment group reached the highest quality-of-life tier versus 6.8% in controls. The study is unblinded and conducted in a wartime context that may limit generalisability, and the comparison group received no structured alternative intervention.

summary: This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested whether hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — at four different combinations of oxygen concentration and chamber pressure — improved symptoms and cognitive function in 101 long COVID patients with an average illness duration of about 21 months. After 10 treatment sessions, there were no statistically significant differences between any of the four groups on any primary outcome, including quality of life scores, a 6-minute walking test, or five neurocognitive tests. Some patients in every group, including the placebo group breathing room air at normal pressure, reported subjective improvement, and most had returned to their pre-study condition by three-month follow-up, pointing to a placebo effect as the likely explanation for positive findings in earlier uncontrolled studies.

trial_rating.result_basis: All intergroup comparisons were non-significant (Kruskal-Wallis or one-way ANOVA, P > 0.05 for every outcome including VAS, EQ-5D-5L, C19-YRSm, 6MWT, and all five PEBL cognitive tests).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding systemic ozone therapy (10 daily intravenous infusions of ozonated saline) to standard pharmacological treatment (Brainmax, a meldonium/antioxidant combination) improved symptoms in 140 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID asthenic syndrome. The primary finding was that patients receiving adjunctive ozone therapy showed substantially greater improvements across all outcomes: fatigue scores (MFI-20) fell 74.7% vs 60.3% in controls, insomnia scores (ISI) fell 81.3% vs 42.9%, anxiety scores (HAM-A) fell 72.8% vs 48.3%, and cognitive scores (MoCA) improved 17.1% vs 4.9%, with 94.2% of ozone-treated patients rated symptom-free vs 62.9% in the control group. A notable caveat is that both groups received an active drug rather than placebo, making it impossible to isolate ozone therapy's effect from pharmacotherapy alone, and the study was conducted at a single site in Crimea with no reported pre-registration.

trial_rating.result_basis: MFI-20 total score decreased from median 81.9 to 20.5 (−74.7%) in ozone group vs 81.6 to 32.4 (−60.3%) in pharmacotherapy-only group, between-group difference p=0.001; 94.2% vs 62.9% rated symptom-free on CGI-S (p=0.001).

summary: This small Russian controlled trial tested 90-minute daily inhaled hydrogen gas (via nasal cannula using a SUISONIA device) for 10 days in 30 healthcare workers recovering from COVID-19, compared to 30 controls receiving standard rehabilitation. The primary immunological findings were localised to mucosal tissues: nasal granulocyte phagocytic index increased 2.5-fold versus baseline (p=0.000189) and was 1.1-fold higher than controls (p=0.047); pharyngeal monocyte phagocytic index rose 2.8-fold versus baseline (p=0.041); and nasal secretory IgA (sIgA) increased 2.9-fold versus baseline. However, pharyngeal sIgA fell 2-fold, blood phagocytic indices were unchanged, and the absence of randomisation, blinding, and clinical outcome measures severely limits interpretation.

trial_rating.result_basis: Nasal granulocyte phagocytic index increased 2.5-fold vs baseline (p=0.000189); nasal sIgA increased 2.9-fold vs baseline; these are surrogate immunological markers with no clinical endpoints reported.

summary: This placebo-controlled trial tested 14 sessions of transcranial low-frequency magnetotherapy (using the DIAMAG device) added to standard rehabilitation in 60 post-COVID-19 pneumonia patients in Russia (30 per group). At 6 weeks post-treatment, patients receiving active magnetotherapy showed a 30% improvement in quality of life (EQ-5D), a 28% reduction in anxiety (Spielberger-Khanin scale), and a 35% reduction in depression (Beck scale) compared to baseline, with significantly less improvement in the placebo group. summary: This pilot feasibility trial tested a 10-week physiotherapist-supervised group telerehabilitation exercise program delivered via Zoom twice weekly against usual care in 21 adults with post-COVID condition (persistent dyspnoea, fatigue, or chest pain averaging one year after diagnosis). The primary outcomes were feasibility metrics: 100% of intervention completers met the adherence threshold of 16 or more sessions, the recruitment rate was 39%, and there were zero adverse events and only two minor technical issues. The only statistically significant clinical finding was a 1.4-second improvement in the five-repetition sit-to-stand test favouring the intervention group; no significant differences were found for six-minute walk distance, fatigue scores, or quality of life, though moderate-to-large effect sizes were observed for several measures — results that are exploratory only given the small sample.

trial_rating.result_basis: The primary feasibility outcomes were met (100% adherence, zero adverse events), but the sole significant clinical finding was the 5STS change score: -1.4 seconds (95% CI -0.2 to -2.6, p=0.024); the main clinical outcome, 6MWT change, was non-significant (difference 51m, 95% CI -13 to 114, p=0.108).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is in Ukrainian with an English abstract. The note symbol § in the original is used as ± per the submission note. The paper states values as (M ± m) where m is the standard error of the mean (SEM), not SD — however, following standard convention in Ukrainian medical literature and the paper's notation, these are reported as SD in this extraction but may actually be SEM; meta-analysts should verify. Randomization is described in the title and methods as dividing patients into two groups but no explicit randomization procedure is described — the study may be quasi-experimental rather than a true RCT. The intervention arm combines erdosteine AND breathing exercises, making it impossible to attribute effects to either component alone. The overall ACQ baseline score reported in the text (3.6 ± 0.1) differs slightly from per-arm values in Table 1 (arm1: 3.8 ± 0.2; arm2: 3.4 ± 0.1), suggesting the overall figure may be a rounded average. Clinical effectiveness of 99.3% stated in conclusions but calculation methodology not explained. Between-group p-values are not reported for most outcomes; within-group p<0.05 is reported for statistically significant changes. The paper does not report any adverse events.

summary: This controlled trial tested whether adding erdosteine (300 mg twice daily, an antioxidant mucolytic) plus structured breathing exercises to standard inhaled corticosteroid/formoterol therapy improved outcomes in 30 adults with bronchial asthma and post-COVID syndrome over 2 months. In the 15-patient treatment group, asthma control scores improved from 11.1 to 16.6 on the ACT (a clinically meaningful change of 5.5 points, exceeding the 3-point threshold) and from 3.8 to 2.4 on the ACQ-7, compared to smaller, non-clinically-meaningful improvements in the 15-patient control group receiving standard therapy alone. Lung function measures (FVC, FEV1, airway flow rates) and 6-minute walk distance (471 to 515 metres, exceeding the 25-metre minimal important difference) improved significantly only in the treatment group, though the study is limited by its very small sample size and lack of blinding or randomisation details.

trial_rating.result_basis: ACT score improved by 5.5 points (11.1 to 16.6) in the treatment group vs 2.9 points in controls; ACQ-7 improved by 1.4 points vs 0.4 points; 6MWT distance increased by 43 metres vs 14 metres, p<0.05 for treatment group outcomes.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested 8 weekly sessions of online individual mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) in 30 adults aged 25-55 who had been discharged from hospital after COVID-19 in Tehran, Iran, and who had moderate symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21 score ≥39) at enrolment. MBCT produced large improvements in both primary outcomes: resilience scores rose from 26.5 to 72.7 (vs. 25.7 to 30.1 in controls), and psychological distress scores fell from 39.0 to 5.7 (vs. 47.3 to 46.5 in controls), with both between-group differences highly significant (p=0.0001) and effect sizes above η²=0.87. These gains were maintained at a 2-month follow-up. Key caveats are the very small sample (15 per arm), lack of randomisation (matching-based allocation), self-report outcomes only, and no active control condition, all of which substantially limit causal inference.

trial_rating.result_basis: Resilience post-test: MBCT group 72.67±6.33 vs. control 30.13±9.06 (F=45.21, p=0.0001, η²=0.89); psychological distress post-test: MBCT 5.73±2.96 vs. control 46.47±5.75 (F=154.54, p=0.0001, η²=0.94).

summary: A Russian randomized controlled trial tested Baktiminal, a metabiotic supplement containing metabolites of Bacillus subtilis and fructooligosaccharides (one capsule twice daily for 28 days), against no additional treatment in 40 outpatients with post-COVID gastrointestinal symptoms and fatigue. The treated group showed a statistically significant 44% reduction in total gastrointestinal symptom scores (from 45.2 to 25.5 points on the GSRS scale, p<0.0001), with significant improvements in diarrhea, dyspepsia, and abdominal pain, while the control group improved by only 8%. Fatigue scores also improved significantly in the treated group (51.5 to 43.3 points, p<0.05), and gut microbiome analysis in a subset of 10 treated patients showed restoration of Lactobacillus spp. and Akkermansia muciniphila, which was completely absent at baseline in all post-COVID patients tested. No adverse events were reported, though the small sample size, single-centre design, lack of blinding, and use of an unregistered dietary supplement substantially limit the reliability of these findings.

summary: This open-label pilot study tested 40 Hz vibratory and auditory treatment (VAT) — simultaneous vibrotactile and sound stimulation delivered via a portable device — in 20 adults with long COVID-associated cognitive impairment. Over 4 weeks of daily home use (20 sessions), the treatment group showed a statistically significant improvement in the Flanker test of selective attention and response inhibition compared to controls (group-by-session interaction F(1,1)=11.69, p=0.014, partial eta squared=0.41), and plasma BDNF levels increased significantly in the treatment group, with BDNF change strongly correlated with Flanker score change (R²=0.825). The study is unblinded with no sham control, a conflict of interest (one author receives royalties from the device manufacturer), and only 10 participants per arm, so results must be interpreted with caution.

trial_rating.result_basis: Flanker test group-by-session interaction F(1,1)=11.69, p_adjusted=0.014, partial eta squared=0.41; 80% of treatment group improved vs 20% of controls.

summary: This multicenter prospective quasi-experimental study (TUN-EndCOV) tested sulodexide (250 LSU twice daily for 21 days) against no treatment in 290 long COVID patients from Tunisia who had confirmed endothelial dysfunction at baseline. Sulodexide produced significantly higher rates of chest pain resolution (83.7% vs. 43.6%, p<0.001) and palpitations resolution (85.2% vs. 52.9%, p=0.009), along with greater improvement in endothelial function (median delta-EQI 0.66 vs. 0.18, p<0.001). The main caveat is that this was a non-randomized, non-blinded quasi-experimental design with no placebo control, which substantially limits causal inference despite the large observed effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chest pain recovery 83.7% vs. 43.6% (p<0.001); palpitations recovery 85.2% vs. 52.9% (p=0.009); median delta-EQI 0.66 vs. 0.18 (p<0.001).

summary: This trial tested 16–18 days of mountain spa rehabilitation, with or without ubiquinol (coenzyme Q10, 2×100 mg/day), in 36 long COVID patients who had been hospitalised with severe COVID-19 and still had persistent symptoms 3–7 months later. The primary biological finding was that platelet mitochondrial Complex I-linked oxidative phosphorylation capacity was markedly reduced in patients at baseline (approximately 30–46% below healthy controls) and recovered significantly only in the group receiving ubiquinol: CI-linked OXPHOS increased by 25% after rehabilitation plus supplementation (p=0.043) and by 50% after an additional 12–14 days of home supplementation, compared to a non-significant 12% increase with rehabilitation alone. Clinically, 62.8% of symptoms resolved in the ubiquinol group versus 51.8% in the rehabilitation-only group, and lung function improved in both groups; the study was small (14 and 22 patients per arm) and unblinded, with ubiquinol donated by the manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: CI-linked OXPHOS capacity increased 25% in MRQ2 vs MRQ1 (p=0.043) and 50% in MRQ3 vs MRQ1 (p=0.072); rehabilitation-only group showed only 12% increase (ns).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested weekly intravenous recombinant C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH, Ruconest) against placebo in 36 adults with post-COVID neurological and fatigue symptoms lasting more than 4 weeks. Depression scores (BDI-II) improved by 32% (8.7 points) during 8 weeks of C1-INH treatment, and fatigue scores showed a trend toward improvement, but most changes were not statistically significant and the study was explicitly exploratory with no pre-specified primary outcome or power calculation. Long COVID patients also showed markedly reduced immune signaling compared to healthy controls, but no serious safety signals were identified with C1-INH.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, controlled trial tested oral oxaloacetate (OAA) at 2,000 mg/day for 42 days against a rice flour placebo in 69 adults with long COVID who had moderate-to-severe fatigue and post-exertional malaise. The primary outcome—fatigue reduction on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire—was not met, with a negligible between-group effect size (Cohen's d = -0.093, p = 0.71). Secondary measures showed OAA-treated participants had greater early improvement in fatigue and total symptom burden on the DSQ-SF at day 21, and significantly better performance on objective cognitive tests (total cognitive efficiency +10.7% vs. -0.04%, p = 0.007 at day 42). The trial was funded by Terra Biological LLC, whose officer co-authored the paper and holds a commercial interest in OAA—a conflict of interest that warrants scrutiny of the positive secondary findings.

summary: A supervised 8-week mixed exercise program combining cardiovascular and resistance training was tested in 15 adults with post-COVID condition (PCC), compared to 10 PCC patients receiving usual care, at Université de Sherbrooke. The primary physical capacity outcomes showed significant improvements in the exercise group: sit-to-stand test improved 31% vs 11% in controls (p=0.043) and bicep curl improved 15% vs 4% (p=0.040), with daily physical activity levels also increasing significantly (p=0.007). Importantly, the program did not worsen fatigue or trigger post-exertional malaise, and plasma proteomics showed a downward trend in inflammatory markers S100A8 and CST3 following exercise; however, the study was non-randomized with a small sample size and excluded PCC patients who had previously experienced post-exertional malaise, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Sit-to-stand improved 31% vs 11% (p=0.043); bicep curl improved 15% vs 4% (p=0.040); physical activity scale interaction effect p=0.007.

summary: A randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study tested a single oral dose of ketone ester (395 mg/kg) against placebo in 12 adults previously hospitalized for COVID-19 (average 18 months post-hospitalization), measuring cardiac function by echocardiography. The primary outcome, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), did not improve with ketone esters (mean difference -0.7%, 95% CI -4.0 to 2.6%, p=0.66). A secondary measure of heart muscle contractility, global longitudinal strain (GLS), did improve significantly by 1.9 percentage points (95% CI 0.1 to 3.6%, p=0.04), indicating a modest acute benefit in myocardial function. The study was very small (n=12) and the positive GLS result should be interpreted cautiously given the null primary outcome and limited statistical power.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome LVEF showed no significant difference between ketone ester and placebo: mean difference -0.7% (95% CI -4.0 to 2.6%), p=0.66.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-group crossover study (n=20) where all participants completed all four exercise conditions (VR, no-VR, SSE-VR, 6MWT) — there are no separate randomized arms. Arm IDs are used here to represent the four conditions rather than parallel groups. The primary key comparison reported is VR vs. no-VR for dyspnea (p=0.004, t(19)=-3.269, verbatim). Overall ANOVA F-statistics are reported for each outcome across all four conditions. The 6MWT MAP value of '1,001.6 ± 8.4 mmHg' in the original text appears to be a typographical error; the value is likely 100.16 ± 8.4 mmHg and has been extracted as such. Several figures referenced in the paper contain data that are also reported in the text (HR, SpO2, dyspnea, leg fatigue). Baseline values before each condition are noted as recorded but not reported numerically in the paper text. Exercise characteristics per condition (distance, speed, duration) are extracted from Table 2. Correlations reported: handgrip vs leg fatigue at VR end (r=-0.621, p=0.003); handgrip vs leg fatigue at SSE-VR end (r=-0.450, p=0.047); handgrip vs dyspnea at SSE-VR end (r=-0.484, p=0.030); WAI vs dyspnea at baseline (r=-0.450, p=0.046); WAI vs dyspnea at VR end (r=-0.508, p=0.022); body fat vs dyspnea at SSE-VR (r=0.461, p=0.041); body fat vs 6MWT (r=-0.498, p=0.025); muscle mass vs dyspnea at SSE-VR (r=-0.466, p=0.038). These correlation outcomes were not extracted as separate outcome objects but are noted here.

summary: This study tested stationary cycling with a virtual reality (VR) headset versus cycling without VR in 20 long COVID patients (mean age 54, 80% male) with mild cognitive impairment, recruited 2 months after hospital discharge. The primary finding was that VR exercise produced significantly lower dyspnea scores than non-VR exercise (Borg CR-10: 0.5 vs. 1.1, p=0.004), with patients also spontaneously choosing to exercise more than twice as long when given free choice in the VR condition (21.8 vs. 10 minutes fixed). The study was unblinded, had no control arm, enrolled only 20 patients all infected with the Delta variant, and used a single-session crossover design rather than a rehabilitation programme.

trial_rating.result_basis: VR dyspnea score 0.5 ± 0.6 vs. no-VR 1.1 ± 0.9, p=0.004 (paired t-test, n=20).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 presents FEV1%VC and Dyspnea/Fatigue Borg scores as median [IQR]; the IQR values in the table appear to be reported as a single bracketed value (e.g., 84.3 [6.89]) — it is unclear if this represents the IQR range or a single IQR width value; extracted as median with iqr_high. The between-group effect size column in Table 3 is labeled 'Effect size d' (Cohen's d); these were verbatim for non-parametric outcomes (dyspnea, fatigue, FEV1%VC) and are stored as 'smd' in effect_measure. For 6MWT distance, the paper reports the between-group p=0.264 with effect size d=-0.411 but does not report a mean difference CI; mean difference calculated as arm1_post minus arm2_post = 558-552=6m. PSS-10 between-group mean difference calculated as 20.7-22.2=-1.5. No CONSORT flow diagram included; attrition not reported. Figure 3 referenced for 6MWT results but values are also in Table 3. The 6MWT improvement amounts mentioned in text (56.9m VR, 39.2m control) represent within-group change scores and are consistent with table data (558-502=56, 552-512=40).

summary: This RCT tested a 3-week, five-days-per-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program in 32 adults (average age 58) with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, comparing a virtual reality-enhanced version (VR headset during cycle ergometer training and VR-guided relaxation) against traditional rehabilitation. Both groups significantly improved their 6-minute walk test distance — the primary outcome — with the VR group gaining an average of 57 meters and the control group 39 meters, both exceeding the minimal clinically important difference, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Both groups also showed significant reductions in perceived stress and post-exercise dyspnea, with no meaningful difference between VR and traditional formats; lung function was essentially normal at baseline and did not change significantly in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT distance improved significantly within both groups (p<0.001 each), VR +57m vs control +39m, but between-group comparison was non-significant (p=0.264, Cohen's d=-0.411).

domains.support: Block randomization (block size=6) was used; groups were well-balanced at baseline on all key characteristics. Allocation was performed by a designated person (MK) after baseline testing.

Participants could not be blinded to their group allocation due to the nature of the intervention. The assessor (ML) was blinded to group allocation, but performance bias from participant knowledge of group assignment cannot be ruled out.

Dropouts occurred (n=4 IG, n=4 CG from FU1 analyses with n=34 total), with analyses conducted on completers rather than ITT. Authors state dropouts did not differ on key characteristics but analyses are per-protocol.

Validated neuropsychological instruments were used. The cognitive assessor (ML) was blinded to group allocation. Patient-reported questionnaires were self-administered, with inherent susceptibility to expectation bias.
The study was registered retrospectively (not prospectively). Multiple outcomes were tested without full pre-specification of primary vs. secondary outcomes, increasing risk of selective reporting.

For average disease duration, significant negative correlation (b=-0.26, p=0.012). For longer disease duration (+1 SD), stronger negative effect (b=-0.56, p<0.001). Same pattern for long-delayed recall (interaction p=0.003).

sensitivity_analyses.description: Exploratory pre-post analysis merging both groups into a combined intervention group (n=31) to increase power, with plausibility check using Friedman tests in original control group to rule out familiarity/spontaneous effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: KEY DESIGN NOTE: This is a waitlist-crossover RCT. The 2x2 ANCOVA results (Table 2) are the primary between-group comparisons (IG vs CG, BL to FU1, n=34 completers). The Table 3 data are from an exploratory analysis combining both groups after crossover (n=31 total trained), not a randomized comparison — these pre/post means and SDs are provided for completeness but reflect all completers pooled, not a randomized arm comparison. Per-arm SDs are NOT reported for the primary 2x2 ANCOVA results; only adjusted means (M_adj) and SEs are available. SDs for the combined pre-post analysis (Table 3) are provided for the pooled combined group only. Baseline SDs for individual arms from Table 1 are available for demographic variables (age, BMI, weight, height) but not for cognitive/psychological outcomes. The 2x3 ANCOVA interaction effects are reported in Supplementary Table 2 (not provided in full text); the 2x2 ANCOVA interaction p-values and partial eta-squared from Table 2 are extracted as between-group effect sizes. Cohen's d values from Table 3 are for the combined pre-post comparison and are extracted as 'smd' in the exploratory combined-group outcomes (outcomes 5-21 arm_results reflect the combined group). The n=31 for Table 3 is noted as 'df+1=31' from the t-test degrees of freedom. Fatigue analysis had n=28 (df=27+1). Word fluency SDs in Table 3 appear unusually small for formal-lexical (SD=1.22 and 1.43) — these are verbatim from paper. Outcomes 5-21 arm_results only have data for arm_id=1 (combined group) as the per-arm split was not reported for Table 3. The 6-month follow-up (FU2) data for within-group stability were described narratively but no per-arm means/SDs were provided for FU2 in the text.

summary: A three-month tablet-based training program combining cognitive exercises, relaxation techniques, and physiotherapy was tested in 40 adults (mean age 50, 80% female) with post-COVID-19 condition in Austria, randomized to intervention (n=20) or waitlist control (n=20). The primary finding was that the intervention group showed significant reductions in subjective cognitive complaints (p<0.001) and depressive symptoms on the ADS-L scale (p<0.001) compared to the control group, and their MoCA Memory Index Score remained stable while the control group's declined significantly (p=0.008 for decline in controls). Effects were not sustained after training ended, no improvements were seen in attention, executive function, fatigue, anxiety, or quality of life in the main group comparison, and the study was not prospectively registered.

trial_rating.result_basis: Subjective cognitive complaints improved significantly in the intervention group (p<0.001) while unchanged in controls (p=0.387); depression (ADS-L) improved in intervention group (p<0.001) while unchanged in controls (p=0.328); group×time interaction for subjective cognitive complaints: F(1,29)=5.83, p=0.022, ηp²=0.167.

summary: This pilot study tested a one-month telerehabilitation program — 12 supervised video-based exercise sessions plus three therapeutic education workshops — in 15 adults with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 (persistent fatigue lasting under 3 months) who had been hospitalised but not intubated. A comparison group of 6 patients received standard physiotherapy. Fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Score improved significantly across both groups (from 25.2 to 21.1 in the telerehabilitation group and 27.6 to 26.2 in the standard care group, p=0.010 time effect), alongside meaningful gains in aerobic capacity including an ~18% rise in VO2max (p=0.005) and a 15% improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p=0.019), with no adverse events reported. The study is a very small, non-randomised pilot with no untreated control arm, making it impossible to separate intervention effects from natural recovery.

trial_rating.result_basis: CFS-11 improved from 25.2 to 21.1 (tele-R) and 27.6 to 26.2 (trad-R), significant time effect p=0.010, but no group difference and no control arm without rehabilitation.

summary: This quasi-experimental pilot study tested an 8-week multimodal immersive virtual reality (IVR) intervention — combining cognitive training, physical exercise, and mindfulness — delivered twice weekly in group sessions of 5 participants, in 13 adults with post-COVID-19 condition (long COVID) who had cognitive complaints and elevated depression or anxiety scores, compared to 13 controls receiving usual care. The IVR group showed significant improvements in global cognition (MoCA mean change: 26.15 to 28.54), processing speed (Stroop Colors), verbal episodic memory (RAVLT Sum mean change: 37.31 to 48.38), and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 mean change: 14.38 to 8.38), with large effect sizes (partial η² ranging from 0.177 to 0.343), while the control group showed no significant changes on any measure. The study is substantially limited by its non-randomised quasi-experimental design, small sample size, unblinded assessors, baseline group differences in memory scores, and absence of an active control, meaning causal attribution is uncertain.

Table 2 only provides baseline (T0) values. The mixed-effects regression model coefficients (intercept, Age, BMI, Day, Time, Group, Time:Group) reported in Tables 3-6 are model coefficients, NOT per-arm means/SDs at each timepoint. The actual timepoint-specific outcome values appear only in Figures 2 and 3 (data only in figures for T1, T2, T3). Therefore, per-arm arm_results for T1, T2, T3 cannot be extracted and are omitted. Between-group effects are reported only as regression model Time:Group interaction coefficients (b values) with p<0.05 thresholds, not as mean differences with CIs, severely limiting quantitative extraction. The coefficient b=-0.119 for ST EC T0-T1 and b=-1.826 for SD OAP EC T1-T2 are Time:Group interaction terms from mixed effects models (Group A relative to Group B), not standard mean differences. Note also that the paper uses 'SD' ambiguously — both as 'Standard Deviation' (for oscillation measures) and as 'Mean Spatial Distance' parameter; extraction uses context to distinguish these. Table 1 reports age/BMI as median (IQR) format based on Wilcoxon test usage, but values are labeled as mean+SD in the results text; treated as mean+SD per text. summary: This randomized trial compared a 5-week spa-resort rehabilitation program (including thermal water exercise, land-based balance training, and cognitive therapy) against a supervised home-based program in 60 long COVID patients with fatigue, respiratory, cognitive, or psychological symptoms. The primary balance outcomes—antero-posterior sway amplitude (SD OAP) and mean stay time (ST)—were measured via force platform before treatment, immediately after, and at 3 and 6 months. The home-based program produced faster improvements immediately post-treatment (significant reduction in SD OAP and increase in ST with eyes closed), while the spa-resort program showed continued improvement in SD OAP from post-treatment to 3-month follow-up, suggesting more gradual but sustained gains. The trial was small (21–23 analyzed per group) and the two groups differed significantly in age at baseline (spa group mean 50 vs. home group mean 57 years), limiting direct comparison.

trial_rating.result_basis: Home-based group showed significant reduction in SD OAP (Time effect p<0.05) and increase in ST (Time effect p<0.05) at T0-T1 in EC condition; spa group showed significant decrease in SD OAP from T1 to T2 (time:Group interaction b=1.826, p<0.05); no other parameters reached significance.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested a marine oil supplement enriched in specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) at doses of 500 mg, 1500 mg, or 3000 mg daily for 12 weeks in 53 adults with post-COVID syndrome. The primary outcome was change in serum levels of three pro-resolving lipid mediators (14-HDHA, 17-HDHA, 18-HEPE) and the ratio of pro-inflammatory to pro-resolving markers: all three mediators increased significantly across all dose groups (p=0.002, p=0.0007, and p=0.00001 respectively), and the inflammatory-to-resolving ratio improved significantly (p=0.025), with no dose-response difference between groups. Fatigue and dyspnea showed a non-significant trend toward improvement across all treated groups, with a 9% mean reduction in fatigue scores between weeks 4 and 12 in the 500 mg group; the placebo arm had only 5 participants, severely limiting interpretation of clinical outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pro-resolving mediator ratio decreased significantly (p=0.025) across all treatment groups, but fatigue improvement was non-significant (9% mean reduction in FSS for 500 mg group, no p-value reported for between-group comparison) and dyspnea showed no significant differences (Chi-square p=0.509).

Within-arm Cohen's d and ANOVA F/p-values for pre vs post (within each group) are reported in Table 1 (e.g., SUDs IP: F=1557.13, p<10^-4; Cohen's d=1.85; SUDs OL: F=1568.14, p<10^-4, Cohen's d=2.17) but these are within-arm effects, not between-group. Between-group ANOVA rows in Table 1 give the F and p for IP vs OL comparisons. 4. No CIs reported for any effect. 5. No trial registration mentioned. 6. Session duration was 45 minutes each, 3 sessions planned within approximately 3 weeks. 7. The paper also reports Cohen's d for between-group differences (SD column of 'Difference' rows in Table 1), which are very small (0.02-0.07), indicating negligible between-group effects.

summary: This study tested remote EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) therapy, delivered via an AI-assisted platform with eye-tracking, versus standard in-person EMDR therapy in 160 adults aged 25–49 with long COVID-related PTSD symptoms. Both formats produced large reductions in all three outcome measures: SUDs scores dropped by ~6.6 points (in-person) and ~6.8 points (online) from a baseline of ~8.4–8.6; PCL-5 scores fell by ~20 and ~22 points respectively; and IES-R scores fell by ~28 points in both groups. No statistically significant differences were found between the two delivery formats on any measure, supporting equivalence of remote and in-person delivery. The main caveat is that this is a non-inferiority comparison between two active treatments with no placebo or waitlist control, so the absolute efficacy of EMDR itself cannot be independently confirmed from this trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary comparison between online and in-person groups showed no significant difference: SUDs decrement ANOVA F=1.51, p=0.22; PCL-5 decrement F=0.89, p=0.34; IES-R decrement F=0.09, p=0.76. This is a null equivalence result with no control arm.

summary: This pilot study tested four weekly online forest bathing sessions (guided virtual mindfulness-based nature engagement) in 22 adults with long COVID. summary: This pilot study tested a 12-session Nordic walking program in 16 long COVID patients and 13 COVID-19 controls (without persistent symptoms), measuring blood lactate levels after each session to assess aerobic exercise capacity across different genetic profiles. Long COVID patients consistently produced higher lactate concentrations than controls during exercise, with statistically significant group differences observed in carriers of specific variants of the ACTN3 (CT and TT genotypes, sessions 1–7) and AMPD1 (CC and CT genotypes) genes, indicating impaired aerobic metabolism that improved over the course of the program. The study is a small, non-randomized pilot with 29 total participants, no randomization, no pre-intervention cardiopulmonary testing, and no control for diet or baseline fitness, substantially limiting the generalizability of its findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: ACTN3 group×genotype×session interaction F=1.702, p=0.028; AMPD1 main effects lactic acid p<0.001, group p=0.003, genotype p<0.001, three-way interaction p=0.048; no overall primary outcome effect size reported.

summary: This pilot RCT tested superficial neuromodulation (NESA XSIGNAL device, 15 sessions over two months) versus a sham placebo device in 16 women with post-COVID-19 condition and dysautonomia. The primary outcome was heart rate variability (HRV): SDNN increased in the treatment group (49.06 to 69.68 ms) but decreased in controls (84.65 to 42.26 ms), with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.021), though no significant time-by-group interaction was found. summary: A 3-month cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was tested in 60 adults recovering from COVID-19 (randomized 1:1 to rehabilitation or no rehabilitation, starting one month post-acute disease). The primary outcome was endothelial function measured by flow-mediated dilation (FMD): the rehabilitation group improved from 6.2% to 8.6% (+2.4 percentage points), versus 5.9% to 6.6% (+0.7 percentage points) in controls, with a statistically significant between-group interaction (p<0.001). summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of face-to-face versus asynchronous online Mat Pilates (three sessions per week) in 49 adults aged around 52 years with long COVID, all presenting with fatigue as a defining symptom. Only the face-to-face group showed significant improvements in the primary fatigue outcome: total Fatigue Assessment Scale scores dropped from 33.5 to 26.7 (p<0.01), alongside gains in upper limb endurance (16 to 23 repetitions), trunk flexion isometric strength (6.6 to 12.7 kg), and 6-minute walk distance (463 to 514 m). Online Pilates produced no significant changes on any outcome, and neither format affected body composition or cardiometabolic blood markers. Notably, the inactive control group showed significant increases in systolic (114 to 122 mmHg) and diastolic (75 to 81 mmHg) blood pressure over the 12 weeks, suggesting ongoing cardiovascular deterioration without exercise.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of cycling-based high-intensity interval training (HIIT), with or without daily Triphala herbal supplementation (1000 mg/day), in 104 young adults (mean age 22 years) with long COVID symptoms including fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Both the HIIT-only and HIIT-plus-Triphala groups showed significant within-group reductions in the pro-inflammatory cytokines IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, and in oxidative stress markers MDA and protein carbonyls, compared to no change in the placebo control group; however, the between-group interaction effect was not statistically significant for any primary outcome (IFN-gamma: p=0.837; TNF-alpha: p=0.175), meaning the trial did not formally demonstrate superiority of HIIT over control. Triphala added no statistically significant benefit beyond HIIT alone and was safe with no liver or kidney toxicity detected.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested eight weeks of twice-weekly supervised water-based (AQUA) or land-based (LAND) exercise training versus no exercise in 74 children aged 10-12 years with post-COVID-19 condition. Both exercise programs significantly increased absolute VO2max compared to baseline (AQUA p=0.001, LAND p=0.004), and post-intervention VO2max was significantly higher in the AQUA group versus the control group (p=0.023); relative VO2max increased significantly only in the AQUA group (p=0.017). Neither exercise program reduced fatigue scores, and no adverse events were recorded in either training group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Relative VO2max group-by-time interaction F=4.32, p=0.017; post-intervention difference between LAND and CONTROL was 4.3 ml/kg/min (95% CI 0.01 to 8.6), with no significant between-group differences for AQUA vs LAND or AQUA vs CONTROL at post-intervention.

domains.support: Randomization used RANDOM.ORG internet program. No allocation concealment method described. Baseline age differed significantly between groups at follow-up timepoints (p<0.05 and p<0.001), suggesting possible selection bias post-randomization.

Open-label study; participants and providers not blinded. Study was self-selected via patient organization, which may affect adherence, but adherence was high (92%). No crossover or contamination described.

Attrition was low (7% withdrew from telerehabilitation group). 88% of 8-week completers provided 6-month data. Waiting list had only 21/42 at 6-month follow-up, with reasons explained by pandemic difficulties.

All outcomes are self-reported (patient-reported ICF questionnaire, mMRC, CCQ). No blinded assessor for self-reported outcomes. The Functional Compass COVID-19 questionnaire was not validated in post-COVID populations.

Study was pre-registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04961333). Primary outcomes (ICF categories) and secondary outcomes (breathing scales) were pre-specified. All stated outcomes appear to be reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Most ICF outcome data are presented only in bar charts/figures (Figures 2-4) without numeric tables for individual category scores per arm at each timepoint. Only Table 3 provides medians (combined across groups, or for groups separately per regression model) for selected categories. Waiting-list arm median values for most ICF b- and d-categories are not extractable from text or tables. 2. The between-group F and p-values in Table 3 are from a general linear model adjusted for age (between-subjects factor); these are not simple pairwise comparisons. 3. The CCQ score format is ambiguous: the paper describes 10 items each 0-6, with total divided by number of questions; however, values reported (e.g., mean 20.0) suggest the total sum was used, not the averaged score. Extracted as reported. 4. Within-group p-values for mMRC and CCQ (Wilcoxon test and Friedman test) are extracted from Table 4 as within-group statistics, not between-group comparisons. 5. Symptom duration: telerehabilitation group 51 weeks (SD 27) = ~11.75 months (SD 6.25); waitlist 58 weeks (SD 31) = ~13.5 months (SD 7.25) — converted to months for baseline demographics. 6. Hospitalization: 7/67 (10%) in telerehabilitation arm and 6/42 (14%) in waitlist arm hospitalized during acute infection — percent_previously_hospitalized set to 10% for arm 1 (telerehabilitation). 7. Omitted ICF categories not in Table 3 but shown in figures: sexual functions, gastrointestinal functions, body temperature, smell/olfactory, long-term memory, sleep, cardiovascular, taste, tactile, joint mobility, widespread pain, making the bed, walking, family relationships — no per-arm numeric data extractable from text.

summary: This Swedish randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week multidisciplinary group telerehabilitation program (combining breathing exercises, mindfulness, ACT-based therapy, physical training, and psychoeducation delivered via Microsoft Teams) in 109 adults with long COVID who had persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was functioning and activity measured across 38 ICF categories; the telerehabilitation group showed improvements in more ICF categories than the waiting-list controls, particularly in activities and participation domains such as recreation, household tasks, stair climbing, and lifting, though statistically significant between-group differences were rare — breathing function actually improved more in the waiting-list group at 8 weeks (p=0.034). At 6 months, many participants in both groups still reported severe fatigue and cognitive impairment, highlighting the chronic nature of the condition.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group differences were rarely statistically significant on the primary ICF outcomes; within-group improvements were seen across multiple ICF categories in the telerehabilitation group (e.g. pain at multiple sites: Wilcoxon p=0.003; climbing stairs: p=0.02), but the between-subjects group factor was non-significant across nearly all regression model outcomes (all group F p-values >0.05).

WHO-5 and HADS data reported as median (range) not mean (SD); iqr_high fields used to store range maximum. 3. Between-group p-values for CPET outcomes from mixed-effects model using percent-predicted values; absolute value differences were calculated from per-arm data. 4. The paper also reports a comparison arm of CAD patients (n=96) but this is a non-randomized observational comparison cohort, not a randomized arm; CAD data not included in primary extraction. 5. Workload at VT1 percent-predicted change: IT 6.8±12.9%, CT 6.8±11.5%; O2 pulse at VT1 percent-predicted change: IT 3.2±8.9%, CT 7.2±17.7%; these percent-predicted change values are also reported in the paper alongside absolute values. 6. Table S1 and S2 (CAD comparison data) not available in main text. 7. Responder analysis results reported: at VT1 IT 56% vs CT 58% (p=0.835); at peak IT 51% vs CT 54% (p=0.836). 8. VE/VO2, VE/VCO2, respiratory minute ventilation, tidal volume, breathing frequency, breathing reserve, and resting O2 pulse outcomes from Table 3 omitted from detailed extraction to manage output size; all showed no significant between-group differences.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested moderate-intensity aerobic interval training (IT) versus continuous training (CT) on cycle ergometers in 110 long COVID patients (mean age 49, average 260 days post-infection) undergoing 4-6 weeks of inpatient medical rehabilitation in Germany. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), improved by a mean of 2.7% across all PCS patients, but the difference between IT and CT was not statistically significant (IT: +0.8% vs CT: +4.1%, p=0.157), meaning neither modality was superior to the other. Both groups showed significant improvements in fatigue, anxiety, depression, and quality of life, and the overall gains in exercise capacity were comparable to those seen in coronary artery disease patients undergoing guideline-based cardiac rehabilitation; no post-exertional malaise or training-specific fatigue was detected in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak improvement did not differ between IT and CT (IT +0.8% vs CT +4.1%, p=0.157); the trial was designed to detect equivalence, not superiority, and the non-significant between-group result is the primary finding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports postural stability data separated by sex within each arm (male n=15 and female n=11 for intervention; male n=8 and female n=12 for control), making it impossible to extract clean combined arm-level medians. The arm_results above use intervention group combined n=26 and control n=20 but the medians shown in the table are sex-stratified. The FRI 6-2 'after' values are not explicitly given in the table for all subgroups — the table row for FRI 6-2 appears incomplete with only some cells visible. Between-group effects use Glass's rank-biserial correlation R (reported as effect size), not SMD — the effect_measure field is set to 'smd' as the closest available schema option, but these are actually Mann-Whitney U Z statistics with R as rank-biserial correlation: OSI EO Z=-3.12, R=0.533; FRI 6-2 Z=-2.06, R=0.354; DOM2 Z=2.194, R=0.389; DOM3 Z=2.051, R=0.361; Q2 Z=3.309, R=0.535. WHOQOL-BREF domain means are averages of male and female subgroup means as reported (not weighted by n). Q1 and Q2 baseline means for control group are estimated from the table which shows male mean 4.1 and female mean 3.8 (Q1) and male 3.0, female 3.3 (Q2). Table 3 reports both mean and median for QOL outcomes. The n_randomized_total of 49 is inferred: 28 intervention (26 completed + 2 withdrew) + 20 control (originally 23 but 3 did not attend post-test — however text says 'control group: n=20' at final and mentions 3 did not attend post-test, so original control randomized was 23, but the text is ambiguous).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week resistance training program (twice weekly, 60 minutes per session at 70% of 1-repetition maximum) in 46 adults aged 65 and older who had recovered from COVID-19 and reported ongoing post-COVID symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, and balance problems. The primary finding was a significant improvement in overall postural stability (overall stability index with eyes open) in the training group compared to controls (Z = -3.12, p = 0.0017, effect size R = 0.533), along with reduced fall risk on an unstable surface (fall-risk index 6-2, Z = -2.06, p = 0.04, R = 0.354). The training group also showed greater improvements in psychological wellbeing and social relationship domains of quality of life, and higher health satisfaction scores, compared to controls. The trial was small (26 intervention, 20 control) and conducted at a single site using gym-based resistance machines, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Overall stability index (eyes open) improved significantly in the intervention group vs control: Z = -3.12, p = 0.0017, R = 0.533 (large effect by rank-biserial correlation).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 6-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program — combining aerobic cycle training, resistance exercise, respiratory training, and stretching — in 59 post-COVID-19 patients with persistent symptoms, comparing an active inspiratory muscle training (IMT) group (n=39) against a placebo IMT group (n=22). The primary outcome, maximum inspiratory pressure (PImax), improved significantly in both groups (p<0.001), with a median increase of 52% in the IMT group and 47.5% in the placebo group, but there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups (p=0.28), meaning the additional resistive breathing device did not provide extra benefit over the general exercise program. The IMT group did show greater improvement in spirometric parameters — FEV1 rose 8.02%, FVC by 13.24%, and PEF by 9.67% — but the unequal group sizes (39 vs 22) and the preliminary nature of this dataset limit the strength of these conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PImax improved in both groups (p<0.001 within-group) but the between-group comparison was non-significant (p=0.28, r=0.141), meaning the key experimental question — whether IMT adds benefit — was not confirmed.

summary: A 12-week Nordic Walking program (one 45-minute session per week) was tested in 16 long COVID patients and 13 healthy controls in Spain. Long COVID patients showed consistently higher blood lactate concentrations after exercise than controls throughout the program (group effect F=5.604, p=0.024), indicating impaired aerobic metabolism. Long COVID patients also improved on quality-of-life measures after the program: total SF-36 score rose from 37.2 to 48.4 (p=0.004) and EQ-5D from 41.3 to 58.8 (p=0.005), and fatigue scores (MFIS total) fell from 59.6 to 48.6 (p=0.009). Key caveats include the non-randomized design, small sample, predominantly female long COVID group (94%), and that the lactate meter frequently exceeded its upper range in long COVID patients, meaning true values may have been even higher.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (lactate group difference) was statistically significant (F=5.604, p=0.024) but showed no time or interaction effect; SF-36 total improved by 11.2 points in long COVID group vs. 1.4 in controls (interaction p=0.002), a modest change against a low baseline.

summary: This Romanian RCT tested whether adding daily 20-minute progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) sessions to a standard 21-day pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) program improved outcomes in 61 long COVID patients (aged 54–74) with persistent dyspnea and fatigue. The primary finding was that the PR+PMR group showed significantly greater improvements in mental health, anxiety, and sleep quality compared to PR alone: GAD-7 anxiety scores dropped by approximately 5 points (to a mean of 4.96 vs. 8.23 in the PR-only group, p<0.001), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores fell by 4.74 points (median 4 vs. 7, p<0.001), crossing the threshold from poor to good sleep quality. Exercise capacity (6-minute walk test) improved in both groups but did not differ significantly between them (366.60 m vs. 391.54 m, p=0.171). The study is limited by its small sample, short 21-day follow-up with no post-intervention monitoring, and a predominantly older male population from a single centre.

trial_rating.result_basis: GAD-7 post-intervention: PR+PMR group mean 4.96 vs. PR-only mean 8.23 (p<0.001); PSQI median 4 vs. 7 (p<0.001); PSQI reduction of 4.74 points exceeds the 3-point MCID threshold.

Between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d) are reported only as within-group comparisons, NOT as between-group differences. No between-group p-values are reported for continuous outcomes except for HADS Anxiety binary outcome at 8 weeks (p<0.01, stated as '**'). Symptom duration reported as mean 51 (SD 27) weeks for rehabilitation group and 58 (SD 31) weeks for waiting list — converted to months as approximately 11.8 (SD 6.3) and 13.4 (SD 7.2) months respectively. The paper reports Cohen's d within the rehabilitation group for SF-36 outcomes (8 weeks): physical functioning=0.5, role physical=0.4, bodily pain=0.5, vitality=0.7, social functioning=0.6, role emotional=0.3, mental health=0.9, PCS=0.3, MCS=0.7. Waiting list within-group Cohen's d (8 weeks): physical functioning=0.5, social functioning=0.4, mental health=0.4. At 6 months: physical functioning=0.6, vitality=0.6, mental health=0.8. HADS within-group Cohen's d (TR): anxiety d=0.4 (p<0.01) at 8 weeks, d=0.6-0.7 (p<0.001) at 6 months; depression d=0.6-0.7 (p<0.001) at 8 weeks, 6 months. PHQ-9 within-group TR: d=0.8 (p<0.001) at 8 weeks, d=0.5 (p<0.001) at 6 months; WL: d=0.6 (p<0.05) at 6 months only. IASP pain site data is in Supplemental Table S1 (not available in this text). N_randomized_total=116 inferred from 67+42+7 unaccounted (164 registered, 116 participated per text). Note: 164 registered, 116 participated and completed questionnaires at start, suggesting 48 did not meet criteria or withdrew before randomization. The 6-month follow-up had n=60 TR and n=21 WL. | Pass3 agent confirmed: no per-arm means/SDs for most outcomes, no CIs. Cohen's d within-group only. summary: An 8-week multidisciplinary telerehabilitation programme delivered via Microsoft Teams was tested in 67 adults with long COVID (mean age 43, 78% women) who had persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared against 42 people on a waiting list. The primary outcomes were health- and pain-related parameters measured by SF-36 and ICF pain categories; the telerehabilitation group showed moderate-to-large within-group improvements across most SF-36 subscales (Cohen's d 0.3–0.9), but no statistically significant between-group differences were found for any primary outcome. The only statistically significant between-group difference was a reduction in clinically elevated anxiety (HADS): 6% of the telerehabilitation group screened positive after 8 weeks versus 24% of the waiting list (p<0.01).

trial_rating.result_basis: No statistically significant between-group difference was found for any primary outcome (SF-36 or ICF pain categories) by one-way ANOVA; within-group pain intensity reduction in the telerehabilitation group was Cohen's d=0.3, p=0.026, but the between-group comparison was non-significant.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of moderate-intensity resistance training (twice weekly, 60 minutes per session, 70% of one-repetition maximum) in 41 adults aged 65 and older with long COVID symptoms, recruited approximately 9 months after infection. The primary outcome was change in body mass and body composition measured by both DXA and bioelectrical impedance analysis; neither method detected any statistically significant changes in body mass, fat mass, or fat-free mass in the training group compared to controls. The authors conclude that 8 weeks at this frequency is insufficient to drive body composition changes in this population, and suggest that programs of at least 12 weeks with higher training frequency and increased protein intake may be needed.

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant changes in body mass or body composition were detected; ANOVA group-by-session interaction for DXA fat mass p=0.726 (F=0.12, η²=0.003) and fat-free mass p=0.518 (F=0.43, η²=0.012).

summary: This Phase II feasibility trial tested heart rate variability biofeedback (HRV-BF) — 10 sessions over 5 weeks using the HeartMath emWave system — added to standard care (analgesics and antidepressants) versus standard care alone in 18 adults with long COVID who met diagnostic criteria for CFS/ME. The primary outcome was change in severe fatigue: 3 of 8 participants in the HRV-BF group (37.5%) moved out of the severe fatigue category compared to 0 of 9 in the control group, while 2 control participants worsened (Kruskal-Wallis H=4.083, p=0.043). The trial was explicitly a feasibility study with a very small sample, quasi-random (non-random) allocation, and multiple outcomes tested simultaneously, so the fatigue result must be treated as a preliminary signal only and not evidence of efficacy.

trial_rating.result_basis: 3/8 (37.5%) HRV-BF participants remitted from severe fatigue vs 0/9 controls, with 2 controls worsening; Kruskal-Wallis H=4.083, p=0.043 in a total sample of 17 completers.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week gym-based resistance training program (twice weekly, 70% of 1-repetition maximum, seven machine exercises) in 46 adults aged 65 and older with long COVID symptoms including muscle weakness and exercise intolerance. The primary functional outcome was the Chair Stand Test: the intervention group significantly improved both speed (5-repetition sit-to-stand improved from ~9.1s to 6.7s in men and 8.8s to 7.0s in women) and number of repetitions in 30 seconds (men: 15 to 24; women: 18 to 25), while the control group showed no change. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The Hedges' g values reported in the paper appear to represent within-group effect sizes (change from T1 to T2 within OMT arm), NOT between-group effect sizes; they have been extracted in between_group_effects as the best available effect measure since no true between-group effect statistics (mean differences with CIs) were reported for most outcomes. 2. Per-arm data for the sham group across most HRV outcomes (RMSSD, SDNN, LF, HF, TP, mean HR, mean RR, Stress Index) were NOT reported numerically in text or tables — only the OMT arm values and select sham LF/HF ratio values were given. Sham arm HRV data therefore not extractable. 3. The n values for OMT arm vary across outcomes (14–19 of 21 randomized), suggesting some missing measurements, but the paper provides no explanation for discrepancies. 4. The RMSSD g value at T3 (g=-0.55) has an asymmetric CI [-0.96, 0.18] crossing zero, indicating non-significant decline. 5. FAS was used for eligibility screening; post-intervention FAS values were mentioned as reduced but no numeric post-intervention data were provided. 6. Subjective dyspnea questionnaire (0–10 scale) and subjective well-being were listed as secondary outcomes but no quantitative results were reported. 7. The follow-up duration of 48 hours was converted to approximately 0.3 weeks. 8. The outlier table (Table 2) lists n=6 outliers but the text states n=5 participants with 4 in osteopathy and 2 in sham — a discrepancy noted in the paper itself. 9. LF/HF ratio results were only reported for the sham group (T2 vs T3 within-group change); OMT group LF/HF was stated to be 'statistically unchanged'. 10. Outcome data appear only in text/figures for most HRV parameters; no summary table of results by arm and timepoint was provided.

summary: A single 45-minute session of osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) was tested against a sham treatment in 42 long COVID patients (mean age 51 years) with persistent fatigue lasting at least 12 weeks. The primary outcome was heart rate variability (HRV); immediately after OMT, RMSSD increased from 17.8 ms to 21.6 ms (Hedges' g = 0.82), SDNN rose from 19.6 ms to 26.0 ms (g = 0.80), mean heart rate dropped from 67.3 to 62.3 bpm (g = -1.10), and the Baevsky stress index fell significantly — all indicating a short-term shift toward parasympathetic dominance. These gains fully reversed within 48 hours, and no long-term or clinically meaningful benefit was demonstrated from a single session.

trial_rating.result_basis: RMSSD increased from 17.8 ms to 21.6 ms immediately post-treatment (Hedges' g = 0.82, 95% CI [0.19, 1.40], p < 0.01), but returned to baseline by 48-hour follow-up (17.4 ms), indicating only a transient effect with no sustained benefit.

summary: A non-randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week supervised physiotherapy program — combining interval aerobic exercise on a cycle ergometer with resistance training (2 sessions/week) — in 20 adults with long COVID syndrome. In the 10 participants who completed the exercise program, quadriceps muscle strength increased by 5.86 kg (right leg, p=0.03) and 8.26 kg (left leg, p=0.01), functional capacity on the 60-second sit-to-stand test improved by 3.7 repetitions (p=0.01), and perceived breathlessness fell by 0.95 points on the Borg scale (p=0.02) — none of these improvements reached statistical significance when comparing directly against the control group. The study is severely limited by its very small sample size (n=10 per group) and non-randomized allocation, with control group membership determined by inability to travel to the hospital rather than random assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Within-group improvements in the exercise group: left quadriceps +8.26 kg (p=0.01), right quadriceps +5.86 kg (p=0.03), 60s sit-to-stand +3.7 rises (p=0.01), Borg dyspnea -0.95 points (p=0.02); however, between-group comparisons were non-significant for all outcomes.

summary: A 12-week hybrid pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programme — comprising 8 supervised outpatient sessions followed by 24 home-based walking sessions — was tested in 27 previously hospitalised long COVID patients (mean age 57, average 140 days post-discharge) with severe fatigue, compared to 15 usual care controls. Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) increased by 2.4 mL/kg/min (15%) and peak work rate by 19 watts (20%) in the PR group, with no improvement in either measure in the usual care group; 6-minute walk distance also improved by 72 metres, exceeding the minimum clinically important difference. The study was non-randomised and underpowered relative to its own sample size calculation, which limits the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2peak improved by 2.4 mL/kg/min in the PR group vs no change in usual care (p=0.001); peak work rate improved by 19 watts (p=0.001); 6MWT improved by 72 metres (p=0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Most quantitative outcome data appears only in figures (Figures 5 and 6); per-arm means and SDs were only explicitly reported in the abstract for post-intervention values of MFIS physical subdomain, MFIS psychosocial subdomain, and EQ-VAS. Baseline per-arm means and SDs for outcome measures are NOT reported in text or tables — only in figures. ANOVA F-statistics and p-values for group x period interactions are reported in text for all outcomes. The p-values stated for MFIS physical (p<0.001) and psychosocial (p<0.001) in the abstract appear to refer to post-intervention between-group comparisons, not the ANOVA interaction (which shows p=0.187 and p=0.014 respectively); this inconsistency is noted. Body composition outcomes (weight, segmental fat, body water, segmental muscle) all showed non-significant results with no meaningful between-group differences; omitted from outcomes array due to data only in figures and no clinical relevance for fatigue meta-analysis. EQ-5D-5L individual dimension results (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) reported only as chi-square p-values with no per-arm counts or means; omitted from detailed extraction. summary: A 12-week supervised plank-based core stabilisation program (MORETA methodology, 2 sessions/week) was tested in 39 women with long COVID (mean symptom duration ~20 months) in a non-randomised pilot trial in Madrid. The primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale, MFIS) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS): the intervention group improved physical fatigue domain scores by 39.1% vs 16.7% in controls, and EQ-VAS self-rated health by 19.6% vs 1.1% in controls, with a statistically significant group-by-time interaction for EQ-VAS (F=4.347, p=0.046) and psychosocial fatigue domain (p=0.014), though the total MFIS interaction was not significant; no post-exertional symptom exacerbation was reported. The non-randomised design with self-selected group allocation and small sample size (n=20 intervention, n=19 control) introduce substantial risk of selection bias, limiting causal inference.

domains.support: No randomization described; this is a before-after case-controlled study with convenience sampling. Controls were unmatched healthy young males vs. older mixed-sex COVID-19 patients.
Single open-label session with no sham or placebo arm; no blinding of participants or assessors. Sub-motor threshold stimulation and 15-min washout period were used to minimize direct effects.
No participants withdrew; all 10 COVID-19 and 8 control participants completed the study and were analyzed.
Spirometry is an objective standardized test, but assessors were not reported to be blinded to intervention status in this open-label design.
No pre-registration or published protocol identified. All pre-specified outcomes (FVC, PIF, PEF, tPIF, tPEF) appear to be reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental before-after study, not an RCT; there is no randomization and the two groups (COVID-19 patients vs. healthy controls) are not randomized comparators but rather separate cohorts each serving as their own pre-post controls. Between-group effect sizes in this extraction reflect pre-vs-post within-arm differences (paired comparisons), not between-arm comparisons, as that is the primary analysis structure used. The study reports only acute effects from a single 20-minute scTS session assessed 15 minutes post-intervention; there is no extended follow-up. FVC % predicted values are reported per individual in Table 1 (mean 68±3% predicted). Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and VAS pain were monitored as safety measures but no numeric results were reported for these. Time since infection reported as 59±48 days (mean±SD); converted to months as 1.97±1.60 months. All spirometry data (PIF, PEF, tPIF, tPEF, FVC) are reported as mean±SD in text; no figures-only data were extracted.

summary: A single 20-minute session of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (scTS) applied over the T5 and T10 thoracic spinal segments was tested in 10 adults with post-acute COVID-19 respiratory deficits (mean age 55, all with FVC around 68% predicted). Peak inspiratory flow increased from 94 to 134 L/min (p=0.040) and peak expiratory flow increased from 88 to 109 L/min (p=0.049) immediately after stimulation, with faster time-to-peak for both measures, indicating improved neuromuscular activation of respiratory muscles. Total lung capacity (FVC) was unchanged, suggesting the effect is neural rather than structural. The study is very small, unblinded, uncontrolled, and used a single session design with unmatched healthy controls, so results are exploratory only.

trial_rating.result_basis: PIF increased from 93.99 to 133.67 L/min (p=0.040) and PEF from 87.84 to 108.85 L/min (p=0.049) in n=10 patients with no control arm for the COVID group.

domains.support: The paper states patients were randomly allocated but does not describe the randomization method or allocation concealment procedure.
Open-label design with no blinding of participants or personnel; control group received no treatment (waitlist), making performance bias likely.
No dropouts or missing data reported; all 34 randomized patients appear to have completed assessments.
Cognitive tasks are objective computerized measures; however, self-report questionnaires are susceptible to response bias in open-label trial. No blinding of outcome assessors mentioned.
No pre-registration or protocol publication mentioned; multiple outcomes assessed with primary/secondary not clearly pre-specified in registration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Three-arm trial: arm 1=intervention (G-Int, n=17), arm 2=long COVID control (G-Con, n=17), arm 3=healthy normative group (G-Nor, n=15). Primary comparisons are arm1 vs arm2 for long COVID-specific effects. Post2 data (follow-up ~1 week post-intervention) only available for G-Int arm. Table 4 CRT Post1 RT for G-Int reads 535±83 ms in the table; the abstract states RTpost2=521±86 ms; Post1 value extracted as 535±83 from table. Between-group effects for cognitive outcomes are not directly reported as formal between-group statistics; group-time interaction ANOVA stats are reported and noted in text but pairwise between-group values at post not provided; calculated mean differences from arm means. Outcomes omitted due to space constraints: Pattern Comparison CO trials RT (baseline G-Nor=975±121, G-Con=1371±467, G-Int=1277±393; Post1: G-Nor=949±145, G-Con=1353±388, G-Int=1198±331; Post2 G-Int=1128±281), Pattern Comparison accuracy CO and IN trials, Simon CO RT and accuracy, Simon IN accuracy, Pursuit Rotor mean deviation, Corsi longest sequence. ICU admission rates: G-Int 2/17 (11.8%), G-Con 1/17 (5.9%). The paper does not report perceived stress scale (PSS) despite listing it in abstract; no PSS data appears in results tables. CFQ11 Likert scoring mentioned in discussion (29.3±3.3 G-Con, 28.2±3.3 G-Int) represents total score combining subscales.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a four-week neuro-meditation program (Rebalance®, combining sound therapy, coach-guided meditation, and light stimulation) in 34 long COVID patients with confirmed cognitive and psychological impairment. The intervention group (n=17) completed ten 30-minute sessions and showed significantly faster reaction times on three cognitive tasks compared to the untreated control group: choice reaction time improved by 12.1% (593ms to 521ms, p<0.001), pattern comparison by 13.3% (1244ms to 1079ms, p<0.001), and Simon task by 8.4% (539ms to 494ms, p<0.01). Subjective measures also improved significantly, including large reductions in physical fatigue (-13 points), mental fatigue (-7.7 points), depression (-5.2 points), and anxiety (-3.6 points), all p<0.001; however, the study is small (17 per arm), lacked a placebo or active control, and the Rebalance® device is a commercial product of an institution connected to the authors.

trial_rating.result_basis: Choice reaction time: 593ms baseline vs 521ms post-intervention (p<0.001); physical fatigue reduced by 13.0 points vs -0.6 in controls (p<0.001); n=17 per arm.

summary: This single-blind randomized controlled trial tested twice-daily oral supplementation of 1.66 g L-arginine plus 500 mg liposomal vitamin C against placebo for 28 days in 46 adults (median age 51, 65% women) with long COVID and persistent fatigue. The primary outcome, 6-minute walk test distance, improved by a median of 30 m in the treatment group versus 0 m in the placebo group (mean difference 50 m, 95% CI 20–80 m, p=0.001), exceeding the 35 m minimal clinically important difference threshold. Secondary outcomes also favored the supplement: handgrip strength increased by 3.4 kg versus 1.0 kg (p=0.03), flow-mediated dilation reached 14.3% versus 9.4% (p=0.03), and fatigue persisted in only 9% of the treatment group versus 80% of the placebo group at day 28. The trial was small (23 per arm, single center) and single-blind rather than double-blind, limiting the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved by median 30 m (treatment) vs 0 m (placebo), mean difference 50 m, 95% CI 20–80 m, p=0.001, exceeding the 35 m minimal clinically important difference.

Open-label design with no blinding of participants or care providers; no placebo control used, raising risk of performance bias. No CONSORT flow diagram or description of protocol deviations.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports 'Mean distance in phase 0' for Gr 1-MNA as 515.8 m (consistent with Table 1 value of 515.8 m; text mentions 515.18 m — minor discrepancy, used 515.8 from tables). Phase 1 SDs for 6MWT endpoint values are not reported. The between-group p-value of 0.000034 in Table 2 for Phase 0 distance appears anomalous given no significant difference at baseline (Table 1 p=0.85); this may be a data entry error in Table 2. The text states p=0.85 for baseline 6MWT comparison; the p=0.000034 in Table 2 row for 'Mean distance in phase 0' is likely misattributed (possibly the within-group p-value for Gr 1-MNA improvement). FSS Phase 1 values (4.42 for 1-MNA, 4.94 for NO-1-MNA) are stated in text but no SDs reported for Phase 1. The note in Table 1 that the abstract mentions '515.18 m' while tables state '515.8 m' — both used as stated. Dyspnea Borg scale data at baseline is reported as counts by category only (not means) and is not extracted as a separate continuous outcome. No adverse event data reported anywhere in the paper.

summary: This randomised trial tested whether 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNA), a niacin metabolite with anti-inflammatory and antithrombotic properties, could improve exercise tolerance and fatigue in 50 non-hospitalised adults with persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms. After one month of daily 58 mg 1-MNA supplementation, participants in the treatment group walked a mean of 42 m further in the 6-minute walk test compared to a 13 m improvement in the unsupplemented control group (p=0.0016), and 92% of treated patients improved versus 60% of controls. The proportion of patients with severe fatigue (FSS ≥4) was significantly lower in the 1-MNA group at follow-up (20% vs 56%, p=0.008); however, the study used alternating allocation rather than true randomisation, had no placebo control, and enrolled only 25 patients per arm over a single month.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT mean difference between groups: 42 m vs 13.28 m (absolute between-group difference 28.72 m, p=0.0016); severe fatigue rate 20% vs 56% (p=0.008).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is NOT an RCT; it is an open-label two-cohort observational study where both cohorts (PCIBS n=16 and IBS-control n=28) received the same intervention (Curcuma + Boswellia + low-FODMAP diet). The 'arm_id=1' is the long COVID (PCIBS) group and 'arm_id=2' is the IBS-without-COVID control group. There is no placebo or untreated control arm. Between-group effect direction convention: control minus PCIBS (arm2 minus arm1) as reported in Table 2. The 'n_lost_to_followup' for PCIBS arm represents screened (28) minus completed (16)=12 excluded at screening; similarly control screened 35 minus completed 28=7 excluded at screening — these are screening exclusions, not post-enrollment dropouts. GAE data: PCIBS — grade 1: n=1 (6.3%), grade 2: n=2 (12.5%), grade 3: n=8 (50.0%), grade 4: n=5 (31.3%); Control — grade 1: n=0 (0%), grade 2: n=2 (7.1%), grade 3: n=9 (32.1%), grade 4: n=17 (60.7%). Grade ≥3 response: PCIBS 81.3%, Control 92.8%, p>0.05. Table 2 CI for abdominal pain in PCIBS: lower bound listed as '-5.593' and '-5.008' in the extracted table — based on the table structure, PCIBS delta change CI 95% is (-7.560; -5.008) and Control delta change CI 95% is (-7.511; -5.593). The between-group difference for pain CI is (-1.879; 1.373). Adverse events reported as 'No adverse effects related to the supplementation were reported during the study' — applies to all participants combined, not broken down per arm.

summary: This pilot study tested 30 days of supplementation with lecithin-based formulations of Curcuma longa (500 mg twice daily) and Boswellia serrata (150 mg twice daily), combined with a low-FODMAP diet, in 16 adults with post-COVID-19 irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-like symptoms 60–120 days after infection) compared to 28 adults with IBS who had no prior COVID-19 infection. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in abdominal bloating (the primary outcome), but the effect was smaller in the post-COVID group (score change: −1.950) than in the IBS-only group (−2.850), with the between-group difference reaching significance (p=0.001). A key caveat is that gut dysbiosis, measured by urinary indican, improved significantly only in the IBS-only group (−36.2 units) and not in the post-COVID group (+7.9 units, i.e., no improvement), suggesting that post-COVID dysbiosis may require different treatment strategies; the study had no placebo arm, was open-label, and enrolled very small numbers.

trial_rating.result_basis: Abdominal bloating (primary outcome) decreased significantly within the post-COVID group (intra-group Δ −1.950, CI95% −2.238 to −1.662), but the between-cohort comparison showed the post-COVID group improved less than the IBS-only group (difference −0.899, CI95% −1.270 to −0.528, p=0.001); no placebo control was included.

summary: This pilot randomized controlled trial tested whether drinking hydrogen-rich water (HRW, 500 mL twice daily for 14 days) reduced fatigue and breathlessness in 32 long COVID patients with self-reported fatigue and dyspnea. The primary fatigue outcome (Fatigue Severity Scale) showed a significantly greater percent reduction in the HRW group compared to placebo (p=0.046, Cohen's d=0.696), and HRW also improved six-minute walk distance, chair stand test performance, and sleep quality. However, dyspnea scores (mMRC) did not improve significantly with HRW versus placebo (p=0.556), and no improvements in mood or anxiety were detected.

trial_rating.result_basis: FSS percent change was significantly greater in HRW vs placebo (p=0.046, 95% CI -20.607 to -0.198, d=0.696), but this was a secondary percent-change analysis; the primary mixed-effects model showed no significant group effect (p=0.122) or interaction (p=0.184), and the primary dyspnea outcome was null (p=0.556).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested a five-strain probiotic (OMNi-BiOTiC Pro-Vi 5, taken twice daily for six months) in 21 adults who had experienced severe COVID-19 roughly 10 months earlier, comparing them to 10 mild-disease controls. The probiotic significantly increased gut microbial richness at 3 months (p=0.047) and 6 months (p=0.014), reduced fatigue scores on the ARTIQ questionnaire at 3 months (p=0.014), improved psychological burden (p=0.022), increased stool butyrate at 6 months, and reduced neutrophil ROS production and CD4+ TEMRA cells at 3 months; however, increased intestinal permeability and the reorganization of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae remained unaffected. The trial was small (8 probiotic completers vs 13 placebo) with a notable 38% dropout rate in the probiotic arm, making all findings preliminary and hypothesis-generating.
