summary: This randomized placebo-controlled trial tested daily oral supplementation with 28g of fermented Carica papaya and Morinda citrifolia syrups (BioRex Papaya and BioRex Noni) added to standard rehabilitation care in 188 adults recovering from moderate or severe COVID-19 (primarily the delta variant). After 20 days, patients receiving the fermented fruit supplements showed significantly greater reductions in plasma IL-6 and IL-8 levels, normalization of elevated nitrite/nitrate levels, improved immune cell function (phagocytosis restored toward normal range in severe COVID survivors), and greater improvement in self-reported symptoms including weakness, physical and mental working capacity, heart pain, arrhythmia, and tachycardia compared to placebo. The study has notable limitations: it was single-center with no pre-registration, blinding adequacy is unclear, several co-authors have commercial ties to the tested products, and the placebo (diluted honey water) may not have been inert.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total average symptom score decreased from 1.2±0.2 to 0.5±0.1 in FFS group vs 0.9±0.1 in placebo (severe COVID, p<0.05); IL-6 normalized in FFS groups vs remained significantly elevated in placebo groups (p<0.01); oxygen desaturation during 6-minute walk test occurred in 53.3% of FFS patients vs 71.4% of placebo patients.

summary: This 12-week open-label randomized controlled trial tested vitamin D replacement therapy guidance (25 µg daily vitamin D3 supplement plus dietary counseling, sun exposure, and exercise) versus alfacalcidol (active vitamin D preparation) alone in 85 adults with ME/CFS developing after COVID-19 infection or vaccination who had vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency (serum 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL). The intervention group reduced their ME/CFS symptom count by a mean of 6.7 symptoms versus 1.2 in the control group (between-group difference -5.6; 95% CI: -7.2 to -3.9; p<0.001), and 16 of 42 intervention participants versus 1 of 38 controls no longer met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria at 12 weeks. summary: This 24-week randomized controlled trial tested daily supplementation with 2000 IU vitamin D3 and 240 µg vitamin K2 (MK-7 form) against standard of care in 151 adults with established long COVID (at least 2 moderate symptoms persisting 3+ months after confirmed infection). The vitamin K2/D3 group showed a 7.1% decrease in the proportion meeting the RECOVER Long COVID Research Index threshold of ≥12, compared to a 7.2% increase in the standard-of-care group (p=0.01); in adjusted models, the LC Research Index was 3.2 points lower in the treatment arm (p=0.04), and the treatment group had nearly 2 fewer total symptoms (-1.7, 95% CI -3.2 to -0.1, p=0.02). summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding personalized normobaric interval hypoxic-hyperoxic therapy (IHHT) — alternating low-oxygen (10–15%) and high-oxygen (30–40%) breathing via the ReOxy device — to a standard 10-day inpatient rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 120 patients recovering from moderate COVID-19 pneumonia with long COVID symptoms. The intervention group showed significantly greater gains in exercise capacity (six-minute walk test improved by 19.9% vs 12.0% in controls), breath-hold tolerance (Stange test improved by 51.2% vs 24.1%), and spirometric measures including FVC and FEV1, compared to standard rehabilitation alone. No adverse events were reported, though the study lacked a placebo arm, did not assess outcomes beyond the 10-day program, and did not analyze results by age or sex.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk test improved by 19.9% (374.8m to 449.3m, p=0.000) in the intervention group vs 12.0% (376.5m to 421.7m, p=0.001) in controls; Stange breath-hold test improved 51.2% vs 24.1%; FVC improved 12.8% vs 8.1% (both p<0.05).

summary: This randomised open-label trial from Uzbekistan tested four rehabilitation programmes in 166 adults (average age 46) with neuropsychological symptoms of long COVID, including fatigue, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, and anosmia. The main group (n=46) received acupuncture combined with therapeutic exercise incorporating yoga elements and small-group psychotherapy; comparator groups received massage plus physiotherapy, acupuncture alone, or home exercise only. The combined acupuncture-plus-exercise group showed the largest improvements across all outcomes: the six-minute walk test distance increased by 18% (from ~364m to ~430m), dyspnoea on the Borg scale fell by 53%, depression severity on the HADS fell by 66.7%, and quality-of-life scores (EQ-5D) rose from ~57 to ~87 points (+53%), all significantly better than comparator groups (p<0.05). The study had no blinding, no placebo control, and outcomes were self-reported, which limits confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk distance increased 18% (363.6m to 429.8m) vs 9.6% in home-exercise control; Borg dyspnoea fell 53% vs 25.5%; EQ-5D quality-of-life score rose from 56.8 to 86.7 (+53%) vs +29% in control; all between-group differences p<0.05.

summary: This pilot study tested two bacteriophage cocktails — one oral and one inhaled — in 30 post-COVID patients who had persistent gut dysbiosis and lung involvement at least 3 months after hospital discharge. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the addition of audiovisual stimulation (binaural brainwave entrainment shifting from beta to theta activity over 22-minute sessions) and cognitive behavioral therapy (5 sessions of 40 minutes each) to standard rehabilitation in 59 long COVID patients with emotional disturbances 1–6 months post-infection, mean age ~60 years. In the intervention group (n=29), anxiety and depression scores on the HADS improved significantly compared to the control group receiving standard rehabilitation alone, with 93.1% of treated patients showing no signs of anxiety or depression after treatment versus 64% in controls; situational anxiety on the Spielberger-Khanin scale dropped from a median of 46 to 42 points (p<0.001), and high-level situational anxiety was eliminated in all 21 patients who had it at baseline (p<0.001 between groups). The main caveat is that three of the five authors hold a patent on the intervention, and the lead editor of the publishing journal is also a study author, raising conflict-of-interest concerns.

summary: This single-blind randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week calisthenics exercise program (jumping jacks, burpees, squats, planks, and related movements) in 176 adults with post-COVID syndrome, comparing therapist-supervised sessions against a home-based program. Both groups showed statistically significant improvements across all five EQ-5D-3L quality-of-life dimensions and the general health score, with the home exercise group's health score rising from 58.5 to 75.8 and the supervised group's from 58.0 to 68.6. No significant difference was found between the two delivery formats, suggesting that a well-instructed home program is as effective as supervised exercise for improving quality of life in this population.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested acupuncture added to a standard multi-modal rehabilitation program versus rehabilitation alone in 160 post-COVID-19 patients (average age 61, 76% women) hospitalized at a rehabilitation center in Kazakhstan. summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a rehabilitation programme combining robotic mechanotherapy with biofeedback (Con-Trex lower-limb trainer), interactive balance therapy (Stabilan 01-2), and virtual reality training (Nirvana system) against a standard rehabilitation programme (therapeutic gymnastics, low-intensity laser, speleotherapy, chest massage) in 120 adults aged 40-70 with post-COVID syndrome assessed 1-6 months after infection. The experimental group showed significantly greater gains in cardiorespiratory fitness: maximum work performed increased by 12.9% versus 3.0% in controls (post-rehabilitation difference 25.3% higher, p=0.006), oxygen consumption at the first ventilatory threshold rose 6.3% versus 5.0% (p=0.016 between groups), and diastolic blood pressure at peak exercise fell by a mean of 7 mmHg (p=0.003). Dyspnoea severity also improved more in the experimental group: the proportion with moderate-to-severe dyspnoea fell from 78.3% to 13.3%, and 86% had mild or no dyspnoea after treatment, compared with 58.3% in the control group. No safety concerns were reported, but notable conflicts of interest exist: four authors hold a patent on the intervention tested.

trial_rating.result_basis: Maximum work performed increased 12.9% in the intervention group vs 3.0% in controls, with post-rehabilitation values 25.3% higher in the intervention group (p=0.006); diastolic BP at peak load fell by 7 mmHg (p=0.003); proportion with mild or no dyspnoea reached 86% vs 58.3% in controls (p<0.001 for mild dyspnoea category).

summary: This randomized trial tested whether adding personalized normobaric interval hypoxic-hyperoxic therapy (NBIHHT) — alternating breathing of low-oxygen (10–15% O2) and high-oxygen (up to 40% O2) gas mixtures, individually dosed via real-time pulse oximetry feedback — to a standard rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 120 adults (mean age 62) with persistent symptoms more than 12 weeks after moderate COVID-19 pneumonia. Quality-of-life gains were sustained at 3 months in the NBIHHT group and stable at 6 months, whereas the control group showed a declining trend by 6 months; no safety concerns were reported, though the trial lacked a sham-control arm and did not pre-register.

summary: This study tested 16-18 days of mountain spa rehabilitation with or without ubiquinol (reduced coenzyme Q10, 200 mg/day) in 36 non-vaccinated post-COVID-19 patients (3-6 months after hospitalization) at a high-altitude sanatorium in Slovakia. The primary biochemical finding was that ubiquinol supplementation markedly raised CoQ10 levels in platelets (+68%), whole blood (+194%), and plasma (+232%), while CoQ10 remained unchanged in the rehabilitation-only group. Clinically, the ubiquinol group showed greater symptom reduction across multiple domains: for example, overall fatigue fell from 85% to 35% of patients and shortness of breath from 65% to 30%, compared to more modest improvements without supplementation. summary: The EXER-COVID trial tested a 6-week supervised muscle power resistance training program (two sessions per week, 50–70% of daily 1RM, performed at maximum speed) in 100 adults with long COVID (mean age 48, 68% women) in a randomized crossover design conducted in Spain. The primary outcome, peak VO2, improved by 2.10 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.25–2.94, p<0.001) compared to usual care. The program also increased upper and lower body strength, reduced psychological distress, improved quality of life and cognitive performance, and reduced 7 of 22 long COVID symptoms including dyspnea (RR=0.56, 95% CI 0.39–0.82) and weakness (RR=0.75, 95% CI 0.59–0.95), with no notable safety signals reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Peak VO2 improved by 2.10 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.25 to 2.94, p<0.001) in the exercise vs. usual care condition; per-protocol analysis showed 2.40 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.56 to 3.25, p<0.001).

The exercise group showed significant improvements across multiple outcomes: the 6-minute walk test improved significantly (F=22.56, p<0.001), blood pressure fell (systolic and diastolic, p<0.001), lung function measures including FVC and FEV1 increased, and oxidative stress markers improved (MDA decreased, SOD and catalase increased). summary: This Russian trial tested whether adding the probiotic Bifiform (containing Bifidobacterium longum BB-46 and Enterococcus faecium ENCfa-68, 3 capsules daily for 2 weeks) to standard IBS treatment improved outcomes in 70 adults who developed irritable bowel syndrome following COVID-19 infection. Both groups showed statistically significant improvements in IBS symptom severity (IBS-SSS) and quality of life (IBS-QOL) scores, but improvements were larger in the probiotic group; however, the trial was open-label with no blinding, limiting confidence in the results.

summary: This pilot trial tested 4 g/day of creatine monohydrate plus breathing exercises (2-3 times daily for 10-15 minutes) versus breathing exercises alone in 8 long-COVID patients with moderate fatigue lasting at least 3 months. The primary outcome was tissue creatine levels measured by MRS: the creatine plus breathing group showed significant increases at 6 of 14 tissue locations, while the control group showed significant decreases in 2 brain regions. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week telerehabilitation program (24 supervised video-call sessions, 3×45-60 min/week of multicomponent exercise) against a control group in 32 adults who had recovered from COVID-19 (mean age 48 years, ~57% with severe initial disease). Depression scores (Beck Depression Inventory) fell significantly more in the telerehabilitation group (p=0.00 between groups), though the between-group difference in anxiety reduction was not statistically significant (p=0.26); the small sample size (16 per arm with substantial dropout from initial allocation) limits generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk test improved by 122 m in telerehabilitation group vs 8 m in controls (p=0.01); sit-to-stand improved 3.6 vs 0.1 repetitions (p=0.00); depression score difference between groups p=0.00.

summary: This randomised-design study tested whether adding balloon blowing exercise (30 min/day) to diaphragmatic breathing (10 min/day) for 8 weeks improved lung function, exercise tolerance, and quality of life in 30 post-COVID-19 survivors aged 25–50, compared to diaphragmatic breathing alone. summary: This pilot RCT tested individualized homeopathic treatment versus placebo in 77 adults with long COVID (mean symptom duration ~9 months, 80% female) over 12 weeks via telemedicine. The primary outcomes — Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), and the physical and mental composite scores of the SF-36 — showed no significant difference between the homeopathy and placebo groups at any time point (4, 8, or 12 weeks). Repeated-measures ANOVA found a statistically significant interaction favoring placebo over verum for fatigue (FAS: F(3,210)=3.3, p=0.021) and physical health (PCS: F(3,210)=3.28, p=0.022), meaning the placebo group improved earlier; both groups improved overall, likely reflecting natural recovery. The verum group reported nearly twice as many transient symptom worsening events (19 vs. 10), which the authors attribute to a homeopathic aggravation effect.

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant between-group difference at any time point for FAS, PCS, or MCS; the only significant ANOVA interaction (FAS p=0.021, PCS p=0.022) favored placebo over verum.

summary: A 3-month hybrid integrated care program combining 8 outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation sessions with 24 home-based ICT-supported sessions was tested in 27 long COVID patients with significant fatigue (mean FACIT score 26), compared to 15 patients receiving usual care. The primary outcome of exercise tolerance improved substantially in the rehabilitation group: peak work rate increased by 19±10 watts, 6-minute walk distance by 72±63 meters, and FACIT fatigue score by 15±9 points (all p=0.001), while the usual care group showed improvement only in breathlessness (mMRC). Patient compliance with the home-based program was 95%, supporting feasibility, though the study is limited by its small, non-randomised design and conference abstract format with no pre-registration or blinding details reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Peak work rate increased by 19±10 W (p=0.001), 6MWT improved by 72±63 m (p=0.001), and FACIT score improved by 15±9 points (p=0.001) in the PR group vs no significant change in UC except mMRC (0.7±0.6, p=0.008).

summary: This study tested osteopathic manual treatment (sessions every two weeks for 10–12 weeks) in 20 adults with post-COVID fatigue and autonomic symptoms (astheno-neurotic syndrome), compared against 20 untreated controls. The primary outcome was severity of asthenia on the Scale of Asthenic State (SAS): the treated group improved by 4.7 points versus 0.8 points in the control group. Treated patients also showed normalization of autonomic balance (Kerdo index moving from −3.29 to −0.35) and improvements in mental health and general health on the SF-36. The trial was small, unblinded, and conducted at two Russian osteopathic medicine institutes with a non-treatment (rather than sham) control group, introducing high risk of placebo and expectation bias.

trial_rating.result_basis: SAS asthenia score decreased by 4.7 points in the treated group (p=4.16E-17) versus 0.8 points in the control group (p=1.30E-3); no between-group statistical comparison reported, and the absolute difference of ~4 points on a scale of 30–120 is modest.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week circuit training program combining aerobic, strength, and breathing exercises (50 minutes, three times per week, at 65-75% maximum heart rate) in 60 Indonesian women with post-COVID-19 syndrome. The exercise group showed significantly greater improvements than controls in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume; interaction p=0.010, effect size d=-0.66), FEV1/FVC ratio (interaction p=0.006), peak expiratory flow (interaction p=0.009, effect size d=-0.67), and oxygen saturation (interaction p=0.041), while FVC and maximum voluntary ventilation improved in both groups equally. The FEV1/FVC ratio actually declined in the control group over the 8 weeks, underscoring the value of the exercise program, though the study was limited to women only and lacked long-term follow-up beyond the intervention period.

summary: This randomized controlled trial compared physiotherapist-supervised synchronous telerehabilitation (STR) against unsupervised asynchronous telerehabilitation (ATR) in 31 Brazilian adults with post-COVID syndrome, using an 8-week progressive exercise program including aerobic, strengthening, and breathing exercises. The primary outcome—lower limb functional strength measured by the Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test—improved significantly within the STR group (from 11.02s to 9.63s at 8 weeks, p=0.03) and showed a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.027, Cohen's d=0.52), though post-hoc testing did not confirm this between-group difference. STR also produced significant within-group improvements in dyspnea, fatigue, stress, and quality of life, while ATR improved only fatigue and anxiety; notably, dropout was substantially higher in the ATR group (13 of 21 lost by 20-week follow-up vs. 8 of 23 in STR), limiting the reliability of comparisons.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group difference in FTSTS was p=0.027 (Cohen's d=0.52), but post-hoc testing did not confirm this difference; within-group improvement in STR was from 11.02s to 9.63s (p=0.029, 95% CI 0.10–2.40).

summary: This randomized trial tested daily home-based transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS), delivered via a standard TENS device clipped to the left ear tragus, in 114 adults with post-COVID fatigue. Among the 24 participants in the active treatment arm who met minimum adherence (at least 1 hour/day on at least 50% of days), fatigue measured on a Visual Analogue Scale improved by 11.9 points (±17.8) after 8 weeks, compared to non-significant reductions of 8.0 points in both the sham and placebo groups; the active group also showed significant improvement across all domains of the Fatigue Impact Scale and in an objective measure of peripheral muscle fatigue. A major caveat is that this is a per-protocol subgroup analysis of adherent participants only — one-third of the 114 enrolled did not meet minimum usage — and the main between-group intention-to-treat analysis is reported separately; the experimenter was also not blinded after randomization.

trial_rating.result_basis: VAS fatigue score improved by 11.9 ± 17.8 points in the active nVNS group (p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.939, N=24), versus non-significant reductions in sham (p=0.018) and placebo (p=0.141) groups; this is a per-protocol subgroup analysis, not the pre-specified primary analysis.

summary: This double-blind randomized controlled pilot trial tested 2,100 mg/day of omega-3 fatty acids (EPA+DHA) versus a soybean oil placebo for 12 weeks in 18 healthcare workers with long COVID symptoms including shortness of breath, cough, fatigue, and loss of taste and smell. Notably, the omega-3 group did show a larger drop in the AA:EPA inflammatory ratio (mean change of 11.4 vs. 3.06 in placebo), but this change did not correspond to clinical symptom improvement, and the study was too small to draw conclusions about efficacy.

summary: This randomized trial compared 15 sessions of continuous aerobic training (CT) at 40% peak workload versus low-intensity interval training (LIIT, alternating 3-minute loaded and 1-minute unloaded intervals at 40% peak workload) in 63 COVID-19 survivors with residual symptoms including dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced walking distance. T-statistics are given for HADS-A (t=-3.636, t=-5.167) and HADS-D (t=-2.823, t=-2.458) and ISI (t=-8.801, t=-3.569) but not CIs. 3. The insomnia categorical outcome (absence of insomnia 53.2% vs 30.4%) was reported with chi-square statistic (x=4.944, p=.026) — this appears to be the chi-square value not the ISI mean score as stated in the abstract. 4. The abstract states insomnia score '53.2 vs 30.4' which matches the categorical percentages in Table 2 (not ISI continuous scores), suggesting the abstract conflated percentage data with score data. 5. Control group n at 12 months is 43 per Table 2 (not 46), consistent with 3 additional dropouts noted in limitations. 6. Baseline demographic table shows n=93 for analyzed population but randomization was 105 total (52 IG + 53 CG). The 12 missing patients (5 IG + 7 CG) are the dropouts. 7. The paper uses 'psychoeducation' as the label for the MBSR intervention in the abstract methods section but the intervention is clearly MBSR throughout.

summary: This Italian RCT tested an 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) program (2 hours per week in small groups) added to usual drug therapy versus usual care alone in 105 COVID-19 survivors who had been admitted to intensive care and developed new-onset chronic pain, anxiety, depression, or insomnia. The primary outcome was chronic pain assessed by the Brief Pain Inventory; the MBSR group showed statistically significant reductions in 'least pain in the last 24 hours' at 6 months (0.91 vs 1.43, p=0.035) and 12 months (2.20 vs 2.83, p=0.012), alongside significant improvements in anxiety (HADS score 11.28 vs 13.15, p<0.001), depression (9.95 vs 11.23, p=0.007), and insomnia at 6 months (53.2% vs 30.4% absence of insomnia, p=0.026). The authors themselves noted that the pain reductions, while statistically significant, appeared clinically small, and the study was single-centre with a sample size below its original target of 125.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (least pain in last 24h) improved by 0.52 points at 6 months (0.91 vs 1.43, p=0.035) and 0.63 points at 12 months (2.20 vs 2.83, p=0.012); authors themselves characterised these reductions as statistically but not clinically significant.

summary: A 6-week outpatient cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program — combining respiratory muscle training, inspiratory muscle training, upper limb resistance exercises, and treadmill aerobic training — was tested against an educational control in 33 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Brazil. The rehabilitation group walked 100.5 m further on the 6-minute walk test than controls (95% CI: 7.4–193 m, p=0.002), a clinically meaningful improvement in functional capacity. Dyspnea also improved significantly (mMRC inter-group difference: −1.45, 95% CI: −1.98 to −0.92), and upper limb muscle mass increased by 0.63 kg more than controls; fatigue scores did not differ significantly between groups. The trial was small (n=33) and unblinded to participants, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT inter-group difference of 100.46 m (95% CI: 7.40–193 m, p=0.002), exceeding the commonly cited minimal clinically important difference of ~25–54 m.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot RCT tested 14 days of beetroot juice supplementation (200 mL/day, ~600 mg nitrate) versus placebo in 25 adults with long COVID aged 20–60 years who reported persistent fatigue. The primary outcome—change in fatigue resistance—improved significantly within both groups over 14 days (+21.8 s overall, p<0.001), but there was no significant difference between beetroot juice and placebo (median change +26.6 s vs +15.0 s; mean difference 1.3 s, 95% CI −13.5 to 19.6 s; p=0.92). Beetroot juice did produce beneficial changes in gut microbiota composition (increased Akkermansia, Oscillospira, Prevotella, Roseburia, Ruminococcaceae) and inflammatory markers (IFN-γ and MIP-1β) compared to placebo, though the clinical significance of these biological changes is unclear.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (fatigue resistance) showed no significant between-group difference: mean difference 1.3 s, 95% CI −13.5 to 19.6 s, p=0.92.

summary: This pilot study tested fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), administered four times via upper and lower endoscopy over 8 weeks, in 60 long COVID patients with clinically significant insomnia (ISI ≥8) at a Hong Kong tertiary hospital. At 12 weeks, insomnia remission (ISI <8) was achieved by 37.9% of FMT recipients versus 10.0% of untreated controls (OR 5.50, 95% CI 1.34–22.51, p=0.018), with significant improvements in sleep quality, anxiety, daytime sleepiness, and blood cortisol. The study was non-randomized and open-label with group allocation based on patient preference, limiting causal inference; no serious adverse events were reported.

summary: This double-blind RCT tested a combined plant extract (CPE) supplement — containing lime, bamboo grass, cannabis leaves, galangal, and black pepper — at 4500 mg/day for 7 days in 66 Thai adults with long COVID symptoms. The two co-primary outcomes were CRP levels and a total symptom score: CRP did not significantly change (median difference −0.05 mg/L, 95% CI −0.49 to 0.39, p=0.823), but the symptom score was significantly reduced in the CPE group (median difference −4.00 points, 95% CI −7.58 to −0.42, p=0.029). Secondary analyses showed CPE was associated with 75% lower risk of moderate-to-severe fatigue (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.08–0.81) and 65% lower risk of moderate-to-severe post-exertional malaise (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16–0.78), though the trial was small, used a newly developed unvalidated symptom questionnaire, and early dropout of 10 placebo participants may have inflated apparent treatment effects.

summary: This uncontrolled pilot study assessed three intravenous infusions of human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs, 1×10⁶ cells/kg on days 0, 7, and 14) in 10 long COVID patients with persistent symptoms and lung lesions. summary: This open-label randomized controlled trial tested oral thiamine (vitamin B1, 600 mg/day for 8 weeks) plus supportive therapy versus supportive therapy alone in 66 long COVID patients in Tehran, Iran. The primary finding was that thiamine significantly accelerated symptom resolution: by week 7, 67% of the thiamine group had resolved symptoms versus 33% of controls, and by week 8, recovery rates were 87% versus 40%. Multiple individual symptoms including fatigue, anosmia, myalgia, anorexia, dyspnea, palpitations, skin rash, and hair loss showed significantly greater improvement in the thiamine group by week 6 (p<0.05 to p<0.0001). summary: This pilot RCT tested major ozone autohemotherapy (O3-MAH) added to conventional treatment versus conventional treatment alone in 73 Chinese patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), most of whom were elderly (median age ~70) with symptoms persisting for ~20 weeks after Omicron infection. The primary outcomes favored O3-MAH: 71% of O3-MAH patients achieved ≥50% symptom score reduction versus 45% of controls (p=0.0325), with significantly better 6-minute walk distance (6MWD %predicted, p=0.0032) and tidal volume (p=0.0374). O3-MAH also improved inflammatory markers (CRP, SAA, PCT) and cellular immunity markers (lymphocyte, CD3, CD4 counts), with no adverse events reported. Key limitations include inability to blind participants to treatment allocation and imbalanced baseline severity between groups, which may have inflated apparent benefits.

trial_rating.result_basis: 71% response rate (≥50% symptom reduction) in O3-MAH vs 45% controls (p=0.0325); 6MWD %predicted significantly higher in O3-MAH group post-treatment (p=0.0032); tidal volume p=0.0374.

summary: This Italian multi-centre survey (LINCOLN) tested whether 30 days of combined L-Arginine (3.32 g/day) plus liposomal Vitamin C (1 g/day) reduced long COVID symptoms compared to a B-vitamin multivitamin combination in 1,390 COVID-19 survivors. The L-Arginine + Vitamin C group had significantly lower total symptom scores (8.15 ± 1.3 vs 13.9 ± 2.3, p<0.001) and better effort perception on the Borg scale (p<0.0001), with improvements seen across all nine individual symptoms. A critical limitation is that this was an observational survey rather than a randomised trial: physicians were not blinded, no baseline symptom data were collected, and treatment allocation was not randomised, making it impossible to rule out selection bias or regression to the mean.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total symptom score 8.15 ± 1.3 (L-Arg + Vit C) vs 13.9 ± 2.3 (multivitamin), p<0.001; Borg effort perception significantly lower, p<0.0001.

summary: This bicentric randomized feasibility study tested singing-based respiratory training (SBRT) in 47 adults with post-COVID syndrome and respiratory symptoms at a university outpatient clinic and inpatient rehabilitation center in Germany. summary: The PERCEIVE RCT tested a 6-month personalised supervised aerobic and resistance exercise program (plus cardiovascular risk factor management) versus usual care in 133 adults with long COVID who had reduced exercise capacity at least 12 weeks post-infection. The primary outcome, indexed VO2 peak, improved significantly more in the exercise group than usual care at 6 months (between-group difference: 1.74 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.71–2.76, p=0.001), with concurrent improvements in absolute VO2 and peak watts. summary: This RCT compared two 8-week telerehabilitation programs — functional exercise (bodyweight strengthening) versus aerobic exercise (progressive walking), both combined with breathing techniques — in 43 adults with long COVID averaging 17 months post-infection. The primary outcome was fatigue (Fatigue Assessment Scale): the functional exercise group showed a statistically significant reduction of 6.7 points (95% CI -11.9 to -1.3), while the aerobic exercise group showed a non-significant reduction of 5.1 points (95% CI -10.3 to 0.1), and there was no significant difference between groups. Both groups improved perceived stress and reached the minimal clinically important difference for quality of life; no adverse events were reported.

summary: A 3-week inpatient, multimodal symptom-based rehabilitation program was tested against usual care in 104 adults with post-COVID condition, stratified by dominant symptom cluster (fatigue, somatic, or cognitive). summary: This secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial examined whether individuals with long COVID respond differently to 8 weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT), using data from 111 IMT participants and 36 usual-care controls. The primary finding was strong heterogeneity in inspiratory muscle strength responses: mean improvements of 26.6 cmH2O for maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP) and 141.2 pressure time units for sustained MIP, with the intervention group showing substantially greater variability than controls (Bayes factor >100 for both). Greater training dose was the strongest predictor of improvement, with each standard deviation increase in cumulative power associated with a 10.9 cmH2O gain in MIP; however, no evidence of heterogeneous treatment effects was found for perceived dyspnea or health-related quality of life.

summary: A multimodal immersive virtual reality (IVR) intervention combining cognitive training, physical exercise, and mindfulness was tested in 18 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCC) in Spain, comparing 16-session (reduced) versus 24-session (extended) formats over 8–12 weeks, with heart rate variability (HRV) as the primary outcome. Contrary to expectations, time-domain HRV parameters (RMSSD, SDNN, SDSD) significantly decreased from baseline to mid-intervention in both groups, with partial recovery by the end, and no significant improvements were observed in either time-domain or frequency-domain measures at final assessment. There were no significant differences between the two session-length groups, and no control arm was included, making it impossible to isolate intervention effects from natural disease course.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary HRV outcomes showed no significant group-by-time interactions (p > 0.05 for all); RMSSD decreased significantly from baseline to mid-term (MD = 0.079 ms, p = 0.044) with no significant improvement at endpoint relative to baseline.

This is a secondary analysis of a stress-recovery trial with COVID-19 status determined by self-report only, small subgroup sizes (n=38-51 per arm), and outcomes measured partly with non-validated Likert scales, limiting the strength of conclusions.

summary: An 8-week selected exercise rehabilitation (SER) program combining breathing, stretching, strength, and aerobic exercises was tested against standard care in 35 COVID-19 survivors with pulmonary damage and persistent fatigue, recruited from Al-Zahra Hospital in Isfahan, Iran. The SER group showed significantly greater improvements than controls across all measured outcomes at 8 weeks, including fatigue (Chalder scale: 24.5 to 16.3), CRP (7.8 to 3.7 mg/L), WBC (14,491 to 8,223 cells/µL), handgrip strength (25.3 to 28.9 kg), two-minute walk test (62.5 to 81.1 m), and quality of life scores, with large effect sizes (Cohen's d 0.63–1.93). The study had notable limitations including a small final sample (n=35 across both arms), no long-term follow-up beyond 8 weeks, and no control for natural recovery given that pre-tests were conducted near hospital discharge when inflammatory markers were still acutely elevated.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chalder Fatigue Scale improved from 24.5 to 16.3 (Cohen's d=1.46), CRP from 7.8 to 3.7 (d=1.80), WBC from 14,491 to 8,223 (d=1.93); between-group p<0.001 for all outcomes.

summary: This small Russian RCT (n=28) tested aquatic walking exercises in a pool containing diluted sodium chloride-bromine brine versus plain freshwater pool exercises in long COVID patients at a Moscow rehabilitation centre, all of whom also received a standard rehabilitation programme including physiotherapy and massage. The primary finding was that the brine group showed a 40% increase in 6-minute walk test distance (p=0.01), a twofold increase in oxidative metabolism index (p<0.01), and compared to controls, a threefold greater oxidative metabolism index (p<0.001), doubled microcirculation index (p<0.05), and 20% greater reduction in BMI (p<0.05). No serious adverse events occurred in either group. The trial is very small, open-label, and uses non-standard physiological measures as endpoints, limiting the interpretability of results.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk test improved 40% in brine group (T=10.0, p=0.01); oxidative metabolism index threefold higher vs control (U=32.0, p<0.001); microcirculation index doubled vs control (U=120.0, p<0.05).

summary: This placebo-controlled RCT tested Chatushashti Prahari Pippali (CPP) — a processed long pepper (Piper longum) preparation — at 500 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, added to WHO rehabilitation guidelines, versus rehabilitation plus placebo in 112 Indian adults with post-COVID syndrome. The CPP plus rehabilitation group showed statistically significant improvements over placebo plus rehabilitation across all primary symptom outcomes (cough, dyspnea, fatigue, headache) and the 6-minute walk test, with intergroup percentage differences ranging from 76% (fatigue) to 96% (cough); 49 of 54 CPP-treated patients achieved complete symptomatic relief versus 1 of 56 controls. The trial was open-label (not blinded) and conducted at a single Ayurvedic institution in India, limiting generalisability; no adverse events were reported.

summary: The PAX LC trial tested a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (Paxlovid) versus placebo–ritonavir in 100 adults with long COVID across the USA, using a fully decentralised design. The primary outcome—change in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score from baseline to day 28—showed no significant difference between groups (adjusted mean difference –0.55, 95% CI –2.32 to 1.21, p=0.54), well below the 5-point threshold considered clinically meaningful. No deaths or serious adverse events occurred, though dysgeusia was markedly more common with nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (48% vs 6%), partially compromising blinding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA LIMITATION: All quantitative outcome tables (Tables 1-6) were only available as supplementary files (Table1to6.docx) not included in the preprint text. The figure (Fig. 1) showing categorical recovery period distributions for each symptom across the 4 recovery categories is also only in graphical form with no extractable numeric values. As a result, per-arm recovery proportions (good/moderate/slow/resistance) for each symptom domain cannot be extracted. Only prevalence counts at enrollment and qualitative descriptions of recovery ordering are available from the text. The paper is observational, single-arm, no control group. Main findings are: (1) pulmonary symptoms had best recovery with inhaled budesonide; (2) hair loss worst recovery; (3) brain fog and smell disorder second-worst; (4) smoking, COVID-19 severity, number of symptoms, and delay to treatment all significantly associated with slower recovery. No effect sizes, ORs, HRs, or quantitative between-group statistics reported in text — only chi-square significance statements. This paper provides very limited extractable quantitative data for meta-analysis.

This is an observational prospective cohort study (POSTCOV registry) with embedded case-control substudy, NOT an RCT or interventional trial. The 'intervention' is COVID-19 vaccination (monovalent, self-selected). Arm 0 used for longitudinal within-group analyses (n=131 mixed vaccination status at second sampling). Many outcomes (EBV VCA IgG quantitative titer, HSV IgG/IgM, VZV IgG/IgM, EBV EBNA IgG) have data in Table 4 but no significant between-group p-values reported; these are partially captured. Quantitative figure data (EBV IgG vs time correlation; parvovirus-B19 IgM vs time correlation) not extractable from text alone. Substudy comparing long-COVID vs healthy controls uses n=105 per group (first 105 consecutive long-COVID patients age- and sex-matched to biobank controls). IQR for parvovirus-B19 IgM in vaccinated group appears inverted in source (median 0, IQR 0.05-0.41) which may indicate the median is between the IQR bounds — extracted verbatim. Promise score context: this is a vaccine (non-pharmaceutical intervention) observational study with moderate effect sizes on biomarkers and symptom frequency; design is seriously confounded by self-selection.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is primarily a cross-sectional biomarker study with observational comparison of vaccination groups, not a treatment trial with randomized allocation. Quantitative cytokine values (means, SDs, SEs) for IL-1β, IL-18, TNF, IL-6 per vaccination group are presented only in figures (Fig. 3a, Fig. 4a) without tabulated numeric values — set as not_reported. Arm definitions are complex: the 'treatment' groups are post-infection vaccination (1x or 2x) vs unvaccinated PCC controls. The study also includes resolved PCC and no PCC groups as comparators but the main intervention comparison is within the ongoing PCC group. The n=13 for GI symptom subgroup refers to ongoing PCC patients with GI symptoms regardless of vaccination status. The ranges reported for IL-1β and IL-18 in the GI subgroup analysis appear to represent full observed ranges, not IQR, so they are stored in iqr_low/iqr_high fields as approximations. The symptom frequency data (Fig. 5) with percentages per vaccination group is presented only in a figure without tabulated values. No formal statistical test results (p-values) for the primary IL-1β/IL-18 comparisons between vaccination groups are reported as exact values in text — results described as significant only in figure panels using ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc. Multiple testing across 25 cytokines without correction is a notable limitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm prospective observational cohort study — all 327 patients received SPA rehabilitation without a control group. Primary reported outcomes are post-SPA improvement scores on a 0-3 FSS scale, subgrouped by obesity, chronic respiratory disease, and DLCO status. Multivariate logistic regression results for predictors of fatigue/dyspnea and rehabilitation outcomes were reported as 'data not shown' with only select OR values disclosed in text. Barthel Index improvement values reported only for dyspnea-improved vs. not-improved subgroups (13.2±9.9 vs. 5.9±6.7, p=0.02) — not for overall cohort pre/post. Table 2 (dyspneic vs. non-dyspneic) and Table 3 (normal vs. reduced DLCO) and Table 4 (fatigue vs. no fatigue) contain extensive comparative data reported as subgroup cross-sectional comparisons at baseline, not pre-post treatment comparisons. DLCO data available only in ~one-third of patients (n=96). The mMRC overall mean 1.5±1.1 is reported in text but not in tables. Some column headers in Table 5 use 'Sì' (Italian for 'Yes') for chronic respiratory conditions presence. No long-term follow-up data available. Pre-post within-group change data not quantitatively reported for mMRC, Borg, or Barthel Index at the overall cohort level — only improvement scale scores (FSS) and Barthel Index change in dyspnea-improved subgroup.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily a metagenomics/microbiome study of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) in COVID-19 patients, not a clinical outcomes trial of long COVID symptoms. The probiotic intervention (SIM01) is tested for its effect on gut resistome, not on long COVID symptom resolution. All quantitative outcomes are metagenomic measures (ARG counts, abundances); no per-arm means or SDs are reported in text — all data appear only in figures (box plots, scatter plots). PACS is reported as a binary outcome (prevalence %). The study includes: (1) longitudinal cohort of 90 COVID-19 patients (66 antibiotic-naive, 24 antibiotic-experienced) + 66 matched non-COVID-19 controls; (2) open-label pilot of SIM01 during acute infection (n=22 SIM01 + n=10 controls); (3) open-label pilot of SIM01 after viral clearance (n=20). Detailed demographics are in supplementary tables (not in main text). P-values reported mostly as ranges (p<0.001, p<0.01) or exact values (e.g., p=2.85e-05). Control group for acute probiotic study (n=10) was from independent infectious disease team. Antibiotic-experienced group used: amoxicillin clavulanate (n=12) or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline (n=12).

The abstract states GHQ-12 decreased from 14.5 to 9 at follow-up (combined groups), consistent with Table 6 combined column. The abstract also states average Borg reduction of 3.5 points, but per-arm data shows FZYF reduction of 3 and FZAS reduction of 4. The note in Table 7 states assessments used GHQ-12 but the abstract/methods describes PHQ-9 for depression and mMRC for dyspnea inconsistently. Given the fabricated data concern, this paper should be flagged for exclusion from meta-analysis pending verification.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm retrospective cohort; no control group. Outcomes are ordinal Likert severity (none/mild/moderate/severe), so events/total represent 'any severity present' (mild+moderate+severe combined). Exact baseline prevalence counts for Table 2 outcomes derived from 'None' column: events_at_baseline = 79 minus n_reporting_none. Exact end-of-treatment prevalence similarly derived. Some outcome prevalences at end of treatment calculated from Table 2 'None' column (e.g., fatigue end: 79-42=37, but paper states 36(45%) — using verbatim 36 where stated, otherwise calculated). Additional outcomes from Table 2 not extracted as separate outcome objects (due to size): general pain (p<0.001), joint pain (p=0.006), symptoms of PTSD (p=0.004), hair loss (p=0.006), diarrhea (p=0.046), fever episodes (p=0.034), tinnitus/paralysis/sensory disturbance/skin rash/earache/voice loss/emerging metabolic diseases/thromboembolism — all non-significant (n.s.). subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Higher PS (fatigue) at baseline was significantly positively correlated with worse delta QIDS (%) in all three MANCOVA models (Model 1: partial regression coefficient 0.50, 95%CI 0.01-0.98, p=0.04; Model 2: 0.53, 95%CI 0.04-1.02, p=0.04; Model 3: similar significant result). sensitivity_analyses.description: MANCOVA Model 1: PS, QIDS, PHQ9, GAD7 initial scores + Long-COVID/Post-Vaccine dummy as independent variables for delta QIDS (%)
MANCOVA Model 2: Added propensity score to Model 1 to handle Long-COVID/Post-Vaccine confounders as single variable

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preprint (medRxiv, not peer reviewed). The study has two 'arms' (Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine) but both receive TMS with no control group — it is fundamentally a before-after single-arm design analyzed by subgroup. Treatment duration in days is reported as median IQR (Long-COVID: 12 days IQR 7.75-19.5; Post-Vaccine: 5.5 days IQR 3.75-22.75) but number of sessions was fixed at 10. Correlation matrices (Figure 2) and MANCOVA coefficients (Figure 3) are partially reported in table form in the text but full coefficient tables for Model 3 were not provided with numeric CIs. The delta X (%) formula means lower values = better improvement (score after/score before × 100), so for improvement rate outcomes higher_is_better=false. PS data was missing for 7 Long-COVID and 2 Post-Vaccine patients at baseline (N=39 and N=12 respectively); for delta PS calculation further exclusions reduce to N=34 and N=11. No adverse events were formally reported. MANCOVA partial regression coefficients for PS predicting delta QIDS are extracted in sensitivity_analyses section.

Incremental QALY and cost data by pathway appear only in figures (Figures 2 and 3 forest plots) with only the absolute values in Table 4; incremental effects not numerically extractable from the text except for the overall ICER. summary: This retrospective cross-sectional study examined bronchodilator responsiveness in 134 post-COVID patients presenting with exertional dyspnea to an inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation clinic in Germany. Following inhalation of 200 mcg Salbutamol, the post-COVID cohort (n=94 for primary analysis) showed a mean FEV1 increase of 181.5 mL (SD 186.6), significantly greater than a historical Swedish reference population (118 mL, p<0.0001) and an internal healthy control group (n=19; mean delta-FEV1 107.9 mL). Approximately 29% showed >200 mL FEV1 response and 12% met full significant bronchodilator criteria, with no significant difference by sex, age, BMI, or prior hospitalization, suggesting post-viral airway hyperresponsiveness may occur in a substantial minority of long COVID patients regardless of acute disease severity.

summary: This single-arm prospective observational feasibility pilot study examined individualized Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) delivered via telehealth to 61 patients with COVID-19 symptoms or sequelae (including 10 'long haulers') at a Seattle EAM school clinic beginning in 2020. summary: This retrospective single-arm before-after study evaluated oral prednisolone (10mg twice daily) plus zinc gluconate (10mg three times daily) for 2-4 months in 71 long COVID patients with persistent olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction (≥1 month) following Omicron-variant infection in Taiwan. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No control group — improvements cannot be distinguished from natural recovery. Approximately 50% of enrolled patients did not return for the second objective testing visit (18/34 returned in smell+taste group, 21/36 in smell-only group), creating serious selection/attrition bias. The UPSIT-TC score range for smell-only group at second visit (mean 23.81, SD 8.10) reuses the same SD value as baseline — this may be a paper reporting issue. Follow-up duration is approximate: treatment was 2-4 months and phone follow-up mean was ~10.35-10.42 months from first visit; total duration calculated as ~45 weeks. Baseline UPSIT-TC scores for the smell+taste group (n=34, mean 23.50, SD 7.02) and WETT scores (n=34, mean 25.82, SD 6.96) are for the full enrolled group, while second-visit scores (n=18) are for those who returned. The paper authors note no sample size calculation was performed.

summary: This uncontrolled pilot study tested the feasibility of patient-reported outcome measures (PSS-10, GAD-2, SSS, MYMOP) among 14 Long COVID patients who completed an 8-week virtual Integrative Medical Group Visit (IMGV) program called Nourish to Flourish at a university post-COVID clinic. Statistically significant pre-post improvements were observed in perceived stress (PSS-10 decreased 3.43 points, p=0.007) and the MYMOP primary symptom score (decreased 1.25 points, p=0.004), while GAD-2 showed a non-significant trend (decreased 1.43 points, p=0.091); Fibromyalgia SSS subscales showed no change. The authors conclude that PSS-10, GAD-2, and MYMOP are feasible and potentially useful PROMs for future efficacy trials of IMGV in Long COVID, but the absence of a control group and 48% dropout rate preclude causal inference.

summary: This prospective multicenter cohort study (PoCoRe, N=1,028) assessed outcomes of multimodal inpatient post-COVID rehabilitation across 6 German centers, comparing depressed (PHQ-2 positive, n=734) versus nondepressed (n=294) patients. summary: This single-center retrospective study of 65 US military veterans discharged from a Chicago VA hospital with new domiciliary supplemental oxygen following COVID-19 hospitalisation found that 52% had oxygen therapy discontinued within 8 weeks, yet 46% developed PASC persisting beyond 8 weeks. The majority of patients did not undergo formal 6-minute walk test reassessment of ongoing oxygen requirements (only 6% within 8 weeks, 23% thereafter). There was no comparison group, so it is not possible to determine whether domiciliary oxygen therapy influenced PASC development, and the findings are descriptive only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm retrospective descriptive study with no comparator group and no statistical testing reported. There are no between-group effects or within-group change statistics. Table 2 has some parsing ambiguity due to merged cells; the PASC row data was partially unclear (noted as 'nn (%%)' for aggregate at 8 weeks), but individual timepoint values are reconstructed from text. The study does not report PASC symptom breakdown, oxygen flow rate changes over time, or formal statistical analyses. Median time to death 130 days noted in Table 3 footnote. Race/ethnicity data for the overall cohort: 69% African American, 25% Caucasian, 6% other.

summary: This prospective cohort study of 730 severe COVID-19 survivors evaluated a multidisciplinary post-COVID programme (pulmonary rehabilitation, nutrition, psychology, and specialist medical care) against usual follow-up without programme attendance over 18 months. Programme attendants showed significantly greater improvement in SF-12 physical and mental component scores (adjusted differences of +2.64 and +2.18 points per assessment, respectively; both p≤0.002) and faster resolution of fatigue, respiratory, neuropsychiatric, musculoskeletal, and gastrointestinal symptom clusters (adjusted HRs 0.62–0.81 for symptom persistence, all statistically significant except cardiovascular). However, the non-randomised self-selected design introduces substantial confounding by indication, limiting causal inference.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study with prospective follow-up surveyed 200 post-COVID patients attending a German university hospital post-COVID center between December 2022 and July 2023, describing utilization frequencies and patient-reported effectiveness of over 15 symptomatic treatment modalities. At follow-up (mean 6.3 months post-baseline, n=165), beta-blockers had the highest proportion of users reporting strong-to-very-strong symptom improvement (31.6%), followed by plasmapheresis (33.3% of 15 users), antibiotics (29.6%), and glucocorticoids (24.4%), while psychotherapeutic interventions yielded lower rates (3.6-11.0%). The study had no control group, no randomization, and no validated outcome instruments, precluding causal inference about any treatment's effectiveness.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a descriptive observational study with no comparison group and no validated continuous outcome measures — all effectiveness data are proportions of therapy users reporting 'strong' or 'very strong' improvement on a non-validated 4-point ordinal scale. The denominators for follow-up effectiveness outcomes (Table 5) do not always match baseline utilization rates (some patients may have started or discontinued therapies between baseline and follow-up); the paper notes follow-up n=165. Follow-up duration calculated as approximately 6.3 months (SD=2.2) after baseline presentation = ~27 weeks. Figure 2 shows distribution of all improvement levels per therapy but only Table 5 numerical data were extractable. The paper states 15% of follow-up users reported plasmapheresis (n=15 of 165), while baseline records showed only 3.5% (n=7) underwent plasma exchange — discrepancy likely because some patients received plasmapheresis after baseline presentation. No p-values reported for any outcome. No adverse event data reported.

summary: This single-arm, open-label pilot observational study evaluated MYP plus — an herbal formulation of Astragali Radix, Salviae Radix, and Aquilariae Lignum — in 50 South Korean long COVID patients with severe fatigue and/or brain fog over 4 weeks. All primary and secondary clinical outcomes significantly improved (p<0.01), including a 46% reduction in mKCFQ11 fatigue score, 52% reduction in brain fog VAS, and 59% improvement in SF-12 quality of life. However, the absence of a placebo control group means these improvements cannot be causally attributed to the intervention and may reflect natural recovery or placebo effects.

summary: This single-arm retrospective before-after study evaluated pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) in 55 PASC patients (mean age 57.9 years, 63% previously hospitalized for COVID-19) at a US tertiary center. All 8 pre-specified functional and psychological outcomes improved significantly after PR: 6-minute walk distance increased by ~405 m, chair rise repetitions by 4.3, gait speed by 0.27 m/s, TUG time decreased by 3.3 seconds, mMRC by 1.2 points, SOBQ by 28.8 points, HADS by 3.6 points, and CAT by 9.6 points (all p<0.0001); only PHQ-9 did not improve significantly (p=0.74). Regression analyses identified hypertension, diabetes, ILD, prior outpatient COVID management, and specific inpatient drug therapies as factors associated with attenuated PR response, though the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Preprint (not peer-reviewed). Single-arm pre-post design with no control group; all between-group comparisons are subgroup regression analyses within the treated cohort, not RCT arms. The paper_id used is the preprint DOI. Rehabilitation program duration not reported in paper. The T-value reported for PHQ-9 was 'S-value of 4' (Wilcoxon signed-rank test), not a parametric T; p=0.7402. Balance test is mentioned in methods but no pre/post values reported for it. N analyzed per outcome not individually specified; assumed n=55 for all based on overall cohort size. Change means calculated as post minus pre.

summary: This ambispective longitudinal cohort study in China enrolled 104 outpatients with post-COVID-19 chronic cough (>8 weeks) during the Omicron wave, comparing inhaled budesonide/formoterol (ICS, n=51) to conventional symptomatic treatment alone (NICS, n=53) over 60 days. Both groups showed significant improvements in cough (CET) and dyspnea (mMRC) scores, with no statistically significant between-group differences at either 30 or 60 days. However, ICS treatment was associated with significantly greater improvements in spirometric parameters (FEV1%, FEV1/FVC, MMEF%, MVV%) and FeNO50 at 60 days, indicating that ICS improves lung function but not symptom burden compared to usual care in this population.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Between-group effect values (actual differences) for CET, mMRC, and pulmonary function outcomes are not reported — only p-values for group comparisons are given. Lung function secondary outcome n varies (35 ICS / 32 NICS for spirometry; 34 ICS / 31 NICS for FeNO/CaNO; 30/30 for BPT) because only patients attending face-to-face day 60 visits were tested. The p=0.000 for MMEF% between-group change is reported as '0.000' in the paper (likely p<0.0005). BPT change column reports n converting from positive to negative (12/29=41.4% ICS; 6/26=23.1% NICS). Some pulmonary function data may also appear in figures (Fig 3) but Table 3 contains the key quantitative values. Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 (asthma subgroup) were not provided in the main text.

summary: This retrospective single-center cohort study assessed the effectiveness of pacing strategies in 86 patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome (WHO definition, >12 weeks symptoms) at Angers University Hospital, France, followed for a median of 10 months. All patients were advised to implement energy-envelope pacing; adherence was measured by the Engagement in Pacing Subscale (EPS). Recovery (return to work with full remission) occurred in 33.7% and improvement in 23.3% of patients; on multivariable logistic regression, EPS score was the only independent predictor of recovery (adjusted OR 40.43, 95% CI 6.22–262.6, p<0.001), and patients with high EPS adherence had substantially higher recovery (60%) and improvement (33.3%) rates than those with moderate (4.3%/17.4%) or low (5.5%/5.5%) adherence.

summary: This prospective observational cohort study of 145 long COVID patients (36% female, 64% male) undergoing ~4-week inpatient multimodal exercise-based rehabilitation in Germany found significant pre-post improvements in cardiopulmonary exercise capacity (VO2peak +1.1±2.9 ml/min/kg, p<0.001; peak workload +14.2±18.9W, p<0.001) and pulmonary function, with no control group. Women presented with higher relative baseline exercise capacity but greater fatigue and lower wellbeing; they showed significantly greater improvement in submaximal workload at VT1 (time×group interaction p=0.026) and FEV1/VC (p=0.027) compared to men, suggesting potential sex-specific benefits of intensified respiratory muscle training in long COVID rehabilitation.

summary: This prospective longitudinal observational study followed 114 post-COVID patients (predominantly healthcare workers with occupationally acquired SARS-CoV-2) through multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation and for 12 months afterward, assessing work ability and return to work (RTW). At 12 months post-rehabilitation, only 48.6% had returned to work and median WAI total score (21.0) indicated poor work ability, which had significantly worsened from baseline (median 24.5; p<0.001, r=0.484). Fatigue severity (FIS total) was the strongest predictor of both RTW (OR per unit=0.969, p<0.001) and perceived work ability, with physical capacity (6MWD) and subjective health perception (SPSH) also independently predicting WAI total, suggesting that targeted fatigue management and physical rehabilitation are critical unmet needs in post-COVID occupational reintegration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm observational study with no control group; all within_group_change data reflect T1-to-T4 change without a comparator. Predictor variables (FIS, 6MWD, SPSH, HADS-D, DSST1, DSST2, PIA, MVPA) are reported as regression coefficients only at T4 — individual means/SDs at T4 are stated to be in Supplementary Material Table A5, which was not available in the provided text. WAI dimensions 2, 5, 7 showed no significant change (p=0.110, 0.315, 1.000 respectively) and are not separately extracted as outcome objects to limit size; their T1/T4 medians and IQRs are in Table 2. Logistic regression for RTW: FIS total B=-0.031, SE=0.009, OR=0.969 (95%CI 0.953-0.986), p<0.001, Nagelkerke R2=0.247. Multiple linear regression for WAI total: FIS beta=-0.399, 6MWD beta=0.196, SPSH beta=0.237, adjusted R2=0.473. Mediation analyses reported with path coefficients (beta) and bootstrap CIs. RTW denominator: text states 54 (47%) returned to work and 57 (50%) did not, totaling 111 with 6 in reintegration — percentages in Table 1 use n=114 as denominator including those in reintegration.

summary: This retrospective proof-of-concept study examined the effects of oral lactoferrin, a Multi-Element Product (MEP; containing magnesium, quercetin, curcumin, resveratrol, vitamin E, zinc, folic acid, selenium, and cholecalciferol), or their combination in 294 children diagnosed with long COVID at 3 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection, followed in a single tertiary clinic in Rome. Using logistic regression (reference: lactoferrin alone, OR 7.6, 95% CI 5.1–11.4), MEP alone (OR 5.7, 95% CI 3.8–8.5) and MEP+lactoferrin (OR 5.06, 95% CI 3.3–7.6) were associated with lower odds of persistent long COVID at 6 months — suggesting a potential benefit compared to lactoferrin monotherapy — though no significant associations were found when treatment was initiated at 6 months or later. The study is severely limited by the absence of an untreated control group, non-randomized allocation, and inability to separate treatment effects from spontaneous recovery.

summary: This multicenter single-arm observational study in Hong Kong evaluated individualized Chinese Medicine (herbal prescriptions based on CM syndrome differentiation) for 3-6 months in 150 post-COVID-19 patients discharged from public hospitals, with a 3-month no-treatment follow-up. summary: This prospective observational cohort study assessed sex differences in response to six weeks of outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (OPR) among 263 post-Covid syndrome patients (54.4% female) in Vienna, Austria. All participants improved significantly across all outcomes (6MWD, PCFS, MIP, FEV1, DLCO, dyspnea; all p<0.0001), but women — despite less severe acute Covid-19 — retained greater symptom burden at discharge, with only 19.4% of women vs. 38.5% of men achieving full functional remission (PCFS=0). Women showed significantly worse inspiratory muscle strength, FEV1, dyspnea scores, and functional status than men both before and after rehabilitation, indicating that current OPR protocols do not fully bridge the sex gap in post-Covid recovery.

summary: This prospective observational cohort study compared CPET-derived cardiorespiratory fitness in 57 post-COVID-19 endurance athletes with exercise intolerance to 34 COVID-unaffected matched endurance athlete controls in South Africa, with both groups reassessed after 8 weeks of self-directed endurance training. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is in Russian with English abstract and bilingual tables. summary: This single-center retrospective study from China compared 72 long COVID patients with cardiac injury who received potassium and magnesium supplementation plus lifestyle advice against 72 controls receiving lifestyle advice only, assessed over 14 days. summary: This non-randomized quasi-experimental study examined the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin 10mg added to metformin) versus continued metformin/sulfonylurea therapy on cardiovascular biomarkers (ST2 peptide and homocysteine) in 43 type 2 diabetes patients followed for 9 months after COVID-19 recovery, compared to 32 non-diabetic COVID-19 controls. Both T2DM groups showed significant reductions in homocysteine to normal levels, while ST2 decreased significantly in the SGLT2i group (5.4 to 4.8 ng/mL, p<0.05) but increased in the standard therapy group (4.9 to 5.7 ng/mL, p<0.05), suggesting a cardioprotective effect of SGLT2i in the post-COVID period. However, the study has serious methodological limitations including non-randomized retrospective group allocation with known confounding by indication, as SGLT2i was preferentially prescribed to higher-severity heart failure patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is primarily in Ukrainian with English abstract. The table for group 2 homocysteine post-treatment has Q1=20.4 which appears to be a data entry error in the original paper (Q1 > Q3 at 10.8, and Q1 > median at 10.1); extracted verbatim as reported. Group 3 (non-diabetic control) homocysteine data only reported at baseline as mean±SD (9.9±3.1 µmol/L) without full table data; folic acid data for group 3 not reported. summary: This prospective non-randomized study conducted in Baghdad, Iraq enrolled 500 COVID-19 patients and identified 183 (36.6%) with severe headache, who were assigned to one of three groups: Group A (ibuprofen + acetaminophen, n=91), Group B (ibuprofen + acetaminophen + phenytoin 100-300 mg/day, n=92), and a third group (Group C, n=92, not clearly described in methods). At the 6-month follow-up, Group C showed the lowest rates of persistent headache requiring treatment (2.16% at 24 weeks vs 21.7% for Group A and 13.32% for Group B), and Group B showed lower need for ongoing treatment than Group A at 24 weeks. No formal statistical testing was reported, no randomization was performed, and Group C's identity is unclear, severely limiting interpretability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Multiple serious data quality issues: (1) A third arm 'Group C' (n=92) appears in all outcome tables but is not described in the Methods section — its identity and treatment are unknown. (2) Group A enrolled 91 patients (Table 2) but only 46 appear in outcome tables (Tables 3-5); Group B enrolled 92 but only 45 appear in outcome tables — the reason for this ~50% attrition is never explained. (3) No statistical tests, p-values, or effect sizes are reported anywhere. (4) Mean age is referenced in Table 1 caption ('The mean age of the patients was years') but the actual value is missing from the text — appears to be a typographic omission. (5) The abstract states '63% women' but the body text states '46.6% female' — these are contradictory; the body text table (n=233/500=46.6% female) is used here. (6) Outcome data presented only as frequency distributions across pain scale scores, not as summary means/SDs — no poolable continuous summary statistics are available. (7) This study covers COVID-19 acute headache with post-recovery follow-up; its relevance to long COVID is marginal — headache persistence post-infection is documented but the study was not designed as a long COVID intervention trial.

summary: This prospective observational cohort study followed 61 post-acute COVID-19 patients (65.6% severe disease by WHO-CPS) through a multidisciplinary inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation programme of ~3.2 months duration at a single Israeli medical center. All functional outcomes improved significantly from admission to discharge, including total FIM (103.7 to 118.7, p<0.001), 6MWT (195 to 336 m), hand grip strength, and gait speed, with 88% of patients weaning off supplemental oxygen. Critically, despite severe patients having significantly lower functional status at admission, there was no significant correlation between disease severity and functional outcomes at discharge, suggesting that even severely ill COVID-19 survivors can achieve comparable functional independence with appropriate rehabilitation.

summary: This retrospective observational study examined 779 long COVID patients who underwent a 3-week inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation programme in Austria, comparing those who also received additional respiratory muscle training (RMT, n=352) versus standard rehabilitation alone (non-RMT, n=427). Across the total cohort, all outcomes improved significantly: 6MWD increased by 100.8 m (Cohen's d=0.81), EQ-VAS by 17.65 points (Cohen's d=1.16), EQ-5D-5L index by 0.11, and PHQ-4 decreased by 0.55 (all p<0.001). The RMT group, who had worse baseline respiratory muscle strength, showed significantly greater improvements in 6MWD and EQ-5D-5L index scores compared to the non-RMT group (interaction p<0.001 and p<0.05, respectively), though no significant between-group difference was found for EQ-VAS or PHQ-4.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm pre/post means and SDs for 6MWD and EQ-5D-5L index are not reported separately by arm in tables; only total-group means/SDs appear in Table III, with between-group data in Table IV (GLMM fixed effects with SE). All per-arm arm_results for 6MWD are set to null with arm_id=0 used for total-group values as a workaround. The GLMM interaction estimate for 6MWD (20.96m, SE 5.04) represents the additional improvement in the RMT group over non-RMT. Cohen's d values are reported in Table III for completeness (6MWD: 0.81; EQ-5D-5L index: 0.75; EQ-VAS: 1.16; PHQ-4: -0.21). Heart rate context: baseline value appears to be resting heart rate before 6MWT and the post-PR value is peak heart rate after 6MWT (not directly comparable as a pre-post rehabilitation metric in the traditional sense — the increase reflects exercise capacity). subgroup_analyses.results_summary: IR patients (mild course) had medium to large effect sizes during rehabilitation; FUR patients (severe course) had smaller effects, contrary to one previous study. FUR patients had greater improvements in lung function and perceived rehabilitation success.

IR patients had more neurocognitive symptoms at baseline that improved over time; FUR patients showed an increase in neurocognitive symptoms during follow-up (e.g., word-finding difficulties: 6.6% at baseline vs. 27.4% at 12 months, p<0.01).

summary: This multicenter prospective observational study compared 12-month outcomes between 253 long COVID patients undergoing standard inpatient rehabilitation (IR; predominantly mild initial COVID-19, mostly female) and 91 patients undergoing follow-up rehabilitation after hospitalization (FUR; predominantly severe COVID-19, mostly male) across four German pulmonary rehabilitation facilities. Both groups showed statistically significant improvements in fatigue, quality of life, participation restrictions, and work ability during the 27-day rehabilitation program (medium to large effect sizes), with effects largely maintained at 12 months. Return to work rates were high in both groups (~87-89%) at 12 months, but FUR patients returned to work a median of 4.5 weeks later than IR patients (median 5.5 vs. 1 week, p<0.01), and FUR patients showed a concerning increase in neurocognitive symptoms during follow-up, suggesting that post-hospitalization long COVID patients require ongoing monitoring beyond rehabilitation discharge.

summary: This prospective cohort study examined psychocognitive status in 134 Russian patients with controlled arterial hypertension, comparing 73 with post-COVID syndrome (PCS) to 61 without COVID-19 history. PCS patients showed significantly higher rates of depressive syndrome (41% vs. 12%, p<0.001) and more severe depression on HADS. Among PCS patients with depression, those who self-selected to take agomelatine 25 mg/day for 8 weeks (n=22) had significantly lower rates of psychocognitive impairment on SPMSQ compared to those who refused treatment (n=16): 32% vs. 94% any impairment (p=0.001), with no moderate impairment in the agomelatine group vs. 38% in the untreated group (p=0.004); however, treatment assignment was not randomized.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. The study uses a 3-group structure but the agomelatine comparison (arms 1 vs 2) is from a quasi-experimental self-selected subgroup within PCS patients only. The no-COVID group (arm 3, n=61) and full PCS group (Group 2, n=73) are used for depression/anxiety comparisons; the SPMSQ agomelatine comparison uses only Subgroups 2A (n=22) and 2B (n=16). Group 2 total n=73 includes subgroups 2A+2B (n=38) plus PCS patients without depression (n=35 estimated). Arm_id=4 used in outcomes 2-4 and 8 refers to the full PCS Group 2 (n=73) for cross-sectional depression/anxiety comparisons vs. Group 1 (arm_id=3). The paper reports no per-arm means/SDs for HADS subscale scores in the agomelatine subgroups; SPMSQ data are proportions only. No baseline SPMSQ data reported. Anxiety outcome 8: events calculated as sum of subclinical (n=21, 30%) + clinical (n=10, 15%) for Group 2 = 31/73 (42%), and Group 1: 18+5=23/61 (38%); percent and CI values extracted from text for subclinical and clinical categories separately. The paper does not clearly state whether SPMSQ was assessed at baseline or only post-treatment; it appears to be assessed at the end of the 8-week treatment period. Mild SPMSQ impairment in agomelatine group: paper states all 32% had mild impairment, so events=7 (32% of 22); figure 3 referenced but values extracted from text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a community service program report (pengabdian masyarakat), not a formal clinical trial. There is no control group, no pre/post quantitative scores (only symptom prevalence counts at baseline), and no statistical testing. The primary outcome (90% improvement) is based on a single binary self-report question in a telephone follow-up, with high risk of social desirability bias. Age is reported only as grouped percentages (18-39y: 65%, 40-64y: 27%, ≥65y: 2%), not as mean/SD — no continuous age data available. summary: This non-randomized prospective cohort study compared surgical correction of isolated horizontal venous reflux (EVLO, subfascial ligation, or foam sclerotherapy of perforant veins) versus conservative treatment (compression, wound dressings, phlebotonic drugs) in 59 post-COVID-19 patients with new-onset complicated chronic venous insufficiency (CEAP C3/C4/C6). At 6 months, the surgical group (n=39) showed significantly greater reductions in VCSS edema, pain, pigmentation, and inflammation scores compared to the conservative group (n=20), and achieved complete trophic ulcer healing (100% vs. 84% area healed). However, the study is limited by self-selected group assignment, no statistical adjustment for confounders, and baseline CEAP severity imbalance favoring the surgical group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English abstract and tables. The p-values reported in tables appear as 'p(00,2)' etc., which likely encode values like p<0.02, p<0.03, p<0.04, p<0.05, p<0.06 — these are p-value thresholds, not exact values (set p_value_exact=false throughout). The exact p-value encoding convention is ambiguous (possibly '00,2' means 0.002 in Russian decimal notation, or could mean <0.02). Per-arm N for the CEAP subgroups: Group I C3=29, C4=6, C6=4 (sum=39); Group II C3=11, C4=5, C6=4 (sum=20). Note that the within-group p-values in Table 4 for pain (Group II, C4) appear as '00,2' which was assigned 0.002, same as Group I — these may differ; original ambiguity noted. Microcirculatory Doppler findings are described qualitatively only (depletion of spectral pattern / parietal stasis) with no quantitative values extractable. The study enrolled patients from April 2020 to November 2023 (3.5 years); it is not a long COVID trial per standard definition but rather a post-COVID vascular complication study.

summary: This was a 15-day uncontrolled pilot observational study in 20 post-COVID patients with persistent fatigue who self-selected to take a daily oral supplement containing hydroxytyrosol, acetyl-L-carnitine, vitamins C, D, B6, B12, thiamine, and folic acid, compared descriptively to 20 healthy non-COVID controls who took no supplement. Using the AD ACL questionnaire, group-summed energy scores increased 123% in supplement users versus 10% in non-users, and tiredness scores decreased 51% versus 21%; no statistical tests were performed. The study provides no reliable evidence of efficacy due to the absence of randomization, blinding, statistical analysis, or an appropriate placebo control group, but the authors propose it as a basis for a future randomized trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUE: Table I reports group-summed item scores across all 20 participants (e.g., Energy total=155 at baseline = sum of all 20 respondents' scores on 5 items), NOT per-person means or SDs. Individual-level means and SDs are not reported anywhere in the paper, making it impossible to compute standard effect sizes or conduct meta-analysis. No p-values, CIs, or any inferential statistics are reported for any outcome. The comparison group (non-users) had no COVID history and no placebo — fundamentally different from the treatment group. AE percentages are reported for the supplement arm only (e.g., stomachache 25%), which translates to approximately 5 of 20 participants, but exact Ns are not stated. Percentage changes (+123%, -51%, -48%, +40% for supplement users; +10%, -21%, -22%, +6% for non-users) are reported in Table I but are derived from group-summed scores, not per-person means. The 'mean' fields in arm_results for outcome_id 2-5 contain the group sums as reported in the table, not per-person means — this should be interpreted accordingly.
