summary: This two-center prospective cohort study from Russia assessed respiratory outcomes and treatment of broncho-obstructive syndrome (BOS) in 10,456 post-COVID-19 patients. In the treatment comparison (n=7,497 with BOS), extra-fine beclomethasone dipropionate/formoterol (EMD BDP/FORM) in MART mode was superior to nebulized budesonide plus salbutamol at 24 weeks, with significantly better ACQ-5 scores and fewer as-needed inhaler uses (p<0.05), particularly in patients with eosinophils ≥150 cells/mcL. In a separate cohort of 89 patients with moderate-to-severe COVID-19, DLCO remained impaired in 94% at 6 months and 85% at 12 months, with severe disease, ICU admission, and high-flow oxygen therapy identified as risk factors for persistent DLCO reduction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper presents TWO distinct study populations: (1) Center 1 (n=10,456) for BOS treatment comparison between EMD BDP/FORM (n=3,245) and nebulized budesonide+salbutamol (n=4,252) — note these are both within the 7,497 BOS subgroup, and further split into 4 subgroups by eosinophil level and COVID severity; (2) Center 2 UNIF (n=89) for longitudinal DLCO/pulmonary function follow-up at 6 and 12 months comparing moderate (n=49) vs severe (n=40) COVID-19. Outcomes 1-4 pertain to Center 1 treatment groups; outcomes 5-7 pertain to Center 2 observational groups. The arm_ids 3 and 4 are used for Center 2 moderate and severe COVID-19 groups respectively, as this is a distinct sub-study. Table 1 subgroups: 1-a (n=1780, eos<150, mild COVID, arm 1), 1-b (n=1465, eos≥150, moderate/severe COVID, arm 1), 2-a (n=2050, eos<150, mild COVID, arm 2), 2-b (n=2202, eos≥150, moderate/severe COVID, arm 2). Per-arm means in Table 2 are reported as M±m (mean±SE, not SD) per the statistical methods section. The total arm 1 n=3,245 and arm 2 n=4,252 — these include all subgroups; the treatment outcomes are reported for n=974 newly diagnosed asthma patients specifically at treatment period 3 (weeks 8-24). These results should be interpreted cautiously given non-random group allocation and lack of statistical adjustment for baseline differences.

summary: This prospective 4-arm cohort study (n=113) conducted in Russia compared a respiratory rehabilitation program including aquatic training (main group, n=25) versus no rehabilitation (n=25), Eastern medicine methods (n=29), or balneotherapy/physiotherapy (n=34) in post-COVID syndrome patients over 6 months of follow-up via structured telephone interview. The respiratory rehabilitation program showed the largest reduction in relative risk of hospitalization (85.7% vs no rehabilitation, 66.0% vs balneotherapy, 42.0% vs Eastern medicine), suggesting sustained preventive benefits over 6 months post-treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English abstract. No continuous/scale outcome data reported — study focuses exclusively on healthcare utilization (binary) endpoints at a single 6-month follow-up timepoint. No baseline per-arm demographics reported (only overall sample: mean age 58.4, 73.45% female, median age Q1-Q3 48-70). Groups were stated to be comparable on sex, age, and rehabilitation routing scale but no per-arm values provided. Chi-square statistics for hospitalization comparisons reported as chi2=5.357 p=0.021 (arm1 vs arm2), chi2=0.125 p=0.724 (arm1 vs arm3), chi2=0.856 p=0.355 (arm1 vs arm4). Table note indicates chi2 was not applicable for some cells (zero events), which limits statistical interpretation of pulmonologist and EMS outcomes. The study was nested within a larger RCT but uses observational cohort design for this sub-study. Overall time since infection at enrollment was 6.5±2.5 months (mean±SD). 7 patients (5.83%) withdrew; arm-level attribution not reported.

summary: This retrospective cohort study from a single clinic in South Korea evaluated a multi-drug 'Cocktail' treatment (Covi Wonder, comprising up to 17 medications including ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, and others) versus no treatment in 47 long COVID patients who completed serial blood tests. The primary outcome was a proprietary 'blood toxicity score' based on stereomicroscopic identification of purported graphene oxide, microchips, and microrobots in blood samples. Treated patients (n=37) showed a statistically significant decrease in toxicity score (12.92±5.18 to 7.76±2.99, Wilcoxon z=-4.783, p<0.001), while untreated patients (n=10) showed a significant increase (12.90±7.20 to 18.30±5.25, p=0.011); however, the study is critically limited by its use of a pseudoscientific, unvalidated outcome measure, lack of randomization or blinding, very small sample size, and severe confounding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL SCIENTIFIC VALIDITY CONCERN: This paper's primary outcome measure — a 'blood toxicity score' based on stereomicroscopic identification of 'graphene oxide,' 'microchips,' 'microrobots,' and 'polyacrylamide hydrogel filaments' in blood — reflects pseudoscientific claims unsupported by mainstream biomedical evidence. The paper explicitly references COVID-19 vaccine conspiracy theories (including 'shedding,' VAIDS, self-assembling nanoparticles, and microchips) and is published in a low-impact open-access journal (Granthaalayah). The acknowledgment section honors a conspiracy figure jailed in Germany. Symptoms were assessed narratively without validated patient-reported outcome instruments — no quantitative symptom scores were extracted. The treatment duration of ~5 months 10 days was used to calculate treatment_duration_weeks (~22 weeks). Per-arm Ns for vaccinated/unvaccinated subgroups were inferred (treated arm: 27 vaccinated + 10 unvaccinated = 37; untreated arm: vaccination status not reported, so subgroup Ns for untreated arm are unknown). The Wilcoxon test p-values for the primary outcome are reported as z=-4.783, p<0.001 (treated) and z=-2.536, p=0.011 (untreated). This paper should not be included in a meta-analysis of evidence-based long COVID treatments.

summary: This retrospective single-center chart review evaluated 10 weekly sessions of red LED photobiomodulation (630 nm, 37 J/cm2) as adjuvant therapy for post-COVID telogen effluvium (TE) with or without androgenetic alopecia (AGA) in 140 long COVID patients divided into four groups. At 12 weeks, cessation of hair loss (negative hair pull test) occurred significantly more often in LED-treated TE patients (86.8% vs 48.1%, p<0.001) and TE+AGA patients (78.7% vs 46.2%, p=0.035) compared to controls without LED therapy. LED-treated groups also showed significant within-group increases in thick hair proportion and follicular unit density across frontal and occipital areas, while controls showed no significant improvement or worsening, supporting LED photobiomodulation as a promising adjuvant for post-COVID hair loss.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. summary: This multicenter prospective single-arm observational study (LIRA-COVID, n=83) evaluated oral L-ornithine L-aspartate (LOLA) 9 g/day for 4 weeks in Russian post-COVID syndrome patients with hyperammonemia, elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST >2x ULN), cognitive symptoms, and asthenia. summary: This single-center prospective observational study compared 32 patients with biopsy-proven post-COVID myocarditis (SARS-CoV-2 RNA/protein positive) to 45 patients with non-COVID myocarditis, all treated with methylprednisolone-based immunosuppressive therapy. Post-COVID myocarditis was associated with significantly higher myocardial CD45 and CD68 cell counts and a broader morphological spectrum (including eosinophilic and giant cell variants). At follow-up, post-COVID patients had a significantly higher rate of excellent echocardiographic response (86% vs. 53% achieving ≥10% EF increase, p<0.05) and higher mean LV EF (49.8±7.6% vs. 43.9±12.3%, p<0.05), despite shorter follow-up and less frequent cytostatic use, though this comparison is substantially confounded by era-related differences in heart failure therapy.

Table 1 reports overall sample (n=83); Table 3 reports NAFLD subgroup (n=23); Table 4 reports no-NAFLD subgroup (n=60). Ammonia is measured at 3 timepoints (day 0, 14, 28), other outcomes only at day 0 and 28. The paper does not report exact arm-level p-values for the within-group changes in NAFLD and no-NAFLD subgroups — p-value thresholds used (p<0.01 for NAFLD, p<0.001 for no-NAFLD). summary: This prospective cohort study from Ukraine followed 266 hospitalized moderate-to-severe COVID-19 patients for one year; 25 (9.4%) were diagnosed with post-COVID-19 interstitial lung disease (ILD), of whom 9 received off-label nintedanib 300 mg/day for 3 months in addition to corticosteroids. summary: This prospective single-arm cohort study in Kazakhstan enrolled 98 older adults (aged ≥65) with post-COVID syndrome and arterial hypertension, transitioning them from multiple antihypertensive medications to a single-tablet combination (valsartan + amlodipine ± hydrochlorothiazide) over 8 weeks. summary: This single-center prospective observational study evaluated Japanese traditional medicine (Kampo medicine, predominantly saikokeishito and/or kamikihito) in 112 long COVID patients at Tohoku University Hospital, Japan, assessing HR-QOL via EQ-5D-5L at baseline and 3 months. The entire cohort showed a statistically significant improvement in median HR-QOL from 0.711 to 0.833 (change +0.087, exceeding the minimally important difference of 0.065; p<0.0001), with 90.2% of patients receiving JTM formulations. Multivariate logistic regression identified the combination of kamikihito and saikokeishito as independently associated with QOL improvement in all patients (adjusted OR 5.4, 95% CI 1.4-30.1) and in the brain fog subgroup (adjusted OR 6.1, 95% CI 1.6-30.8), though the absence of a control group precludes attribution of improvement to treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm before-after design with no control group; all outcome data are within-group pre-post comparisons. The KKT/SAKT combination analysis is an internal comparison within the cohort using multivariate logistic regression, not a separate arm — extracted as between_group_effects for outcomes 11 and 12 for convenience but represents an adjusted OR from regression, not a randomized comparison. The EQ-VAS change IQR for the brain fog subgroup was reported as '7.5 (-9.3 to -24.3)' in the paper — the negative upper bound appears to be a typographic error (likely should be +24.3); extracted as iqr_high=24.3. Table numbering in the paper is inconsistent — 'Table 4' contains outcome data for HR-QOL/EQ-VAS, and both Table 4a (all patients) and Table 4b (brain fog) are extracted. Supplementary tables 1 and 2 referenced but not available in the provided text.

summary: This multicentric prospective cohort study in Ecuador enrolled 477 adults who received 8 weeks of multidisciplinary rehabilitation (3x/week) at 14 centers, comparing functional and perceived health outcomes between 354 patients with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) and 123 without PCC over 12 weeks. Overall, PCFS functional status improved significantly (mean decrease 0.48 points, 95% CI -0.65 to -0.31, p<0.0001) and perceived health (AVS) improved by 0.68 points (95% CI 0.56-0.80, p<0.0001); however, PCC patients had substantially lower odds of achieving a favorable PCFS outcome at Week 12 compared to non-PCC patients (aOR 0.27, 95% CI 0.13-0.56, p<0.001), while AVS improvement did not differ significantly by PCC status (aOR 0.58, p=0.062). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm intervention study (all participants received the same rehabilitation) stratified by exposure status (PCC vs non-PCC) rather than a true two-arm trial. Symptom trajectory data (Figure 1) is available only for the PCC subgroup (not non-PCC). arm_id=0 used in within_group_change entries to indicate overall cohort (both arms combined), as the paper reports these as overall mixed-effects model results without arm stratification. summary: This single-arm retrospective medical records review (n=40) evaluated 10 sessions of major ozone autohemotherapy (MBO) in post-COVID syndrome patients at a Turkish university hospital, measuring fatigue (FACIT), anxiety and depression (Beck scales), sleep quality (PSQI), and quality of life (SF-36) before and after treatment. Statistically significant pre-to-post improvements were observed across nearly all outcomes: FACIT fatigue (median 31 to 9.5, p=0.001), Beck anxiety (7.5 to 4.0, p=0.001), Beck depression (5.5 to 1.0, p=0.002), global PSQI (15 to 13, p=0.016), and 8 of 9 SF-36 subscales (all p<0.05), with emotional well-being the only non-significant subscale. The study lacks a control group, so causal attribution to MBO is not possible.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm before-after study only; no control group. All data reported as median (min-max) using Wilcoxon signed-rank test — no means or SDs available. The min-max range is reported in tables, not IQR; iqr_low and iqr_high fields have been populated with the min and max values respectively as the only range data available. Treatment session duration in weeks not explicitly stated (10 sessions at 2-3x/week implies approximately 3.3–5 weeks but not confirmed). No adverse events reported. Vaccine status: 85% vaccinated (n=34 of 40). The PSQI sleep duration subscore median is identical pre and post (both 7) yet p=0.008, consistent with a non-parametric rank-based test on the full distribution. Post-treatment follow-up appears to be at end of treatment only (no subsequent follow-up visits described).

summary: This single-center, uncontrolled, prospective observational cohort study enrolled 72 patients (mean age 54.6 years, 67% female) hospitalized with post-COVID-19 intestinal lesions (GI symptoms arising 2-4 weeks after COVID-19 recovery with negative PCR) during the first and second COVID-19 waves in Russia (June 2020-September 2021). All patients had diarrhea (mean 6.8 episodes/day), with highly variable endoscopic findings including pseudomembranous colitis (17.9%), focal hemorrhagic colitis (16.4%), erosions (28.4%), newly diagnosed ulcerative colitis (3%), and normal or near-normal mucosa (31.3%); C. difficile toxins were detected in 38.9%. Treatment was symptomatic; 56.9% improved during hospitalization, 27.8% achieved complete recovery within 4-8 weeks, while 3 patients (4.2%) required emergency colectomy and 2 (2.8%) died, with no consistent correlation between clinical severity and endoscopic/histologic findings.

summary: This multicentre prospective observational cohort study followed 88 post-COVID-19 patients (mean age 54.4 years, 48.9% male) from five Dutch hospitals, measuring symptoms monthly from 4 to 18 months post-infection. Using latent class mixed modelling, three distinct trajectories were identified for both fatigue and dyspnoea: decreasing, high persistent, and low persistent. Participation in a lifestyle intervention (personalised dietary and physical activity counselling) was significantly associated with higher odds of symptom improvement (decreasing fatigue OR 1.58; decreasing dyspnoea OR 2.21), while female sex, older age, comorbidities, and mild acute COVID-19 severity were associated with persistent high-burden trajectories.

summary: This prospective single-center before-after observational study enrolled 64 post-acute COVID-19 patients (88% with cognitive impairment/brain fog) undergoing a 30-day inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation program in Italy, including daily 45-minute individualized neuropsychological cognitive stimulation sessions. The primary outcome, MoCA global score, improved significantly from 20.4±5 at admission to 24.7±3.7 at discharge (p<0.0001), with significant improvements in attention, language repetition, memory recall, orientation, visuospatial abilities, and abstract reasoning. At discharge, 43% of cognitively impaired patients had normalized cognitive function; the improvement remained significant after multivariate adjustment for age, sex, COVID-19 severity, and other confounders, though the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study has a partial informal comparator: 8 patients with normal MoCA at admission received standard rehabilitation without neuropsychological treatment (MoCA 27±0.9 vs 28±1.7, p=0.138). This subgroup is not a formal control arm and was not randomized, so the study is classified as single-arm before-after. The IES-R baseline value was reported in two places inconsistently: abstract states 16.6±15.6 (overall) and Table 4 shows 19.6±15.6 — Table 4 value used as it is more likely arm-level. Acute COVID hospitalization duration was 55.8±25.8 days (not rehabilitation duration). Rehabilitation duration was 30±10 days. No adverse events were formally reported. summary: This single-arm longitudinal pilot study assessed the Adaptive Force (AF), a measure of neuromuscular holding capacity, in 17 long COVID patients at three time points: during long COVID state (pre), immediately after first individualized integrative medicine treatment (post), and at recovery (end, ~71 days later). The maximal isometric Adaptive Force (AFisomax) was severely reduced at baseline (elbow: 87.9 N, hip: 88.3 N, ~47-49% of maximal AF) and increased significantly to near-normal levels post-treatment and at recovery (elbow: 187.2 N, hip: 174.1 N, ~100% of maximal AF; all p<0.0001, Cohen's d >2.4). Symptom intensities across 13 domains (fatigue 7.75, post-exertion malaise 8.14, and others) also decreased significantly from long COVID state to recovery, though the uncontrolled design, self-selected recovery endpoint, and heterogeneous individualized treatments preclude causal attribution.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a single-arm before-after study with no control group; the 'end' timepoint was defined as recovery/substantial health improvement, creating major ascertainment bias (only recovered patients were included). 2) The 20 patients who had not recovered by July 2022 were excluded, so the sample is highly selected. 3) Demographic data reported separately by sex (14 female, 3 male) with separate age/height/weight statistics; combined mean age not explicitly reported. 4) The weeks_from_enrollment for 'end' was calculated as 71.06 days ÷ 7 ≈ 10.15 weeks. 5) Some AFmax hip flexor CI values in Table 2 appear to have a typographical error (pre CI lower bound listed as 148.77;148.77 — likely should be 148.77;201.20); extracted as printed. 6) Symptom data n=14 at pre and n=13 at end (one patient did not complete follow-up questionnaire). 7) Additional symptoms reported in Table 3 (fever) were omitted from outcomes extraction but noted: fever pre=2.14±3.66, end=0.23±0.83, p=0.023. 8) Ratio of AFosc to AFisomax (%) and Ratio of AFosc to AFmax (%) outcomes were partially extracted via narrative but full per-timepoint tabular data are available in Table 2 for completeness — these were not separately entered as outcome objects to keep JSON manageable. 9) The integrative medicine treatment involved PEMF, mental stress treatment, and lymphatic/osteopathic techniques; it was individualized and non-standardized.

summary: This 12-week prospective observational study in Romania enrolled 505 post-COVID-19 patients with fatigue, assigning 146 to Astenor Energy (arginine aspartate + B6 + biotin + magnesium) and 359 to Astenor Forte (L-arginine + malic acid) based on physician-assessed liver enzyme levels. summary: This single-arm prospective observational study followed 45 non-hospitalized, complex post-COVID-19 patients (mean age 49.6 years, 62% female, mean 86% with comorbidities) who received individualized multidisciplinary rehabilitation (exercise, respiratory, olfactory, speech/cognitive therapy, and/or psychological support) coordinated by a post-COVID team, with outcomes assessed by structured phone consultations at approximately 15 and 22 months post-infection. Despite the coordinated rehabilitation program, the most prevalent symptoms (fatigue >90%, neurocognitive disorders >75%, muscle/joint pain) did not significantly resolve; however, dyspnea (p=0.013), anxiety (p=0.004), and chest pain (p=0.007) showed statistically significant reductions by McNemar's test. At 22 months, only 9% felt fully recovered, 53% reported some improvement (moderate 33%, minimal 20%), 38% reported no improvement, and 36% of working-age patients had not returned to any work activity.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Exact post-intervention (22-month) symptom prevalence percentages are only shown in Figure 4 (bar chart) and not provided as numeric values in the text or any table — thus timepoint_id=2 percent values for outcomes 1-8 are set to null with result_source='not_reported'. Baseline symptom frequencies at 15 months are described in approximate terms ('more than 90%', 'more than 75%', 'more than half', 'around 40%') rather than exact counts — these were recorded as approximate percent values with result_source='inferred'. Patient-perceived improvement breakdown: 9% healthy/complete recovery, 33% moderate improvement, 20% minimal improvement, 38% no improvement. Return-to-work breakdown (n=40 excluding 5 retired): 36% no work, 24% partial (>=50%), 40% full-time. No validated questionnaires were used; all symptom data are non-standardized self-report. The follow-up duration of ~30 weeks is calculated from mean time differences: 22.6 - 15.1 = 7.5 months between phone calls.

summary: This prospective before-after cohort study assessed 34 post-acute COVID-19 patients undergoing a 28-day inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation program (exercise, nutritional therapy, psychiatric support) in Italy, comparing outcomes in those with sarcopenia (n=20) versus without (n=14) at admission. Both groups showed improvements in TUG performance, appendicular skeletal muscle mass, and SpO2 across positions, but sarcopenic patients demonstrated significantly greater improvements across respiratory, body composition, muscle strength, and functional domains. Sarcopenia prevalence was 58% at admission, and early identification of sarcopenia was associated with more pronounced rehabilitation gains, suggesting that targeted assessment and intervention in sarcopenic post-COVID patients is clinically important.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Spirometry (FEV1, FVC) was performed only at baseline (T0) and not repeated at discharge; no post-treatment spirometry values available. The paper reports values as 'mean ± SD' but the statistical analysis section states 'continuous variables expressed as median and interquartile range' — it is possible the table values labeled as SD are actually IQR; however, the tables explicitly state 'mean ± standard deviation (SD)' in their legends, so values are extracted as mean ± SD. Table values for Dyspnea Borg lying at T0 NS show SD=0.1 which seems implausibly low; extracted verbatim. The NS group BMI at T0 is reported as 28.4 (8.9) in text and 27.3 (9.0) in Table 1 — small discrepancy noted; Table 1 value used for arm_results. No between-group statistical comparisons were reported for any outcome (only within-group pre-post p-values are given); between_group_effects arrays are empty throughout.

summary: This single-arm observational study of 10 post-COVID ME/CFS patients with elevated ADRB2 autoantibodies assessed the effect of immunoadsorption (5 sessions over 10 days) on physical function. Seven of ten patients (70%) were classified as responders, with SF36-PF scores improving by 10–45 points at 4 weeks post-treatment (baseline median 25, post-treatment median 42.5; p<0.05), with significant improvements also observed in muscle pain and immune symptom scores. No control group was included, limiting causal inference; autoantibody levels did not correlate with treatment response, suggesting mechanisms beyond simple IgG depletion.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post study; no SDs reported for any outcome (only medians, ranges, and p-values from Wilcoxon tests). SF36-PF individual patient data available in Table 1 for baseline and 4-week timepoints (all 10 patients). Months 2 and 3 SF36-PF data are in figures only with no tabular values. FSS, cognitive score, immune score, muscle pain, and headache data are in figures only — no numeric values extractable from text. Bell score at baseline ranges 20–40 (individual patient values in Table 1) but no post-treatment Bell score values reported in text or tables. Age range given (33–59 years) but no mean or median calculated by authors. Time since COVID-19 ranges 9–32 months per Table 1. IgG range after 4 IAs stated as 0.57–3.23 but this appears to be the full range, not IQR.

summary: This prospective single-arm before-after study (PCR-SIRIO 8) enrolled 90 adults (54% female, mean age 61.7 years) with post-COVID-19 syndrome characterized by persistent dyspnea, who underwent a 6-week personalized outpatient rehabilitation program combining HIIT, resistance training, and therapeutic education. Statistically significant improvements were observed for all functional and patient-reported outcomes including fatigue (MFIS: 37.4 to 29.1, p<0.0001), dyspnea (mMRC: 2.21 to 1.00, p<0.0001), 6-minute walk distance (328 to 384 m, p<0.0001), and functioning (FCIS total: 86.1 to 91.7, p<0.0001), with no statistically significant differences in the magnitude of improvement between males and females, though females showed specific improvements in abdominal fat and skeletal muscle mass while males showed improvements in grip strength.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. SD values for grip strength in Table 3 appear to be printed as rounded to the nearest integer (e.g., SD=12.00, 11.00, 10.00) which is implausible and likely a table formatting artifact — SD values for grip strength should be treated with caution. 2. The 'after' SD for phase angle in Table 2 for the studied group is listed as 9.25 which appears inconsistent with the female (0.62) and male (0.72) subgroup SDs — likely a typographical error. 3. The paper states SPPB is 0-12 points but reports means of 13.68 and 15.09, which exceeds the stated maximum — authors likely used a modified/extended version; values extracted as reported. 4. No adverse events reported. 5. Gender-specific subgroup data (means ± SD by female/male) for all outcomes in Tables 2-5 are available in paper but only delta (change) means and SDs are reported for subgroups, not separate baseline and follow-up values for per-sex subgroup arm_results beyond what is captured; key subgroup deltas captured in subgroup_analyses. 6. Outcomes not separately extracted but reported: total body mass, BMI, fat-free mass, rate of fat-free mass, fat mass, rate of fat mass, total body water, rate of total body water, extracellular water, rate of extracellular water, muscle mass of right arm/left arm/right leg/left leg/dominant arm/non-dominant arm (subgroup level), left-hand grip strength, dominant-hand grip strength, non-dominant-hand grip strength, oxygen desaturation during 6MWT.

summary: This Romanian single-center RCT (n=84) assigned post-severe-COVID-19 patients discharged from hospital to either low-intensity (cyclo-ergometer 20-30W, 3x/week) or high-intensity (40-50W, 5x/week, HIIT) cardiopulmonary rehabilitation over 3 months. Both groups showed significant within-group improvements across all pulmonary function measures (FVC, FEV1, MVV, PEF, FEF25-75), cardiopulmonary exercise testing parameters (VO2 peak, VO2 at AT, breathing reserve), and cardiac measures (ejection fraction, SPAP), with no statistically significant differences between the two intensity groups at 3 months on any outcome.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Central neurological deficit was positively correlated with higher disability scores across all six WHODAS 2.0 domains (p<0.01 for all), with correlations ranging from r=0.495 (mobility) to r=0.683 (self-care).

ICU admission was negatively correlated with disability scores in cognition (r=-0.397, p=0.041), mobility (r=-0.579, p=0.002), self-care (r=-0.455, p=0.017), life activities (r=-0.433, p=0.024), and participation in society (r=-0.420, p=0.029), suggesting possible rehabilitation benefit.
DM was significantly correlated with higher mobility disability scores (r=0.383, p=0.048) but not significantly associated with other WHODAS 2.0 domains.

summary: This single-center Romanian cohort study assessed long-term disability ~3 years after post-acute rehabilitation in 27 survivors of severe/critical COVID-19 using the WHODAS 2.0 questionnaire administered by telephone. The rehabilitation intervention was an inpatient multidisciplinary program (median 18 days) based on the STM ASAP protocol, applied immediately post-discharge from acute COVID-19 care. The overall disability score at 3-year follow-up was 35.09%, with highest impairment in household activities (51.79%) and participation in society (39.81%); central neurological deficits were significantly associated with higher disability across all six domains (r=0.495–0.683, p<0.01), while ICU admission was paradoxically negatively correlated with disability scores in most domains, possibly reflecting a rehabilitation benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm observational cohort study with no control group and no baseline WHODAS 2.0 measurement — disability was assessed only once at ~3-year follow-up, so no pre-post within-group change can be extracted. WHODAS 2.0 domain scores are reported as percentages (0-100%) without SDs, so only point estimates are available. The 'work/school activities' subscore was completed by only 6 of 27 patients (those still working). The rehabilitation hospitalization duration is reported as both 'median 18 (11.5, 24) days' (IQR) in one table and 'average 19.14 ± 8.06 days' (mean ± SD) elsewhere — both are noted. The study reports Spearman/Pearson correlation coefficients between WHODAS domain scores and clinical variables (DM, ICU admission, central neurological deficit), extracted in subgroup analyses. No formal between-group comparisons with effect sizes (mean differences, ORs) are reported. The overall disability score is stated as 35.09% in the Results table but as 35.9% in the Discussion — 35.09% used as primary value.

summary: This single-center retrospective study evaluated PIRV-F20 (a supplement combining lactoferrin, lysozyme, lactobacillus, resveratrol, vitamins, zinc, and copper) in 44 post-COVID-19 patients with exercise impairment, comparing 23 who self-selected the supplement for ≥6 weeks against 21 who declined treatment. The treatment group showed a statistically significant improvement in 6-minute walking distance (median +40m vs +10m in controls; p=0.01 between groups), though treatment and control groups differed significantly in age (57.8 vs 39.7 years). No significant differences were observed in muscle strength, echocardiographic parameters, or symptom perception between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 24-week follow-up data for 6MWD reported only as 'a further increase of 15.3 ± 2.4 m' from the 6-week value in the treatment group (n=17); baseline and absolute 24-week values not provided. The between-group p-value for 6MWD change (p=0.01) was reported for the median change comparison; no exact effect size (mean difference) reported for the primary endpoint between groups. Note: two patients who discontinued due to AEs are counted in arm 1 n_enrolled=23 as they appear to have completed follow-up (AEs led to discontinuation of supplement, not withdrawal from study).

summary: This prospective single-arm longitudinal observational study enrolled 127 post-COVID patients (predominantly healthcare workers with work-related COVID-19) who completed a mean 29-day multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation program in Germany, with follow-up at 6 months (T3, n=108-121) and 12 months (T4, n=95-115) post-rehabilitation. Significant improvements were observed 6 and 12 months after rehabilitation in functional exercise capacity (6MWT: +68.5m at T3, +50m at T4), VO2max, Wattmax, 1-min sit-to-stand, quadricep strength, balance, and subjective physical ability (all p<0.05, effect sizes r=0.189-0.755), while handgrip strength did not improve significantly. Despite these gains, post-COVID symptom burden remained high 12 months post-rehabilitation (prevalence 28.6-94.7% depending on symptom), and participation in outpatient exercise groups after rehabilitation was associated with significantly greater improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and symptom reduction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm before-after study with no control group; all comparisons are within-group (Wilcoxon signed-rank, T1 vs T3 and T1 vs T4). Symptom cluster prevalence data (Figures 1 and 2) not fully extractable as numeric percentages were in figures only; qualitative descriptions used. The study reports median (IQR) for all continuous outcomes due to non-normal distributions. Effect sizes reported as Wilcoxon r (not Cohen's d). The T1 sample size for spiroergometry outcomes (VO2max, Wattmax) differs slightly between T3 (n=50) and T4 (n=51) analyses, likely due to different paired samples. Time since infection mean 409.52 days (SD=143.97) = ~13.65 months (SD ~4.8 months). Treatment duration calculated as ~4 weeks (mean 28.99 days). Total follow-up from T1 to T4 approximately 56 weeks (29 days rehab + ~12 months follow-up). PCFS p-value at T3 stated as 0.790 in text but r=-0.219 in table (r value may be from Friedman or different analysis; extracted as stated). Baseline T1 n for 6MWT and quadricep at T3 is 108 vs 107 for 1MSTST at T3; minor discrepancy likely due to missing values. T2 (end of rehabilitation) data are published separately (Müller et al. 2023) and not included in this paper.

summary: This retrospective before-after study evaluated the effectiveness of inpatient health resort treatment (mean ~24.6 days) for cardiopulmonary symptoms of long COVID in 122 patients (mean age 64.4 years) at a Polish sanatorium in 2021. The complex multimodal intervention included balneotherapy, respiratory and general exercises, physical medicine modalities (LLLT, cryotherapy, TENS, electromagnetic fields), and health education. All assessed cardiopulmonary symptom domains improved significantly after treatment (p<0.05 for 7 of 8 outcomes), including mMRC dyspnoea (62% decrease, from 1.37 to 0.52 points, p<0.0001), exercise-induced dyspnoea (63% decrease), sputum (82% decrease), and cough intensity (81% decrease), with fast heart rate being the only non-significant outcome (p=0.06). The absence of a control group precludes conclusions about treatment efficacy beyond natural history.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm before-after study with no control group; all comparisons are within-group pre-post. Table 4 in the paper contains a formatting artifact where some rows appear duplicated in the original text (palpitations and fast heart rate rows appear twice with slightly different values — values used are from the structured table). Treatment duration mean 24.59 days calculated to ~3.51 weeks. Subgroup data extracted from Tables 4, 5, and 6 (sex, age group, and balneotherapy subgroups respectively). Between_group_effects left empty for all outcomes as no control arm exists. Change_mean values are calculated (post minus pre). The effect size calculation (f=0.306 per G*Power) is a pre-study power estimate, not a post-hoc effect size, so not extracted as an outcome effect. No objective measures (spirometry, 6MWT, ECG) were used — all outcomes are subjective patient-reported numeric scales.

summary: This single-arm service evaluation assessed long-term outcomes in 112 patients (of 460 contacted; 24% response rate) discharged from a specialist multidisciplinary long COVID community rehabilitation service in Leeds, UK, at a mean of 9.7 months post-discharge and 37.6 months post-infection. While patients showed clinically meaningful improvements in EQ-5D-5L index score (0.52 to 0.65) and symptom severity (18.4 to 13.0) during service engagement, these gains partially eroded after discharge (EQ-5D-5L 0.53, symptom severity 15.1). At follow-up, 90.2% of respondents had not returned to pre-COVID-19 health status, and 43% met NICE criteria for suspected ME/CFS, indicating that long COVID had become a long-term condition for the majority of engaged service users.

summary: This single-arm prospective cohort study evaluated an 8-week WHO Borg CR-10 structured pacing protocol combined with active rest guidance in 31 adults with persistent long COVID (median symptom duration 29 months) who had post-exertional symptom exacerbation (PESE). PESE episode frequency declined significantly by 15% per week (95% CI 11%-20%, p<0.001), with reductions in episode duration, symptom count, and severity; statistically significant improvements were also seen in C19YRSm functional disability and PESE subscores by week 8, and in symptom severity, overall health, and EQ-5D-5L VAS by week 12. However, improvements in C19YRSm did not reach the minimal clinically important difference (MCID of 4 points), and EQ-5D-5L utility index did not improve significantly, reflecting the long-term nature of the condition in this cohort.

summary: This open-label, single-arm before-after cohort study evaluated personalized, algorithm-based intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia conditioning (IHHC) in 199 Danish patients with post-COVID-19 condition (mean symptom duration 14.1 months), using SF-36 quality of life and NRS pain as primary outcomes. At 6 weeks (n=93) and 6 months (n=37), SF-36 total scores increased by 102 points (95% CI 78.4-127, p<0.001) and 106 points (95% CI 57.0-154, p<0.001), respectively, while NRS pain at rest and during activity decreased by approximately 29-35% at both timepoints (all p<0.05). The study lacks a control group and has high attrition at follow-up, and three of six authors are co-founders of the company providing the treatment, which substantially limits interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm study with no control group; all within_group_change p-values are stated as thresholds (p<0.001, p<0.01, p<0.05), not exact. The 6-week and 6-month analyses use different (nested) subsets of the 199-patient total cohort (n=93 and n=37 respectively), with paired analyses only for patients who returned questionnaires — substantial attrition noted. Per-arm n for NRS pain analyses not reported separately (only that patients with NRS≥1 at rest or activity were included). Baseline NRS CI values appear inverted in paper text (stated as '95% CI 0.90 to 1.95' for a reduction — extracted as negative change). Total PCC cohort baseline SF-36 total score (380) represents all 199 patients; the 6w cohort baseline is 357 and 6m cohort baseline is 389 — these are separate cohorts, not sequential. The paper reports all outcomes also for the Total PCC cohort at baseline only (no follow-up for the full 199); these baseline-only values are noted in Table 2 but not extracted as separate arm results since no follow-up data available for the full 199. risk_of_bias.key_concern: Serious confounding by indication: MetS and non-MetS groups differ substantially at baseline in age distribution, BMI, prevalence of diabetes (50% vs 8%), hypertension (88% vs 39%), and pneumonia during COVID-19 (86% vs 65%), and regression adjustment was limited to four variables; additionally, the actual sample size (n=146) was underpowered relative to the post-hoc estimate of n=278 needed, per the authors.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Both MetS and non-MetS groups showed significant within-group improvements in 6MWT (both p<0.001); in regression analysis, age was a significant negative predictor of 6MWT in both groups (MetS: p=0.002 at both timepoints; non-MetS: p<0.001 at both timepoints); hypertension was an additional significant negative predictor in the non-MetS group only (delta 6MWT: OR -66.33, 95% CI -116.03 to -16.63, p=0.011).

Both MetS (p=0.025) and non-MetS (p=0.021) groups showed significant within-group improvements in FEV1% predicted; diabetes was a significant negative predictor of FVC at end of rehabilitation in the non-MetS group only (OR -25.07, 95% CI -46.74 to -3.40, p=0.024).

summary: This prospective observational study compared outcomes of a 2-6 week supervised inpatient post-COVID-19 rehabilitation program (breathing exercises, aerobic training, and strength training) in 84 patients with metabolic syndrome (MetS) versus 62 without MetS at a single rehabilitation hospital in Poland. Both groups showed statistically significant within-group improvements in 6-minute walk test distance (both p<0.001) and FEV1% predicted (MetS p=0.025; non-MetS p=0.021) following rehabilitation. After multivariable adjustment for age, sex, diabetes, and hypertension, MetS itself was not a significant independent predictor of rehabilitation outcomes; rather, older age was a consistent negative predictor of 6MWT performance in both groups, and hypertension and diabetes were additional negative predictors specifically in the non-MetS group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: per-arm means and SDs for the primary outcomes (6MWT distance in meters, FEV1% predicted, FVC% predicted) at baseline and follow-up are NOT reported in any table or text — only p-values for within-group change are given (and these appear to come from Figure 2, which contains bar charts without numeric labels). The regression tables (Tables 3 and 4) provide OR (regression coefficients, not odds ratios despite the label) with 95% CIs for predictors of outcomes, not per-arm summary statistics. Rehabilitation duration was variable (2-6 weeks, median 28 days for MetS and 23 days for non-MetS); total_duration_weeks set to null as individual-level variation precludes a single value. The OR label in Tables 3-4 appears to represent unstandardized regression coefficients (beta), not odds ratios — the authors label them 'OR(95% CI)' but the outcomes are continuous, making this a misnomer. Percent hospitalized: 75% in MetS arm (63/84) and 62.9% in non-MetS arm (39/62) were hospitalized during acute COVID-19, but this refers to acute-phase hospitalization, not the rehabilitation hospitalization.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study examined 59 long COVID patients with extremely severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <50 mmHg) admitted to an ICU in Romania between October 2021 and December 2022, comparing outcomes between HFNC-only (n=23), CPAP-only (n=13), and combined HFNC+CPAP (n=23) non-invasive ventilatory strategies. Overall ICU mortality was 85%, with CPAP-only showing the numerically lowest mortality (76.9%) versus HFNC-only (82.6%) and HFNC+CPAP (87.0%), though none of these differences reached statistical significance (p=0.5). Post-ETI mortality was also high at 86%, with CPAP-only prior therapy associated with the lowest post-intubation mortality (60%), but again without statistical significance (p=0.124); the authors conclude the data are hypothesis-generating only and require larger multicenter studies.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Baseline demographics (age mean/SD, percent female) are not reported per treatment arm — only per survivor/non-survivor subgroups. The n_analyzed values for PaCO2/PaO2 survivors subgroup (arm_results outcome_id 4 and 5) are not explicitly stated and were inferred from survivor counts per arm (arm1=4, arm2=3, arm3=3). Kaplan-Meier survival curve data are in figures only with no numeric table; time-to-event HR values not extractable. Post-ICU sequelae (impaired pulmonary function, persistent dyspnea, reduced physical performance) described narratively but without quantitative data. risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:serious, classification:moderate, deviations:moderate, missing_data:low, measurement:low, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Groups differed systematically by presence of musculoskeletal comorbidities (HILT group had 100% musculoskeletal disorders vs. 0% in comparator), making it impossible to separate the effect of HILT from the effect of different underlying pathology on 6MWT performance.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Normal BMI patients had highest admission mean (437.62m) and discharge mean (505.77m); overweight had admission 398m, discharge 476.12m; obese had admission 358m, discharge 420m. Normal BMI patients also had lowest Borg scores throughout.

Patients without lung damage walked further at admission (466m) and discharge (536.18m) compared to those with lung damage (370.29m and 440.58m respectively); lung damage correlated negatively with 6MWT at both timepoints (p<0.05).

Patients without musculoskeletal damage had lower admission 6MWT (386.82m) but also lower discharge 6MWT (458.73m) compared to those with musculoskeletal damage (admission 424.57m, discharge 498.24m), likely confounded by HILT treatment in the musculoskeletal group.

Patients with cardiac damage had substantially lower admission 6MWT (336.29m) and discharge 6MWT (426.43m) vs. those without (429.15m and 494.50m); cardiac damage correlated with higher Borg exertion at discharge (p<0.05, r=0.382).

Patients with neurological damage had higher admission 6MWT (426.80m) and discharge 6MWT (488.13m) vs. those without (383.42m and 457.83m), possibly reflecting confounding with the HILT group composition.

summary: This retrospective before-after study compared 10-day rehabilitation programs in 33 post-COVID patients: HILT plus kinesiotherapy (n=18, all with musculoskeletal disorders) versus kinesiotherapy alone (n=15, without musculoskeletal disorders). Both groups improved on the 6-Minute Walk Test, with the HILT group achieving a higher mean discharge distance (519m vs. 445.73m) and a statistically significant association between HILT and greater distance yield (p<0.01, r=-0.666 in the correlation analysis). However, the two groups differed fundamentally in their comorbidity profiles, making attribution of benefit specifically to HILT versus differences in underlying pathology unreliable.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Several issues: (1) Tables had significant rendering artifacts with merged/duplicated cells requiring careful parsing. (2) The correlation between HILT and discharge distance was reported as r=-0.692 (negative), which appears counterintuitive — likely a coding artifact where HILT=0 and no-HILT=1, so the negative r actually indicates HILT associated with higher distance. (3) No SDs were reported for any outcome means — only min/max ranges provided. (4) The 6MWT yield (distance yield, %) was referenced in correlation analyses and figures but arm-specific means were not tabulated in numeric form. (5) Overall cohort O2 saturation ranges given but not broken down by arm. (6) One patient (of 33) could not complete 6MWT (96.96% completion = 32/33); unclear which arm this patient belonged to. (7) No p-values reported for within-group pre-post changes; only between-group correlations with HILT variable reported. (8) The between-group effect for 6MWT yield is from the correlation analysis (r=-0.666, p<0.01) not a formal group comparison.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a purely descriptive prescription-pattern study with no treatment outcomes measured. There are no pre-post comparisons, no control group, no efficacy endpoints, and no quantitative symptom severity data. The 'outcomes' extracted here are all cross-sectional symptom prevalence counts at initial visit and prescription frequency counts — not treatment response data. BMI median (22.9, IQR 20.8-26.6) is reported overall but not stratified by Kampo vs non-Kampo. Percent vaccinated calculated as (13+22)/102 = 34.3% for 1 or 2 doses; 64.7% unvaccinated, 1% unknown. Figure 3 (Kampo medicine frequencies by symptom) contains additional data but values are only in a bar chart figure with no accompanying table — not extractable numerically. The study has severe limitations for meta-analysis purposes as it reports no treatment effectiveness data whatsoever.

summary: This prospective single-center observational study assessed predictors of response to a 3-week comprehensive inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) program in 183 severe post-COVID-19 patients in Switzerland. Responders (n=94, 51%) who reached their predicted reference 6-minute walking distance showed significantly higher baseline 6MWD (250 vs 119 m), FIM motoric scores (73.0 vs 64.2), FVC% predicted (80% vs 62%), and DLCO% predicted (62% vs 47%) compared to non-responders. Multivariable logistic regression and CART analysis identified 6MWD at admission, FIM motoric, and FVC% predicted as the strongest independent predictors of failing to reach the target walking distance, with both groups showing significant within-group improvements in 6MWD, FIM, and wellbeing (all p<0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study defines 'responders' and 'non-responders' post-hoc based on the outcome itself (reaching predicted 6MWD), making it a prognostic/predictor analysis rather than a true treatment comparison — arm_id=1 (responders) and arm_id=2 (non-responders) both received identical PR; the grouping is purely by outcome. PFT data (FEV1, FVC, DLCO) available only for ~75% of patients (n approximately 136 with FVC). HADS questionnaires completed by 156 of 183. FEV1/FVC ratio also reported: overall 80.28 (SD 10.74), responders 80.53 (SD 9.24), non-responders 79.97 (SD 12.45), p=0.760 — not extracted as separate outcome due to JSON size. summary: This prospective single-center cohort study from France followed 288 COVID-19 survivors discharged from hospital during the first wave (March–April 2020), focusing on 136 patients (47.2%) who had persistent malnutrition, impaired muscle strength (SES <7/10), or performance status >=2 at 30 days post-discharge; these patients received multimodal nutritional rehabilitation including dietary counseling, oral supplements, adapted physical activity, and physiotherapy. At 6 months post-discharge, 119 of these 136 patients were re-evaluated and showed significant improvement across all nutritional and functional measures — weight, SEFI, SES arm/leg, fatigue VAS, and performance status — though 36% still had persistent malnutrition and 14.3% retained significantly impaired muscle strength. Obesity (BMI >=30) and prior ICU admission were independently associated with worse outcomes at 6 months, but the absence of an untreated comparator group means the contribution of the intervention versus natural recovery cannot be disentangled.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cohort study with no randomization and no untreated control group — the 'recovered' arm (arm 2) represents patients who did not meet impairment criteria at D30 and were not followed to 6 months, so the comparison is cross-sectional at discharge only, not longitudinal. summary: This single-arm prospective cohort study (n=37) followed severe COVID-19 ICU survivors through inpatient rehabilitation and 6 months post-discharge in France. Before infection, all patients were fully autonomous (GIR 5–6); upon rehabilitation admission, 39% were highly dependent (GIR 1–2), and 81% had severe malnutrition by GLIM criteria. Following individualized rehabilitation, autonomy recovered substantially (30.5% → 69% GIR 5–6 at discharge, 80% at 6-month follow-up), and most symptoms resolved; however, fatigue persisted in 70.2% of patients at 6 months, and patient adherence to nutritional recommendations was poor. The study had no control group, so these changes cannot be definitively attributed to the rehabilitation program rather than natural recovery.

summary: This retrospective population-based observational study from the Consorci Sanitari de Terrassa (n=192,651), Spain, compared long COVID incidence and thrombotic events in patients chronically prescribed antihistamines versus those not on antihistamines over five years (March 2020–March 2025). No long COVID cases were observed among antihistamine users with two or more SARS-CoV-2 infections vaccinated before first infection, and zero cases among those with three or more infections, though subgroup sizes were small and between-group comparisons did not reach statistical significance. Thrombotic events were significantly less frequent in antihistamine users across multiple polypharmacy strata and calendar years (overall 1.6% vs 3.3%, p<0.0001), with ORs ranging from 1.5 to 9.0 in individual annual/polypharmacy subgroup comparisons, and logistic regression confirmed an independent inverse association between antihistamine use and thrombosis after adjusting for age, sex, and number of chronic treatments.

summary: This single-center before-after study examined how TLR4 Asp299Gly genetic polymorphism modifies rehabilitation outcomes in 92 post-COVID syndrome patients with respiratory manifestations who received inpatient multimodal rehabilitation (climatotherapy, exercise therapy, massage, aromatherapy, respiratory therapy) in Yalta, Russia. Patients were stratified by genotype into AA (n=22), AG (n=37), and GG (n=33) groups, with no randomization or control arm. All genotype groups showed within-group improvements in fatigue, dyspnea, SpO2, and quality of life, but AG heterozygotes demonstrated the largest and most statistically significant improvements across clinical symptoms, pulmonary function, 6MWT distance (+49m vs +13m in GG), and anxiety scores, while AA homozygotes showed the least functional improvement; however, between-group differences did not reach statistical significance for most outcomes.

summary: This retrospective comparative review examined the impact of COVID-19 pandemic-related restructuring on inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation across a network of 8 Italian hospitals, comparing 2,089 patients admitted during March 2020–March 2021 (including 265 with post-COVID sequelae, 12.7%) to 3,912 patients admitted in the preceding year. Despite a 47% reduction in admissions and significant case-mix changes, rehabilitation outcomes (6MWT, MRC dyspnoea, CAT, SPPB, Barthel dyspnoea) were broadly similar between periods, though COVID-era patients had worse baseline disability (Barthel 60 vs 69) and achieved greater functional gains. In-hospital mortality (2.2% vs 1.6%) and acute hospital transfers (8.0% vs 3.3%) were higher in the COVID era, while home discharge rates were lower (88.5% vs 93.6%); no statistical tests or p-values were reported for any between-group comparisons.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a health service reconfiguration review, not a long COVID treatment trial. The 265 post-COVID sequelae patients represent only 12.7% of the COVID-era cohort; all outcome data are reported for the entire mixed-diagnosis cohort (CRF, COPD, OSAS, ILD, tracheostomized, post-COVID), not specifically for the post-COVID subgroup. No statistical tests or p-values are reported for any between-group or within-group comparisons. LOS means are reported (23.84±16.14 vs 23.37±12.37 days) but not extracted as a formal outcome. Nursing home discharge rates also reported (1.24% COVID vs 1.47% pre-COVID). Individual patient follow-up duration is not reported; LOS approximates treatment duration but exact rehabilitation duration per patient is not given.

summary: This retrospective multicenter observational study examined whether COVID-19 vaccination status influenced outcomes of an inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) program in 96 severe COVID-19 survivors (46 vaccinated, 50 unvaccinated) admitted to three ICS Maugeri IRCCS hospitals in Italy between September 2021 and April 2022. Both groups achieved statistically significant within-group improvements in all outcome measures — Barthel Index, 6-Minute Walking Test, Short Physical Performance Battery, and P/F ratio — following the PR program (all p<0.01). There were no statistically significant between-group differences in any outcome measure at baseline or at discharge, indicating that vaccination status did not influence PR outcomes, though the groups were inherently non-comparable due to significant differences in age, comorbidity burden, and acute disease severity.

summary: This retrospective single-arm before-after study from India evaluated outcomes in 49 long-COVID patients (symptoms >4 weeks post-COVID-19) managed in an outpatient pulmonary clinic over 12-14 weeks. Of these, 24 patients with HRCT abnormalities plus resting hypoxia or exertional desaturation received tapering oral deflazacort (equivalent to prednisolone 0.25-0.5 mg/kg) over 8-10 weeks. Across all 49 patients, breathlessness declined from 91.8% to 44.9% (p<0.001), fatigue from 93.9% to 51.0% (p<0.001), and cough from 77.6% to 8.2% (p<0.001); in the steroid-treated subset, MMRC dyspnoea score (median) improved from 3 to 1 (p<0.001) and 6-minute walk distance increased by 75.9 meters on average, but the absence of a control group precludes causal attribution of improvement to corticosteroids.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study has two overlapping analysis populations: all long-COVID patients (n=49) and the corticosteroid-treated subset (n=24); outcomes are reported separately for each in Tables 2 and 3. The n=49 group received heterogeneous treatments (oral corticosteroids, inhaled corticosteroids/LABA, domiciliary oxygen, acebrophylline in various combinations), so improvement cannot be attributed to any single agent. CT/CXR findings extracted from Tables 2 and 3 but not repeated as separate outcome objects for every sub-finding (e.g. diffuse reticulations, GGOs) to manage output size; key radiological summary outcomes (normal CXR, normal HRCT) are included. Arterial blood gas values (pH 7.43±0.024, pCO2 36.14±2.53, paO2 51.28±2.54) reported for the 7 hypoxic patients only at baseline — no follow-up ABG data available for extraction. Wheezing, chest tightness, chest pain, tachypnoea all resolved to 0% at follow-up in the full cohort (Table 2) but McNemar test not applicable (NA); these are not extracted as separate outcome objects.

summary: This retrospective observational study examined 90 patients with post-COVID-19 lung sequelae followed for 6 months at a single Egyptian center, comparing outcomes in 46 patients who received steroids plus pirfenidone (off-label) versus 44 who received steroids alone. Both groups showed significant improvement in CT scores and oxygen saturation over 6 months, with one-third of patients returning to normal CT findings; however, there was no statistically significant difference in CT score change (p=0.191) or oxygen saturation change (p=0.240) between the pirfenidone-treated and steroid-only groups. summary: This single-arm prospective observational cohort study enrolled 24 patients with severe-to-critical COVID-19 pneumonia complicated by platypnoea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) who received inpatient multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation in Singapore. The mean duration of POS was 12.9 ± 8.3 days and total orthodeoxia 28.5 ± 14.6 days; all 24 patients achieved orthodeoxia resolution before hospital discharge and none required home oxygen. At follow-up (mean 88.7 days post-discharge), 22 of 23 patients achieved independence in ADLs and ambulation, and 65.2% had unlimited community access; ICU admission and higher maximal respiratory support were the only independent predictors of prolonged orthodeoxia duration.

summary: This propensity score-matched cohort study used the TriNetX US network (60 healthcare organizations) to evaluate long-term cardiovascular outcomes among 1,320 COVID-19 survivors who underwent exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation compared to 1,320 matched controls who did not. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper reports only HRs with 95% CIs for all outcomes — no per-arm event counts, Kaplan-Meier curves with numeric data, or absolute risk data are provided. The study enrolled COVID-19 survivors broadly (not restricted to those with post-acute/long COVID symptoms), so applicability to long COVID specifically is inferred. Pre-matching group sizes were asymmetric (6,420 rehabilitation vs. 1,605 controls), suggesting the control group was the limiting factor for matching. Mortality outcome is reported as all-cause.

summary: This prospective non-randomized case-control study (n=119) from a single Greek center compared an 8-week supervised multidisciplinary rehabilitation program (n=47) to usual care (n=72) in patients with post-COVID-19 sequelae. summary: This single-arm before-after study evaluated a 3-month supervised Physical Rehabilitation Program (breathing exercises, strength training, aerobic exercise 2-3x/week) in 18 post-COVID-19 patients with long COVID sequelae in Brazil. The program produced large-to-huge improvements in handgrip strength (26.5 to 31.8 kgf, Cohen's d=2.7, p=0.001), maximal inspiratory pressure (80.6 to 108.3 cmH2O, d=1.6, p<0.001), maximal expiratory pressure (106.4 to 131.8 cmH2O, d=2.7, p=0.001), and estimated VO2peak (17.2 to 27.8 ml/kg/min, d=2.3, p<0.001) and 6-minute step test performance (93.3 to 140.6 steps, d=1.6, p<0.001). Despite these functional gains, heart rate recovery at 1 minute (a mortality risk marker) did not significantly improve (p=0.052), with 72% still showing abnormal recovery post-PRP.

summary: This single-arm prospective observational study from Bangladesh examined the outcomes of pulmonary rehabilitation in 126 long COVID patients (83% male, age 18–52 years) attending a tertiary hospital between May and December 2023. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Multiple serious data quality issues: (1) No SDs reported for any continuous outcome. (2) No p-values or statistical tests reported for within-group changes. (3) Rehabilitation program duration not specified — the referenced '20 days' is cited from a different study in the literature review, not from this study's own protocol. (4) 6MWT data only reported as a range (350–850 m) with no mean or SD, and it is unclear whether this is baseline, post-treatment, or both. (5) Fatigue data reported only as baseline categorical distribution, no post-treatment fatigue data extracted. (6) Study design described as 'prospective observational study' in the abstract but 'cross sectional study design' in the methodology — treated as before-after single-arm. (7) Abstract states '880.9%' center-based (obvious typo for 88.09% or 88.1%), and table section confirms 111/126 = 88.1% center-based. summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study examined 42 hospitalized COVID-19 patients who developed post-COVID organizing pneumonia (OP) between March 2020 and June 2021, comparing outcomes among those treated with high-dose prednisone (60-80 mg, n=18), standard dexamethasone 6 mg (n=15), or no glucocorticoids (n=7). At discharge, the prednisone group had higher average oxygen requirements (3.5 L/min) than the dexamethasone group (2 L/min), reflecting confounding by severity; at 12-month follow-up, most patients in all groups no longer required supplemental oxygen. Mortality was highest in the high-dose prednisone group (4/18, 22%), likely reflecting baseline severity differences, with no formal statistical comparisons performed between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm before-after study with no control group. Statistical tests are McNemar paired proportions tests comparing pre- vs. post-treatment symptom prevalence across all 41 patients (not just among those with a given symptom), so the 'difference in proportions' in Table 3 reflects change in prevalence across the full cohort. summary: This retrospective cohort study compared 33 self-selected adults who received neurologic music therapy (NMT — diaphragmatic breathing, vocal intonation therapy, therapeutic singing) as an adjunct to standard inpatient rehabilitation after acute COVID-19 or PASC against 36 who declined NMT. Despite the NMT group having significantly higher oxygen requirements at baseline, both at rest and during activity, NMT participants showed significant within-group reductions in oxygen demand from admission to discharge (−0.78 L at rest, −0.85 L during activity; both p=0.003) and a significantly greater reduction in activity-based oxygen use compared to controls (Cohen's d=2.06, p=0.014). Additionally, NMT participants demonstrated significant dose-dependent improvements in sustained phonation (Pearson r=0.45 for minutes of therapy, p=0.009) and were discharged home at a significantly higher rate (97% vs. 78%, p=0.018), though no post-discharge follow-up was conducted.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) Phonation outcome was measured only in the NMT arm (n=32 with final data; 1 participant missing discharge phonation); no comparator phonation data exists. 2) The between-group change in activity-based oxygen (outcome_id=2, timepoint null) represents the admission-to-discharge change comparison between groups (Cohen's d=2.069, p=0.014) as reported in Table 4, not a cross-sectional between-group difference at a single timepoint. 3) Days between COVID test and rehab admission differed significantly: NMT 47.3±33.0 vs non-NMT 18.9±21.3 days (p<0.001), indicating groups were not comparable at baseline — a major confounding concern. 4) Number of NMT sessions: mean 4.2±2.33 sessions; minutes mean 174±114. 5) Midpoint p-value for activity oxygen reported as <0.001, coded as p_value_exact=false. 6) The change in oxygen use from admission to discharge comparison between groups (Table 4 row: 'Change in oxygen use from rehab admission to discharge with activity') reports MD=-1.117, 95% CI -2.1126 to -0.1223, Cohen's d=2.069, p=0.014 — this is the key between-group effect for the primary outcome. 7) No subgroup analyses were conducted due to small sample size. 8) Pearson correlations (outcomes 5 and 6) reflect within-NMT-arm correlations only, not between-group effects; structure adapted accordingly.

summary: This single-arm retrospective survey-based cohort study evaluated the effect of stellate ganglion block (SGB) on PASC symptoms in 52 patients treated at a single US institution between September 2022 and September 2024. summary: This single-arm observational cohort study examined 61 post-COVID-19 patients undergoing 4–6 week inpatient multidisciplinary neurological rehabilitation in Germany, investigating whether baseline treatment expectations predicted outcomes. Higher side-effect expectations at baseline were significantly associated with worse outcomes at 3-month follow-up, including greater illness-related disability (PDI: β=0.42, p=0.007), reduced physical fitness on the 6MWT (β=−0.24, p=0.04), and more somatic symptoms (PHQ-15: β=0.33, p=0.006); unexpectedly, higher positive treatment expectations were associated with poorer functional status (PCFS: β=0.35, p=0.011). These associations remained significant after false discovery rate correction, suggesting that baseline expectation management may be an important target in post-COVID rehabilitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study reports regression coefficients (standardized β and unstandardized B) for associations between baseline expectations and outcomes, not per-arm means/SDs at each timepoint. The paper states that means and standard deviations for outcomes are reported in Table 1 and Table 2, but these tables are not included in the text provided — only narrative results are available. No per-arm means or SDs could be extracted for any outcome at any timepoint. The study is single-arm (no comparison group), so between_group_effects are not applicable. Positive treatment expectations mean=6.22 (scale 0–10); negative treatment expectations mean=0.82; side-effect expectations mean=1.63 at baseline. Rehabilitation duration was 4–6 weeks (mean 32 days in inpatient stay). The primary analyses are regression associations between baseline expectations and outcomes, not pre-post efficacy estimates — this is fundamentally an expectation/placebo mechanisms study, not a treatment efficacy trial. Duration unit set to weeks with value 4 as lower bound (range 4–6 weeks); total follow-up calculated as ~5 weeks treatment + 12 weeks post-treatment = ~17 weeks.

summary: This prospective single-center cohort study in China compared TCM syndrome-differentiation treatment (CRPRF or YTRF herbal decoctions; n=1204) versus standard Western symptomatic medicine (n=202) in 1426 long COVID patients over a 90-day follow-up. summary: This open-label pilot study randomized 14 adults with long COVID brain fog (≥5 months post-acute cognitive decline) to 12 sessions of either transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM; 1070 nm helmet, n=7) or whole-body photobiomodulation (wbPBM; 660/850 nm light bed, n=7) over 4 weeks. summary: This single-arm prospective cohort study evaluated a 6-week WHO Borg CR-10 structured pacing protocol in 31 adults with long-standing post-COVID syndrome (median symptom duration 17 months) attending a community rehabilitation service in the UK. The primary outcome, total weekly PESE episodes, decreased significantly from a mean of 3.4 in Week 1 to 1.1 in Week 6, representing an average 16% reduction per week (95% CI: 9%-24%; p<0.001), with improvements across physical, cognitive, and emotional exertion triggers. Quality of life (EQ-5D VAS) also improved significantly from 51.4 to 60.6 points (paired difference 9.2 points, 95% CI: 3.2-15.2; p=0.004), though the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study (no randomization, no control group); the study_design RCT schema does not fully apply. Rate ratios for weekly change were back-calculated from reported percentage decreases (e.g., 16% decrease = rate ratio 0.84). The 95% CIs for cognitive dysfunction symptom trajectory (-12% to 16%) indicate the lower CI is -0.12, upper 0.16 relative to the rate, so rate_ratio CI is 0.88 to 1.16. The n=34 consented but n=31 analyzed; the 3 excluded did not complete the full 6 weeks. The study notes 4 participants 'could not comply' but 3 were excluded from analysis - slight ambiguity in reporting. summary: This single-arm pre-post pilot study examined the effect of an 8-week online peer support program (8 weekly 1-hour group sessions via Zoom, 3-6 participants plus 2 trained facilitators per group) on mental health in 18 Japanese adults with self-reported PASC and mild-to-moderate depression (PHQ-9 ≥5). summary: This single-arm pre-post intervention study evaluated individualized stress-controlled training therapy (Blended Therapy: computerized system + home exercises) followed by intensified cognitive behavioral therapy in 78 vaccinated long COVID patients with fatigue and sensorimotor instability at the Post-COVID-19 Center Lausitz, Germany, over 3 years (2021–2023). summary: This single-arm pre-post study evaluated low dose naltrexone (LDN; 1 mg/day escalating to 2 mg/day over 2 months) in 52 patients with long COVID (median symptom duration 333 days) at a single Irish tertiary hospital. Among the 36 participants who completed follow-up questionnaires, significant improvements were observed in 6 of 7 Likert-scale outcomes including pain (largest effect size r=0.534), recovery from COVID-19, activities of daily living, energy, concentration, and sleep (all p≤0.001); mood improvement was not statistically significant (p=0.054). The study lacked a control arm, so improvements cannot be attributed solely to LDN versus placebo effect or natural recovery, but LDN appeared safe with only 2 of 38 participants (5.3%) discontinuing due to adverse events.

summary: This single-arm open-label pilot study (N=36, efficacy N=31) tested 12 weeks of combined low-dose naltrexone (4.5 mg/day orally) and NAD+ iontophoresis patches (weekly) in patients with persistent moderate-to-severe fatigue after COVID-19. Mean total SF-36 quality-of-life scores improved significantly from 36.5 (SD 15.6) at baseline to 52.1 (SD 24.8) at 12 weeks (p<0.0001), and Chalder Fatigue Scale scores decreased from 25.9 (SD 4.6) to 17.4 (SD 9.7) (p<0.0001). summary: This single-arm open diagnostic study enrolled 30 long COVID patients (median age 41, 73% female) with symptoms persisting ≥6 months, assessing airflow limitation via methacholine bronchial provocation test and app-based diurnal FEV1 variability monitoring, followed by 3 weeks of inhaled corticosteroid-based asthma treatment. Airflow limitation was detected in 29/30 patients (97%), either by positive methacholine BPT (8/30, 27%) or excessive diurnal FEV1 variability (21/22 BPT-negative patients, 95%). Three weeks of asthma treatment significantly normalized mean diurnal FEV1 variability from 18.0% to 7.3% (p<0.001), eliminated dyspnoea (3.0 to 0, p<0.001), and significantly reduced fatigue scores (8.3 to 6.1, p<0.001), suggesting that unrecognized airflow limitation may contribute to long COVID symptoms and respond to asthma therapy.

summary: This single-arm pilot study administered a 6-week course of oral minocycline (200mg loading then 100mg/day) to 55 patients with ME/CFS, including 19 with long COVID, at a single Japanese clinic. Among the 51 who completed treatment, 80% achieved a clinically meaningful improvement in Performance Status score (>=2 point decrease), with particularly high response rates in those with disease duration <6 months (90%; HR 3.6, p=0.02). Statistically significant improvements were observed in fatigue, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, brain fog, orthostatic intolerance, and disequilibrium, but the study lacks a control group, blinding, or randomization, making placebo effects and natural disease course impossible to exclude.

summary: This single-arm interventional cohort study tested Psychophysiologic Symptom Relief Therapy (PSRT) — a 13-week program combining psychophysiologic education, desensitization, and mindfulness-based stress reduction — in 23 adults with long COVID (PASC) without organ injury who had experienced symptoms for a median of 267 days. summary: This single-arm pilot clinical trial enrolled 14 adults with long COVID in a 10-week supervised aerobic exercise training program (cycle ergometer and treadmill, twice weekly). The primary biomarker finding was that exercise training enabled a significant acute exercise-induced response in serum extracellular vesicle RNA, with 53 differentially expressed genes (predominantly downregulated, including immune/inflammation-related genes MYL9, NRGN, B2M, CCL5) identified at peak exercise after training but not before, and no SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in EVs at any timepoint. Clinically, peak VO2 increased significantly by 7.4% (1.88 to 2.03 L/min, p<0.05) and peak work rate increased 16% (139 to 155 W, p<0.05) after training, though absence of a control group prevents attribution to exercise versus spontaneous recovery.

summary: This single-arm before-and-after feasibility study examined 8 weeks of home-based personalized computerized cognitive training (CogniFit CCT) in 73 adults with long COVID-related cognitive dysfunction (brain fog), most of whom had been symptomatic for over a year. summary: This single-arm interventional cohort study (n=23) tested Psychophysiologic Symptom Relief Therapy (PSRT), a 13-week group-based mind-body program combining psychophysiologic education, desensitization, and MBSR, in adults with long COVID (PASC) without objective organ injury. The primary outcome, SSS-8 somatic symptom score, decreased by a mean of 10.9 points (55% reduction) from baseline to 13 weeks (p<0.001; 95% CI: -13.5 to -8.3). Statistically significant improvements were also observed across all secondary outcomes including fatigue (FSS-9), dyspnea (MDP), pain (BPI), pain anxiety (PASS-20), physical functioning (PROMIS-29), and brain fog at all three follow-up timepoints; however, the absence of a control arm limits causal inference.

summary: This pilot RCT (n=14 completers) tested Constraint-Induced Cognitive Therapy (CICT) — combining Speed of Processing Training with behavior change techniques — versus treatment-as-usual in adults with long COVID brain fog and IADL impairment. CICT produced very large improvements over TAU in daily-life cognitive task performance (COPM Performance MD=3.7, 95% CI 2.5–4.9, p<0.001, d=2.6) and brain fog (MCS MD=−4.0, 95% CI −5.3 to −2.6, p<0.001, d=−3.1), as well as a significant return-to-work advantage (80% vs. 0%, p=0.048). Results support feasibility and provisional efficacy, warranting a larger blinded RCT with an active comparator.

summary: This was a prospective open-label pilot study in South Korea testing three traditional Korean herbal medicines — Bojungikgi-tang (BIT), Kyungok-go (KOG), and Cheonwangbosim-dan (CBD) — in 45 long COVID patients with fatigue or cognitive dysfunction, allocated by clinician syndrome differentiation (no randomization or control group). After 12 weeks of treatment, fatigue VAS treatment success rates were 80%, 53%, and 47% for BIT, KOG, and CBD respectively, with significant within-group improvements in CIS and ChFS scores across all arms, though no statistically significant between-group differences were found at the primary endpoint. Cognitive dysfunction outcomes showed little significant improvement across arms, with the exception of K-MoCA in the KOG group and CFQ in the CBD group at later timepoints; no adverse events were causally related to the medications, confirming feasibility but not efficacy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a non-randomized, uncontrolled pilot study — all outcomes are within-group change from baseline (ANCOVA-adjusted mean differences vs baseline with 95% CI), not between-group comparisons vs a control arm.
