summary: This was a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover phase IIa trial (reCOVer) evaluating BC007 (Rovunaptabin, 1350 mg IV single infusion), a GPCR functional autoantibody (GPCR-fAAb) neutraliser, in 30 PCS patients with confirmed GPCR-fAAb positivity and prominent fatigue at a single German centre. The primary safety endpoint showed no significant difference in TEAEs between sequences (p=0.1299 at day 28; p=0.1352 at day 70), and BC007 was well tolerated. For secondary efficacy endpoints, BC007 produced statistically significant improvements in fatigue (FACIT +2.91, p=0.038; Bell +7.54, p=0.0004; FSS −0.43, p=0.009) and quality of life (SF-36 vitality, general health, social functioning, and MCS) over 28 days, with crossover analysis confirming significant effects on FACIT, Bell, and CCC; no significant effect was observed on Chalder Fatigue Scale, 6MWT, or DSQ-PEM.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preprint (medRxiv, not peer-reviewed). Per-arm means and SDs for all secondary outcomes are reported only in supplementary tables 9-27/28 which were not included in this document — only treatment effect estimates (mean difference, 95% CI, SE, p-value) from Table 2 were available for extraction; arm-level raw values set to null. Adverse event counts at day 70 (n_any_ae) were extracted as the number with at least one TEAE from baseline to day 70 per arm (Seq A: 8/14; Seq B: 9/16); note that Seq B's 9 TEAEs include exposure to both placebo and BC007 phases. The SAE (1 event, not treatment-related) occurred in the context of sequence B which received placebo first — it is attributed to arm_id=2 (placebo) for coding purposes but is stated as not treatment-related. The withdrawal for 'allergic reaction after first infusion' in the trial profile figure refers to a participant in sequence B who received placebo first and had an allergic reaction — this is listed under arm_id=2. Duration of PCS was 1136±283 days for Seq A and 1061±232 days for Seq B (converted to months: ~37.9 and ~35.4 months respectively). Outcomes not shown in Table 2 (Chalder Fatigue Scale, SF-36 Physical Component Summary, SF-36 Physical Functioning, SF-36 Role Physical, SF-36 Role Emotional, SF-36 Bodily Pain, BORG scales, GPCR-fAAb titers) had non-significant results or data only in supplementary figures — omitted from outcomes array due to no quantitative data available. The t-value column in Table 2 appears mislabeled as it contains t-statistics for the treatment effect model.

summary: This 8-week double-blind RCT (n=80) conducted in Thailand tested high-dose oral vitamin D2 (60,000 IU/week; total 480,000 IU) versus placebo in patients with post-COVID syndrome experiencing fatigue or neuropsychiatric symptoms, all of whom had baseline vitamin D deficiency (mean ~18 ng/mL). Vitamin D supplementation significantly improved fatigue (CFQ-11 adjusted coefficient −3.5, p=0.024), anxiety (DASS-anxiety −2.0, p=0.011), and global cognitive function (ACE-III +2.1, p=0.012) compared to placebo, while depression (p=0.085), sleep quality (p=0.052), Trail Making Test, IL-6, and CRP showed no significant between-group differences. The intervention was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.

summary: This single-arm feasibility study tested a 6-week theatre-based wellness programme (including breathing, movement, voice, and drama exercises) delivered to 20 adults with diagnosed long COVID either in-person or online. Retention was high (80% completed follow-up), and exploratory analyses demonstrated statistically significant improvements in self-rated health (mean difference=0.12, 95% CI 0.00–0.23, p=0.04) and chronic fatigue symptoms (mean difference=−3.50, 95% CI −6.97 to −0.03, p=0.05) at 8-week follow-up. As a single-arm study without a control group, no causal inferences can be drawn, but findings support the feasibility and acceptability of this intervention and provide a rationale for a larger controlled trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm feasibility study — there is no randomization and no control arm; the 'between_group_effects' for outcomes 1 and 2 represent pre-post within-group paired t-test results (baseline vs 8-week follow-up), not between-arm comparisons. Outcome 7 captures the within-study comparison of in-person vs online delivery subgroups, treated as arm_id=1 (in-person) vs arm_id=2 (online) for data structure purposes only. Follow-up values for most secondary outcomes (GAD-7, PHQ-9, WEMWBS, UCLA Loneliness Scale, MOS Social Support, Dyspnoea-12, PEM) were described qualitatively as improved but numeric follow-up means/SDs are reported only in online supplemental tables not included in the paper text. Baseline means and SDs for these outcomes were also not reported in the main text. Outcome 7 adds a notional second 'arm' for online participants to capture the delivery-mode comparison — not a true RCT arm.

summary: This single-arm pilot study enrolled 13 adults with neurologic long COVID (PASC) symptoms and reduced glucagon-stimulated GH secretion (<10 ng/mL) and treated them with daily subcutaneous recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) for 9 months, followed by 3 months of off-treatment observation. GH treatment was associated with significant improvements in fatigue (BFI, MFSI-SF), quality of life (QoL-AGHDA), mood (POMS), and depression (BDI-II), but not sleep quality (PSQI) or cognition (MoCA). Improvements in submaximal physical performance (walk distance at 25% and 50% effort, isometric/isokinetic torque at 25% effort) were also significant, but maximum-effort measures and body composition did not change; critically, symptoms largely returned after GH was discontinued, suggesting symptomatic but non-curative benefit.

summary: This Norwegian pilot study tested a 3-4 day concentrated micro-choice based interdisciplinary group rehabilitation program in 241 patients with chronic low back pain, long COVID, or type 2 diabetes using a single-arm pre-post design with 3-month follow-up. Among the 76 long COVID participants (83% female, mean age 41 years), there were significant improvements at 3-month follow-up in work/social functioning (WSAS: 24.38 to 16.72, Glass Δ=1.04, p<0.001), illness perception (BIPQ1: 24.55 to 14.86, Glass Δ=1.89, p<0.001), and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L: 0.748 to 0.796, p=0.014; EQ VAS: 54.2 to 67.1, Glass Δ=0.78, p<0.001). The study lacks a control arm, preventing causal inference, but results are promising and the authors recommend a controlled trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post pilot study with no control/comparator arm; therefore between_group_effects are empty throughout, and no randomization occurred. The long COVID subgroup (n=76) is the relevant cohort for this meta-analysis. The paper presents results for all three diagnostic groups combined and separately — long COVID-specific values are extracted as primary arm results. Table 2 reports estimated means with standard errors (from mixed regressions), not raw SDs; SE values are placed in the 'se' field accordingly. The CSQ-8 table reports means with SD in parentheses. EQ-5D-5L dimension data (Table 3) are binary proportions rather than continuous scores. Effect sizes reported are Glass's Delta (not Cohen's d or SMD). Total N included=241; long COVID n=76; low back pain n=104; type 2 diabetes n=61. Age for long COVID group reported as mean=41 years (from text comparison). Note: n in Table 3 for long COVID appears to be approximately 55 (sum of no problem + any problem for most dimensions); exact per-group n at follow-up not explicitly stated for all dimensions. Adverse events not reported. BIPQ1 subscale covers 4 items (illness affect, control, concern, understanding); BIPQ2 covers 8 items (the additional 4 being: illness timeline, symptom experience, treatment help, emotional impact).

summary: This single-arm open-label feasibility study tested 4 weeks of twice-daily heart rate variability biofeedback (HRV-B) using diaphragmatic breathing in 13 long COVID patients with dysautonomia symptoms. All pre-specified patient-reported outcome measures showed statistically significant improvement post-intervention, including the primary C19YRSm symptom severity score (19.5 to 13.5, p=0.001, Cohen's d=1.09), COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom score (p=0.008), WHODAS disability (p=0.021), and EQ-5D-5L global health (p=0.008); Fitbit-measured RMSSD also improved significantly (p=0.048). However, the absence of a control group means these improvements cannot be attributed to the intervention, and the authors recommend a larger randomised controlled trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post feasibility study (not an RCT); the 'between_group_effects' fields have been used to record pre-vs-post Wilcoxon signed rank test results as this is a within-subject design. The paper reports p-values slightly inconsistently: the abstract states COMPASS-31 p=0.007 and RMSSD p=0.047, while Table 4 shows COMPASS-31 p=0.008 and Table 5 shows RMSSD p=0.048 — table values were used as primary. The paper enrolled 15 participants, 13 completed, and 2 were excluded from analysis (not lost to follow-up per se). No formal sample size calculation was performed per feasibility study norms. Cohen's d effect sizes were reported in the tables and have been noted but not re-extracted into a separate field as the schema uses between_group_effects for within-subject comparisons. EQ5D-5L VAS exact scale not fully specified in text. NASA Lean Test results at baseline are tabulated (Table 3) but no post-intervention NLT data with means/SDs were reported numerically in the paper.

summary: This pilot RCT (n=14 completers) compared two 8-week virtual pulmonary rehabilitation approaches in adults with post-COVID syndrome: physiotherapist-led group video conference sessions (PR_VC, n=8) versus self-directed pre-recorded video sessions (PR_SD, n=6), both delivered 3x/week. The PR_VC group showed significantly greater improvement in sit-to-stand capacity (median change +3 vs -3.5 repetitions, p=0.012, Cohen's r=0.67), while the PR_SD group showed significantly greater worsening in fatigue, neurocognitive, and autonomic symptoms on the DSQ-SF. Both approaches were feasible and safe with 83% session completion, high satisfaction, and no adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pilot feasibility study — not powered for efficacy; between-group effect values (mean differences) not reported, only p-values and Cohen's r effect sizes. All outcome data reported as median change scores (post minus pre) with IQR and 95% CI of median using non-parametric Mann-Whitney tests. EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS domain scores (pre/post) shown only in radar plots and box plots (Fig. 2) — absolute endpoint values not extractable from text; only change scores reported in Table 3. Additional DSQ-SF items not included as separate outcomes but all change score data extracted in Table 3: next day soreness (p=0.789), tiredness after minimum exercise (p=0.232), feeling unrefreshed (p=0.691), muscle pain (p=0.548), bloating (p=0.694), problems remembering things (p=0.051), irritable bowel (p=0.351), feeling unsteady (p=0.407), cold limbs (p=0.791), flu-like symptoms (p=0.940), smells/chemicals make you feel sick (p=0.224) — all non-significant and omitted as separate outcome objects to manage output size.

summary: This single-arm open-label pilot study (N=45) tested the Muse-S EEG wearable brain-sensing headband with guided meditation app as an adjunct treatment in long COVID patients over 90 days, with follow-up to 180 days. Statistically significant within-group improvements were observed at end of treatment (day 90) in perceived stress (PSS-10: -5.0±5.3, p<0.001), emotional distress (PROMIS: -4.5±5.5, p<0.001), sleep, cognitive function, self-efficacy, and quality of life, with improvements persisting at day 180. However, as a single-arm uncontrolled trial, the findings cannot be attributed to the intervention versus natural recovery or placebo effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post study with no control group; all between_group_effects arrays are empty as there is no comparator arm. No randomization was performed. STAI score is labelled in Table 4 as significantly associated with usage (p=0.028) but Table 3 shows no significant within-group change at any timepoint by paired t-test — this discrepancy is noted. PHQ-2 (depression) and Fitbit wearable data (heart rate, steps, SpO2) were collected but no quantitative results were reported in the paper text or tables; these outcomes are omitted. PROMIS Cognitive Function Abilities Short Form 4a results were not separately reported from the main Cognitive Function form. The LASA-6 baseline mean of 5.0 (SD 2.1) appears to be a per-item score (0-10) not the total (0-60).

summary: This single-arm, uncontrolled expanded access program enrolled 10 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome who received 5 intravenous infusions of autologous adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (2×10^8 cells each) over 14 weeks, with follow-up to 40 weeks. The primary outcomes — total VAS symptom severity and Fatigue Assessment Scale scores — both improved significantly from baseline to end of study (VAS: median 37.6 to 4.90, p=0.0039, ES=0.91; FAS: median 33.0 to 15.0, p=0.0039, ES=0.91). All eight SF-36 quality-of-life subscales also improved significantly (p=0.0039–0.0078), and the treatment was well tolerated with 40 mild-to-moderate AEs and no serious adverse events; however, the absence of a control group makes it impossible to rule out natural disease course or placebo effects as explanations for the improvements.

summary: This open-label single-arm pilot study evaluated 4 weeks of oral paraprobiotics (Abiprol + Brexibiol, 1.92 g/day total of inactivated bacterial strains) in 6 long-COVID patients followed for >12 months at a Swiss university hospital. Improvements in multiple clinical measures (dysautonomia, fatigue, depression, daily steps) were observed in 30%–80% of measurements per patient, but no quantitative effect sizes or p-values for clinical outcomes were reported, limiting interpretation. Significant immunological changes included reduced HLA-DR expression on B cells and NK T cells, reduced CD40 on nonclassical monocytes, and reduced TLR2 expression on CD4+, CD8+, and NK T cells (all p<0.05 by paired Wilcoxon test), suggesting paraprobiotics may modulate immune activation; however the uncontrolled design and very small sample size preclude causal conclusions.

summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study (n=42) tested a single 10-minute virtual pet-assisted therapy (VAT) session — interaction with a virtual dog via VR headset — in long COVID outpatients at a Japanese university hospital. summary: This single-arm retrospective study from Turkey evaluated 2 months of low-dose oral methylprednisolone (total 680 mg, mean 11.3 mg/day in tapering doses) in 97 long COVID-19 patients with persistent symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitation, cough) at least 4 weeks after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study was uncontrolled with no comparison group, making it impossible to attribute improvements to treatment rather than spontaneous resolution; the treatment was generally well tolerated with only 3% reporting dyspepsia.

summary: This blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial (n=101 completers; 52 intervention, 49 placebo) from Uzbekistan tested whether electroacupuncture Voll (EAV) medicament testing could determine daily ribavirin dosing in long COVID patients aged 16-50, with observations over three years (2020-2023). The primary finding was that EAV-determined ribavirin doses increased over the observation period (e.g., Ne-3 meridian: 232.8 mg in 2020-21 to 607.8 mg in 2023) and were inversely correlated with electrodermal activity pre-test readings (Spearman ρ = -0.766 to -0.919, p<0.001), while the placebo group showed no normalization of EAV post-test readings. Importantly, this paper was retracted in June 2025, no clinical outcomes were measured, and the intervention is based on pseudoscientific electroacupuncture dosimetry with no demonstrated clinical benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper was RETRACTED on June 6, 2025. The paper does not measure any validated clinical outcomes (e.g., symptom scales, functional measures, quality of life) — all outcomes are electrodermal activity readings (AMV) on the EAV/Voll pseudoscientific device. No clinical benefit of ribavirin was assessed. Table 2 has garbled row ordering (Le-1a* pre/post-test rows appear swapped in the source). The ± values in Table 1 appear to be SDs (labeled as such in context), but Table 2 states 'means and standard errors' — SE values are used accordingly in outcomes 1-3. Table 3 placebo group data appears to be single pooled timepoint values (not repeated per year for placebo), and the between-group comparisons use Mann-Whitney test with significance stars. Spearman correlation n values (32 for Ne meridian, 41 for Kr meridian) are used as proxy n_analyzed. Ribavirin dose data in Table 1 values for other meridians (3E-1b, He-8c, Le-1a, Pa/Mi-1a S&D, Ge-1b, Hau-1-3, Ni-1-3b, Bl-66, Pa/Mi-11) not extracted as separate outcome objects due to output size constraints — all available in Table 1 with mean±SD format. Fig 2 shows individual patient scatter plots but no additional numeric data beyond what is in text/tables.

summary: This single-center, open-label, non-randomized interventional study in Ukraine enrolled 320 reproductive-age women with long COVID and menstrual cycle disturbances, divided by presence (n=160) or absence (n=160) of GI symptoms and further assigned to oral vs vaginal micronized progesterone (200mg twice daily x10 days) combined with vitamin D, magnesium, and valerian. At 3 months, approximately 78% of GI- and 71% of GI+ patients reported symptom relief, rising to 89% and 87% respectively at 6 months; vaginal progesterone showed 2.5–14% better outcomes than oral, with fewer side effects. No control arm, no validated outcome instruments, and no between-group statistical testing were reported, severely limiting interpretability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical data quality issues: (1) No randomization described — this is NOT an RCT despite being labeled 'interventional'; design is quasi-experimental at best. (2) There is no placebo or control arm — all 4 groups received active treatment. (3) Primary outcome data (% relief) is reported only as group-level averages pooled across the 4 arms, not broken down by arm; per-arm percentages appear only in Figures 2 and 3 which were not readable. (4) No means, SDs, or validated outcome instrument scores are reported anywhere. (5) Arm allocation: paper states 'two subgroups: oral n=90 and vaginal n=90' but this is ambiguous — it likely means 90 oral and 90 vaginal within EACH of the two GI groups (total 180+180=360 or possibly 45+45+45+45=180 within 320 total). Given n_total=320 and 4 subgroups, n=80 per arm is also plausible; n=90 per subgroup stated but adds to 360 not 320. Discrepancy unresolved. (6) Baseline demographics are reported only for GI+ vs GI- groups combined, not by progesterone route. (7) Side effect data shown only in Figure 2 (not readable). (8) No p-values, CIs, or formal statistical comparisons between arms reported.

Both programs (aerobic, strengthening, and pulmonary exercises, 3×/week) significantly improved resting and post-exertion oxygen saturation, physical activity (IPAQ), dyspnea, fatigue, heart rate, and 30-second sit-to-stand performance at 8-week post-treatment and 8-month long-term follow-up (p<0.05 for all within-group). summary: This open-label single-arm pilot study tested daily 35-minute transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS) for 6 weeks in 15 Long COVID patients who also met 1994 Fukuda CFS criteria. Eight of 15 patients (53%) met the pre-specified composite primary outcome (improvement on ≥2 of 4 measures: PGIC, SF-36 physical function, Chalder caseness, VAS symptom severity), exceeding the a priori success threshold of ≥33%. No adverse events were reported, but the absence of a sham control means placebo effects cannot be ruled out.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label pilot study — no control arm, no randomization, no between-group statistics. All outcomes are reported as responder counts (binary) based on pre-specified thresholds rather than continuous group means or SDs; consequently no per-arm means/SDs or between-group effect sizes are extractable. Table 1 lists individual subject outcomes by criteria met (1 = met, blank = not met) rather than scale scores. No demographic data (age, sex, BMI) are reported in the paper. Brain fog VAS showed no improvement in any patient (noted in text). POMS improvement (≥10 points) was a secondary outcome: 5 of 15 patients met this criterion (including 4 primary responders plus 1 non-primary-responder). The PGIC 'events' count of 5 reflects subjects 1-5 in Table 1 who had '1' in the PGIC column. The VAS 'events' count of 6 reflects subjects 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 in Table 1 who had VAS improvement, but subject 6 also had VAS improvement — total 6 subjects (1,2,4,5,6 = 5 rows, checking table: subj 1,2,4,5,6 have VAS=1, that is 5 subjects). Corrected: VAS improved in subjects 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 = 5 subjects (33.3%); SF-36 PF improved in subjects 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 = 6 subjects (40%); Chalder case→no case in subjects 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 = 7 subjects (46.7%); PGIC improved in subjects 1-5 = 5 subjects (33.3%). Note: Table 1 only shows 14 rows (subjects 1-14), but text states 15 patients were analyzed — subject 15 data appears missing from table. Reported 8/15 overall responders per text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study with no randomization and no control group — it does not meet strict RCT criteria but is described as 'interventional'. summary: This single-arm open-label study (n=60, 90% female, mean age 42.55 years) evaluated VITAMIC BIOSEN® (curcumin + vitamin C + Boswellia serrata oral drops) over 6 weeks in vaccinated Spanish long COVID patients. Narrative results reported improvement in dyspnea, sleep disorders, headache, depression, pain, and concentration, with some Fisher exact test p-values <0.05, but no per-arm means or SDs were reported for any outcome. The absence of a control arm, randomization, or blinding means that causal attribution to the supplement is not possible.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical data quality issues: (1) No per-arm means, SDs, or CIs reported for any outcome — only directional narrative statements and selected Fisher exact test p-values. (2) No control arm — this is a single-arm before-after study, not an RCT; between_group_effects arrays capture only within-group pre-post p-values extracted from the Fisher exact test table. (3) Biomarker data (ENCHEPAX) reported only in figures/heatmaps with no numerical values extractable from text. (4) PCFS and EQ-5D scales are stated as primary outcomes but no numerical results are reported. (5) Baseline symptom prevalence percentages (e.g. Asthenia 79.58%) reflect proportion of patients reporting the symptom, not scale scores. (6) The paper was published in a journal of uncertain quality (Biomedical Journal of Science & Technology Research, BJSTR); the Fisher exact test table notes 'not enough samples, Fisher exact test not done properly' for nearly every variable, undermining reported p-values. (7) Convenience/non-probability sampling explicitly stated. (8) Anosmia and ageusia showed no improvement (not quantified). Omitted from outcomes (data only in figures or fully narrative): anosmia severity, ageusia severity, cough severity, fatigue/Likert score details, individual ENCHEPAX biomarker values (AGP, A2M, CRP, Fetuin-A, SAP, PF4/CXCL4, PDGF-AB/BB).

summary: This single-arm pre-post study examined 30 days of a 5-species Lactobacillus probiotic blend with inulin prebiotic in 126 COVID-19 patients (68% with chronic symptoms persisting >30 days, mean 120 days), recruited from a UK hospital post-COVID clinic. All three primary outcomes — cough score, fatigue (Chandler scale), and subjective well-being — improved significantly at 30 days in both early and chronic cohorts (all p<0.001), with large Cohen's d effect sizes for fatigue (d=1.36) and well-being (d=1.10). However, the absence of a control arm means these improvements cannot be causally attributed to the intervention, and the study has high risk of bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a single-arm pre-post study with no control group — RoB2 is applied but most domains are high risk by design. The paper states n=126 for the whole cohort but Table 2 notes chronic cohort n=96 (not n=86 as stated in text/Table 2 header); both values appear — 86 is stated in methods ('86 (68%) in a chronic phase') but t-test df suggests n=96 (t95). The chronic cohort n used here follows the t-test df (t95 implies n=96). Fatigue analysis used t118/t119 suggesting some missing data (~7 participants). CI direction for subjective well-being in Table 1 appears reversed in paper (5.98 to -2.67) — corrected to positive change direction in extraction. No between-group effects are calculable as there is no control arm. Subgroup analysis sample sizes for the BMI subgroup (n=46+80=126) and hospitalization subgroup (n=79+47=126) are internally consistent. Bowel symptom improvement (25/31, 82%) and sleep improvement (8/10, 80%) are notable self-reported binary outcomes extracted in Table 4 but not in formal outcomes above due to no formal instrument.

summary: This single-arm pilot study tested a 10-week online singing and breathing retraining programme (SingStrong) in 21 adults with long COVID in Ireland who completed at least 50% of classes. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post pilot study with no control group — not an RCT. All 'between_group_effects' entries represent within-arm pre-post comparisons (not between-arm comparisons). summary: This single-arm feasibility study tested 8 weeks of individually tailored internet-based CBT (ICBT) with weekly asynchronous therapist support for COVID-19-related psychological symptoms in 24 Swedish adults (66.7% probable post-COVID syndrome) during the pandemic's final phase. Of 24 enrolled, 15 (62.5%) completed post-treatment assessments. Statistically significant improvements were found in depression (BDI-II, r=0.53), anxiety (GAD-7, r=0.43), health anxiety, post-traumatic stress, loneliness, and exhaustion, while stress, quality of life, cognitive failures, and financial well-being showed no significant change; insomnia paradoxically worsened on one test but not the robustness check. summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study assessed 10 days of twice-daily home-based transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (t-VNS) using the Parasym device in 24 female long COVID patients (mean age 45.8 years, mean 20.2 months post-infection) with prominent cognitive symptoms. summary: This non-randomized experimental repeated-measures study compared three doses of individualized pulmonary rehabilitation (12, 24, or 36 sessions, twice weekly) in 60 Chilean adults with post-acute sequelae of severe COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, assessed at baseline, end of program, and 1-year follow-up. Crucially, at the 1-year assessment there were no statistically significant between-group differences in most outcomes (except physical FAS, total FAS, PCFS, and bodily pain favoring the 12-session group), suggesting that a shorter personalized program may be sufficient, though the non-randomized design with substantial baseline imbalances limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is explicitly non-randomized; group allocation was by clinical criterion (ability to walk 30 minutes continuously at 12 sessions). Significant baseline imbalances existed between groups in key outcomes (6-MWD, FVC, FEV1, FAS, mMRC, PCFS, Borg), making between-group effect comparisons potentially misleading. Between-group p-values reported in Tables 5 for 1-year follow-up comparisons are from omnibus tests (not pairwise); pairwise p-values listed in table footnotes indicate specific pair(s) significant. The table note for Borg in the 36s group (Table 4) lists STST baseline as '25.22 ± 8.27' which appears to be an error (baseline was 15.22 per Table 1). summary: This single-arm pre-post study enrolled 41 ambulatory long COVID patients in a 12-week individualized exercise program combining 15 minutes of endurance training on a Total Body Trainer with 10-15 minutes of breathing, stretching, and strengthening exercises, conducted 2-3 times per week. Statistically significant improvements were observed in FACIT-Fatigue scores (mean increase 7.41 points from baseline, 95% CI 3.81–11.02, p<0.001, Cohen's f=0.67), 1-minute sit-to-stand test repetitions (median increase from 21 to 24, p<0.001), and workload capacity (median increase from 34W to 79W, p<0.001, Kendall's w=0.76), while the Post-COVID Functional Status Scale score (median 3) remained unchanged. summary: This quasi-experimental single-arm pre-post study evaluated a 4-week personalised digital physiotherapy programme (delivered via Physiotec software with videoconference support) in 32 long COVID patients in Andalusia, Spain. After 4 weeks, statistically significant improvements were observed in functional capacity as measured by the 1-minute sit-to-stand test (14.03 to 17.53 repetitions; Cohen's d=0.45, small effect) and the Short Physical Performance Battery total score (7.90 to 9.12 points; Cohen's d=0.66, medium effect), both exceeding the minimal clinically important difference. Adherence was high (mean 18.66 sessions over 4 weeks), but the absence of a control group severely limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Single-arm study with no control group — all 'between_group_effects' entries represent within-group pre-post comparisons, not true between-group effects. The paper reports p<0.05 (threshold, not exact) and Cohen's d for each outcome; no 95% CIs for within-group changes are reported. The paper states an improvement of 1.21 points for SPPB and 3.50 for 1-min STS in text, consistent with calculated differences from table means (SPPB: 9.12-7.90=1.22, minor rounding). Cohen's d values reported: 1-min STS=0.45, SPPB total=0.66, Balance=0.70, Gait Speed=0.46, Chair Stand=0.43. Effect size r also reported (1-min STS=0.22, SPPB=0.31, Balance=0.33, Gait speed=0.22, Chair stand=0.21). Correlation (paired) reported: 1-min STS=0.81, SPPB=0.72, Balance=0.50, Gait speed=0.72, Chair stand=0.66. No trial_rating computed as this is a quasi-experimental study without randomization.

summary: This single-arm before-and-after feasibility pilot study tested 8 weeks of home-based personalized computerized cognitive training (CogniFit CCT) in 73 adults with self-reported cognitive dysfunction at least 3 months after COVID-19 infection. All five cognitive domains assessed (attention, memory, coordination, perception, reasoning) showed statistically significant improvements from baseline to post-intervention, with mean z-score changes ranging from 0.36 (reasoning) to 1.01 (coordination) and mean percentile gains of 11–18 points. However, the absence of a control group means that practice effects, natural recovery, and regression to the mean cannot be ruled out as explanations for the observed gains.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm before-after study with no control group — between_group_effects arrays are all empty as there is no comparator arm. The 0-800 scale scores are also reported in Table 1 (Attention pre: 361 SD 148, post: 472 SD 141; Memory pre: 384 SD 170, post: 525 SD 185; Coordination pre: 280 SD 167, post: 426 SD 192; Perception pre: 332 SD 115, post: 471 SD 146; Reasoning pre: 348 SD 149, post: 440 SD 169) but were not extracted as separate outcome objects to avoid redundancy with the z-score and percentile outcomes. Dropout: 262 candidates enrolled, 103 completed both assessments, 73 also met the 10-session minimum. Figure 2 (relationship between minutes of training and cognitive gain) contains data only in figure form — not extractable numerically. No adverse events were reported anywhere in the paper.

summary: This single-arm pilot clinical trial enrolled 29 post-COVID-19 patients (mild, moderate, or severe) in a 2-month outpatient pulmonary and functional rehabilitation program consisting of inspiratory muscle training, aerobic exercise, and peripheral muscle strengthening, administered twice weekly for 16 planned sessions. Significant pre-post improvements were observed in 6-minute walk test distance (326 to 445 m, p<0.001), FVC (p=0.004), FEV1 (p=0.001), maximal expiratory pressure (p<0.001), handgrip strength (p<0.011), and patient-reported outcomes including mMRC, CAT, and PCFS (all p<0.001). The absence of a control group precludes causal attribution, but results suggest clinically meaningful gains in functional and respiratory capacity following structured rehabilitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post design with no randomization or control group; classified as quasi-experimental. All between_group_effects entries represent within-arm pre-post comparisons (not between-arm comparisons), as this is a single-arm study. FVC% and FEV1% columns in Table 2 appear to represent ratio of achieved/predicted value (not percent predicted in the usual sense), with values of 3.7 and 2.9 at baseline — these may be data entry errors in the paper or a non-standard reporting format; extracted as verbatim. The paper states sample size calculation required 42 participants but only 29 completed, indicating the study was underpowered. No adverse events were reported anywhere in the paper. Systolic BP: baseline 131.7±15.3, post 128.6±14.8, p=0.272; Diastolic BP: baseline 88.2±10.7, post 85.2±17.7, p=0.432; Oxygen saturation: 96.1±2.6 vs 96.2±2.4, p=1.000 — these vital signs outcomes were not included as separate outcome objects to stay within size limits but all data is available in Table 2.

summary: This single-center randomized trial from Mexico enrolled 54 post-COVID-19 condition patients (all with vitamin D deficiency and prior severe COVID-19 hospitalization) and compared 8 weeks of weekly bolus vs. daily oral cholecalciferol supplementation. Both regimens significantly increased GPx activity (an antioxidant biomarker), while only bolus dosing significantly reduced IL-6 levels and only daily dosing significantly improved HADS anxiety and depression scores. Neither regimen produced statistically significant improvements in cough, dyspnea, or fatigue. The absence of a placebo arm and the self-controlled design preclude causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a self-controlled RCT with two active arms (bolus vs. daily vitamin D) — no placebo control. arm_id=1 assigned to bolus (primary intervention), arm_id=2 to daily (active comparator). 2. Within-group p-values (paired t-test) are the primary statistical results; between-group comparisons are secondary. 3. The between-group p-value for GPx at baseline (p=0.006) is noted in text — suggesting non-equivalent groups at baseline. 4. Between-group effect for HADS anxiety at post-treatment (p=0.01) is verbatim; other between-group p-values for HADS depression and IL-6 post-treatment not explicitly reported (stated only as p>0.05 or not significant). 5. Overall combined results (all 54 patients) also reported: GPx pre 182.42±78.33, post 234.12±113.76 (p=0.0001); IL-6 pre 4.92±9.59, post 2.62±6.40 (p=0.07); HADS anxiety pre 4.04±3.98, post 1.07±2.12 (p=0.0001); HADS depression pre 3.81±4.54, post 1.24±2.35 (p=0.001) — these pooled results not extracted as separate outcomes. 6. The obesity % in Table 1 for bolus group appears to contain a typographic error (42.9% listed as 26 participants out of 28, which would be ~92.9%; likely should be 42.9% = ~12 participants). 7. No intermediate 30-day biomarker results were reported numerically. 8. Trial registered at ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06419712.

summary: This single-arm pre-post study enrolled 31 long COVID patients in Poland who underwent 15 sessions of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) at 2.5 ATA. Significant improvements were observed across multiple domains including quality of life (EQ-5D-5L VAS: 67.8 to 83.6, p<0.001), aerobic endurance (two-minute step test: ~92 to 126 steps, p<0.001), venous lactate levels (1.35 to 1.06 mmol/L, p=0.025), working memory (p=0.015), and attention/concentration (p<0.001). However, the absence of a control group severely limits causal inference, as improvements may reflect natural recovery rather than HBOT effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study with no randomization or control group — classified as quasi-experimental, not RCT. Many Fullerton test subscores (dynamometer, back scratch, sit and reach by timepoint) are reported only in supplementary Table S2 which was not available in the full text provided. Spirometry values (FEV1, FVC, FEF25-75) are described narratively and in supplementary figures/tables but specific means/SDs by timepoint were not extractable from the provided text. Anion gap change p=0.0245 is stated but no means/SDs reported for anion gap in text. Subjective symptom questionnaire results (headache, fatigue, sleep, etc.) are described as significant (p<0.001) but numeric scores are in supplementary Table S1, not available here. EQ-5D-5L domain distributions (walking, self-care, daily activities, pain, anxiety/depression) extracted as percentages reporting 'no problems' category. Follow-up duration stated as '2-24 weeks' making precise weeks_from_randomization calculation impossible. Between-group effect entries for pre-post comparisons within a single arm use 'baseline_vs_posttreatment' as the comparison label rather than arm1_vs_arm2, since there is no control arm.

summary: This prospective before-and-after interventional study evaluated an 8-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program (45-min sessions, 3x/week, combining cycle ergometer and progressive resistance exercises) in 60 post-COVID-19 syndrome patients in Brazil. All participants showed significant improvements (p<0.001) in dynamic balance (TUG: 8.2 to 6.2 s), functional capacity (6MWT distance: 482 to 587 m), walking speed, distance-saturation product, and self-reported functional status (DASI: 29.5 to 56.3). Improvements were similar between mild/moderate and severe/critical subgroups with no statistically significant intergroup differences; however, the study lacked a control group, limiting causal interpretation.

summary: This single-arm prospective pilot study enrolled 20 patients with long COVID or post-COVID-19 conditions who had general fatigue and were prescribed hochuekkito (a traditional Japanese Kampo herbal medicine at 7.5 g/day) for 8 weeks at a specialized outpatient clinic in Japan. The primary outcome, the Japanese version of the Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), decreased from a mean of 35.9 (SD 5.9) at baseline to 31.2 (SD 9.4) at 8 weeks in the 13 patients with complete data, a mean reduction of 4.7 points (95% CI: 0.5–8.9), which exceeds the minimal clinically important difference of 4 points. As a single-arm study with no control group, it is not possible to attribute this improvement to hochuekkito versus natural recovery, and the authors note a planned RCT is underway.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm observational pilot study, not an RCT; design_type set to quasi-experimental. There is no control arm, so between_group_effects array is empty for all outcomes. The paper enrolled 20 patients but only 13 had complete baseline and 8-week FAS data; n_analyzed=13 for primary endpoint and baseline (the 13 who completed). The paper reports the 95% CI as 0.5–8.9 for the improvement (decrease), so ci_95_low and ci_95_high are reported as negative values (-8.9 to -0.5) in the change_from_baseline arm_result to reflect direction of change. The paper does not report adverse events. The time_since_infection_months_mean of 5.3 months is the median per the table (shown as '5.3 (1.5–13.5)' with range), treated as mean per abstract. summary: This single-arm pilot trial enrolled 13 post-COVID-19 patients with upper limb impairment following severe COVID-19 hospitalization to evaluate a 6-week robotic hand exoskeleton rehabilitation program (RobHand, 4 sessions/week, 45 min each). summary: This Swiss single-arm pilot study (n=7) of ME/CFS patients with post-COVID-19 condition and elevated GPCR autoantibodies evaluated 4 sessions of therapeutic plasmapheresis plus low-dose IVIG (2g Octagam per session) over approximately 60 days, with repeated measures of psychometric outcomes (EQ-5D-5L, ISI, FSS, HADS) at baseline, after 2nd PE, and after 4th PE. summary: This before-after case-controlled trial (n=5) tested whether adding spinal cord transcutaneous stimulation (scTS) to respiratory training (RT) improved respiratory function in post-acute COVID-19 patients with FVC deficits. All participants first completed 10 daily sessions of RT alone, then 10 daily sessions of scTS combined with RT. Compared to RT alone, scTS+RT produced significantly greater improvements in FVC (2.28 to 2.99 L, p=0.034), percent-predicted FVC (54.4% to 69.6%, p=0.023), PEF (1.52 to 2.11 L/s, p=0.023), and tPEF (0.56 to 0.43 s, p=0.013), with an average effect size twice that of RT alone (1.46 vs 0.78), though the study's single-arm sequential design, absence of a control group, and n=5 severely limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-cohort sequential crossover design, not a true RCT. All 5 participants received RT first (arm_id=2 in this extraction), then scTS+RT (arm_id=1). Arm_id=2 represents the RT-alone phase (both serving as baseline context and as a comparator). The study reports paired within-subject before-after comparisons using paired t-tests and Signed Rank tests, not between-group comparisons in the traditional sense. For PIF and PEF at baseline, the paper uses Median ± MAD notation (non-normally distributed); values labeled as mean±SD in results text are actually median±MAD for these outcomes at some timepoints — noted in context. The PEF outcome at baseline shows '1.15 ± 0.37' and post-RT '1.38 ± 0.04' labeled as Median ± MAD. Pre-scTS PEF is listed as '1.52 ± 0.49' and post-scTS as '2.11 ± 0.49' with mean±SD notation; these may represent a switch to normal distribution at post-scTS timepoint or inconsistent reporting. Effect size data (Cohen's d per outcome) are shown in Figure 5 but not tabulated numerically in text beyond the averages (RT: 0.78±0.70; scTS+RT: 1.46±0.38). Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and VAS pain were monitored as safety outcomes but no numeric data reported. No adverse events formally reported. Conflict of interest noted: Gerasimenko holds shareholder interest in Cosyma Inc., manufacturer of the Neostim-5 device used.

summary: This Ukrainian quasi-experimental study compared one versus two daily sessions of early inpatient physical rehabilitation (positioning, verticalization, breathing exercises) in 102 severe COVID-19 ICU patients (n=51 per group). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study (no control group, no randomization) despite being labelled a 'prospective intervention study'. The paper incorrectly uses 'quasi-experimental' framing. SF-36 Pain subscale shows a counterintuitive direction: baseline mean 84.05 is very high (lower pain burden = higher score in SF-36), dropping to 28.4 post-intervention — this is coded as pain worsening on the scale but authors describe it as improvement; the scale may be reported as a 'pain interference/limitation' subscale where lower is better (pain scales vary in direction). The change score of 55.65 is coded as positive in the paper. The 6MWT was measured in laps of a 30m corridor rather than meters, making cross-study comparison difficult. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study, not an RCT. The SD column in Table 2 appears mislabeled — the values reported as 'S.D' (e.g., fatigue BT S.D = 0.89) are plausible SDs, but the column labeled 'S.E' (e.g., 0.18) and values labeled 't score' appear to be one-sample t-statistics (mean/SE), not two-sample between-group t-tests. The 't score at 0.01 level of significance' column likely represents t = mean/SE for each timepoint separately rather than a BT vs AT comparison t-test; no paired t-test p-value is explicitly stated. The SD field was left null and SE was populated from the paper's 'S.E' column. The '99% confidence interval' column values (e.g., 0.46 for fatigue BT) appear to be half-widths of the CI rather than full CI bounds, and represent 99% CI (not 95%), so ci_95_low/high were left null. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Critical design caveat: this is NOT a randomized trial — the two arms differ by COVID-19 history, not by treatment assignment; both arms received the same hydrogymnastics intervention. summary: This pre-experimental single-arm pre-post study enrolled 60 post-COVID OPD patients in Pune, India with persistent respiratory problems and assessed the effect of diaphragmatic deep breathing exercises on dyspnoea and related symptoms. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed a statistically significant reduction in dyspnoea median score from 1.0 (mild) pre-intervention to 0.0 (no dyspnoea) post-intervention (p<0.001), with the proportion of patients with no dyspnoea increasing from 30% to 78.3%. The absence of a control group means these findings cannot be attributed to the intervention with confidence, and the study duration and exercise protocol details were not reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a pre-experimental (quasi-experimental) single-arm pre-post design — there is NO control group. Between-group effect sizes cannot be calculated. 2) The intervention duration and frequency of breathing exercise sessions are not specified anywhere in the paper. 3) Age is only reported in categorical bands (18-35: 30%, 36-50: 43.3%, 51-65: 26.7%); no mean or SD available. 4) Symptom data for cough, chest pain, and cold are only reported at baseline (pre-intervention); post-intervention data for these outcomes are not reported. 5) Oxygen saturation and respiratory rate are mentioned as measured parameters (Section II-A) but no numeric results are presented in text or tables. 6) The Wilcoxon test result is stated as p<0.001, which is a threshold not an exact value. 7) The table caption for Table 1 appears to have the percentage descriptions reversed for chest pain (text says 70% had no chest pain and 30% had chest pain, but the table header says 'majority 70% patient were reported chest pain' — based on the table data, 30% had chest pain and 70% did not; extracted per table data). 8) Graph 1 and Graph 2 show dyspnoea comparison figures but the underlying data are also captured in tables 1.1 and 1.2.

summary: This single-arm pre-post study conducted in Kazakhstan assessed 11 days of medicinal leech therapy (hirudotherapy) in 83 long COVID patients (symptoms >6 months) with cognitive, autonomic, and sleep complaints. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Study design is highly problematic: authors call it 'case-control' but it is effectively a single-arm pre-post cohort with a separate normative/healthy control group (n=50) for reference comparison only, not as a concurrent intervention control. Between-group effects presented are all within-subject (pre vs post) comparisons, not true between-arm comparisons; these are noted in outcome_id 1 as an example but not calculated for all outcomes to avoid redundancy. summary: This single-arm pre-post study enrolled 21 post-COVID-19 adults (mean age 58 years, 71% female, none previously hospitalized) in an 8-week water-based exercise program conducted twice weekly for 60 minutes per session across sites in Slovenia, Croatia, and Serbia. Fatigue (MFI-20) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) were assessed before and after the intervention. No significant changes were observed in MFI total score (53.43 to 56.24, p=0.10) or EQ-5D-5L VAS (77.06 to 78.76, p=0.84); the only statistically significant within-group change was a worsening of reduced motivation scores (p=0.04), and MFI total worsened significantly in females only (p=0.04). The absence of a control group, high dropout rate (72 enrolled, 21 completed), and low baseline symptom burden severely limit interpretation of these results.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a single-arm pre-post study with no control/comparator arm; all 'between_group_effects' are pre-post within-group comparisons. summary: This double-blind pilot RCT (n=30) in post-COVID women who had undergone lower segment Caesarean section compared 12 weeks of combined body-weight, abdominal strengthening, and breathing exercise (Group B) versus general breathing plus upper/lower limb strengthening exercises (Group A). Both groups showed significant within-group improvements in abdominal muscle thickness (ultrasonography), upper limb strength (dynamometer), and lower limb endurance (sit-up test), but Group B demonstrated substantially greater post-test gains across all three outcomes (post-test means: USG 4.00 vs 2.47; dynamometer 27.87 vs 17.27; sit-up 11.40 vs 9.13). Between-group comparisons were reported as significant but no SDs, CIs, or exact p-values were provided, substantially limiting the interpretability of the results.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical data quality issue: no standard deviations are reported for any outcome mean (baseline or post-test), making effect size calculation impossible. The paper states p<0.0001 for all within-group comparisons but provides no between-group test statistics, exact p-values, or confidence intervals. Arm assignment in text is ambiguous — Group A is described first in methods as the control (breathing + general strengthening) but the results section reports Group B (combined exercises) first; arm_id=1 has been assigned to Group B (intervention) per extraction convention. Graphs referenced (Graphs 1-3) contain no extractable numeric data beyond what is in the text. The 'sit-up test' is described as measuring 'lower limb strength' which is anatomically inconsistent — it primarily measures abdominal/core endurance. Units for ultrasonography and dynamometer measurements are not specified in the text. The odd-even randomization method is quasi-random and does not constitute proper allocation concealment. The paper is from a predatory-risk journal and represents a very small pilot (n=15/arm) with multiple methodological concerns.

summary: This 4-week RCT (n=30) compared aerobic exercise plus balance training plus relaxation versus relaxation alone in post-COVID-19 patients aged 45-65 with anxiety and dizziness. The intervention group showed significantly greater improvements in Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores (17.2 vs 21.73 post-treatment, p=0.005), Berg Balance Scale scores (45.47 vs 35.07, p=0.0002), and Maximum Voluntary Ventilation (117.2 vs 108.13 L/min, p=0.0002) compared to the relaxation-only control group. Both groups improved significantly from baseline, but the combined aerobic and balance exercise program was superior across all three outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Several data quality concerns: (1) The abstract states participant ages 45-65 years but the demographic table reports Group A mean age 28.4±2.11 and Group B 29.6±3.68 — a likely reporting error or mislabeled rows. The discussion also states '30 patients aged between 40 and 60 years', inconsistent with both. Ages used are verbatim from Table 1. (2) Table 4 (MVV) has scrambled column layout with merged/misaligned cells; values were extracted from text narrative which is clearer. (3) Paper is published in Journal of Neonatal Surgery which is unrelated to the topic — possible predatory/hijacked journal. (4) The MVV improvement percentages (77.27% for Group A, 42.20% for Group B) appear inconsistent with the raw means (approximately 13% and 9% change respectively); likely errors in the paper. (5) No blinding described; open-label design is a major limitation. (6) Baseline BBS scores show a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.026) despite randomization, suggesting potential allocation failure. (7) Study conducted May-June 2020 during acute pandemic — patients may not meet contemporary long COVID definitions (symptom duration not reported). (8) No confidence intervals reported for any outcome.

summary: This single-arm retrospective pilot study evaluated stellate ganglion block (SGB) in 17 patients with long COVID symptoms including fatigue, autonomic dysfunction, anxiety, and PTSD. Patients showed statistically significant improvements in Fatigue Severity Scale scores (median 58 vs. 49, p=0.002) and resting heart rate (83.1 vs. 73.1 bpm, p=0.008) one week post-procedure. Reductions in PCL-5 (PTSD) and GAD-7 (anxiety) scores were not statistically significant, though a ~5-point PCL-5 decrease was considered clinically meaningful; the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post observational study with no control group — not an RCT. The design_type is 'quasi-experimental' and there are no between-group effects in the traditional sense; all 'between_group_effects' entries represent pre-vs-post within the single arm (Wilcoxon signed-rank or paired t-test). COMPASS-31 post-procedure numeric values are not reported in Table 2 (only pre-procedure subscales and total given in Table 1); p-value for COMPASS-31 not stated. Table 2 had a merged/partially garbled cell for Heart Rate — values reconstructed from text: pre 83.1±10.1, post 73.1±11.7 bpm. FSS analyzed by Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric), reported as median/IQR; n for post-FSS is 16 (1 patient completed only COMPASS-31 post-procedure). PCL-5 post-procedure n is ambiguous: 10 completed pre+post PCL-5, but footnote b states 'missing pre-procedure data for 3 patients and post-procedure data for 6 patients' — likely n=10 for pre (of 17, missing 3 who didn't complete it) and n=11 for post (missing 6), but reported means appear to be for the 10 who completed both. summary: This quasi-experimental study from Kyrgyzstan evaluated normobaric intermittent hypoxytherapy in post-COVID-19 patients with respiratory dysfunction, comparing spirometric outcomes (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio, peak inspiratory flow) against an untreated post-COVID-19 group and healthy controls. After hypoxytherapy, FVC increased from 3.83 to 4.03 L (p<0.05), FEV1 increased from approximately 2.54 to 3.44 L, the FEV1/FVC ratio improved significantly (mean 94.6% vs 73.8% pre-treatment, p=0.023 Wilcoxon), and peak inspiratory flow improved to near-control levels (5.88 vs 6.08 L/s, p=0.647 vs controls). These findings suggest hypoxytherapy may benefit post-COVID-19 pulmonary rehabilitation, though the study is substantially limited by the absence of randomization, unclear sample sizes, garbled data in tables, and placeholder values in the abstract.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Major data quality issues: (1) The abstract uses literal placeholder text 'X%', 'Y%', 'Z%' for key effect estimates, indicating the paper was published with incomplete results. (2) Table 2 (FEV1 values) has garbled/merged cell content — 'OEF 1' appears to be a transliteration of FEV1; the 'before therapy' column shows '2.54,54' which likely means 2.54 with SE 0.007 and 'after hypoxic' column shows '3.44 4.2' which likely means 3.44 (treated) and 4.2 (control) — values extracted with best-effort interpretation. (3) Sample sizes are never stated explicitly; n=17 per patient group and n=27 for controls are inferred from Table 8 (FEV1/FVC distribution counts: 24+1+1+1 = 27 control, 8+1+1+0+3+2+1+1 = 17 pre-treatment, 4+6+4+0+0+2+1+0 = 17 post-treatment). (4) The paper states 'post-COVID-19 cohort (n = [insert sample size])' — another unfilled placeholder. (5) Treatment protocol duration and frequency are not specified. (6) No randomization: this is a non-randomized controlled study, not an RCT. (7) Table 3 comparisons appear to compare arm1 (treated post-COVID) vs arm3 (controls) and arm2 (untreated post-COVID) vs arm3 (controls); P2→3 Wilcoxon likely compares pre-treatment vs post-treatment within the treated group. Interpretation of group comparisons is uncertain due to ambiguous table labeling.

summary: This target trial emulation used propensity score-matched data from 910 long COVID patients in the French ComPaRe e-cohort to evaluate whether COVID-19 vaccination (first injection) reduces long COVID symptoms compared to remaining unvaccinated. At 120 days, vaccinated patients had significantly lower long COVID symptom severity (ST score MD -1.8, 95% CI -3.0 to -0.5) and life impact (IT score MD -3.3, 95% CI -5.7 to -1.0), and doubled the remission rate (16.6% vs 7.5%; HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.15). summary: This observational cross-sectional study compared post-COVID-19 psychiatric and somatic outcomes in 246 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors who had either received IL-6 receptor inhibitors during acute illness (tocilizumab, n=67; sarilumab, n=21) or had not (controls, n=158). The primary finding was that controls had significantly higher emotion dysregulation scores on the DERS (mean 83.08 vs. 77.06 for tocilizumab; p<0.01 after covariate adjustment), with no significant differences in depression, anxiety, PTSD, sleep, anhedonia, or hopelessness between groups. Controls also had more post-COVID physical symptoms including dyspnea on exertion, cough, headache, and diarrhea, suggesting that receipt of anti-IL-6-R therapy during acute COVID-19 hospitalization may be associated with a lower long-COVID symptom burden, though confounding by indication limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional observational study with no pre/post within-subject measurements — all outcomes reflect status at a single post-COVID evaluation visit. The 'treatment' (tocilizumab/sarilumab) was administered during acute COVID-19 hospitalization months prior to evaluation (mean ~155-173 days from symptom onset). The DERS was the only outcome showing significant group differences. The paper also reports an Anti-IL-6-R combined group (N=88) across Tables 1-2 that pools TOC+SAR; both combined and three-group comparisons were extracted. Three-group Kruskal-Wallis p-values are reported in Table 4; post-hoc Mann-Whitney p-values per pair are also reported and used here. The DERS between-group effect for TOC vs Ctrl (arm1_vs_arm3) p-value of <0.01 was reported verbatim in Table 4; the calculated mean difference of -6.02 is derived from table means. YMRS/MRS (Young Mania Rating Scale) scores are mentioned in Table 2 (0.89 ± 1.44 Ctrl; 0.89 ± 1.43 Anti-IL-6-R) and Table 4 (0.89 ± 1.44 Ctrl; 0.85 ± 1.39 TOC; 1.00 ± 1.58 SAR) but were omitted from outcomes list to stay within size limit — all p-values non-significant. Time-since-infection values converted from days to months as follows: Ctrl 173.38d = 5.78mo SD=3.23mo; TOC 152.96d = 5.10mo SD=3.00mo; SAR 163.29d = 5.44mo SD=2.78mo. The study enrolled patients between April 2020 and May 2022 prior to vaccine availability.

summary: This prospective observational before-after study evaluated 12-day spa therapy (balneotherapy and/or inhalation crenotherapy) in 78 post-COVID-19 patients with pre-existing chronic joint, musculoskeletal, skin, or respiratory diseases at three Italian spas. Spa therapy produced statistically significant reductions in VAS scores for nearly all post-COVID-19 symptoms including chronic fatigue (-47%), muscle pain (-48%), brain fog (-41%), and persistent cough (-68%), as well as significant improvements across all eight SF-36 quality of life dimensions (all p<0.0001), with the largest gains in role limitations due to physical (+72%) and emotional (+66%) functioning. The study lacked a randomized control arm, making it impossible to distinguish treatment effects from natural recovery or placebo effects; nonetheless, improvements were consistently observed across sexes, with females tending to show greater percent improvements in QoL dimensions despite lower baseline scores.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm before-after study for the post-COVID-19 group; arm 2 (never-infected subjects, N=38) also received spa therapy and serves only as an unexposed comparator for QoL, not as a true control. The N for never-infected subjects used for QoL comparison was stated as 38 in Table 4 but the total cohort of subjects who never had COVID-19 is not clearly enumerated (the 159 total minus 121 who contracted SARS-CoV-2 = 38 never-infected). Table 2 provides sex-stratified VAS data for post-COVID-19 patients but note that in Table 1 the joint pain VAS before=2.0±0.8, after=1.6±1.0, while Table 2 shows females joint pain before=2.9±0.9, after=1.6±1.1 and males=3.2±0.7, after=1.7±0.9 — the Table 1 overall value appears inconsistent with sex-stratified values; likely different sub-Ns were used for the overall vs sex-stratified analyses. Cohen's d values for SF-36 comparisons between post-COVID and never-infected groups were reported in Supplementary Table S3 (not extracted in full). Logistic regression results are reported in Supplementary Table S4 (summary included in text). VAS scores for symptoms in Table 1 reflect only the subset of patients who reported each symptom, not the full N=78. The Tinnitus, pseudo-freezing, gastroesophageal reflux, sore throat, persistent loss of smell, burning skin, hair loss, dysphony, nausea, itching, earache, dysphagia, vomiting, nasal congestion, and irritability outcomes are omitted from the outcomes array due to output size constraints but all numeric data are present in Table 1 and Table 2.

summary: This single-center retrospective open-label cohort study evaluated palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) 600 mg twice daily for approximately 3 months in 33 long COVID patients in Italy, comparing outcomes between those previously hospitalized (n=12) and those managed at home (n=21) during acute COVID-19. Both groups showed statistically significant improvement in Post-COVID-19 Functional Status (PCFS) scores after PEA treatment (p<0.0001 for home care; p=0.0004 for hospitalized), but home care patients achieved substantially greater functional improvement (PCFS T1: 1.03±1.19 vs. 2.2±1.1, p=0.01). No adverse effects from PEA were reported. The absence of a control group and no adjustment for confounding (particularly disease severity and co-treatments) substantially limits causal interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is effectively a single-arm pre-post design with a post-hoc subgroup comparison (hospitalized vs. home care); the two 'arms' are defined by prior acute illness management, not by treatment assignment — all 33 patients received the same PEA intervention. The overall PCFS values in Table 2 for 'Total' show PCFS T0=3.12±0.65 and T1=1.03±1.19, but the T1 value listed for 'Total' matches the home care arm exactly (both 1.03±1.19), which may be a table error. The overall within-group p-value is reported as p=0.0000 for the total sample. The SI score in Table 2 also lists Total and Home Care identically (2.03±1.05), suggesting a possible data entry issue in the original paper. Odds ratio for hospitalization in smokers vs. non-smokers reported as 8.13 with CI [0.233, 1.167] — this CI appears to be on the log scale or contains a typographic error in the original paper (a CI spanning less than 1 would indicate a non-significant result, inconsistent with stated RR of 4.17). Extracted verbatim from paper without correction.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:critical, selection:serious, classification:moderate, deviations:serious, missing_data:low, measurement:moderate, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Critical confounding: all 152 patients had pre-existing autonomic dysfunction and were already on autonomic therapy before COVID-19, making it impossible to separate COVID-19 effects from pre-existing disease trajectory; no comparison group of long COVID patients without pre-existing autonomic dysfunction; unblinded; proprietary device (lead author is co-founder of device manufacturer).

summary: This retrospective, hypothesis-generating, single-arm before-after study followed 152 patients with pre-existing autonomic dysfunction who had undergone P&S (parasympathetic/sympathetic) testing and treatment prior to COVID-19 infection, then were re-tested and re-treated after developing long COVID. Post-COVID-19, patients showed a significant increase in autonomic dysfunction burden (mean 2.34 to 3.67 dysfunctions, p=0.004) and symptom burden (mean 9.74 to 14.6 of 28 symptoms), with parasympathetic excess becoming the dominant dysfunction (27.0% to 46.7%) and sympathetic withdrawal decreasing in relative prevalence. Following resumed autonomic therapy (Midodrine, Alpha-Lipoic Acid, Nortriptyline, and low-intensity exercise), both autonomic dysfunction count (3.67 to 1.63, p=0.003) and symptom count (14.6 to 7.44, p=0.004) were significantly reduced, supporting the hypothesis that targeted autonomic therapy may be beneficial in long COVID, though the lack of a control group and highly selected population (pre-existing autonomic disease) severely limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study has a highly unusual and confounded design: all participants had pre-existing autonomic dysfunction and were already receiving autonomic therapy BEFORE COVID-19 infection. This is not a typical long COVID treatment trial but a retrospective outcomes study in a pre-selected clinical population. 2. The paper does not report SDs for any of the continuous outcomes (symptom counts, dysfunction counts) — only means and p-values are given, limiting meta-analytic utility. 3. The pre-COVID follow-up therapy duration was stated as 'less than 9 months' and post-COVID therapy duration as 'less than 6 months' — no exact durations are reported, making follow-up_weeks not calculable. 4. The p-values reported in Table 3 compare row to row within the pre-COVID or post-COVID phase (e.g., pre-COVID baseline vs. pre-COVID follow-up; post-COVID baseline vs. post-COVID follow-up) — not all pairwise comparisons are reported. The p-value for post-COVID vs. pre-COVID baseline for symptoms is stated in text as p<0.001 for the increase to 14.6. 5. Lead author (Colombo) has a conflict of interest as co-founder of Physio PS, Inc., manufacturer of the P&S Monitor 4.0 device used for all measurements. 6. IRB statement is non-standard (HIPPA rather than HIPAA, no formal IRB approval stated). 7. The paper states results are based on Pearson correlation and Student's t-test (SPSS v.20) but does not report test statistics or effect sizes beyond means and p-values.

summary: This propensity-score matched retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX global health research network to investigate whether omega-3 PUFA supplementation (taken before COVID-19 diagnosis) was associated with lower risk of post-COVID-19 psychiatric sequelae in 16,962 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients matched 1:1 to controls. Omega-3 users had a significantly lower risk of developing any psychiatric sequelae (HR 0.804, 95% CI 0.729–0.888, p<0.001), including depression (HR 0.828), anxiety (HR 0.833), and insomnia (HR 0.679) in the 90-day to 1-year follow-up window. Significant protective associations were also observed for cough and myalgia, but not for fatigue, cognitive symptoms, chest pain, or abnormal breathing, and benefits were consistent across most demographic subgroups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm event counts for individual psychiatric outcomes (depression, anxiety, insomnia) and all somatic secondary outcomes were not reported in the paper text — only composite psychiatric sequelae counts (633 omega-3, 1048 non-omega-3) were stated. All individual outcome HRs are from Table 2 and Table 3 (tables not included in full text provided). Pre-matching sample sizes reported (16,962 omega-3; 2,248,803 non-omega-3) but post-matching Ns for matched cohort not stated. Omega-3 dose, formulation, and duration of supplementation were not captured in the TriNetX database and are not reported. The study examines pre-COVID-19 omega-3 exposure as a preventive intervention rather than a long COVID treatment — the 'long COVID' framing refers to post-acute sequelae emerging 90 days to 1 year after infection.

summary: This randomised pilot trial tested a single half-day online group intervention combining narrative therapy ('journey of life') and breathing retraining, co-designed with young people, for 32 adolescents aged 12–18 with Long COVID attending tertiary NHS clinics in London. The primary outcome was the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) Impact Score; both intervention and control groups improved slightly over six months (mean reduction of 1.17 vs 0.92 respectively), but there was no statistically significant difference between groups on any measure. All secondary outcomes—wellness score, quality of life, fatigue, Nijmegen breathing questionnaire, and exercise capacity—improved over time in both groups with no between-group differences. A notable finding was that 84% of participants had breathing pattern disorders at baseline despite normal spirometry, highlighting this as an underrecognised feature of Long COVID in adolescents.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper states 'timepoint 2' without specifying the exact weeks; 6 months is inferred from the intervention period described. 2. For the SDQ primary outcome, baseline n for intervention arm is 15 and for control is 10 (per Table 2), which is less than randomized Ns, suggesting missing baseline data. 3. summary: This study tested weekly intravenous C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH, RUCONEST) against placebo in 10 adults with persistent neurological symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection, using a randomized double-blind crossover design. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a proteomic mechanistic sub-study of parent RCT NCT04705831 (Melamed et al. Front Neurol 2025); it does NOT report per-arm means, SDs, or between-group effect sizes for the clinical outcome measures (MoCA, FSS, RBANS, MIDAS, GSRS, HIT-6, BDI-II, present pain intensity) — those quantitative data are exclusively in the parent trial publication. All quantitative outcome data in this paper are proteomic: log2 fold-changes and Spearman rho correlation coefficients between protein changes and clinical change scores. The 'effect_value' fields in outcomes 10-17 contain Spearman rho values (not SMDs); the 'smd' effect_measure type was used as the closest available field since rho is a correlation coefficient rather than a between-group effect size in the conventional sense. Protein-level log2FC data appear predominantly in figures and supplementary Excel files (not reproduced as numeric tables in the text), preventing full numeric extraction. Arm 1 n=4 and Arm 2 n=6 reflect an imbalanced crossover allocation noted by the authors as a feasibility constraint. summary: This randomized sham-controlled pilot trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — a non-invasive ear-based electrical nerve stimulation device — in 45 adults with persistent fatigue following COVID-19 infection, comparing above-threshold stimulation, sub-threshold stimulation, and sham (inactive electrode) over 4 weeks. Fatigue scores on the MFI-20 improved across all three groups, but no statistically significant differences were found between the active stimulation arms and sham, meaning taVNS did not outperform placebo on the primary outcome. The device was well tolerated with only mild side effects (skin irritation and vertigo each in 7.7% of participants), though the 8.9% dropout rate was higher than prior taVNS studies.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: All quantitative outcome data (per-arm means, SDs, medians for MFI-20 subscales, BDI-2, PCSS, and all SF-36 domains) are presented exclusively in figures (Fig. 1A-R) and in a Supplementary Table 1 that was not provided in the paper text. No numeric values (means, SDs, CIs, or p-values for between-group comparisons) are reported in the main text or any extractable table. Only selected within-group intragroup p-values are mentioned narratively (e.g., General Fatigue Verum1 baseline-to-visit1 p=0.009; Physical Fatigue Verum1 p=0.037; Mental Fatigue Sham p=0.03; Reduced Activity Sham p=0.025; Reduced Motivation Verum1 p=0.035; BDI Verum1 p=0.015; SF-36 Physical Functioning Sham p=0.013; SF-36 Bodily Pain Verum2 p=0.043; SF-36 Vitality Sham p=0.018; SF-36 Social Functioning Verum2 p=0.009; SF-36 Health Transition Sham p=0.026). No between-group p-values or effect sizes are reported numerically. The 236 min/day mean stimulation duration is an overall mean across all groups; per-arm breakdown not reported. Adverse events are reported as overall counts (not broken down by arm). The primary endpoint (MFI-20) was powered for the 20-item total score but the paper only discusses subscales; the power calculation referenced MFI-20 total but no total score data are extractable. Study design was modified mid-trial to add a crossover extension phase for Sham and Verum1 participants; outcomes at visit 2 (week 8) reflect crossover to Verum2 for those subgroups, not continued original allocation. Dropout allocation: 2 Sham, 1 Verum1, 1 Verum2 dropped out shortly after visit 0; additionally 2 Verum1 and 2 Sham declined crossover after visit 1 (these are separate from the primary 4-week completers).

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant between-group differences detected on MFI-20 at any timepoint; paper reports 'no significant differences (Pdiff) could be observed between the visits or within the groups' with no p-value for the primary between-group comparison exceeding the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of p=0.017.

summary: This retrospective multi-center study from three hospitals in Zhejiang, China developed and validated a machine learning model to predict which Long COVID patients (n=330) would respond to a 14-day course of low-dose oral methylprednisolone (8 mg daily). The primary outcome was a clinically meaningful improvement in quality of life, defined as a greater than 10-point increase in SF-36 total score; 266 of 330 patients (81%) met this threshold. A logistic regression model using seven clinical features—fatigue, SF-36 score, lung function (FEV1/FVC), sleep quality (PSQI), IL-6, CRP, and neutrophil percentage—achieved AUC values of 0.87–0.87 across external validation cohorts, and the study found that patients with higher inflammation markers (CRP, IL-6) and lower baseline quality of life were most likely to respond. This is a prediction tool study with no control arm, so the overall effectiveness of methylprednisolone itself versus no treatment cannot be determined from this data.

summary: This study tested whether a single session of the six-minute step test (6MST), a submaximal stepping exercise, could acutely improve blood vessel function in 26 adults with long COVID compared to 21 healthy controls. The primary outcome was brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD%), a measure of endothelial function: long COVID participants showed a significant increase in FMD% immediately after the 6MST (4.53% before vs. 6.83% after, p=0.0005, Cohen's d=1.038), though their post-exercise values remained well below those of healthy controls (6.83% vs. 10.07%, p=0.002). The long COVID group also had reduced exercise capacity, lower peak oxygen uptake, higher diastolic blood pressure, and greater leg fatigue during the test; notably, cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 peak) did not independently predict the vascular improvement after adjustment for confounders.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a non-randomized cross-sectional observational study, not an RCT — the 'arms' represent comparison groups (long COVID vs healthy controls), not randomized treatment allocations. Per-arm means and SDs for VO2 peak (mL/kg/min) are referenced in the univariate regression table (Table 3) and in-text but exact group-level means and SDs are not explicitly tabulated — only the regression coefficient and R² are reported. Cardiorespiratory variables (VO2, VCO2, VE, RER over time during 6MST) are presented only in figures (Fig. 4) with no tabular data available. SBP data across time points are fully tabulated but no significant between-group differences were found; these are not extracted as separate outcomes to manage output size. The paper does not report formal adverse events. The study self-describes as cross-sectional observational. Risk of bias applied using RoB2 adapted for the non-randomized design context. The FMD% pre-control value is stated as '9.88 ± 2.67' in one paragraph and the between-group post-6MST comparison references '10.07 ± 2.66' — both verbatim values are extracted at their respective timepoints.

trial_rating.result_basis: FMD% increased from 4.53% to 6.83% post-6MST in long COVID group (p=0.0005, Cohen's d=1.038); no control intervention arm, cross-sectional design only.

summary: This pilot randomised controlled trial tested a 12-week remotely delivered physical activity (PA) coaching programme — combining wearable activity tracking, weekly one-to-one physiotherapist sessions, personalised feedback, and collaborative goal-setting — against usual care in 50 adults with Long COVID (mean age 46, 76% female, averaging 42 months post-infection). The primary outcome was feasibility: recruitment (89%), retention (92%), and adherence (83%) all met pre-specified thresholds, with no adverse events. At three months, the coaching group walked approximately 4,600 more steps per day and covered 119 metres further on the six-minute walk test compared to usual care, with improvements in fatigue (FACIT-FS +11 points), dyspnoea (mMRC −1 grade), and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L +21 points); these gains were maintained or grew at six months. Anxiety and depression scores did not improve, and baseline imbalances in dyspnoea severity and time since infection between groups are a notable limitation of this small pilot.
