summary: This randomized controlled trial tested speleotherapy (underground climate therapy — spending 2 hours per session, six sessions over three weeks, in certified therapeutic caves) as an add-on to standard treatment in 42 adults with Long COVID across nine centers in Germany, Austria, and Italy. The primary outcome for the Long COVID subgroup was improvement in lung function (FEV₁, FVC, PEF) and respiratory muscle strength, neither of which improved significantly in the speleotherapy group; FEV₁ actually improved more in the control group. However, patients receiving speleotherapy reported significant improvements in dysfunctional breathing (Nijmegen Questionnaire, p=0.014), dyspnea (p=0.026 post-treatment, p=0.001 at 3-month follow-up), problems with stair climbing and muscle exertion (p=0.042), and anxiety and sleep disturbances (p=0.021). The trial was underpowered for the Long COVID subgroup (n=42, power 0.7), was retrospectively registered, and the lead investigator is president of the German Speleotherapy Association and received payment for organizing the study.

summary: This Belgian feasibility RCT tested whether adding personalised nutritional counselling (via weekly dietitian teleconsultations) to pacing-based physiotherapy improved physical performance in 65 adults with Long COVID (mean symptom duration ~78 weeks), compared to standard physiotherapy alone over 12 weeks with 6-week follow-up. The primary exploratory outcome was the 1-minute sit-to-stand test (1-MSTS): the combined therapy group gained roughly 1 more repetition than controls at 12 weeks (mean difference 0.97 repetitions, 95% CI −1.75 to 3.70), a non-significant and clinically uncertain difference, though the gap widened to 2.14 repetitions (95% CI −1.26 to 5.54) at 18-week follow-up. The trial was primarily designed to assess feasibility rather than efficacy, and was not powered to detect significant effects; dropout reached 27.7% by follow-up, partly due to high study burden from frequent hospital visits.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Participants with lower baseline capacity (<75% predicted) achieved substantially greater 6MWD improvements (r=0.257, small-to-moderate effect size); higher-performing participants showed smaller gains.
Younger participants (<65 years) achieved significantly greater 6MWD gains (Z=2.117, r=0.244); weak negative correlation between age and 6MWD change (r=-0.262, p<0.05).

No significant sex differences in magnitude of 6MWD change (p>0.05). However, men achieved significantly greater respiratory muscle strength (PImax: r=-0.578, p<0.001; PEmax: r=-0.538, p<0.001) and chest expansion at 10th rib (r=-0.241, p=0.037). Women were more likely to report headaches, chest pain, and muscle/joint pain at 6 months.

summary: A six-week outpatient multi-component rehabilitation programme — combining aerobic cycling, respiratory muscle training with an inspiratory muscle trainer (at 45–80% of PImax), strength training, stretching, and speech/voice exercises — was tested in 75 Long COVID patients (median age 65, all with dyspnoea and functional impairment) in a randomised controlled trial with six-month follow-up. The primary outcomes of six-minute walk distance (6MWD), maximal inspiratory pressure (PImax), and maximal expiratory pressure (PEmax) all showed large, statistically significant improvements immediately post-intervention that were sustained at six months: median 6MWD rose from 300 m to 368 m (+50 m from baseline to follow-up, p<0.001, r=0.615), PImax rose from 49 to 77 cmH₂O (+25 cmH₂O, p<0.001), and PEmax from 63 to 95 cmH₂O (+23 cmH₂O, p<0.001). A notable caveat is that after the six-week programme ended, cough and headache prevalence increased slightly at the six-month follow-up, and marginal declines in PImax and PEmax occurred between the end of treatment and follow-up, though both remained far above baseline.

summary: This German RCT (RELOAD, NCT05172206) tested a 3-week inpatient, multimodal, symptom-based rehabilitation programme versus usual care in 132 adults with Long COVID, 90% of whom had mild non-hospitalised acute COVID-19. The programme was tailored to each participant's dominant symptom cluster (fatigue, cognitive problems, or somatic symptoms) and delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Physical quality of life (SF-12 PCS) improved significantly more in the rehabilitation group at 3 weeks (mean difference +2.9 points, 95% CI 0.2–5.7, p=0.038), with the benefit persisting and widening at 3 months (+4.2 points, p=0.003); mental quality of life, depression, and anxiety also improved significantly at 3 weeks. No adverse events occurred, though unblinded participants and the modest effect size on the primary outcome limit confidence in the magnitude of benefit.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) at 50% of maximal inspiratory pressure in 19 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome, measuring lung aerosol deposition and pulmonary perfusion using gamma scintigraphy. The IMT group showed significant increases in total lung aerosol deposition (p=0.028, effect size r=0.50) and total lung perfusion (p=0.013, r=0.57), while the sham control group showed no improvement and actually declined in perfusion. Peripheral oxygen saturation also rose significantly in the IMT group (95.5% to 98%, p=0.028) but not controls. The trial is small (10 vs 9 participants) and lacked CT imaging to confirm lung boundaries, limiting precision of regional measurements.

summary: This Canadian RCT tested an 8-week individualized tele-rehabilitation program (three supervised video sessions per week with kinesiologists, including aerobic, strengthening, and flexibility exercises) against usual care in 132 adults with long COVID — 78% of whom had never been hospitalized, and 93% of whom had post-exertional malaise at enrollment. summary: This Norwegian randomized controlled trial tested a brief outpatient rehabilitation program using a cognitive-behavioral approach (2–8 sessions with a doctor and physiotherapists) versus care as usual in 314 non-hospitalized adults with Long COVID. The primary outcome—SF-36 Physical Function Subscale at approximately 6 months—was significantly higher in the intervention group (mean difference 9.2 points, 95% CI 4.3–14.2), with the effect sustained at 12 months. The cost-effectiveness analysis found the intervention dominated care as usual: it produced 0.056 more QALYs (95% CI 0.024–0.077) while costing NOK 20,682 less per patient (~$1,958 USD), largely because the intervention group used far less inpatient rehabilitation and other healthcare services.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) companion to the primary trial (Nerli et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(12):e2450744). Detailed clinical outcome data (per-arm means, SDs for SF-36-PFS and secondary clinical outcomes) are NOT reported here — only the primary between-group effect size is cited from the original paper. EQ-5D-5L utility values are reported as group means without SDs at each timepoint. QALY data are reported as group totals without SDs. Cost data are reported as per-patient means without SDs per arm. Adverse event data are referenced as lower in the intervention group but not quantified in this paper — refer to original trial paper. Arm randomization numbers (157 per arm) are inferred from the 1:1 ratio and total of 314; the paper provides analyzed n as 125 (intervention) and 106 (CAU) at T0-T1, and 125 (intervention) and 102 (CAU) at T1-T2. T1 mean was 200 days (SD=75) and T2 mean was 396 days (SD=37) from inclusion. Weeks from randomization for T1 estimated as 200/7 ~29 weeks; T2 as 396/7 ~57 weeks. The cost mean difference of -20,682 NOK is stated verbatim (intervention minus CAU is negative, meaning intervention is cheaper). Sensitivity analysis: with extreme CAU patient excluded, CAU costs drop to 33,178 NOK (CI -20,443 to -781). Complete case analysis (n=204): QALY gain 0.035, cost difference 31,537 NOK savings.

trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 Physical Function Subscale mean difference 9.2 points (95% CI 4.3–14.2) in favor of intervention at T1; QALY gain 0.056 (95% CI 0.024–0.077) with cost saving of NOK 20,682 per patient (95% CI −47,230 to −1,614).

summary: This triple-blind randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle strength training (IMST) at 50% of maximal inspiratory pressure in 40 adults with Long COVID who had CT-confirmed pulmonary involvement, comparing it against thoracic expansion exercises. The primary outcomes were quadriceps femoris muscle oxygenation and functional exercise capacity: the IMST group walked an average of 96.4 metres further on the six-minute walk test than the control group (p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.65), and maintained muscle oxygen saturation during exercise while the control group's levels declined (p<0.001). Secondary benefits included large gains in inspiratory muscle strength (MIP improved by ~52 cmH2O more than controls, Cohen's d=1.24), significant increases in upper and lower limb muscle strength, and meaningful reductions in fatigue (FSS score fell by ~14 points in IMST vs ~1 point in controls, p<0.001) and dyspnea during daily activities; physical activity levels did not improve.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper describes the study as 'triple blind' (participants, researchers, data analysts), though the control group used a clearly different exercise (thoracic expansion), making participant blinding questionable. The between-group effect size CI for 6-MWT% was reported as [7.94-22.40] in the text (note: lower bound reported as 7.94 in one place and 7.94 in another — used verbatim). Some outcome CIs (e.g., for deltoid effect size) were given in the text as Cohen's d ranges, not mean difference CIs — for deltoid the mean difference CI [39.62-79.15] N was extracted as stated. LCADL self-care subscale (p=0.240 between groups, not significant) and LCADL leisure subscale (p=0.445, not significant) were not included as separate outcomes to save space but data is available in Table 4. Non-dominant deltoid muscle strength also showed significant treatment effect (p<0.001) — data available in Table 4 but not included as a separate outcome item. Physical activity sub-outcomes (total energy expenditure, active energy expenditure, steps, sleep duration, lying down) not included as separate outcomes; summary data available in Table 4. Additional SmO2 sub-measures (SmO2 min, SmO2 max, recovery values, THb measures) available in Table 3 but not all extracted as separate outcomes given volume; ΔTHb showed within-group but not between-group significant effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome 6-MWT distance improved by 96.44 m more in IMST vs control (95% CI 51.39–141.49 m, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.65); ΔSmO2 during 6-MWT was significantly better in IMST vs control (p<0.001).

summary: This study evaluated the measurement properties of the 30-second sit-to-stand test (30s-STS) as a functional capacity measure in 150 adults with Long COVID, using data from the PYCNOVID randomised controlled trial. The 30s-STS showed good test-retest reliability (ICC 0.82) and was safe and feasible to administer, with no adverse events; however, 46% of participants scored below the 5th percentile for functional capacity, indicating widespread impairment in this population. The study's primary aim was psychometric validation rather than treatment efficacy — no intervention effect on functional capacity was tested — and a provisional minimal important difference of 2 repetitions was proposed based on distribution-based methods alone, as anchor-based approaches failed due to weak correlations (all below 0.3) between changes in test performance and symptom measures.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL LIMITATION FOR META-ANALYSIS: This paper presents measurement properties data from the PYCNOVID RCT but does NOT report per-arm (Pycnogenol vs placebo) outcome data. All reported means and SDs are for the combined sample (arm_id=0 used as placeholder). Between-group efficacy data for the RCT intervention are not reported here and would require the primary PYCNOVID efficacy paper. The 30s-STS data at 12 weeks and change-from-baseline at 12 weeks are referenced (S3 Table) but not reproduced in this paper. Construct validity correlations: 30s-STS vs FACIT Fatigue r=0.22, vs CRQ fatigue r=0.29, vs CRQ dyspnoea r=0.32; physical activity correlations: r=0.22-0.26. Arm-level demographic/clinical data not reported by treatment allocation. Test-retest reliability: ICC=0.82 (95% CI 0.76-0.86), SEM=2.35 repetitions, MDC95=4.25 repetitions. Bland-Altman mean bias 0.84 repetitions (95% CI 0.26-1.42), LOA -6.21 to 7.89. Sensitivity analysis excluding submaximal effort: mean bias 1.17 (95% CI 0.48-1.87). Time since symptom onset: mean 111 weeks (SD 58.1). Light PA 26 min/day, moderate PA 48 min/day, vigorous PA 0.8 min/day, inactivity 1050 min/day (n=141).

trial_rating.result_basis: No treatment effect was the primary focus; this is a measurement properties study. Anchor-based MID calculation was not possible as all Spearman correlations between 30s-STS change and anchor variables were below 0.3 and all AUC values were below 0.7.

summary: This small Ukrainian trial tested whether adding L-arginine (1000 mg twice daily) and phenibut (500 mg twice daily) for three months to standard cardiac therapy improved neuropsychiatric and autonomic outcomes in 31 patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) who had experienced moderate-to-severe COVID-19 and had Long COVID symptoms. The primary findings were statistically significant reductions in anxiety (35.97% decrease on the HADS Anxiety subscale) and depression (20.81% decrease on HADS Depression subscale), a 9.47% improvement in MoCA cognitive scores, and improved heart rate variability with the stress index falling 1.89-fold in the active period and 2.03-fold in the passive period. The study is very small (n=16 in the treatment arm), lacked blinding, and used 'elements of randomization' rather than full randomization, substantially limiting confidence in the findings.

The study was uncontrolled and had no comparison group; the post-COVID subgroup comprised only 11 participants, limiting confidence in the estimates.

Baseline 6MWD distance not reported; only change from baseline provided. FEV1/IVC ratio data also extracted from Table 4 but not included as separate outcome to avoid redundancy. trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWD increased by 82 m (p<0.01) and mMRC improved by 2.1 points (3.5 to 1.4, p<0.01) in the post-COVID group (n=11).

summary: Ten sessions of individualized respiratory and motor physical therapy were tested in 26 adults with Long COVID (symptoms persisting beyond 12 weeks) attending a multidisciplinary post-COVID rehabilitation service in Bahia, Brazil. Across functional tests, patients showed significant improvements: Timed-Up-and-Go improved from a median of 10 to 8 seconds (p=0.002), the 2-minute step-in-place test improved from 55 to 80 steps (p=0.006), and global muscle strength increased from MRC grade 4 to 5 (p<0.001). summary: This study tested a tailored topical and systemic treatment regimen for chronic non-infectious conjunctivitis in 66 post-COVID patients (aged 50–70), with treatment assigned based on laser Doppler flowmetry (LDF) classification of conjunctival microcirculation as either hyperemic or stagnant. Patients with hyperemic microcirculation received topical antioxidant eye drops (emoxipine), sodium hyaluronate, heparin eye drops, and systemic metabolic agents; those with stagnant microcirculation received sodium hyaluronate, heparin, and systemic venotonics. Treated patients in both groups showed meaningful improvement in perfusion parameters over 3–6 months (e.g., mean perfusion normalised to 24.8 ± 5.5 perfusion units in the hyperemic group at 3 months; stagnant group showed 35% increase in mean perfusion and 52.2% reduction in coefficient of variation by 6 months), while control subgroups receiving only hyaluronate drops showed no statistically significant change. No safety concerns were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is observational/quasi-experimental without formal randomization; patients were stratified by hemodynamic type on baseline LDF, then divided into treatment vs. minimal-care subgroups within each stratum. Outcomes data reported in text and Table; no adverse events reported. Follow-up structured at 1, 3, and 6 months; only 3 and 6-month data presented numerically in results.

trial_rating.result_basis: Stagnant-type treated group (2a): mean perfusion increased 35% at 3 months and coefficient of variation decreased 52.2% by 6 months (Kv = 15.2 ± 7.4%); control subgroups showed no statistically significant changes (p > 0.05).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding a flow-based incentive spirometer to standard inpatient rehabilitation improved outcomes in 82 previously hospitalized adults with post-COVID-19 condition in Cyprus. summary: This Swedish RCT tested whether adding inspiratory muscle training (IMT) twice daily to a standard individualized exercise program improved breathing muscle strength in 44 adults with Long COVID who had confirmed inspiratory muscle weakness. The intervention group showed significantly greater gains in maximal inspiratory pressure than the exercise-only control group, with a mean between-group difference of 18 percentage points (95% CI: 5–30), and were 7 times more likely to achieve a clinically meaningful improvement (OR 7.08, 95% CI: 1.31–38.32). The IMT group also reduced cough frequency more than controls. The trial enrolled only 44 of the 90 planned participants, and those with the most severe fatigue were largely unable to participate, limiting how broadly these results apply.

summary: This open-label controlled trial tested 10 days of inhaled nitric oxide (iNO, 60 ppm) combined with inhaled molecular hydrogen (iH2, <4%) versus iNO alone versus standard rehabilitation care in 60 Long COVID patients (average symptom duration ~2 years) with persistent respiratory symptoms. Both inhaled gas groups showed significant improvements in dyspnea, fatigue, anxiety, depression, and quality of life scores compared to controls, with microcirculation improvements in venular blood flow velocity. The iNO/iH2 combination outperformed iNO alone on exercise capacity (6-minute walk distance improved by 44.7±41.5 m, p<0.05) and was the only group to significantly reduce oxidative stress markers (FORT dropped from 595 to 409 units, p<0.05). Adverse events were mild and non-specific across both treatment groups.

Specific p-values comparing iNO/iH₂ vs iNO monotherapy vs control are reported as p<0.05 for various comparisons without exact values. All numeric baseline and outcome data from tables (Table 1-4, Table 3) were extracted. One post-treatment follow-up visit at day 7 and day 60 post-treatment mentioned for telemetry monitoring but no numeric outcome data provided. Adverse events reported as frequency (n, %) per Table 4. Paper states effects sustained at 7 and 60-day follow-up telemetry checks with no late adverse events reported, but numeric follow-up data not provided.

summary: This feasibility study tested whether machine learning models trained on wearable sensor data could predict next-day fatigue levels in 68 adults with post-COVID fatigue. Participants wore a wrist accelerometer and a chest ECG patch for up to 21 days, generating heart rate variability (HRV), activity, and sleep features that were used to train XGBoost and Random Forest models. The XGBoost model achieved strong predictive accuracy (R² = 0.79, mean absolute error = 3.18 on a 0–100 fatigue scale), with HRV non-linear measures (sample entropy, approximate entropy) and low-frequency power emerging as the top predictors, followed by activity timing and demographics. A key caveat is that the cross-validation did not separate participants between training and test sets, so performance likely overestimates true generalisability to new individuals.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a machine learning feasibility study, not a traditional clinical trial comparing interventions; the three randomized arms (active taVNS, sham, placebo) are from the parent RCT, but the analysis reported here uses all 68 participants with complete data pooled across a machine learning prediction task (no between-arm comparisons reported). Baseline demographics only reported for the overall sample, not per-arm. No adverse events reported. Only 68 of 114 enrolled participants had complete datasets; reasons for exclusion (Bluetooth connectivity, device malfunction, questionnaire non-completion) detailed but per-arm dropout not specified. Feature importance rankings (top 5 features) reported narratively for both XGBoost and Random Forest but full feature importance values not provided in tabular form. Five-fold cross-validation results presented with individual fold values for R², MAE, and correlation. Study is a predictive modeling feasibility analysis rather than an efficacy trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: XGBoost mean R² = 0.789 ± 0.041, MAE = 3.18 ± 0.63 on 0–100 VAS; however, standard 5-fold CV (not leave-one-subject-out) was used, inflating estimates.

summary: This Brazilian pilot RCT tested creatine monohydrate supplementation (6 g/day or 18 g/day for 4 weeks) combined with supervised physical rehabilitation in 67 adults with Long COVID who had significant fatigue. The primary outcome was fatigue as measured by the Revised Piper Fatigue Scale (PFS-R): the 6 g/day group showed a statistically significant reduction in fatigue score of 2.05 points compared to placebo (95% CI: -3.47 to -0.63; p=0.005), along with a 4.40 kgf improvement in handgrip strength (p=0.037); the higher 18 g/day dose showed no significant benefit on fatigue. Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, bloating, diarrhea) were more common at higher doses but resolved within days without medical intervention, and both creatine groups showed small but statistically significant increases in serum creatinine that were not considered clinically meaningful.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Data extracted per intention-to-treat analysis as stated in methods. Baseline tables indicate n=24, 22, 21 randomized to 6g, 18g, placebo groups respectively, with 21, 19, 18 completing the protocol. Between-group effects presented as DiD (difference-in-differences) estimates per prespecified statistical approach. The 18g/day group showed one isolated ultrasonographic finding (biceps brachii short head left): DiD 0.52 cm (95% CI 0.01 to 1.03; p=0.045), but this was noted as clinically not meaningful and should be interpreted cautiously given multiple comparisons. Supplementary Table 1 referenced for additional laboratory parameters (eosinophil count, serum sodium) but full detail not provided in main text — effect estimates extracted as reported in main text Results section.

trial_rating.result_basis: PFS-R score decreased by 2.05 points in the 6 g/day group vs. placebo (95% CI: -3.47 to -0.63; p=0.005) on a scale where scores range roughly 0-10, representing a moderate absolute change but from a small pilot with 21 completers in the effective arm.

summary: A 12-week non-aerobic core stabilization exercise program (the MORETA program, 24 sessions of plank-based trunk exercises) was tested in 17 women with Long COVID symptoms lasting over one year. The primary outcomes were body fat percentage and perceived fatigue; total body fat decreased significantly from 37.1% to 35.4% (p=0.003, ES=1.08), and overall fatigue scores on the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale dropped from 66.6 to 52.6 (p=0.012, ES=0.94), with the largest gains in physical fatigue (29.7 to 21.1, ES=1.20). The study had no control group, enrolled only 17 participants, and cognitive fatigue did not improve significantly, limiting causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is non-randomized, pre-post quasi-experimental with single arm; no control or comparison group. IPAQ-3 (walking days per week without minimum duration) also reported (pre: 2.00±0.88, post: 2.21±1.19, p=0.796) and IPAQ-5 (sitting time weekends) (pre: 4.88±2.21, post: 5.38±1.62, p=0.455) and IPAQ-7 (total physical activity time) (pre: 7.08±3.98, post: 7.92±2.81, p=0.517) presented in Table 5 but excluded from outcomes list due to space constraints. TSK-11 individual item scores reported in Table 6 but omitted from outcomes extraction per output size management. All 11 individual TSK-11 items showed minimal changes (all p > 0.112). Muscle mass percentages reported for right arm, left arm, right leg, left leg, and trunk regions—all non-significant changes (all p > 0.05). Body water data for regional distributions (right arm, left arm, right leg, left leg, trunk) reported but omitted. Correlations between fat mass reduction and outcome changes (MFIS r=-0.84 p=0.765; EQ-5D-5L r=-0.121 p=0.694; IPAQ r=-0.241 p=0.532; TSK-11 r=0.014 p=0.961) reported but effect sizes not sufficient for extraction. Paper reports t-statistics, degrees of freedom, and FDR-adjusted p-values for all outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Overall MFIS fatigue score decreased from 66.59 to 52.59 (p=0.012, ES=0.936); total body fat from 37.09% to 35.41% (p=0.003, ES=1.079) in n=17 with no control group.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Failure to complete active 10-minute standing test (orthostatic intolerance)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Among 9 patients with disequilibrium (positive Romberg and/or tandem gait tests), 6 (67%) failed to complete the 10-minute standing test. Among 23 patients without disequilibrium, only 1 failed to complete the test. Multiple regression analysis showed disequilibrium was significantly positively associated with OI (partial regression coefficient: 0.64, p<0.001, 95% CI 0.32-0.96), whereas POTS was significantly negatively associated (partial regression coefficient: -0.38, p=0.049, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.62).

Six patients with disequilibrium received 6 weeks of oral minocycline therapy (5 patients) or minocycline followed by 2 weeks of rTMS (1 patient). After treatment, 5 of 6 treated and retested patients showed resolution of OI associated with improvement in disequilibrium, although 1 patient experienced symptom recovery without a repeat standing test.

summary: This single-centre observational study of 32 long COVID patients (all meeting ME/CFS criteria) assessed whether balance dysfunction (disequilibrium) or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) better explained orthostatic intolerance (OI) — the inability to sustain standing. In a multiple regression analysis, disequilibrium was the only factor significantly associated with OI (partial regression coefficient 0.64, p<0.001), while POTS was actually negatively associated (coefficient -0.38, p=0.049); 6 of 7 patients who failed the 10-minute standing test had disequilibrium, versus none with POTS alone. A subset of 7 patients with OI was then treated with oral minocycline and/or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and 5 of 6 re-tested showed resolution of OI alongside improvement in balance. The study is very small and uncontrolled, making it impossible to attribute treatment outcomes to the interventions rather than natural recovery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study design: not a randomized controlled trial; single-arm quasi-experimental design with prospective enrollment and pre-post treatment assessments in a subset. No control group or randomization. Table 1 provides individual patient data for 7 patients with OI who received treatment; 6 were retested post-treatment. Table 2 compares patients with and without OI at baseline (25 with OI, 7 without). Multiple regression CI for POTS association reported as (-0.31 to -0.62) which is unusual formatting; extracted as written. Death noted was of co-researcher Yukichi Inoue, not a study participant, during the conduct of the research. Risk of bias tool (RoB2) is not appropriate for this quasi-experimental design; overall judgment reflects that this is not an RCT and lacks key design features necessary for RCT bias assessment.

trial_rating.result_basis: 5 of 6 re-tested patients resolved OI after minocycline/rTMS, but no control group; disequilibrium-OI association: partial regression coefficient 0.64, p<0.001 in n=32.

interventions: Oral minocycline and/or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS)

summary: This open-label randomized controlled trial tested 4 g/day of L-citrulline supplementation for three months in 43 adults who had been hospitalized for moderate-to-severe COVID-19 and were attending a post-COVID clinic in Mexico City. The primary outcome was endothelial function measured by ICAM-1; the L-citrulline group showed a significant reduction in ICAM-1 of 32.59 ng/mg protein (95% CI: -52.85 to -12.33, p=0.001) compared to no change in controls (p=0.034 for group × time interaction). A notable secondary finding was greater improvement in six-minute walk test distance in the L-citrulline group (+141 m vs +68 m in controls, p=0.011 between groups), though both groups improved, likely reflecting natural recovery. The study is limited by its small sample size (21 per arm), open-label design, single centre, and the primary endothelial biomarker ICAM-1 may not directly reflect physiological endothelial function.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 baseline characteristics included median and IQR for hospital stay (reported in days as 18 [11-26] vs 30 [11-47]); these were not extracted as outcome data. The study was open-label (not blinded). Adherence to L-citrulline was reported as 85%. All 43 randomized participants completed the study with no reported withdrawals or loss to follow-up. Nutrient intake data were reported but showed no significant changes between groups; these were included in Table 2 but not extracted as separate outcomes since they are secondary measures of intervention exposure. The p-value of 0.034 for the ICAM-1 between-group effect was from a repeated-measures ANOVA adjusted for E-Selectin and hospital stay; the paper did not report the unadjusted comparison, so the calculated mean difference (305.61 - 32.59 = 273.02 for intervention vs 305.67 - 2.31 = 303.36 for control, difference = -30.34) is approximate.

trial_rating.result_basis: ICAM-1 decreased by 32.59 ng/mg protein in the intervention group vs -2.31 in controls; group × time interaction p=0.034.

summary: This Brazilian randomized controlled trial tested two 6-week supervised rehabilitation programs in 29 adults who survived severe COVID-19 requiring hospitalization: multicomponent exercise alone (aerobic, resistance, and balance training) versus the same program combined with inspiratory muscle training (IMT) using a threshold loading device. Both groups showed large improvements across all primary functional outcomes, including a 123-meter increase in 6-minute walk distance (378m to 501m, +32%), a 27% reduction in Timed Up and Go time (9.6s to 7.0s), a 38% increase in sit-to-stand repetitions, and significant gains in handgrip strength and respiratory muscle pressures. No statistically significant differences were found between the two groups on any outcome, and no adverse events occurred; the study lacked a no-treatment control arm and was underpowered for between-group comparisons, so natural recovery cannot be ruled out.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CPET was performed only at baseline per study design (high cost/logistical constraints), so no post-intervention VO2peak data available. Table 3 header indicates '1 o' and '2 o' denote first and second assessments. Within-group p-values in Table 5 all highly significant (p<0.05 or p<0.001), indicating robust within-group changes. Cardiovascular CPET outcomes (FC_LV1, FC_LV2, FC_Peak measured in bpm) extracted from Table 4 but not included in main outcomes as they represent heart rate rather than primary outcome measures. No between-group interactions reported in tables; p-values shown reflect between-group comparisons at each timepoint (p(GEm vs. GEmTMI/1o) and p(GEm vs. GEmTMI/2o)).

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance improved by 122.9m (+32%) across both groups combined, p<0.001; TUG improved from 9.59s to 7.00s, p<0.001; no between-group differences detected (all p>0.05).

summary: A 12-week multi-strain probiotic (Saccharomyces boulardii DBVPG-6763, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, and two Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains) was given to 34 adults with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (13 with Long COVID, 21 fully recovered) in a non-randomised double-blind trial in Serbia, with 25 healthy non-supplemented adults as reference controls. The primary outcomes were gut microbiota composition and biochemical markers: overall microbial diversity did not change significantly, but in Long COVID participants the probiotic significantly increased Bifidobacterium (delta +0.026 vs -0.007 in controls, p=0.037) and reduced Prevotella_9 abundance (p=0.013), with non-significant trends toward lower CRP, ALT, and AST. The study was small (only 23 Long COVID participants total, 13 in the probiotic arm), non-randomised, and lacked a placebo control group, severely limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is quasi-experimental (non-randomized allocation) rather than RCT. Initial enrollment n=90, but final analyzed sample was n=74 (34 probiotic recipients: 13 long COVID + 21 convalescent; 40 non-supplemented controls: 10 long COVID + 5 convalescent + 25 healthy). Exclusions due to unclear labeling (n=9) and incomplete paired sampling (n=7). Alpha and beta diversity results reported as p-values only with no per-arm numeric data; set as not_reported. Multiple secondary outcomes related to microbiota composition changes reported as log-fold changes or relative abundance changes with p-values; prioritized major findings. Several MetaCyc pathway results omitted from Table 5 (6 of 7 reported) as detailed in extraction; all 7 are now included. Biochemical parameters reported as median changes with Wilcoxon test p-values; no raw means/SDs reported for baseline or endpoint values. Correlation analysis results (30 associations in all participants, 217 in long COVID) noted but not separately extracted as distinct outcomes due to scope; summarized in text. Probiotic compliance monitored by self-report only; no objective compliance measure reported. Study used flow-pack technology packaging but no viability testing beyond manufacturer validation. No serious adverse events, withdrawals, or mortality reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary microbiota and biochemical outcomes were largely non-significant; the strongest finding was a significant increase in Bifidobacterium relative abundance (delta +0.026 probiotic vs -0.007 control, p=0.037), but overall diversity metrics showed no change (PERMANOVA p=0.422) and biochemical trends did not reach p<0.05.

interventions: Multi-strain probiotic (Saccharomyces boulardii DBVPG-6763, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum LP6595, L. plantarum HEAL9), No probiotic supplementation, No intervention (reference control)

summary: This exploratory immunological sub-study of the PAX LC trial tested a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) versus placebo/ritonavir in 82 adults with Long COVID, measuring immune and virological markers in blood before and after treatment. Neither arm showed changes in circulating SARS-CoV-2 spike protein levels, immune cell populations, or anti-spike antibody responses after treatment, providing a biological explanation for why nirmatrelvir failed to improve symptoms in the parent trial. Across both treatment arms regardless of drug assignment, participants who reported symptom improvement showed significantly lower levels of the inflammatory chemokine RANTES (CCL5), identifying it as a candidate biomarker of recovery rather than a treatment effect.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an exploratory immunological sub-study of the main PAX LC trial, not the primary efficacy trial itself. The study reports no between-group differences in major endpoints (spike protein, antibodies, immune cells) and focuses on within-group changes and post-hoc analyses of symptom improvers. Data on per-arm means and SDs for most biomarkers are not provided in the text/tables; values are only in figures (volcano plots, scatter plots). Per-arm baseline sample sizes for most biomarkers were not explicitly stated but inferred from the n=45 placebo and n=37 nirmatrelvir participants analyzed. The paper includes extended data tables referenced but not fully reproduced in the preprint; extracted p-values for within-arm comparisons are from text statements (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank test p-values for baseline vs day 28). Multiple outcomes measured 105 circulating cytokines; RANTES and IL-5 are highlighted as having the strongest associations with symptom improvement. A permutation test was used to validate the clustering of improvers vs non-improvers based on the top 10 immune modulators.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome of the parent PAX LC trial showed no significant difference in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score between arms; circulating spike protein unchanged in both arms (NMV/r p=0.9580, PBO/r p=0.1468).

summary: This phase IIb randomized controlled trial (Neuromod-COV) tested whether working-memory cognitive training (CT), with or without transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over the left prefrontal cortex, could improve cognition in 60 adults with Long COVID cognitive complaints (mean 13 months post-infection, 77% female). CT alone did not improve untrained working memory compared to progressive muscle relaxation (the primary outcome). However, among CT participants, those receiving active tDCS outperformed those receiving sham tDCS on harder working memory tasks at both post-intervention and one-month follow-up, and on a visuospatial memory task immediately after treatment; no intervention improved functional status or quality of life. The trial was well-conducted but small and single-site, limiting generalizability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Study conducted at single site (University Medicine Greifswald, Germany). Behavioral interventions (CT and PMR) were open-label, while tDCS was double-blind. Paper reports p-values for primary outcome comparisons. Detailed cognitive and self-reported outcome data presented in figures and supplementary tables; between-group effects extracted from text and figures. Per-protocol analysis included 38 of 60 participants (n=12/12/14 by arm) but was not the primary analysis. Risk of bias assessed as low overall based on adequate randomization, allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessors, minimal missing data, and pre-specified analysis plan. No subgroup analyses stratified by sex, age, or other factors reported in the paper. Follow-up assessment 1 month after post-intervention visit (approximately 4 weeks post-treatment). The paper does not report raw per-arm means and SDs for all outcomes; between-group effect estimates were extracted from linear mixed-effects models reported in the results and figures.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (N-back accuracy, CT vs. PMR at post-intervention): β = 1.59, 95% CI -1.30 to 4.48, p = 0.278 — non-significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an interrupted time series (ITS) observational study, not a conventional intervention trial with separate arms. The study uses a self-as-control design: participants serve as their own pre-vaccination comparators. All effect estimates are expressed as percentage change in odds (from logistic regression on logit scale), not as absolute mean differences or standard ORs. Key estimates: pre-vaccination trajectory -0.3%/week (OR 0.997, 95% CI 0.991-1.002, p=0.25); first dose level change OR 0.872 (95% CI 0.814-0.934, p<0.001), i.e. -12.8%; slope change after first dose +0.3%/week (OR 1.006, 95% CI 0.996-1.016, p=0.51); second dose level change OR 0.912 (95% CI 0.859-0.969, p=0.003), i.e. -8.8%; slope change after second dose -0.8%/week (OR 0.989, 95% CI 0.979-0.999, p<0.001 per week). Activity-limiting: first dose OR 0.877 (0.805-0.955, p=0.003); second dose OR 0.909 (0.844-0.979, p=0.01). Individual symptom data appear primarily in Fig 4 with only selected values in text; data for 10 symptoms (weakness/tiredness, loss of smell, shortness of breath, loss of taste, headache, trouble sleeping, difficulty concentrating, muscle ache, worry/anxiety, memory loss/confusion) and >3 and >5 symptom composites exist as modelled probabilities in figure only — detailed per-symptom CIs are in supplementary table 6 (not reproduced in main text). Per-arm raw means/SDs are not available; this design produces only trajectory parameters. Follow-up: median 219 days (31.3 weeks) from study start to end; median 67 days (9.6 weeks) post second dose. Time since infection at final visit: mean 308.9 days (SD 129.0).

summary: This prospective case series from a single Spanish tertiary hospital evaluated 29 long COVID patients (symptoms ≥4 weeks post-COVID-19) for SARS-CoV-2 RNA persistence in plasma, stool, and urine, and compared outcomes between 18 patients who received compassionate-use lopinavir/ritonavir ± hydroxychloroquine and 11 who did not. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The study uses a non-validated, non-standard functional disability scale (Grade 0-IV) created by the authors. 2. The p=0.000 reported for overall improvement likely means p<0.001, recorded as p_value_exact=false. 3. Treatment group n reported as 18 in outcomes section but baseline characteristics table says N=18 and Table 3 header says N=18; untreated N=11. These are consistent. 4. Note that Table 1 states 19/29 patients (65%) received antiviral treatment during acute COVID-19, while Table 3 refers to 18 patients receiving compassionate post-COVID antiviral treatment — these are different treatment episodes. 5. Severity distribution in Table 3 appears inconsistent: treated arm shows mild 5 (27.7%), moderate 4 (22.2%), severe 9 (50%) which sums to 18; untreated shows mild 2 (18.1%), moderate 2 (18.1%), severe 7 (63.6%) but 2+2+7=11 which is correct. However, 'severe COVID-19' percentage (63.6%) in untreated group contradicts the overall 24% severe rate — this may reflect that the most severely ill acute patients were in the untreated group at long COVID evaluation. 6. No per-arm means/SDs available for functional scale outcomes — only event counts (binary improvement). 7. Figure 1 referenced for outcome data but specific numerical breakdowns by arm not fully tabulated in text beyond what is extracted above.

summary: This propensity score matched cohort study from a single Hungarian center assessed the effect of remdesivir (RDV) administered during acute COVID-19 hospitalization on post-COVID condition (PCC) outcomes in 188 matched patients (94 SOC+RDV vs. 94 SOC). RDV was associated with significantly earlier attainment of asymptomatic status (adjusted HR 2.28, 95% CI 1.33–3.92, p=0.003) and at least 50% symptom score reduction (adjusted HR 2.08, 95% CI 1.43–3.02, p<0.001), and with significantly better sleep quality (PSQI 5.9 vs. 7.7, p=0.025) and less sleep disturbance at PCC (14% vs. 27%, p=0.003). No significant differences were observed in pulmonary function tests, 6-minute walk test, or other quality-of-life questionnaires.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Pulmonary function test (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, TLC, RV, DLCO, KLCO, PImax, PEmax) and 6MWT data referenced as 'no significant difference' but actual per-arm values reported only in Supplementary Table 4 (not available in full text). VAS and FSS scores also referenced but per-arm values not provided in the main text. The PSQI mean values are given without SD. ESS showed no difference but no values stated. Denominator for sleep disturbances resolved (percentage who had sleep disturbances during COVID and reported resolution) is unclear — percentages taken at face value. Follow-up duration was variable and not standardized; the 6-month timepoint is used for binary outcomes but the time-to-event analyses use time since hospital admission.

summary: This retrospective follow-up study of 1,236 Iranian adults hospitalized for COVID-19 who had previously reported long-COVID symptoms compared the persistence of symptoms (>1 year, termed 'long long-COVID') between vaccinated (n=1,185) and unvaccinated (n=51) individuals. Vaccination with any COVID-19 vaccine was significantly associated with higher odds of persistent long-COVID symptoms at follow-up (44.6% vs. 29.4%; adjusted OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.06–3.63, p=0.032). The study is observational with a very small unvaccinated comparator group and serious confounding risk, limiting causal inference; the authors nonetheless strongly recommend vaccination given its well-established protection against severe disease and death.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational retrospective cohort, not an intervention trial. The 'intervention' is COVID-19 vaccination (self-selected, not randomized). The unvaccinated comparator group is very small (n=51), limiting statistical power for individual symptom comparisons. Table 1 reports p-values for individual symptoms but no ORs per symptom — p-values extracted as chi-square results. Several symptoms had zero events in unvaccinated group (muscle pain, chest pain, palpitation, loss of taste, sore throat, dizziness, concentration difficulty, diarrhea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite) — no p-value calculable for these (listed as '-' in paper). Remaining secondary symptom outcomes with p-values reported: cough (p=0.497), excess sputum (p=0.942), headache (p=0.679), excess sweating (p=0.667) — omitted from outcomes array for brevity but all showed non-significance. Follow-up duration estimated as ~17 months (mean reported as 16.8–17.1 months) converted to ~74 weeks.

summary: This prospective open-label matched-controlled observational study evaluated Actovegin (deproteinized calf blood hemodialysate) versus no Actovegin in 440 post-COVID-19 patients with chronic cerebral ischaemia (CCI) in Russia (n=220 per arm), followed for 90 days. At 90 days, the Actovegin group had significantly lower symptom frequency (38.5% vs 62.1%, p<0.01), greater improvement in fatigue (MFI-20 mean 48 vs 61), sleep (Spiegel SSQ 22 vs 17), and cognition (MoCA +4 vs +1 points), and higher rates of no/minimal quality of life impairment (77.9% vs 33.7%, p<0.001). All between-group differences were statistically significant (p<0.05), though the open-label non-randomized design limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is in Russian with English abstract; all numeric data extracted from figures (Fig 2, 3, 4) and tables. No SDs reported for any continuous outcome — only mean scores at each timepoint from figures. Between-group p-values stated as thresholds only (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001), not exact values. Baseline MFI-20 scores from Fig 2: arm1=69, arm2=66; Day30: arm1=51, arm2=57; Day90: arm1=48, arm2=61. The paper states arm1 decreased 18 pts at Day30 and arm2 decreased 9 pts, which is consistent with 69→51 and 66→57 respectively. MMSE Table 2 reports distribution by severity at Day90 (endpoint only, no baseline severity distribution given separately). Table 3 (MMSE subscores) and Table 4 (MoCA subscores) report % of patients with improvement per cognitive domain — these are proportions of the subgroup who had that impairment at baseline, not of total n=220. Denominators for Tables 3 and 4 are the number impaired at baseline per domain (from Table 1). Depression severity distribution (Table 5) denominator for severity breakdown is among those with depression: arm1 n=69, arm2 n=106. Anxiety distribution (Table 6) is for full n=220 per arm. MoCA baseline arm1=21, arm2=20 from Fig 4 (paper says overall mean ~20-21). Note: paper explicitly states observational design without randomization or placebo control as a limitation.

summary: This retrospective cohort study of 405 post-COVID-19 patients attending a pulmonary clinic in Israel (February 2020–March 2021) compared long-term pulmonary function test (PFT) trajectories between 155 patients who received corticosteroids (CS) during acute COVID-19 and 250 who did not. Despite lower baseline FEV1 (-9.4%) and FVC (-12.3%), CS-treated patients recovered pulmonary function significantly faster (+0.9%/month FEV1, +0.85%/month FVC; both p=0.001), as shown by multivariable linear mixed-effects models adjusting for multiple confounders. The faster PFT recovery with CS was observed across all subgroups including those with BMI ≥30 and chronic lung disease, though substantial confounding by disease severity (CS-treated patients had 93% hospitalization rate vs. 20% in untreated) limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The study uses a mixed effects model reporting rate-of-change coefficients (% per month) rather than discrete endpoint values at fixed timepoints — the between_group_effects and within_group_change fields capture these as the 'Time:steroids' interaction term (0.9%/month FEV1, 0.9%/month FVC). 2. The baseline values reported in Table 1 reflect the FIRST clinic visit (mean 6.4 months post-COVID), not the time of acute infection. 3. Figures 1-4 show predicted values over time but no extractable numeric data from figures. 4. The FEV1/FVC ratio was measured but no numeric results were reported in the text or tables. 5. Follow-up duration: range 23 days to 20.9 months (~91 weeks max), mean 6.4 months (SD 3.9); total_duration_weeks estimated as ~90 weeks (20.9 months). 6. The 'within_group_change' entries for outcomes 1 and 2 represent the monthly rate of change (% predicted per month from the mixed-effects model), not a simple pre-post difference. 7. No adverse events reported.

summary: This retrospective single-arm case series evaluated bisphosphonate combination therapy (intravenous zoledronic acid 5mg plus oral alendronate 35mg twice weekly) in 48 post-COVID-19 patients (88 hips) with osteonecrosis of the femoral head at a tertiary center in India. At a mean follow-up of 10 months, 95.5% of hips had good clinical outcomes without surgery, VAS pain scores improved from 7.03 to 3.13 and Harris Hip Scores from 59.14 to 71.01 at 6 weeks, and only 4.5% of hips required total hip arthroplasty. No comparator group was included, limiting causal inference, but findings suggest bisphosphonate therapy is effective for preventing surgical intervention in post-COVID osteonecrosis, particularly when diagnosed early.

summary: This open-label, four-arm quasi-experimental study enrolled 243 post-COVID-19 patients in the early rehabilitation period in Uzbekistan to evaluate three hepatoprotectors—ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, 10 mg/kg/day), glycyrrhizic acid plus phospholipids (Phosphogliv, 6 tabs/day), and ademeteonine (2 tabs/day)—versus standard care without hepatoprotectors over one month. All groups showed significant improvements in liver biomarkers from markedly elevated baselines; however, UDCA produced the greatest reductions in ALT (to 58.9 vs. 99.3 U/L in controls, p<0.001) and total bilirubin (18.8 vs. 25.7 mmol/L, p<0.01), while ademeteonine showed the largest improvement in alkaline phosphatase. Allocation method was not randomized and baseline LDH differed substantially across arms, raising serious confounding concerns.

summary: This Russian case series (n=44) assessed erectile dysfunction and hormonal changes in men who developed sexual complaints 3 weeks to 2 months after recovery from PCR-confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients were divided by testosterone level into two groups (≥12 nmol/L, n=14; <12 nmol/L, n=30) and treated with PDE-5 inhibitors, antiasthenic therapy (glycine + sulbutiamine), and testosterone gel (for severely low testosterone). At 2-month follow-up, 66.5% of Group 2 patients reported normalization of erectile function with testosterone levels recovering above 12 nmol/L, though 23% had insufficient response and 10.5% had no response. The study had no control group and lacked formal statistical comparisons, but found a strong positive correlation between asthenia severity (MFI-20) and erectile dysfunction severity (IIEF-5).

summary: This single-arm before-after study examined 91 COVID-19 pneumonia convalescents (aged 21-67, 64% female) who underwent a rehabilitation program centered on haloaerosol therapy (dry rock salt aerosol inhalation, 18-20 sessions) in Ukraine. Prior to treatment, patients showed significantly elevated lipid peroxidation end products (Schiff bases), reduced catalase activity, elevated oxidative stress index, endotoxemia (average mass molecules), and circulating immune complexes compared to healthy controls; these abnormalities were present regardless of COVID-19 severity and persisted up to 3 months post-discharge without treatment. After the rehabilitation course, all biomarkers improved significantly (p<0.001) across all severity subgroups, with more pronounced improvement in mild cases, but none reached healthy control reference values, indicating incomplete restoration of oxidative homeostasis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Ukrainian with English abstract and tables. Table values are reported as M±SE (not SD); SE values extracted into the 'se' field. Arm-level data for severity subgroups (mild n=46, moderate n=31, severe n=14) and timing subgroups (≤1 month n=55, 2-3 months n=36) are provided — severity-subgroup pre/post data extracted as separate arm_results entries within each outcome (arm_id=1 used for all COVID-19 subgroups; subgroup identity indicated in n_analyzed and notes). The bacterial pneumonia comparison group (arm_id=2) only has baseline data reported (no intervention or post-treatment values). There is no control group that receives no treatment for COVID-19 convalescents, making it impossible to distinguish treatment effect from spontaneous recovery. The paper does not report the exact duration of the rehabilitation course in weeks — estimated at ~4 weeks based on 18-20 sessions at 5 days/week. Spirography results are mentioned as improving but no quantitative data provided. Post-treatment values for timing subgroups (≤1 month vs 2-3 months) not separately reported — only combined total and severity-stratified post-treatment data available.

summary: This retrospective observational study reviewed 239 medical records of patients with COVID-19-related post-COVID thrombotic complications treated in the vascular surgery department of the National Hospital of Kyrgyzstan (August–December 2020). Venous thromboses (predominantly in lower extremity veins) were 74% more common than arterial thromboses, and women had a 15.4% higher incidence than men. Open surgical interventions — most commonly great saphenous vein ligation (78% of venous cases) and thromboembolectomy (50% of arterial cases) — were the dominant treatment approach, with the paper concluding these are effective for post-COVID thrombotic syndrome; no comparative effectiveness data or post-operative outcomes were reported.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study examined 54 adults with post-acute COVID-19 VTE (PE or DVT within 90 days of infection) at a Romanian tertiary hospital between 2020-2022, comparing 11 patients who received systemic thrombolysis to 43 managed conservatively. Thrombolysis recipients had markedly lower TAPSE (13.0 vs. 20.8 mm), lower SpO2 (90.1% vs. 97.0%), and smaller LVEDD (24.4 vs. 46.1 mm), all statistically significant; in multivariable regression, each 1 mm decrease in TAPSE (OR 1.58) and each 1% decrease in SpO2 (OR 1.34) independently predicted thrombolysis. Inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, fibrinogen) and RV diameter were not associated with treatment group, supporting a non-invasive hemodynamic triad (low TAPSE, low SpO2, reduced LVEDD) as bedside risk-stratification markers for post-COVID VTE.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study using thrombolysis vs. no thrombolysis as a de facto two-arm comparison, but it is not an intervention trial — groups reflect physician-decided treatment. LVEDD values in the thrombolysis group (mean 24.4 mm) are unusually low (normal adult range ~37-53 mm), likely reflecting severe RV-mediated LV compression but should be noted as potentially extreme. Fibrinogen reported as median only without IQR. No long-term follow-up data reported — study captures only in-hospital period. The sPESI data in Table 2 reports mean±SD alongside medians. The paper is primarily a predictive/observational study of biomarkers for thrombolysis, not a treatment efficacy trial; caution is warranted in interpreting as evidence of thrombolysis efficacy.

summary: This propensity-score matched cohort study from the multicenter HOPE-2 registry examined the effect of corticosteroid therapy during acute COVID-19 hospitalization on 18-month all-cause mortality and long-term symptoms in 796 patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Corticosteroid use was not associated with differences in 18-month all-cause mortality (44.0% vs. 39.7%, log-rank p=0.52) or in-hospital mortality (41.2% vs. 36.4%, p=0.167), and no significant differences were found in any long-term post-COVID-19 symptom except for a higher rate of clinically relevant bleeding events in the corticosteroid group (4.1% vs. 0%, p=0.029). However, corticosteroid-treated patients had significantly shorter hospital stays (median 8 vs. 11 days, p<0.001), suggesting a possible benefit in recovery time without clear long-term benefit or harm in this high-risk cardiac subpopulation.

summary: This single-center prospective observational study assessed cognitive function in 63 convalescent COVID-19 patients (mean age 59.8 years, 74.6% male, 63.4% severe pneumonia) admitted for multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation in Italy. Approximately 44% were classified as having reduced cognitive efficiency (RCE), primarily affecting spatial and verbal long-term memory and executive functions. RCE patients were significantly more likely to be non-dippers on 24-hour BP monitoring (75% vs 45.7%, p=0.01), to have had more severe COVID-19 illness (p=0.02), to report PTSD symptoms (p=0.02), and to have cognitive complaints (p=0.002), and showed higher anxiety scores (mean HADS-A 10.39 vs 8.25, p=0.017), suggesting an association between autonomic dysregulation and post-COVID cognitive impairment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study at rehabilitation admission — there is no longitudinal follow-up and no intervention outcomes. The two 'arms' represent RCE vs NCE subgroups defined post-hoc, not pre-specified treatment groups. No adverse events reported (observational study). The paper reports Mann-Whitney U test p-values for continuous variables and chi-square p-values for categorical variables; no effect sizes (OR, RR) or confidence intervals are provided for between-group comparisons. All between-group effect_values for continuous outcomes were calculated as mean differences. Raw neuropsychological test scores (FAS, TMT, RAVLT, Corsi) per arm are reported in supplemental Table S2, which is not included in this paper text and therefore not extractable. FVC% data appears in Table 1 row format but only the overall value 75.59 (SD 20.25) is unambiguously provided — per-arm breakdown not explicitly stated in the table for FVC. Disease duration p-value in Table 3 is stated as 0.739 but abstract says 'longer disease duration (p=0.04)' — this discrepancy likely reflects different variables (disease duration days vs duration of bed stay); extracted as reported in Table 3.

summary: This single-center retrospective case series from Japan evaluated hypothalamic-pituitary function in 15 long COVID patients (mean age 35.6 years, mean 343 days post-infection) using combined CRH, TRH, and GnRH anterior pituitary stimulation tests. While peak hormonal responses were preserved across all axes (ΔACTH 247%, ΔTSH 918%, ΔPRL 820%, ΔLH 1150%, ΔFSH 187%), markedly delayed peaks were observed in FSH (87% of patients), LH (33%), and ACTH (13%), and significant sustained elevations at 120 minutes were detected for TSH, PRL, LH, and FSH. These patterns, particularly the delayed and prolonged gonadotropin responses, suggest functional hypothalamic dysfunction—specifically impaired GnRH pulsatility—rather than primary pituitary pathology, and may contribute to hypogonadism and menstrual abnormalities reported in long COVID patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a diagnostic/observational case series, not a treatment trial — there is no intervention arm with pre/post treatment outcomes in the conventional sense. The 'intervention' is the stimulation test procedure itself, used to characterize endocrine physiology. Some key data (time-course hormone response curves) are in figures only with limited numeric values extracted from text (baseline and 120 min values are in text; peak percent changes are stated but per-timepoint means/SDs at 15/30/60/90 min are only in figures). GH basal values split by sex reported in Table 2 but only male values with SE noted (male mean 0.52±0.25, female 0.6±0.32 ng/mL). The 120 min values for TSH (1.4 vs 5.7 mIU/L), PRL-male (25.7 vs 34.8 ng/mL), LH-male (5.2 vs 31.8 mIU/mL), LH-female (4.9 vs 38.1 mIU/mL), FSH-female (4.3 vs 11.8 mIU/mL) are verbatim from the paper. Significance levels cited as p<0.05 or p<0.01 without exact values. The study provides no treatment outcome data and should be classified primarily as a mechanistic/diagnostic observational study.

summary: The P4O2 COVID-19 study is a multicenter prospective observational cohort study with a nested optional personalized lifestyle counseling intervention in 95 long COVID patients (aged 40-65) recruited from five Dutch post-COVID outpatient clinics at 3-6 months post-infection. This paper reports the study design and baseline characteristics only; no intervention outcome data are yet presented. At baseline (3-6 months post-COVID), the most prevalent persistent symptoms were respiratory (78.9%), neurological (68.4%), and fatigue (67.4%), with the majority (84.8%) showing pulmonary function or radiological abnormalities. Female sex (OR=0.25, p=0.002) and Delta vs. Beta variant infection (OR=3.54, p=0.014) were significantly associated with experiencing more than two symptom categories.

Arm-level N for intervention vs. control not reported at this stage. Baseline outcomes extracted are all cross-sectional at 3-6 months post-COVID. The note '610 have already participated in the second study visit' appears to be a typo in the original (likely '61'). TABLE A1 was truncated in the provided text. Pulmonary function test/radiological abnormality denominator: 14 without + 78 with = 92 (not 95), suggesting 3 missing values. Percent with abnormalities calculated as 78/92 = 84.8%.

summary: This non-randomized prospective study compared olfactory outcomes in 45 long COVID patients (anosmia/hyposmia ≥180 days post-infection) treated with um-PEA-LUT plus olfactory training for 3 months versus 40 MS patients on standard DMTs, using Sniffin' Sticks TDI scoring. At baseline, COVID-19 patients had markedly lower TDI scores (mean 12.6±5.1, mostly anosmic) versus MS patients (mean 33.5±4.9, mostly normosmic); after 3 months, 71.2% of COVID-19 patients recovered normal/borderline-normal olfaction (TDI 34.3±4.6), while MS patients showed stable olfactory function with no significant T0-T1 change. MS patients treated with IFN-beta 1a or glatiramer acetate had no olfactory dysfunction at follow-up (p=0.02 vs. other DMTs), suggesting a hypothesis-generating rationale for investigating DMT in refractory post-COVID olfactory loss.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a hypothesis-generating comparative study, not an RCT; the two arms have different underlying diseases making between-group effect sizes difficult to interpret clinically. Overall T1 TDI means for the full long COVID arm are not reported as a single summary statistic — they are split into 'recovered' (n=32, TDI 34.3±4.6) and 'non-recovered' (n=13, TDI 18.5±8.1) subgroups. MS arm T1 data are only reported for the 10 patients with residual olfactory impairment. Several figures (Figures 1–4) show estimation plots with additional data that could not be extracted numerically from the text. The arm_id=2 (MS) uses multiple different DMTs — heterogeneous comparator. Table rendering in the source appeared garbled (merged cells in DMT treatment table); patient counts per DMT were: Fingolimod 8, Teriflunomide 7, Ocrelizumab 4, Cladribine 3, Dimethylfumarate 6, IFN-beta 1a Avonex 1, Natalizumab 4, IFN-beta 1a Plegridy 3, Glatiramer Acetate 2 (total=38, slight discrepancy with n=40 analyzed — likely 2 counted differently or table formatting issue). EDSS correlation with identification score: Pearson p=0.006 (inverse correlation) — not extracted as separate outcome as no effect size reported.

summary: This retrospective single-center case series described 227 patients with neurological post-COVID-19 syndrome seen at an outpatient clinic in Croatia between May 2021 and June 2022. The most common presenting symptoms were headache (30%) and cognitive impairment (29%), followed by smell disorders, paresthesia, chronic fatigue, and dizziness. Of 109 patients (48%) who attended follow-up at a mean of 9.63 months, 53% had no change in symptoms and 45% had improvement or resolution; therapy was mostly symptomatic (vitamin supplements most common), and no controlled efficacy analysis was performed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a descriptive retrospective case series with no control group and no standardized treatment protocol; there are no pre-post quantitative outcome measures (means/SDs), only symptom frequency counts and categorical follow-up outcomes. The 'therapy' described is not a clinical trial intervention — patients received heterogeneous symptomatic treatments decided by physicians. Follow-up outcomes are only categorical (no change / improved / worsened). Time since infection reported as 6.11 ± 11.15 weeks mean (converted to months: ~1.53 ± 2.79 months). Follow-up duration of 9.63 ± 5.10 months converted to ~41.8 weeks. Table 3 appears to have a data entry error: psychological testing listed as 313 patients (likely should be 31, consistent with text stating 14% of 227 = ~31 patients). Symptom counts in Table 2 sum to more than N=227 because patients had multiple symptoms.

summary: This prospective case series from Chiba University Hospital (Japan) describes 9 long COVID patients (May-September 2021) treated with individualized Kampo (traditional Japanese herbal medicine) formulas — primarily tonic formulas (補剤) and Bupleuri radix-containing formulas (柴胡剤) — combined with lifestyle guidance including restriction of cold foods and drinks. All 9 patients showed a tendency toward symptom improvement within 4-5 weeks of starting treatment, with 7 of 9 showing improvement in their chief complaint within 4 weeks. No control group was included, and individual-level VAS data showed reductions of 20-50 points for pain, fatigue, cough, and taste/smell disturbance in reported cases, though no formal statistical testing was performed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Japanese with an English abstract; table data partially garbled due to OCR issues with Japanese characters. VAS data are reported only for individual cases (not aggregated across all 9 patients), so arm_results n_analyzed=1 for each VAS outcome. Case numbers in Table 2 appear to have row numbering issues (two rows labeled '1' and '7' for different patients — likely a table OCR artifact; row labeled '7' treated as Case 7). Age range (17-69 years) is stated but mean/SD not reported for the group. Time since infection: mean 13.2 weeks (range 3-36 weeks) stated verbatim. BMI values available per patient in Table 1 but no group summary statistics. Percent previously hospitalized: 5 of 9 patients had hospital admission (cases 1, 3, 6, 7 admitted; case 2 stated 'home isolation' but hospitalization status for case 9 is unclear — calculated as 5/9=55.6% based on available data). Narrative description of case 6 provides additional VAS timepoints beyond Table 2. Case 8 olfactory outcome described as 'nearly normal' at 5 weeks but no numeric VAS given for olfaction at that timepoint. The paper notes that final clinical assessment was deferred to 3+ months follow-up, which was not reported in this publication.

summary: This single-arm before-after study enrolled 82 COVID-19 survivors with deranged pulmonary function at AIIMS Bhopal, India, and examined the effect of an 8-week supervised selective yoga regime (pranayama, asanas, and chanting, 30 min twice daily) on spirometric parameters. After 8 weeks, statistically significant improvements were observed in FVC % predicted (63.2% to 77.0%, p<0.001), FEV1 % predicted (65.0% to 77.4%, p<0.001), and FIVC % predicted (53.8% to 69.3%, p<0.001), while FEF25-75% showed a marginal improvement (p=0.014) and PEF and FEV1/FVC ratio did not change significantly. The study lacked a concurrent control group, so natural recovery over time cannot be ruled out as a contributing factor.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post design only; 'Group I (preyoga)' and 'Group II (postyoga)' refer to the same cohort of participants measured at two timepoints (n=82 pre, n=73 post due to 9 lost to follow-up), not two separate groups. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied across-timepoints as the primary within-group comparison. Percent female calculated from Table 4: 24 females in preyoga group out of 82 total = 29.3%. Change means for within_group_change are calculated (post minus pre mean) since the paper reports only p-values for group comparisons, not explicit change scores. The p-value for FVC and FEV1 categorical outcomes and FIVC continuous outcome is reported as '<0.001' (coded as p_value_exact: false). Table 4 baseline demographic data noted as mean (SD) for age and BMI.

summary: This single-arm observational case series followed 60 patients hospitalized in Albania for post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis over 10 weeks. Patients received unspecified inpatient management including supplemental oxygen at varying levels (ventilator to none). At 10 weeks, 25.6% showed significant improvement, 64% showed slight improvement, and 10.4% showed no improvement; 2 patients (3.3%) died by week 2. The study lacks a comparison group, validated outcome instruments, and demographic data, severely limiting interpretability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Major limitations: (1) No specific intervention or drug treatment described — 'management' is undefined. (2) Outcome data for the 10-week endpoint reported only as percentages with no denominator stated for outcomes 5-7 (the 39 patients still hospitalized vs. all 60 enrolled is ambiguous). (3) Week-5 improvement percentages sum to ~100% (31.7+41.7+26.7=100.1%) suggesting they apply to all 60 enrolled patients. summary: This single-arm retrospective cohort study examined the effects of a 14-day inpatient physiotherapy rehabilitation program in 30 post-COVID-19 patients (mean age 62.4 years) at a rehabilitation hospital in India. summary: This uncontrolled retrospective multicenter Russian real-world study assessed the immunomodulator azoximer bromide (Polyoxidonium) in 16,365 adults and children (≥6 months) with acute infectious-inflammatory upper respiratory diseases, including a small number with COVID-19 and post-COVID syndrome. After a 10-day treatment course (mostly intranasal/sublingual, often combined with antibiotics or symptomatic drugs), 40% of patients achieved complete symptom relief and 99.77% showed positive dynamics on a 5-point physician scale; for the post-COVID subgroup, 29% had complete relief and 71% had marked improvement. No comparison group was included, no statistical testing was performed, and improvement cannot be attributed to the study drug rather than natural disease course.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT primarily a long COVID study — it is a large uncontrolled real-world registry study of azoximer bromide for acute upper respiratory infections. Post-COVID syndrome was a minor subgroup (exact N not reported). The study has no control group, no baseline symptom scores, no validated outcome instruments, and physician-assessed outcomes without blinding. Symptom resolution data are reported as proportions resolved by day 3 or day 5, not as continuous scores with means/SDs — no per-arm means or SDs available. Figure 1 (symptom resolution curves) and Figure 2 (5-point scale by disease type) contain additional data not fully captured in text; exact N for post-COVID and COVID-19 subgroups not reported. Median patient age is 28 years overall; sex breakdown given separately for children (48% female / 52% male) and adults (58% female / 42% male) but not for the post-COVID subgroup. The 10-day treatment duration was reported for 85% of cases (range 5–20 days).

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Serious confounding: patients were not randomized to treatment arms, severity-based stratification means the sickest patients received the most intensive treatment, and only 41/84 patients had microbiological samples collected, introducing selection bias in the culture-based analyses.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: 6 deaths (27.3%) in ICU/mechanical ventilation group, 0 deaths in ICU/oxygen group, 2 deaths (4.5%) in ward group; p<0.001.
5 deaths among 22 cases with resistant isolates: 3 in XDR, 1 in PDR, 1 in MDR; prognosis worsens from MDR to XDR; no deaths in sensitive organism group.
Culture positivity was 51% in critically ill, 22.6% in severe category, and 25.8% in ward patients (p=0.003 highly significant).

summary: This retrospective observational study from a tertiary care hospital in India described the microbial profile and antibiotic resistance patterns of 84 long COVID pneumonia patients admitted April–October 2021. Microbiological samples were collected from 41 patients, yielding 32 culture-positive isolates (75.6%), of which 68.75% were drug-resistant organisms (predominantly Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii). Despite high rates of drug-resistant co-infection, severe comorbidities, and raised inflammatory biomarkers, the overall survival rate was 90.5% (76/84), with 8 deaths — 6 in ICU patients on mechanical ventilation and 5 associated with resistant pathogens (XDR/PDR/MDR strains), a finding reported as statistically significant (p<0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective observational microbiological profiling study — not a treatment intervention trial in the conventional sense. The 'intervention' is targeted antimicrobial therapy per culture/sensitivity results, but there is no comparison arm. Subgroup data for biomarkers (CRP, procalcitonin, D-dimer, TLC) are broken out by severity group with medians but without IQRs. Age data is reported as mean ± SD per severity subgroup (58.8±13.13 ICU/ventilated, 53.3±23.3 ICU/oxygen, 50.3±9.13 ward) but not for the overall cohort. Some figures referenced (Figures 1-4) describe resistance patterns and outcome flowcharts but quantitative data from these figures is also available in tables. Mortality in Table 5 shows 6 deaths among 32 culture-positive patients but the paper also reports 8 total deaths among 84 patients (2 culture-negative deaths in ward). Table note discrepancy: abstract states 32 (78.1%) culture-positive out of 41 samples, but results text states 31 samples positive with 32 isolates — likely 31 positive samples yielding 32 isolates (one patient had same organism from two sample types).

summary: In this UK multicenter, single-blind RCT of 78 adults with cognitive impairment associated with long COVID, 10 weekly sessions of individualized, goal-oriented telehealth cognitive rehabilitation (CR) were compared with treatment as usual (TAU). CR produced significantly greater self-reported goal attainment than TAU at both 3 and 6 months (adjusted mean difference at 6 months, 1.72 [95% CI, 0.86-2.57]; P<.001; Cohen d=0.91), a large and sustained effect, though most secondary cognitive and symptom outcomes did not differ between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per review extraction scope, only the primary outcome (BGSI goal attainment) was extracted and only its final (6-month) timepoint; the 3-month primary-outcome data were omitted (adjusted mean difference 2.88 [95% CI, 2.03-3.73], P<.001, Cohen d=1.57; CR 7.84[0.19] vs TAU 4.97[0.53]). All secondary outcomes (goal satisfaction, LSA, SF-DEM, IADL, GAD-7, PHQ-8, CFS, PSQI, DSQ-PEM, RBANS, D-KEFS subtests, WAIS, 4 Mountains Test, Gorilla tasks) were omitted per scope despite being reported in Table 2. Per-arm n_randomized/n_completed/n_analyzed/withdrawal detail and subgroup analyses were also omitted per scope. All *_quote fields were set to null per scope instruction. Discrepancy noted: prose states 258 participants were screened for eligibility, but the Figure 1 flowchart long-description reports '252 Screened'; the verbatim text value (258) was used for n_screened. Per-arm mean/SE reported for the primary outcome are adjusted (multiple-imputation, mixed-effects model) values, not raw unadjusted means; Table 2 reports a single N=78 for the full imputed model rather than a per-arm split, so per-arm n_analyzed was inferred from n_randomized (38 CR, 40 TAU).

summary: This 2016 narrative review/opinion paper by Comhaire and Devriendt argues that chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is primarily an immune-mediated disorder driven by T-lymphocyte dysfunction, cytokine overproduction, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, and proposes renaming it 'Systemic Immune Disorder' (SID). The authors review evidence for genetic/epigenetic predispositions, viral triggers (EBV, HHV-6), and neuro-inflammatory pathways, and critically appraise existing treatments including CBT/GET (deemed minimally effective), Rituximab (moderate-to-important improvement in two-thirds of patients in one open-label study), and a proprietary nutraceutical supplement (Improve®). No original quantitative data are reported; the paper presents consensus opinion based on literature synthesis and the first author's clinical experience.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a narrative review/opinion article published in 2016 about CFS/ME — it is NOT a long COVID treatment study and contains no primary quantitative outcome data. The paper does not study COVID-19 or post-COVID conditions at all (predates the pandemic). No arms, outcomes, sample sizes, or effect sizes can be extracted. All structured fields are null/empty. This record should likely be excluded from the meta-analysis as it does not meet eligibility criteria (not a long COVID study, not a primary intervention trial).

summary: This single-center retrospective case-control study compared JAK inhibitors plus rapidly tapered corticosteroids (n=21) with prolonged corticosteroids alone (n=20) in patients with hypoxic, inflammatory ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 pulmonary disease.
