Primary outcome comprised both proportion liberated from oxygen and time to liberation.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Nonrandomized, self-selected group assignment with ~50% loss to follow-up (differential, highest in the no-exercise group), very small follow-up groups, unblinded virtual testing, and mean imputation of missing test values.

summary: This nonrandomized program evaluation of 106 patients discharged after COVID-19 hospitalization with persistent symptoms compared virtual physical therapy (n=44), home physical therapy (n=25), independent exercise (n=17), and no exercise (n=20); only 53 returned for follow-up at about 2 weeks. Sit-to-stand and step-test scores improved significantly within the VPT and HPT groups (step test also in IE) but not in the no-exercise group, and more VPT/HPT patients met the clinically meaningful difference for sit-to-stand than the no-exercise group (P=.03 and P<.01), while step-test CMD differences were not significant. Interpretation is limited by self-selection, differential attrition and small follow-up groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 footnote says values are percent or median (IQR), so age, BMI and PHQ-4 entries are medians with a single IQR width that cannot be split into low/high; BMI is therefore left null, and age is entered as median only. Within-group Hedges d values (sit-to-stand: VPT 1.14, HPT 1.02, IE .61, None .15; step test: VPT .96, HPT 1.11, IE .85, None .38) and Wilcoxon Z statistics are reported only in Table 3 and are noted in source_location. Within-group change_mean values are calculated from the group means. SpO2 results are pooled across arms (arm_id null). The paper reports Wilcoxon tests but presents means/SDs. Missing exercise test values were mean-imputed (10 sit-to-stand, 15 step test), so n_analyzed is the follow-up group size. Time since infection, vaccination, and adverse events not reported. Figures 1 and 2 hold no additional numeric data beyond Table 3.

summary: Two unvaccinated men with post-COVID-19 organizing pneumonia and inadequate steroid response or relapse were given mycophenolate mofetil added to corticosteroids. Both improved clinically, physiologically and radiologically and could taper steroids, though one stopped MMF at about 10 weeks because of colitis; no statistical testing was done and this uncontrolled report cannot establish efficacy.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: 57 participants were randomized but only 44 (22 per arm) appear in analyses with no reported reasons or flow, and fatigue/QoL outcomes were self-reported by unblinded participants.

summary: In this single-center open-label RCT, 57 non-hospitalized adults with persisting post-COVID fatigue were randomized to 4 weeks of supervised, personalized strength-endurance training (2-3 sessions/week) or no intervention; 44 (22 per arm) appear in the analyses. Training was safe with no adverse events and 96.7% compliance, and improved within-group peak workload, VO2peak, oxygen pulse and strength. VO2peak and oxygen pulse showed group effects on percent change, but MFI-20 fatigue, MQOL and PCFS improved similarly in both groups with no between-group differences at 4 weeks or 3 months. At 6 months the exercise group had higher physical activity and MQOL psychological scores (both p<0.05).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2/3 cells are split across separate XML cells (mean, ' ± ', SD), so result_quote is null for those rows; values and locations are given in source_location. Randomized N=57 but analyzed N=44 (Table 1: 22 per arm); per-arm randomized counts, dropouts and CONSORT numbers appear only in Fig. 1 (image). t2/t3 timepoints set to ~13 and ~26 weeks from 'after 3 and 6 months' (inferred); n_analyzed for t2/t3 is unstated. The primary outcome (MFI-20 improvement in >=2 of 5 dimensions) is not reported numerically; sample size was powered on VO2peak. The 'MFI-20 score or number of dimensions changed' change (-2.2 vs -1.7) is ambiguous in unit. PCFS change p=0.933 in text vs Table 4 group p t1=0.412 (discrepancy). Percent changes: VO2peak and oxygen pulse group-effect p-values are for percent change (text), while Table 3 group p-values are for endpoint t1 values. Control-arm percent changes for VO2peak, oxygen pulse and bench press not reported. Time since infection converted from days to months (/30.44). Several outcomes also shown in figures only (Figs 2-4).

summary: This prospective, non-randomized controlled study compared 12 weeks of classical olfactory training (n=25 analyzed) with no treatment (n=18) in adults with persistent post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction, with groups chosen by patient preference. TDI improved by 5.68 points with training versus 1.46 without; a clinically meaningful improvement (≥5.5 points) occurred in 40% vs 6% (p=0.014). No adverse effects were reported, but allocation was by preference and the sample was small.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Reduction was larger in extreme fatigue (-5.43 points, p=0.002) than in moderate fatigue (-2.20, p=0.014); only the extreme group exceeded the MCID of 4 points.

summary: A retrospective single-arm evaluation of a German telephone coaching programme (Covidcare) teaching pacing strategies to adults with Post-COVID over about 6 months; 85 of 239 participants (36%) had FAS at both time points. Mean FAS fell from 31.94 to 28.81 (difference 3.13, p<0.001), with larger improvement in extreme fatigue (39.73 to 34.30) than in moderate fatigue (28.58 to 26.38). Without a control group and with a low response rate, the effect cannot be attributed to the programme; the authors call for controlled studies.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Table 2 cells were joined from separate lines in the text; reported Differenz is T1 minus T2 (positive = reduction), recorded here as T2 minus T1 (negative values), hence 'calculated'. Cohen's d (0.43, 0.48, 0.65, 0.36) reported but not extracted as effect. Text states p=0.001 as 'p<0,001' for all-participant and fatigue groups (recorded as 0.001 with operator <). Time since infection not reported. Single arm; subgroups by baseline FAS are overlapping/nested populations (n=80 includes n=30 and n=50). Satisfaction survey (447/568 improved health, 473/568 improved quality of life) is a separate non-standardised internal survey, not extracted as outcome.

summary: Retrospective case series of 20 non-hospitalized patients (70% female, median age 40) with new-onset autonomic disorders (75% POTS, 15% NCS, 10% OH) after presumed or confirmed COVID-19, treated with non-pharmacologic measures plus pharmacotherapy in 80%. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm descriptive case series; no continuous outcome data or standardized instruments. summary: This pilot RCT compared a 16-week personalized home-based cognitive and motor telerehabilitation program (46 analyzed) with standard care (33 analyzed) in adults with post-COVID condition or ME/CFS. No between-group differences in cognitive, symptom or 6-minute walk outcomes survived FDR correction, and mixed models showed no Time x Group effects, though an exploratory PCA component was nominally higher in the intervention group (p=0.043, unadjusted). Adherence was high (median about 100%) and usability favorable (median SUS 77.5) under individualized clinical support.

Blinding, allocation concealment and site count not reported; country inferred from Basque ethics committee.

summary: Retrospective single-center German cohort of 122 patients with persistent pulmonary symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection, classified into alveolitis/ILD-dominant (n=61, prednisolone), bronchiolitis-dominant (n=47, azithromycin), asthma-dominant (n=11) and unclassified (n=3) phenotypes after multimodal workup. At 3 months, median paired changes were small but BH-adjusted significant for FEV1 (+2 points), FVC (+1), DLCO (+2) and RV/TLC (-7); KCO, FEV1/FVC, MEF50, TLC, sRtot and oxygen pulse did not reach significance. With no control group, baseline lung function largely normal, and no validated patient-reported outcomes, the authors state results are exploratory and do not establish treatment efficacy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports medians [IQR] only (no means/SDs). Phenotype-specific values are in Supplementary Tables S1/S2 (not available). p_value in within_group_change is the raw Wilcoxon p; BH-adjusted p given in source_location. Month 3 mapped to ~13 weeks. Treatment durations differ by phenotype (prednisolone 6 months, azithromycin 3 months), so treatment duration left null. Paper's ethics section contains boilerplate inconsistencies (singular 'the patient', organ donor statement). Outcome 11 category counts: only one category per timepoint captured in events (restrictive); normal/obstructive counts are in the quotes/source_location. Patient-reported functioning was qualitative only.

summary: This retrospective single-center chart review of 50 Long COVID patients treated with off-label low-dose aripiprazole (0.1-2 mg) found a significant improvement in a modified functional status scale (median 4.0 to 3.0, mean 3.78 to 3.28, p=0.001), while symptom count, composite symptom score, and the seven individual symptom scores did not change significantly. With no control group, concomitant naltrexone use in most patients, and a non-validated questionnaire, the findings are hypothesis-generating and need confirmation in randomized trials.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No per-arm SDs for outcomes (medians with IQR and means only); within-patient change values not reported. Follow-up timing was variable and unstated. Text gives age SD 12.97 and BMI SD 6.35 (table: 6.41); table values used. Text reports mean days on LDA as 315 and also 204.4, so treatment duration left null. Composite score values in Table 1 (about 20) are consistent with a sum of seven items although Methods describe an average. The longitudinal 33-patient results are in Supplementary Table S4 (not provided), and only p-values are available from text. Level II-V distribution extracted for level IV only in arm_results; other levels are described in source_location. Adverse events: 12/76 in the full LDA-exposed cohort; weight changes are among 50 analyzed patients.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: randomization:low, deviations:low, missing_data:some_concerns, measurement:low, reporting:some_concerns
risk_of_bias.key_concern: About 15% of randomized participants (12/78) were lost, no imputation was used, no sample size calculation was performed, and no per-arm randomized numbers or prespecified analysis plan were reported.

notable_aes.event: insomnia, irritability and agitation (led to discontinuation)

summary: This single-center, double-blind RCT in Brazil randomized 78 adults with persistent interstitial lung disease after severe COVID-19 pneumonia to oral prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day for 30 days, then tapered over 21 days) or placebo, with 6 months of follow-up (66 analyzed). Lung function, inflammatory markers, quality of life, functional status and HRCT findings improved over time in both groups, with no significant between-group differences, including for the primary outcome FVC. Only the prednisolone group had a significant 6MWT improvement versus baseline, and the trial was small and had no sample size calculation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm randomized Ns not reported (78 total; 12 lost, 1 prednisolone discontinuation for AEs, other 11 not assigned to arm). Analysis Ns taken from table headers: Table 2 placebo 29 / prednisolone 28; Table 3 placebo 35 / prednisolone 30 (text says final analysis 35 and 31); ESR/CRP Ns not stated. No numeric between-group effect estimates or exact p-values were reported; only qualitative 'no significant difference' statements, so effect arrays hold no values. Within-arm significance vs baseline was flagged only by footnotes. Other HRCT finding rows (ground glass, mosaic attenuation, architectural distortion, bands, bronchiectasis, airway disease) in Table 4 were not extracted, and D-dimer values were not reported. Table 1 race rows are internally inconsistent (e.g., Black 24 (77.5%) in prednisolone vs White/Asian 16 (51.6%)). Table 3 PCFS percentages for prednisolone (33%) do not match 9/30 (30%); reported as printed. Time since infection reported only overall (118.2 ± 19.9 days). Age is labeled median (IQR) but the values look like ranges. Stated sample size of 31 in prednisolone vs 30 in Table 3 is unexplained.

title: Corticosteroid treatment for post-COVID-19 persistent interstitial lung disease: a randomized clinical trial
journal: The Brazilian Journal of Infectious Diseases
authors: Rosângela Villela Garcia; Marcel Koenigkam-Santos; Lucas Botelho de Azevedo; Danilo Tadao Wada; Ada Clarice Gastaldi; Elcio Oliveira Vianna
release_limitations: AI-screened and AI-extracted; eligibility and numerical values have not been independently adjudicated.

arms.label: Yoga
arms.intervention_name: Yoga (Hatha and Kundalini-based program with postures, breathing techniques, brief relaxation/meditation)

arms.label: Health promotion
arms.dose: fortnightly web links (1-2 pages each)

study_design.setting: single-center, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm; yoga studio classes

participants.long_covid_definition: Post COVID diagnosis confirmed by physician; post COVID condition defined as usually within three months of COVID-19 onset, lasting a minimum of two months, not explained by alternative diagnosis
required_symptoms: post-COVID symptoms with negative impact on quality of life
key_inclusion_criteria: Resident in Stockholm County and fluent in Swedish
Able to attend baseline and follow-up assessments
Post-COVID symptoms negatively impacting quality of life
key_exclusion_criteria: Raised blood pressure >=160/100 mmHg or irregular pulse
Currently/recently engaged in regular structured exercise, yoga or meditation

summary: This Swedish pilot RCT randomized 29 adults with physician-diagnosed post COVID to a 12-week supervised yoga program (n=13) or a health promotion web-based comparator (n=16). The yoga program was feasible, with similar adherence and acceptability across arms and no dropouts in the yoga group versus 4 in the HP group. SF-36 PCS and MCS showed no statistically significant between-group differences (PCS B=-1.30, p=.269; MCS B=3.49, p=.054), though the trial was underpowered with notable baseline imbalances.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 post-baseline means are probably imputed values (multiple imputation in HP group), so mean_type is unknown. Time since infection and hospitalization not reported. Several result_quote fields are null for table cells because a single contiguous verbatim table-row span including headers could not be cleanly separated; source_location identifies the cell. Randomization described as sex-stratified, so stratification_factors lists sex. Number of sites inferred from single-center description. Feasibility outcomes (acceptability, retention, adherence) were described as primary; HR-QoL was assessed as a preliminary effect, so is_primary is null for SF-36. Within-group change CIs are for the mean change in each arm; the n_completed for HP calculated as 16-4.

summary: In this German multicentre, double-blind 2x2 factorial phase 3 trial, 323 non-hospitalised adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome (median symptom duration 79 weeks) were randomised to 28 days of prednisolone, B vitamins (B1/B6/B12), both, or placebo. Prednisolone reduced the PROMIS composite T-score significantly more than no prednisolone (adjusted mean difference −1.4, 95% CI −2.5 to −0.4, p=0.008), driven mainly by fatigue, but this fell short of the prespecified 3-point clinically meaningful threshold. B vitamins showed no effect (−0.1, p=0.85), there was no interaction, all groups improved including placebo, and the prednisolone effect did not persist at days 60 and 180.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Factorial design: main-effect contrasts pool arms (prednisolone = arms 1+4 vs 2+3; B vitamins = arms 3+4 vs 1+2). They are bound to arm 1 vs arm 2 and arm 3 vs arm 2 as proxies. Pairwise four-arm contrasts were not reported because the interaction was null. Per-arm table values (Tables 1-3) have null quotes because table cells cannot be quoted contiguously from the supplied XML-stripped text; values are read from the column headers (Prednisolone, B vitamins, Prednisolone + B vitamins, Placebo) and mapped to arm_ids 1, 3, 4, 2. Table 1 ITT Ns (78/80/76/81 = 315) differ from the Table 2 analysed Ns (77/79/74/80 = 310) and from the randomised Ns. Per-arm baseline Ns by outcome follow Table 2 headers, but the Sit-to-Stand arm Ns (77/71/73/74) were mapped from the header order Prednisolone/B vitamins/Prednisolone+B/Placebo, so arms 2-4 are assigned accordingly. Within-arm paired p-values and the PROMIS domain subscores (fatigue subscore −6.4 points; Fig. 2) were not extracted per arm: subscores are figure-only. Also not extracted: NNT 7.5 (95% CI 4.0–55.1), MYMOP fatigue responder 31% vs 23% (no event counts), blinding indices, PROMIS follow-up at days 5, 14, 21, 60, 180 (figure only), and TAP outcomes (not reported). Allocation concealment is not explicitly described. Randomisation lists were stored with no access for enrolment staff, so this was inferred as unclear/central.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:critical, selection:serious, classification:low, deviations:moderate, missing_data:serious, measurement:serious, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Single-arm, retrospective, open-label design without a control group, with co-medications, psychoeducational support, natural recovery and 19% attrition (65/80) confounding the observed pre-post improvements.

summary: Retrospective single-center, single-arm Italian study of 80 adults with a post-COVID-19 major depressive episode treated with flexibly dosed vortioxetine (5-20 mg/day) plus psychoeducational support. Over 3 months (65 with endpoint data), physical symptoms, cognition (DSST, PDQ-D5), depression, anxiety, anhedonia, sleep, well-being and some inflammatory indexes improved significantly (87.7% remission at endpoint), with only mild side effects. The absence of a control group means improvements cannot be attributed to vortioxetine alone.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Mean change column values are MMRM model-based (SE, not SD). Table reports within-group SMDs (e.g., HDRS -1.58/-3.98; DSST 0.25/0.53; PDQ-D5 -0.83/-1.81) with unknown standardization, not extracted as between-group effects. Table 1 percentages (e.g., female 55.6%, hospitalized 37.7%) do not exactly match 80 denominators; recorded verbatim. Per-timepoint n for MMRM changes not stated except 65 with endpoint data; 1-month n left null. Days from infection to MDE diagnosis (79.8±34.6) is not time since infection at treatment, so not entered. Timing of vortioxetine start relative to baseline is unclear (inclusion required >=3 months ongoing treatment yet baseline precedes the 3-month assessment). Response at endpoint (6, 9.2%) excludes the 57 remitters. Number of sites inferred as single center (monocentric per limitations).

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:critical, selection:serious, classification:low, deviations:low, missing_data:moderate, measurement:serious, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Single-arm uncontrolled pre-post design in 9 patients with no disease-matched control and no blinding, so changes cannot be attributed to the drug.

summary: In this small prospective, non-randomized pilot study, nine immunodeficient patients with long-COVID-associated ME/CFS and detectable circulating spike protein received a single dose of Tixagevimab/Cilgavimab (given as COVID prophylaxis) and were assessed before and 30 days after. β1-adrenergic receptor autoantibodies fell nominally (26.8 to 21.2 U/ml, unadjusted p=0.003), but spike protein, the other autoantibodies, handgrip strength, SF-36, CERAD-Plus, Chalder and Bell scores did not change significantly. With no disease-matched control and exploratory unadjusted analyses, the findings are hypothesis-generating and do not show clinical efficacy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Healthy reference cohort (n=11) is explicitly NOT an efficacy control; included as arm 2 for descriptive baseline data only, and has_comparison_group set false. Reference-arm results extracted only for GPCR autoantibodies and CERAD total (reference values for other CERAD subtests are in Table 2 but not extracted). Table 2 CERAD rows use shifted colspans (reference baseline col2-3, reference follow-up col4-6, exposed baseline col7, exposed follow-up col8-9, p col10); mapped accordingly and consistent with prose. Statistical test per outcome (paired t-test vs Wilcoxon) not specified, so sidedness set unknown. Spike protein median(IQR) reported; baseline-only p-values for reference vs exposed are descriptive. Time 30 days converted to 4.3 weeks. SF-36 Role-physical baseline reported as '0' without SD. Spearman correlations between change in spike protein and change in autoantibodies (n=9): β1 rho=0.52 p=0.162; β2 rho=-0.10 p=0.810; M3 rho=0.17 p=0.678; M4 rho=-0.13 p=0.744 (not entered as outcomes). Supplemental immunophenotyping data (Supplemental Table 1) not available. Adverse events not reported.

title: Exploratory clinical and immunological changes following Tixagevimab/Cilgavimab administration in immunodeficient patients with SARS-CoV-2-associated ME/CFS and persistent circulating spike protein
authors: Maximilian Seidel; Moritz Anft; Lea Wiemers; Felix S. Seibert; Sebastian Bertram; Kamil Rosiewicz; Ulrik Stervbo; Timm H. Westhoff; Nina Babel
release_limitations: AI-screened and AI-extracted; eligibility and numerical values have not been independently adjudicated.

study_design.design_type_detail: open-label, parallel-group, 1:1, block randomization (size 12) stratified by sex

arms.label: Tailored exercise + standard care
arms.intervention_name: Individually tailored endurance and resistance exercise with weekly physiotherapist supervision
arms.dose: Up to 5 sessions/week, low-moderate intensity, mainly supine/semirecumbent; median 2.6 sessions/week reported

arms.intervention_name: Standard care (no POTS-specific or tailored exercise program)
co_interventions: alternative activities permitted (walking, breathing, flexibility, balance)

study_design.setting: Recruited in Stockholm via Karolinska University Hospital, primary care rehabilitation and specialized physiotherapy clinics

participants.long_covid_definition: Adults with POTS following COVID-19 or post-COVID-19 condition (PCC)
key_exclusion_criteria: Cognitive or physical impairments preventing participation

summary: In this open-label RCT in Stockholm, 60 adults with POTS after COVID-19 were randomized to 16 weeks of individually tailored, mostly supine low-to-moderate intensity exercise with weekly physiotherapist supervision plus standard care, or standard care alone. There was no between-group difference in the primary outcome of HRQoL (EQ-5D index and EQ-VAS), while upright time (about 31 min/day) and daily steps fell more in the exercise group (P=0.016 and P=0.004). Self-rated health, physical capacity, POTS symptoms and activity limitations improved over time in both groups without interaction effects, so tailored exercise was not superior to standard care.

summary: In this small single-centre Egyptian RCT, 20 post-COVID-19 adults with persistent fatigue/dyspnea and mild cognitive impairment were randomized to 4 weeks (3x/week) of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise with or without non-immersive VR (16 completed). Both groups improved significantly from baseline in fatigue (Chalder), cognition (MoCA) and sleep (PSQI), with no significant between-group differences, while satisfaction was significantly higher with VR (p=0.037, 4/8 'extremely satisfied' vs 0/8). The findings are limited by the small sample, lack of blinding and absence of a non-exercise control.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Very small sample (10/arm, underpowered vs. planned 19), unverified blinding with an unblinded stimulator operator, no reported attrition or flow data, baseline imbalance on two subscales, and no primary outcome designated.

summary: In a single-centre, sham-controlled three-arm trial, 30 women with post-COVID cognitive complaints (10 per arm) received nine sessions of cognitive training combined with active left-DLPFC tDCS, sham tDCS, or no stimulation. Baseline-adjusted ANCOVA showed that active tDCS plus training gave significantly greater improvement in global cognition, memory, fluency, anxiety (BAI 44.7 to 5.6), daytime sleepiness, reaction times and EEG arousal/valence than both comparison groups (FDR-corrected p ≤ .014), with no difference between sham and training-only. The sample was small, blinding was not verified, adverse events and attrition were not reported, and there was no follow-up beyond treatment end.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Post-intervention n per arm not stated; baseline n=10 from Table 1 header, so post n_analyzed left null (ANCOVA df=26 not used to infer). No between-group effect estimates (mean differences/CIs) reported; omnibus ANCOVA F/p and eta2p given (eta2p: global .56, attention .19, memory .51, fluency .40, language .08, visuospatial .02, arousal .29, valence .40, BAI .88, ESS .60, RT simple .71, onset .74, end .73). Tukey r values for global cognition only extracted as p-values; Kruskal–Wallis p values and within-group dz values (e.g. memory 3.30, BAI -4.36) exist but not mapped to effect fields; remaining pairwise contrasts in Supplementary Table S1 not available. Table 2 only has post means (no change scores). Language and visuospatial baseline imbalance flagged. Arm 3 (CT only) typed as active_comparator; arm 2 is sham control. Table cell quotes are single cells; column identified in source_location. Adverse events, hospitalization, vaccination and time since infection not reported.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:moderate, classification:low, deviations:low, missing_data:serious, measurement:moderate, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Care pathways were assigned by clinical need/severity (SNF older, Med most severe, No-rehab least severe), so group comparisons are confounded by baseline severity, and MoCA was repeated only if <26 with substantial missing follow-up data.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: No-rehab had the lowest psychological and cognitive failure scores at 3 and 12 months; Med-rehab had highest CFQ, anxiety, depression and PTSD at 12 months; SNF-rehab had worst MoCA recovery. Group differences are confounded by severity.

summary: Prospective multicenter Dutch cohort (CO-FLOW) of 617 people hospitalized for COVID-19, compared across four post-discharge care pathways (no rehabilitation, community monodisciplinary, medical multidisciplinary, skilled nursing multidisciplinary rehabilitation). Objective cognition (MoCA) and psychological outcomes improved mainly in the first 6 months, with cognitive deficits at 21% and PTSD/anxiety/depression at 7-11% by 12 months. Those with no rehabilitation fared best, while Med-rehab and SNF-rehab groups had worse cognitive failure, psychological or MoCA outcomes, but pathways were assigned by severity so these are not treatment effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Not a Long COVID treatment trial; observational comparison of care pathways after hospitalization, with no baseline measurement (time points are 3/6/12 months after hospital discharge, converted to weeks). Arm_id 5 is the pooled full cohort used for overall time trends; arm ids 1-4 are Med, SNF, Com, No-rehab. Table 2 values are GEE estimated means (SE), not raw. Per-pathway estimated means are only in figures/supplemental tables (not in text). MoCA CI for overall change printed as '0.89 to −1.72' (likely 0.89 to 1.72). SNF MoCA within-group 'p = 0.094' is reported as not significant. Per-group demographic % female taken from Table 1 percentages. Time-since-infection and vaccination not reported.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: No unexposed comparator, selective inclusion of patients referred to rehabilitation, small ward group, and subjective telephone-administered outcomes compared with external population norms preclude inference on treatment effect.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: No large differences in SF-36 dimension scores between ICU and ward groups; dyspnea and persistent symptoms numerically more frequent in ward group (no tests reported).

summary: Single-center cross-sectional study of 59 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia (41 ICU, 18 ward) who received inpatient physiotherapy, assessed by telephone 3 months after discharge. 84.7% had persistent symptoms (59.3% dyspnea, 77.9% other symptoms, 30.5% depression), and SF-36 role physical (40.25) and role emotional (66.10) were well below Spanish norms; no treatment effect was tested as there was no unexposed comparator.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Descriptive study with no inferential statistics or treatment comparison. SF-36 per-dimension values only in Figure 1 (only role physical and role emotional means in text, pooled; no SDs). Table 5 arm-level counts have no verbatim-quotable prose so quotes are null with table location given. Table 4 'días de ingreso previos' columns appear shifted (total blank). Percent female reported only for total sample (33.9%); demographics not given per arm. Discrepancy: text says 47 ICU-admitted patients vs table 3 (41 ICU group + 6 ward). Ward-group mean differences calculated as UCI minus planta.

summary: Two hospitalized patients (56-year-old man, 84-year-old woman) with persistent respiratory failure after acute COVID-19 were diagnosed with secondary organizing pneumonia by transbronchial lung biopsy and treated with oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day, then 0.5 mg/kg/day). Both improved in oxygenation and CT findings; in case 2, DLCO rose from 49.6% to 71.7% of predicted within one week. This is an uncontrolled case report with no statistical testing.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Two-patient case report. Table 1 holds single-patient (case 2) values, with % predicted in square brackets and no dispersion. Case 1 has only post-treatment DLCO and SpO2 values. Time since infection is given as illness day, not weeks. Illness-day timepoints are mapped to weeks relative to steroid start. Age mean (70) is the calculated mean of 56 and 84. CT improvement is shown only in figures.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Post hoc: per 100 mg*day/L AUC increase, OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.07−2.50, p=0.011) for low anti-S, 1.36 (1.04–2.27) for anti-S1, 1.41 (1.07−2.50) for anti-RBD; no association in high-antibody subgroup or low anti-N (OR 1.17, p=0.189).

summary: This exploratory phase 2a, 2:1 randomized, double-blind trial gave a single 1200 mg IV infusion of the long-acting SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibody AER002 (n=24) or placebo (n=12) to adults with Long COVID of about two years' duration. AER002 was safe and well tolerated but did not improve PROMIS-29 physical health (primary, Day 90 adjusted difference -4.1, 95% CI -8.6 to 0.47, p=0.08) or any secondary clinical outcome versus placebo, with numerically larger improvement in the placebo arm. Exploratory PET, proteomic and antibody-exposure analyses were hypothesis-generating only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 values are model-based estimated marginal means (geometric means for labs) without SD/SE; per-arm n set to randomized N (24/12) as outcome-level n not stated. Table values have result_quote null because table cells are not contiguous verbatim text; source_location identifies the cell. Lab percent differences are stored in ci fields with effect_value null (percent difference not mapped to ratio). Baseline VAS given as medians (Table 1). PGIC per-arm proportions only in figure. CPET, PET, biopsy and proteomic results are narrative/figure-only and not extracted per arm. AE counts per arm not reported (112 AEs in 32 participants overall; one unrelated grade 3 AE, arm not stated).

risk_of_bias.key_concern: 6 of 40 randomized participants were excluded before analysis and a further 6 did not complete the protocol (per-arm randomized numbers unreported), and the significant per-protocol VAS result was not replicated in the ITT analysis (p = 0.189).

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: No association of hospitalization (p=0.622) or recovery time (p=0.846) with pain reduction in the multivariate analysis; group effect on pain after treatment was significant (F=12.368, p=0.002).

summary: This pragmatic, double-blind, sham-controlled trial in Brazil tested four weekly 30-minute sessions of transcutaneous 660 nm vascular photobiomodulation over the radial artery in adults with persistent orofacial pain or tension-type headache after COVID-19 (40 randomized, 34 in ITT, 28 per-protocol). In the per-protocol analysis, VAS pain fell more with VPBM (3.42 to 0.33) than sham (3.13 to 1.38; p = 0.001), and some BPI items favoured VPBM, but the ITT analysis showed no between-group difference (p = 0.189) and HIT-6 changes were not significant. The small sample, post-randomization exclusions and discordant per-protocol/ITT results limit confidence.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm randomized numbers not reported (40 total; 34 analyzed in ITT at 14/20; 28 per-protocol at 12/16). Table 3 layout is ambiguous: 'p-value (within groups)' and z-values sit in the 'VAS before' and 'VAS after' rows; text states within-group p<0.001 (VPBM) and p=0.002 (sham). VAS SDs for the per-protocol set were not reported; baseline SDs given only for the ITT set in Table 2. Table 7 parentheses are not defined in the caption and are presumed SD (dispersion unstated). Table 7 'Pain relief with medication (0% to 100%)' values appear to be on a 0-10 scale; unit ambiguous. Table 2 HIT-6 'Some impact' placebo cell reads '2%' (likely 12.5%). Per-session VAS values and ITT end values only in figures. Recovery time from COVID-19 (mean 12.93 and 13.10 months) is not time since infection, so left null. Percent hospitalized of 8.8% calculated from 1/14 and 2/20 in the ITT set. Adverse events not reported.

title: Evaluation of vascular photobiomodulation for orofacial pain and tension type headache following COVID 19 in a pragmatic randomized clinical trial
authors: Mayra Costanti Vilela Campos; Silvana Simões Velloso Schuler; Ana Julia Lacerda; Adriana Cátia Mazzoni; Tamiris Silva; Francine Cristina Silva Rosa; Manoela Domingues Martins; Kristianne Porta Santos Fernandes; Elsa Susana Fonseca; Raquel Agnelli Mesquita-Ferrari; Anna Carolina Ratto Tempestini Horliana; Sandra Kalil Bussadori; Lara Jansiski Motta

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: randomization:some_concerns, deviations:high, missing_data:some_concerns, measurement:some_concerns, reporting:some_concerns
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Poor adherence and unmasked participants (PP/AT analyses depart from randomization), 8 of 62 randomized lost with analysis restricted to completers, and self-reported symptom outcomes in an exploratory pilot with no prespecified efficacy analysis.

summary: This exploratory randomized pilot (SPOVID) tested a 12-week unsupervised aerobic exercise program (3 sessions/week, zones 2-3) versus habitual activity in 62 randomized adults (54 analyzed) with persistent fatigue, concentration, breathing or headache symptoms more than 12 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Adherence was poor (e.g., only 8 of 26 intervention participants logged >=36 sessions), and no hypothesis testing was done; difference-in-differences favored exercise directionally for most symptom outcomes (largest for headache, standardized DID -0.99) but all 95% CIs were wide and included zero, with negligible spiroergometric changes. The authors conclude feasibility of the unsupervised program was limited and efficacy cannot be established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Change-from-baseline values (Difference T1-T0 columns) were not entered as separate arm_results (derivable from endpoints and listed in tables); the PP (Tables 5, 8) and AT (Tables 6, 9) analyses were extracted only for fatigue, headache, physical performance and VO2peak, with other rows omitted for length. Paper reports no p-values (descriptive study). Table 3 quality-of-life standardized CI '[− 1.18,0.47]' appears copied from the previous row (likely a typo). Table 7/8 contain mixed decimals (30.279, − 11.866, 3.066). Withdrawal reasons were reported only for the pooled 8 dropouts, not by arm. n_eligible=215 reflects participants invited (German proficiency). Time since infection was reported as median weeks (101.3 / 99.1), not mean months. Table 1 N is the ITT analysis population (26/28), not the randomized N (31/31).

title: Feasibility of an unsupervised aerobic exercise training program for participants with persistent symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection
authors: Carina Emmel; Oliver Bruder; Niklas Keller; Lukas Schipper; Christoph Schneider; Alexander Ferrauti; Mirjam Frank; Marcus Brinkmann; Mareike Eißmann; Thimo Wiewelhove; Börge Schmidt
release_limitations: AI-screened and AI-extracted; eligibility and numerical values have not been independently adjudicated.

study_design.design_type_detail: single-center retrospective chart review; self-selected pulmonary rehabilitation (>=5 sessions) vs no rehabilitation; ANCOVA with propensity-score covariate

arms.label: Pulmonary rehabilitation (>=5 sessions)
arms.intervention_name: Pulmonary rehabilitation (inspiratory muscle training, pursed-lip breathing, ACBT, diaphragmatic contraction training, interval training)
arms.dose: Median 17 sessions completed (IQR 10-23; range 5-30)
co_interventions: home-based exercise prescription given to all patients at discharge

arms.label: Control (no PR sessions)
arms.intervention_name: No pulmonary rehabilitation (home-based exercise prescription only)
co_interventions: home-based exercise prescription given to all patients at discharge

study_design.data_source: electronic medical record system, patient interviews and documented files (IPAQ-SF)
adjustment_variables: physical activity per week during convalescence
study_design.setting: single-center hospital (First Hospital of Changsha)

participants.long_covid_definition: Not defined; discharged COVID-19 patients followed to 6 months after discharge
key_inclusion_criteria: completed 2-week and 6-month follow-ups and performed blood tests
key_exclusion_criteria: cognitive impairment preventing cooperation in PR sessions (MMSE-2)
signs of respiratory distress or cardiovascular instability

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort in Changsha, China compared 27 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors who completed at least 5 sessions of a 12-week pulmonary rehabilitation program with 71 who did none, assessing outcomes 6 months after discharge. The rehabilitation group had a significantly greater improvement in 6-minute walk distance (unadjusted +194 m; propensity-adjusted +123 m, p<.001) with a dose-response pattern, but no differences in SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulins, T-cell subsets or blood chemistry. Group allocation was self-selected and groups differed at baseline, limiting causal inference.

summary: In this mixed-methods single-arm cohort of 30 purposively sampled Dutch adults recovering from COVID-19 and treated by primary care allied health professionals, patient-reported outcomes were compared from start of treatment to 6 months. Physical functioning (PROMIS-PF T-score 35.9 to 43.8), fatigue (FSS 5.7 to 4.7), anxiety, depression, participation and EQ-VAS (52 to 71) all improved descriptively, yet 83% still had severe fatigue at 6 months. No statistical tests or control group were used, so effects cannot be attributed to the treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports means with ranges only (no SDs); parentheses are ranges. No p-values reported. Within-group changes calculated from table means. Table inconsistencies: HADS-A categories at 6 months for total group (23+2+6=31) and probable anxiety printed as '6 (16)' (6/30=20%); poor HRQoL at 6 months is 12 (40) in the table vs 33% in the text; text lists age range as 62-73 vs 26-73 in Table 1. Time since infection: cohort ~2 months (range 1-6) at inclusion; Discussion says ~3 months. Hospitalised participants: 12/30 (40%). Quantitative data per subgroup extracted as separate outcomes under single arm. Qualitative findings not extracted as numeric outcomes.

summary: This multicenter, double-blind RCT randomized 392 patients with long-term (1-12 months) pulmonary sequelae of COVID-19 to intramuscular bovhyaluronidase azoximer 3000 IU or placebo every 5 days for 71 days. The primary endpoint (change in percent predicted FVC at Day 71) was not met (difference 0.3%, 95% CI -2.24 to 2.84, p=0.817). Secondary findings suggested less exertional desaturation (OR 0.36) and exertional dyspnea (OR 0.62), but these are hypothesis-generating given the failed primary endpoint, with more adverse events in the BA arm (37.2% vs 25.0%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Most efficacy values are model-based approximations ("approximately") from text; per-arm SDs and outcome-specific Ns not reported; Figures 2-4 and Supplementary Tables S2-S5 not available. n_screened not extracted because 'up to 461' was a planned figure. Secondary outcomes without numeric values (resting SpO2, >=50 m 6-MWT gain, cough VAS, EQ-5D-5L) described only as non-significant. Day 71 proportion with >=10% ppFVC increase not reported in text. mMRC OR CI text garbled in source (1.00-2.700.97-2.69); 1.00-2.70 used. Completer counts per arm not given (382 total completed). Time since infection is reported in days in Table 1; converted to months (/30.44). Baseline imbalance noted (fewer females in BA, lower lung damage, greater 6-MWT distance).

authors: Sergey N. Avdeev; Galina L. Ignatova; Oxana M. Drapkina; Veronica B. Popova; Ekaterina V. Melnikova; Tatiana I. Chudinovskikh; Olga V. Ryabova; Natalia V. Egorova; Tamara V. Rubanik; Yury G. arms.label: Active Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT)
arms.intervention_name: Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (27.12 MHz low-amplitude radiofrequency biphasic magnetic field, head-worn applicator, Fareon Restore)
arms.dose: 15-min sessions, 27.12 MHz non-thermal
arms.frequency: twice weekly, at least 70 h apart, self-administered at home

arms.label: Sham device
arms.intervention_name: Sham MMT device (visually identical, same lights and sounds, no magnetic field)
arms.frequency: twice weekly, at least 70 h apart, self-administered at home

study_design.randomization_method: Randomized 2:1 to active or sham; devices pre-programmed by an independent study engineer prior to delivery to the site. Sequence generation method not described.
study_design.setting: single-center outpatient study with at-home self-administered treatment

participants.long_covid_definition: Symptoms (e.g., fatigue, PEM, cognitive dysfunction, mood or sleep disturbance) present at least 6 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and not explained by an alternative diagnosis (ref. 2 criteria)
key_inclusion_criteria: SARS-CoV-2 infection documented by NAAT or antibody test >=6 months before screening
objective cognitive impairment (>=1 SD below normative mean) on at least one executive functioning measure
key_exclusion_criteria: reinfection or vaccination within 30 days of baseline
change in psychoactive medication within 90 days

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: randomization:some_concerns, deviations:low, missing_data:some_concerns, measurement:low, reporting:some_concerns
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Small exploratory pilot with many uncorrected outcomes, complete-case analysis after 3 post-randomization withdrawals, undescribed sequence generation, and a baseline race imbalance; no efficacy result survived FDR correction.

summary: In this triple-blind, sham-controlled pilot RCT, 30 completers (active n=20, sham n=10) with long COVID and objective cognitive impairment self-administered at-home Microtesla Magnetic Therapy or sham twice weekly for 4 weeks, with follow-up to week 8. The primary feasibility outcome was met (100% adherence among completers; 90.9% of the 33 enrolled completed >=80% of treatments and all visits) with no related or serious adverse events. Exploratory efficacy favoured active treatment at week 8 on Digit Span Sequencing, HVLT-R Total Recall, D-KEFS Color Naming and SF-36 Emotional Well-Being (nominal p<0.05), but none survived FDR correction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 values are change-from-baseline per arm (Active-Sham differences, Welch t-test); cell values quoted individually with column identified in source_location. Per-arm randomized Ns not stated (33 enrolled, 3 withdrawn: ankle injury and reinfection [both listed as active-group AEs], one for two missed visits); arm assignment of the missed-visit withdrawal not stated. Raw baseline/endpoint scores are in supplementary tables only (not available). Direction of Trail A/B change scores is unclear (higher_is_better null). Cohen's d for GAD-7 given without timepoint; assigned to week 8 based on matching p=0.057. Mixed-model interaction F-tests recorded as omnibus effects without estimates; other mixed-model results are in Supplementary Table S5 (unavailable). D-KEFS Category Fluency, RCFT, MINT and SDMT-related prose results lack numeric values in the text. Usability and blinding index (Petroff -0.02 to -0.05) not captured as outcomes.

summary: In 114 Japanese outpatients with prolonged symptoms of COVID-19 (median age 41, 57% female, mostly mild acute disease), a single-center, uncontrolled series evaluated Kampo medicine combined with symptom-targeted therapies. Within 3 months 65.8% achieved PS ≤ 2 and 31.6% reached the end-of-visit milestone; higher baseline fatigue (adjusted OR about 0.14) and longer delay to first visit predicted slower improvement. Because there was no control group, no treatment efficacy conclusion can be drawn; the findings are prognostic and exploratory, with unadjusted P-values.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm design; no pre/post outcome values reported (only baseline medians/IQRs in Table 1; Kaplan-Meier curves are in figures only). Table 1 depression IQR printed as '4 (1, 0)' (typo). Table 2 repeats variable rows for the second model (days from onset) and Table 5 likewise; first block is the general fatigue model, second the days-from-onset model. 6-month proportions are 'data not shown' and denominators (76, 78) are inconsistent with the text percentages. Table 3 subgroup medians (achievers vs non-achievers) and supplementary tables S2/S3 were not extracted as arm results. Time since infection reported as median 73 days (IQR 43, 167), not mean.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:serious, classification:low, deviations:moderate, missing_data:serious, measurement:serious, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Participants self-selected the intervention and only 37 of 77 allocated participants (48%) were analyzed, with unblinded assessment, so confounding, selection and attrition bias are likely.

summary: In this non-randomized, open-label study from Brazil, 37 adults with persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms chose either 8 weeks of supervised aerobic and resistance exercise (n=22) or remote monitoring with an educational booklet (n=15). Both groups improved in fatigue and shuttle walk distance (+100.8 m vs +65.9 m), but between-group differences in change were not significant (ISWT p=0.186). Dyspnea, anxiety, peak expiratory flow, and some memory/attention measures improved significantly only within the rehabilitation group, and quadriceps strength improved only in the remote group. Self-selected allocation, small sample, and high attrition limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Figure 2 (PFSDQ-M fatigue, dyspnea, total; ISWT) is garbled OCR, so per-arm PFSDQ-M medians and deltas were not extracted; only text p-values were used and PFSDQ arm_results are empty. Median change (Md delta) values in Tables 2, 4 and 5 were not entered as separate change_from_baseline arm_results; they appear in the quoted rows. Table 2 (n=35) analyzed 13 in the remote arm; Table 5 MVIC/EMG analyzed 15 and 11. Table 4 RAVLT REC lists n=21 and n=14 but printed percentages match denominators of 22 and 15, so total was left null. Table 4 d2-R/RAVLT between-group p-value columns are merged and their baseline/post order was inferred; the text confirms the d2-R and RAVLT within-group findings. Time since infection is reported only categorically (<=3 months vs 4-6 months), so no mean was extracted. The sample-size calculation targeted 41 per group, but fewer participants were analyzed. No adverse event data were reported, although the authors call the protocol safe. Arm-level ISWT baseline/post values were not reported in text.

summary: In this prospective non-randomised two-arm study from Greece, 52 patients recovering from severe/critical COVID-19 pneumonia with significant residual symptoms received either 8 weeks of supervised multidisciplinary rehabilitation (n=25) or usual care (n=27, unable to attend for logistic reasons). Rehabilitation produced significantly greater ANCOVA-adjusted improvements than usual care in CAT, three fatigue scales, SPPB, HADS-anxiety, BDI, MoCA and EQ-5D-5L index/VAS (p≤0.043), while 6MWT, pulmonary function, HADS-depression and IES-R improved similarly or did not differ significantly between groups. Non-random allocation (confounding by distance/access), small samples and open-label self-reported outcomes limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm n_analyzed per outcome not stated (ANCOVA included lost-to-follow-up patients via baseline covariate); completers inferred 21 vs 23 but not used per outcome. Per-arm means for CAT, FACIT, CFQ only in Figure 2 (data only in figures) apart from CAT 95% CIs and FSS means/SDs given in Discussion. Between-group effects are reported as improvement magnitudes (mean±SEM) favouring Rehab; for lower-is-better scales the positive value denotes greater reduction in Rehab. BDI and MoCA table values are median (IQR width only; quartiles not given). PFT details in supplement; p=0.001 operators '<' where text states p<0.001. Percent female calculated from % male.

summary: This conference abstract reports a survey of people with Long COVID breathlessness 3 months after completing the 6-week online singing-based ENO-Breathe programme (483 analysed responses). Respondents reported improved breathlessness (71%), general health and wellbeing (66%) and anxiety (61%), with median programme-impact ratings of 84/100 for mental health and 71/100 for physical health. There was no control group and no significance testing, so effects are descriptive only.

summary: This double-blind pilot RCT randomized 50 adults with olfactory dysfunction lasting 2 months or more after COVID-19 to 12 weeks of twice-daily olfactory training with four odorants or odorless placebo. Objective UPSIT-40 scores did not differ by group or time, while self-rated smell and taste improved significantly only in the training group on post hoc tests, despite a non-significant group-by-time interaction (p=0.091). Parosmia prevalence was lower after training than placebo (p=0.049), and quality of life improved in both groups. With about 18% dropout (6 vs 3) and a pilot sample, the findings are exploratory.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Outcome-level Ns for UPSIT and self-ratings not stated (one intervention participant lacked follow-up UPSIT). QOD data are pooled across groups (SEM, not per-arm) so no arm_results were entered. Table 1 NOSE values lack SDs and quotes are row labels only. Parosmia denominators (20 at baseline in the intervention arm) are as stated. Figures 2-5 contain additional data not extractable.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Women: FSS improved 9.36 (VR-EG) vs 5.53 (Con-EG), MD 3.83 (95% CI -1.24 to 8.88). Men: 2.57 vs 4.67, MD -2.09 (95% CI -7.0 to 2.81). Gender x treatment interaction p=0.24.

Among those fulfilling PEM criteria, FSS improved 4.10 (VR-EG) vs 3.95 (Con-EG), MD 0.15 (95% CI -2.63 to 2.97). Non-PEM subgroup model did not converge. PEM status associated with FSS change overall (p=0.003).

summary: This single-center German pilot RCT compared 12 sessions over 6 weeks of immersive VR neuromuscular exercise (ICAROS) with conventional exercise in 96 analyzed adults with post-COVID fatigue (FSS >= 36). Both groups improved on the FSS (model mean reduction 8.29 VR vs 5.27 control at post-intervention), but the between-group difference (3.03, 95% CI -1.02 to 7.06, p=0.15) was not statistically significant, nor were most secondary outcomes or follow-up differences. VR was feasible and generally safe, with transient vertigo or motion sickness and no serious adverse events; control-arm dropout was higher.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: FSS between-group CI at T1 printed as '–1.02 to –7.06' (likely typo for -1.02 to 7.06); recorded as -1.02 to 7.06. Signs of T2/T3 between-group differences (-2.07, -2.08) are inconsistent with the marginal-mean reductions (VR larger), so direction cannot be resolved; recorded verbatim. FSS reductions entered as negative changes (inferred sign). FSS change values are model marginal means with no SE/CI reported; FSS T1-T3 arm-level Ns not stated. Follow-up timepoint weeks approximated (3 and 12 months after post-treatment assessment). Table 3 values are model marginal means (SE) at T0/T1; Table 3 'hand grip ratio' baseline raw SD in Table 1 for Con-EG (0.51) differs notably. PGIC denominators calculated from percentages. FSS figure (Fig. 2) values only in figure. Primary analysis N at T1 not stated; 46/50 are ITT baseline Ns; complete-case Ns were 43/47.

summary: In a single-center Russian trial of 87 patients (mean age 64.8 years) with post-COVID syndrome after COVID-19 pneumonia, a 14-day program of osteopathic correction plus breathing exercises and chest massage (n=44) was compared with the same program using sham osteopathy (n=43). The osteopathy group showed larger improvements in VC, FVC, MIP, MEP, Stange test, 6MWT, mMRC, HADS and EQ-5D (between-group p 0.003 to <0.001 for most; SpO2 difference not significant, p=0.09). Randomization, blinding and participant flow are poorly reported, no primary outcome was specified, and follow-up ended at course completion.

summary: In 200 adults aged 18-45 with Long COVID (more than 5 months), a 31-day home-based programme of inspiratory muscle training, aerobic walking and smell/taste training was compared with no treatment. The intervention group showed larger improvements in dyspnea (Borg, mMRC), FVC, FEV1/FVC, maximal inspiratory pressure and self-rated smell and taste (group x time p<0.01 or p<0.001), with no significant group x time effect for FEV1 (p=0.09). The control group was untreated and unblinded, outcomes were largely subjective, and there was no follow-up after treatment, so the effects are probably overestimated.

summary: This single-centre UK feasibility RCT tested a 6-week, twice-weekly, physiotherapist-led online yogic breathing programme against usual care in 33 adults with persistent breathlessness and dysregulated breathing after COVID-19. Feasibility was poor: only 5 of 16 intervention participants attended more than 75% of sessions and completed the post-intervention assessment, mainly because of scheduling inflexibility and some IT problems. There were no statistically significant between-group differences; within-group CRQ-D and Nijmegen scores improved in the intervention arm, but the study was unpowered and no serious adverse events were reported.

Table 2 labels CRQ-D and 5RCTS 'Primary Outcomes', while the text names feasibility as the primary objective, so is_primary is true for both feasibility and those two. Within-arm p-values (paired tests) are not captured in arm_results fields. The 3 participants 'lost to both groups' were interpreted as 3 per arm (16-13, 17-14). Week 14 data are reported only for NQ in the intervention arm. Total sample (33) and Table 2 n (13/14) refer to randomised-and-attended and analysed sets respectively.

summary: A nonrandomized, waiting-list-controlled study in Spain tested a 10-session live online respiratory physiotherapy and mindfulness program over 22 days in unvaccinated post-acute COVID-19 patients with dyspnea (50 completers per group). The intervention group improved significantly in dyspnea (Mahler median 7 to 10), anxiety, quality of life, respiratory rate, SpO2 and heart rate, and percentage changes differed significantly from controls (p ≤ 0.001 for all). The controls improved only in dyspnea and quality of life. Interpretation is limited by non-random allocation, completers-only analysis with 32% attrition, baseline imbalances and self-reported outcomes.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:serious, classification:moderate, deviations:moderate, missing_data:no_information, measurement:moderate, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: No untreated control group and groups defined post hoc by treadmill performance (non-independent of outcome), so improvements cannot be attributed to the program and group comparisons are confounded by baseline severity.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Improvement in 6MWT (m) regressed on baseline 6MWT and STS
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Baseline 6MWT predicted improvement: B=-0.58 (95% CI -0.72 to -0.45) without DM (R2 0.56) vs B=-0.45 (-0.62 to -0.28) with DM (R2 0.38); baseline STS B=2.94 vs 3.07 m per repetition.

summary: Single-arm observational study in 133 Chilean patients who required invasive mechanical ventilation for COVID-19, receiving a supervised, individualized pulmonary rehabilitation program (treadmill aerobic, strength, flexibility; 2 sessions/week) of 12, 24 or 36 sessions depending on whether they could walk 30 min on a treadmill. All groups improved significantly pre-post on spirometry, 6MWT, STS, HGS, MIP, fatigue, dyspnea, functional status and SF-36; the 36-session group had the greatest 6MWT gain (median +117 m vs +66 m), but with no control group these gains cannot be attributed to the program. Longer programs were associated with more baseline severity (PCFS, ventilation days, lower baseline 6MWT).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All values are medians (p25-p75, IQR) from non-normally distributed data; no means/SDs reported, so mean fields are null. Per-arm n_analyzed taken from table headers (74/34/25 = 133; text says 132 enrolled, table captions say 133). Time-point weeks not reported (2 sessions/week implies ~6, 12, 18 weeks). Groups are defined post hoc by response to treadmill criterion, not a randomized or control comparison; has_comparison_group set true only because three dose groups are compared. Within-group Pre vs Post Wilcoxon p<0.05 marked by asterisks in tables (exact p not given); not entered as within_group_change. Ordinal logistic regression (Table 4) and linear regression (Tables 5-6) on group membership and 6MWT improvement not extracted as outcomes. Data inconsistency: baseline Table 1 tobacco row values appear as percent (n) swapped.

title: Effects of a pulmonary rehabilitation program on pulmonary function, exercise performance, and quality of life in patients with severe COVID-19
authors: María Fernanda del Valle; Jorge Valenzuela; Claudio Bascour-Sandoval; Gabriel Nasri Marzuca-Nassr; Mariano del Sol; Constanza Díaz Canales; Máximo Escobar-Cabello; Rodrigo Lizama-Pérez; Fernando Valenzuela-Aedo; Rodrigo Muñoz-Cofré

arms.label: Advanced olfactory training (AOT), 8 essential oils

co_interventions: telephone adherence contacts at 1 and 3 weeks

arms.label: Classical olfactory training (COT), 4 essential oils

arms.dose: 15 s exposure per odor, 30 s interval between odors
co_interventions: telephone adherence contacts at 1 and 3 weeks

study_design.randomization_method: Patients randomly assigned to 2 OT groups in a 2:1 ratio (COT:AOT); no further procedure described
study_design.setting: multicenter, otorhinolaryngology services of tertiary hospitals

participants.long_covid_definition: Persistent olfactory alteration for at least 4 weeks after onset of COVID-19 symptoms, with RT-PCR-confirmed COVID-19 less than 3 months earlier (post-COVID olfactory dysfunction)
key_inclusion_criteria: COVID-19 infection less than 3 months before, confirmed by RT-PCR
olfactory complaints persisting at least 4 weeks after COVID-19 symptom onset
key_exclusion_criteria: unable to give written informed consent
sinonasal disease such as chronic rhinosinusitis or nasal masses
previous traumatic brain injury with olfactory sequelae
other current or previous treatments for post-COVID-19 maintenance

summary: In this Brazilian multicenter RCT, 80 adults with post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction lasting at least 4 weeks were randomized 2:1 to 4 weeks of olfactory training with 8 essential oils (AOT, n=26) or the classical 4 oils (COT, n=54). UPSIT scores and olfaction VAS improved overall (UPSIT +1.5 ± 3.9, P = .002), but there were no significant differences between AOT and COT in UPSIT change (1.0 ± 4.2 vs 1.7 ± 3.8, P = .281) or any VAS outcome.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No primary outcome stated; blinding, allocation concealment and analysis population not reported. Group sizes analyzed assumed to be all randomized (26/54) per Table 8, although 1 AOT and 2 COT participants reportedly discontinued, so n_completed is calculated. Adverse events are only summarized overall (18/80, 22.5% with side effects: headache, nausea, worsening nasal symptoms), not by arm. Table 8 IQR values are widths, not quartiles, so iqr_low/high left null. Per-arm months since infection calculated from days (÷30.44). Pooled-sample results (Tables 6, 7, UPSIT initial 25.2 ± 7.1 vs final 26.7 ± 6.3, change 1.5 ± 3.9, P = .002) are not arm-specific and are omitted from arm_results. The paper text for the fluctuation percentages (62.8% to 78.8%) is internally inconsistent.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Non-random convenience allocation produced baseline imbalances (IMT group had more intubation, longer hospital stay, worse lung function), leaving residual confounding despite propensity-score adjustment, with no sham control.

summary: This quasi-experimental study in 53 severe COVID-19 survivors (ICU/ventilatory support) with long COVID dyspnea compared 12 weeks of supervised telerehabilitation inspiratory muscle training (n=29) with usual care (n=24), adjusting for baseline imbalance via a propensity score. IMT produced significantly greater improvements in maximal inspiratory pressure (adjusted difference 20.5 cmH2O), most endurance measures and FVC % predicted, and strongly favored IMT on all TDI dyspnea domains (ORs 12–56). There were no significant between-group differences in 1-min sit-to-stand performance or other spirometry; allocation was non-random, so residual confounding is possible.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 values are propensity-score-adjusted estimated marginal means with 95% CIs (no SDs); n_analyzed assumed 29/24 since no dropouts were reported. Raw baseline means ± SD for many outcomes appear in Table 1 but only BDI was extracted here. Per-group TDI scores appear only in Figure 2 (text gives medians +2 vs +0.5). Table 3 footnote domain labels (motor/mental/fatigue) are inconsistent with the TDI domains in Methods. Abstract reports MIP change +31.6 vs +6.7 cmH2O and endurance time +52.8 vs -9.5 sec, which differ from Table 2 model estimates. Adverse events not reported beyond describing the intervention as safe. Time since infection not quantified (entry: dyspnea >30 days after hospital discharge).

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:moderate, classification:low, deviations:low, missing_data:moderate, measurement:moderate, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: No untreated COVID-19 control group, so pre-post improvements cannot be separated from natural recovery, and severity subgroups differ markedly in age, sex and time since infection.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Severe/critical patients improved 6MWD more (median +124 m) than mild/moderate (+48 m), between-group p=0.009; SF-36 MCS (p=0.036) and D-dimer (p=0.001) changes also differed; lung function changes did not differ.

summary: Fifty post-acute COVID-19 patients (24 mild/moderate, 26 severe/critical) completed a 3-week comprehensive inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation programme in a single German centre. 6MWD improved significantly in both groups (median +48 m and +124 m; 88% and 92% exceeded the 30 m MID), with significant gains in lung function (FVC, FEV1), and in the severe/critical group in ESWT performance, muscle strength, depression, cognition and mental quality of life; no adverse events were observed. There was no untreated control group, so natural recovery cannot be excluded.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All values are medians (IQR) with nonparametric tests; no means/SDs reported. Table 3 stars (*, **, ***) converted to p-thresholds; text gives mild/moderate 6MWD p=0.001 whereas table star implies p<0.001. Between-group p-values in Table 3 appear to compare changes between subgroups. Table 4 outcomes apply only to the severe/critical subgroup. Some Table 4 change entries are internally inconsistent as printed. Table-row quotes are concatenated cell text. Supplementary IPF comparison data not available. Time since infection reported as medians in days (178 mild/moderate; 61 severe/critical), not converted. Number of sites inferred as single centre.

title: Benefits of pulmonary rehabilitation in COVID-19: a prospective observational cohort study
authors: Rainer Gloeckl; Daniela Leitl; Inga Jarosch; Tessa Schneeberger; Christoph Nell; Nikola Stenzel; Claus F. Vogelmeier; Klaus Kenn; Andreas R. Koczulla
release_limitations: AI-screened and AI-extracted; eligibility and numerical values have not been independently adjudicated.

study_design.design_type_detail: single-arm pre-post (T1 two weeks before, T2 two weeks after inpatient rehabilitation), observational, no control group
study_design.data_source: dedicated study measurements (ActiGraph GT9X Link accelerometer, sleep diary, questionnaires, physician anamnesis)
study_design.setting: single-center inpatient rehabilitation hospital (BG Hospital Bad Reichenhall)

participants.long_covid_definition: Persistent symptoms (>12 weeks) due to COVID-19 that cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis
key_inclusion_criteria: post-acute phase without evidence of infectivity
COVID-19 recognised as occupational disease or work-related accident
key_exclusion_criteria: severe cardiological, internist, neurological, psychological and musculoskeletal diseases already present before COVID-19

per_arm.n_enrolled_quote: At T1, out of 127 recruited patients 119 patients were sent an accelerometer

exclusion_reasons.reason: T2 dropouts (reinfection n=1, no longer interested n=2)

summary: Single-arm observational study of 100 post-COVID patients (mostly healthcare workers, about 400 days post-infection) undergoing a ~29-day inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation, with accelerometer-measured physical activity and sleep before and two weeks after. No significant changes in inactivity (~13.9 h/day), PA intensities, or any sleep parameter (all p>0.05), and sleep quality stayed poor, although the prevalence of five self-reported symptom clusters decreased significantly. No control group.

summary: In a single-center Egyptian RCT, 64 adults with post-COVID-19 anosmia (>90 days, TDI <=13) were randomized to 1% intranasal tetra sodium pyrophosphate or 0.9% saline spray three times daily for 1 month. TDI rose from 11.28 to 16.83 with TSPP versus 11.10 to 11.26 with saline, with 26/32 TSPP patients reaching the hyposmia range and nasal calcium falling; the between-group difference in change was statistically significant (p = 0.0008). The trial is small, has unclear allocation concealment and some internal inconsistencies, and only 1-month follow-up.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Text describes study group (TSPP) as 18F/14M, age 36.87, but Table 1 gives TSPP 12M/20F and age 36.87; Table 1 used. Text says 5 TSPP patients did not improve (19%) but Table 2 shows 6 still anosmic after TSPP (26 hyposmic + 6 = 32). Table 1 smoker entries ('5/32','4/32') ambiguous. Table 2 t-values by arm (e.g. 7.97, 11.88) appear to be within-arm pre/post comparisons and were not extracted as between-group effects; within-arm p-values for anosmia counts (0.024, 0.001, 0.0001) not extracted. Days since symptoms to enrollment: NaCl 96.54 ± 4.12, TSPP 94.81 ± 3.89 (days). No primary outcome stated; analyzed N inferred as 32 per arm (no attrition reported). Mean differences and CIs not reported.

summary: In this prospective, open-label, non-randomly allocated Polish single-center study, 75 patients with persistent post-COVID olfactory dysfunction all received intranasal mometasone, vitamin A ointment, saline irrigation and speech therapy-guided olfactory training; 50 additionally received classical olfactory training with applicators. The additional training group improved more on SST total score (+7.9 vs +2.8 points; interaction P < 0.001), thresholds and identification, with 66% vs 24% achieving a clinically significant gain (≥5.5 points). Allocation was systematic, adherence unmonitored and the control group received no applicators, so findings are at serious risk of bias.

summary: This descriptive secondary analysis of the RECOVER-NEURO trial (328 adults with cognitive symptoms of long COVID, 22 US sites, 5 arms) evaluated a centralized NYU hub that delivered remote cognitive training, cognitive rehabilitation and home-based tDCS. The hub supported up to 168 concurrently active participants, 97.6% received at least one session, 81.3% of those were consistently adherent, and 96.9% of shipped kits were recovered. No efficacy outcomes or between-arm statistical tests were reported; the findings support operational feasibility only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Operational/feasibility paper; efficacy outcomes are reported in a separate publication. Arm IDs were assigned as 1=BrainHQ+active tDCS, 2=BrainHQ+sham tDCS, 3=BrainHQ alone, 4=BrainHQ+PASC-CoRE, 5=active comparator. Per-arm n_completed was calculated as randomized minus 'did not complete intervention' from Table 2. Per-arm n_analyzed for sessions and time-to-initiation is not stated (null). Overall (pooled) metrics are recorded in pooled_all_arms because arm_results are per-arm. The text says 'Of the 328 randomized participants, 320 (97.6%) received at least one intervention session, while 28 did not complete the intervention', and Table 2 non-completers sum to 28. The tDCS safety counts (5,508 sessions, 71 technical issue notes, 1 skin reaction) are not split by arm. Concurrent-participant data are only in figures. No between-group effects were reported.

summary: Single-center Japanese retrospective study of 120 outpatients with post-COVID-19 conditions, in which zinc acetate hydrate (50 mg twice daily) was given to those with hypozincemia (n=53). Zinc users improved significantly more for fatigue at 8 weeks (Fisher P=0.030; no zinc user symptomatic at 12 weeks) and for hair loss at 4, 8 and 12 weeks (P=0.002, 0.002, 0.006; 4-week adjusted OR 48.03, 95% CI 2.74-840.50), with no benefit for taste or olfactory disorder. Because zinc was assigned by hypozincemia status, was non-randomized and unadjusted for baseline symptom severity, and outcomes were self-reported, the findings are exploratory.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm event counts (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2) are in figures only, so arm_results are empty. Overall persistence at 4 and 12 weeks is in text but not per arm: taste 39.2% and 20.3%; olfactory 41.8% and 25.4%; hair loss 41.0% and 15.4%; cough/sputum 33.3% persisted at 4 weeks and 92.6% improved by 12 weeks; diarrhea improved in 87.5% at 4 weeks and 93.8% at 8 weeks; dyspnea improved in all patients except one at 4 weeks and in all by 8 weeks. Fatigue OR at 12 weeks was not estimable (no zinc users symptomatic). Zn mean 83.7 ± 17.4 (n=112, µg/dL; text mislabels units as mg/dL). Arm 2 n=67 is calculated as 120 minus 53. Per-arm demographics are not reported. Table 4 fatigue Na (OR 0.64, P=0.045), Cu (OR 1.06, P=0.026) and eGFR (OR 1.06, P=0.033) were univariate-significant, and potassium was significant for hair loss at 4 weeks (OR 123.07, P=0.020) but lost significance when dichotomized at the median.

summary: In this single-centre prospective observational study, 30 hospital-discharged patients with persistent post-COVID-19 organizing-pneumonia-pattern interstitial lung disease at about 6-9 weeks received a rapid 3-week oral prednisolone course (mean starting dose 26.6 mg). After treatment, FVC % predicted rose from 86.8 to 99.2 and TLCO % predicted from 59.7 to 82.6 (both p≤0.004), median MRC dyspnoea improved from 3 to 2 (p=0.002), and CT consensus was improved, with no major complications. There was no control group, so spontaneous recovery cannot be excluded.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm; arm 1 covers before/after treatment. Table 5 inconsistencies: FVC L mean difference 0.42 differs from 3.36-3.07=0.29; reported p-values (e.g. 0.014 for FVC L, 0.025 for KCO) look inconsistent with their CIs; TLCO SI CI lacks closing parenthesis. Baseline demographics (n=35) are for the recommended-treatment cohort, not the 30 completers. Treated-cohort baseline FVC 86.4% (±16.3) and TLCO 56% (±19.6) in prose differ slightly from Table 5 (86.8, 59.7). Per-outcome n for percent-change outcomes unstated (30 completed). Spread on MRC median unspecified (±). Table 3 inflammatory markers (CRP, ferritin, etc.) are hospital-course/clinic values, not pre/post treatment, so not extracted. Three untreated patients had FVC +8.9% and TLCO +6.9% at 3 months (no SDs). One treated patient's 6MWT improved 130 m to 343 m. Adverse events: only 'No major complications of steroid treatment were observed.' CT results descriptive only. 'Time since infection' not explicitly reported; min time based on 6 weeks post-discharge; treatment at day 61 (±19) after discharge.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: MoCA global score, MoCA <26 and 18-25 subgroups, TMT-B errors
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Within-group Wilcoxon: intervention group improved on MoCA global (p=0.022) and TMT-B errors (p=0.046); the non-intervention group showed no significant change (MoCA p=0.915; TMT-B errors p=0.271). No direct between-group test reported.

summary: In this retrospective single-system Brazilian study, 49 adults with new cognitive complaints after SARS-CoV-2 infection were assessed at baseline, and 29 were reassessed at 6 months; 19 of these had received a 4-session cognitive stimulation and psychoeducation program and 10 had not. The whole cohort showed no significant change in MoCA, but improved on TMT-B errors (p=0.029), while depression and anxiety (HAD) were unchanged. Only the intervention subgroup improved significantly on MoCA global (22.1 to 23.3, p=0.022) and TMT-B errors, but this was a small, uncontrolled, non-randomized within-group comparison without a between-group test, so efficacy cannot be established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 percentages use a denominator of 53 (e.g., 37 = 69.8% female) though the analyzed N is 49; sex counts total 53. Text says TMT-B errors p=0.029 and verbal fluency p=0.058 are 'significant' although 0.058 exceeds 0.05. Table 2 MoCA 10-17 at 6 months shows 17.2% vs text 17.4%. TMT-A errors at 6 months (16.3 SD 57.5 intervention; 7.5 SD 38.5 whole cohort) look like outliers/errors in the source. Whole-cohort results are entered with arm_id null (no matching arm in arms list). No between-group effect estimates reported; between_group_effects left empty. Sizes of MoCA-category subgroups in Table 3 are not stated, so n_analyzed is null. Fatigue (17.02 SD 24.1) appears only as a baseline characteristic in Table 1 with no instrument stated in that table (FSS named in methods); no follow-up data. Correlation tables (4, 5) not extracted as outcomes. Adverse events not reported.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Small single-center convenience sample with no control group, self-reported symptoms, and multiple unadjusted exploratory tests.

summary: This cross-sectional study measured TENS sensory (current perception) thresholds in women with a history of COVID-19 attending post-COVID physiotherapy; no treatment was tested. Lower thresholds (higher sensitivity) were associated with more COVID-19 and long-COVID symptoms, shorter time since infection, fewer vaccine doses and being unvaccinated, and with joint/muscle pain, difficulty concentrating, sleep problems and weakness/fatigue. Sample size is not available in the supplied text, there was no control group, and analyses were unadjusted and exploratory.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Sample size, age, BMI and all percentages are stripped from the supplied text. Table 1 Spearman section is garbled; rho and P values were mapped in order (Age, Weight, Height, Doses, Time since onset, Number of symptoms, Number of long-COVID symptoms) and are consistent with text P values. Spearman rho is recorded in outcome names since effect_measure has no correlation option. Subgroup medians are in subgroup_analyses because the study has a single arm. Not a treatment study.

Elbow slope values not in the table (text says non-significant). Table 3 reports no post (1 day after treatment) symptom data and no pairwise p-values apart from text ranges (pre vs end p<0.001 to 0.031 except fever p=0.281, smell/taste p=0.062); only Friedman omnibus recorded. Percent previously hospitalized not clearly stated (2 patients admitted to hospital). Pooled age mean calculated as weighted mean of female/male subgroups; SD not derivable. Time since infection converted from days (274.88 ± 210.70, range 32-688). Unit of analysis for AF means is assumed to be per-participant averages of up to 3 trials. Sample size 17 treated; comparison/p-values for AFisomax pairwise are one-tailed. Paper_id was supplied in the prompt; the published DOI is 10.3390/diagnostics13050882.

summary: A small retrospective, non-randomly allocated study (n=16 university students aged 18-30 with post-COVID-19 syndrome) compared a 4-week, 12-session asynchronous home telerehabilitation program (diaphragmatic breathing plus aerobic/strength exercises) against no intervention. The telerehabilitation group showed within-group improvements in SpO2, 6MWT distance, 1-min sit-to-stand, and decreases in the table-labelled RR and HR, whereas blood pressure did not change significantly. Group-by-time interactions were significant for HR, RR, sit-to-stand and 6MWT but not SpO2 or BP, though the tiny sample and non-randomized allocation limit inference.

Interaction F for 6MWT in text duplicates the physical capacity F value (15.121) with a different p-value. Blood pressure interaction reported once without SBP/DBP separation. Within-group p-values in Table 3 are assumed paired post-hoc (Tukey) tests though the table does not specify.
