summary: This pilot study randomized 53 adults with post-COVID syndrome to an SPM-enriched marine oil at 500, 1500 or 3000 mg/day or to placebo for 12 weeks; the 500 mg group was an unblinded, uncontrolled add-on group and the placebo group had only 5 patients. Serum 14-HDHA, 17-HDHA and 18-HEPE rose significantly from baseline in all treated groups (p=0.002, 0.0007, 0.00001) and the pro-inflammatory/pro-resolving ratio fell (p=0.025), with no differences between doses. Fatigue (FSS) and dyspnea (mMRC) showed non-significant improvement trends with no between-group differences (mMRC chi-square p=0.509), and no placebo-controlled clinical efficacy can be concluded.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 is badly garbled. Only the pro-inflammatory sums (pg/mL) at weeks 0/4/12 could be assigned to doses with confidence. SPM sums and ratio values (e.g. 167.33, 214.84, 455.2562, percent changes) were not mapped to timepoints because the column and row alignment is ambiguous. Raw means for 14-HDHA, 17-HDHA, 18-HEPE and for FSS appear only in figures (figure-only data). The supplied text shows no SDs or n per timepoint for biomarkers. The p-values for biomarkers are pooled pre/post across treated groups, not placebo-comparative. Table 3 shows A n=15 and C n=4 versus 16 and 5 randomized, so the missing patients are unexplained. Arm IDs: 1=X 500 mg, 2=placebo C, 3=B 1500 mg, 4=A 3000 mg. The paper_id is the one supplied in the template, while the paper itself cites Biomedicines 2024, 12, 2221 (10.3390/biomedicines12102221). The text gives no adverse event data, baseline demographics or stratification factors. Table 1 is only the study chronogram. Table 3 caption and text give A n=15 and C n=4, while the Methods give 16 and 5.

summary: In a single-centre, uncontrolled UK service evaluation, 31 adults with long COVID (median duration 29 months) and PESE received an 8-week WHO Borg CR-10 pacing programme with active rest and weekly telephone support. PESE episodes fell by about 15% per week (95% CI 11% to 20%, p<0.001), with shorter, milder episodes. C19-YRSm functional disability and PESE scores improved by week 8, and symptom severity, overall health and EQ-5D VAS improved by week 12, but changes were not clinically significant and EQ-5D-5L utility did not change significantly. There was no control group and no blinding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2/3 report medians (IQR); only baseline Table 1 gives mean (SD) for EQ-5D and C19-YRSm. Per-outcome analysed N not stated (31 completed programme), so n_analyzed is null. Table 3 active resting row week 12 cells are merged/garbled; week 12 values taken from the text. PESE episode, symptom and duration trajectories (weeks 0-12) are partly figure-only (Figures 1-3, Supplemental Material 3). Week 8 and 12 timepoints are labelled on_treatment/post_treatment; no outcome is explicitly primary. Trigger counts (107 at week 0, 47 at week 8, 49 at week 12; patients with no PESE 1, 16, 14) reported in text but not extracted as outcomes. Adverse events not reported.

summary: In this single-arm proof-of-concept cohort of 49 adults with post-COVID condition and self-reported neurocognitive symptoms, a ~6-week course of head and neck manual lymphatic drainage was followed by no change in the primary outcome, life satisfaction (SWLS 22.6 to 22.5, P=0.738). Secondary self-reported brain fog, concentration, headache, sleep (VAS) and fatigue (FSS) improved significantly (all P≤0.014), but without a control group these changes cannot be attributed to MLD.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Within-group P values from Wilcoxon signed-rank tests while means/SDs reported; the t0-t1 interval was not centrally recorded (about 6 weeks planned). N for FSS and subjective-effect VAS not explicitly stated (likely 49 but not confirmed). Per-patient proportions improved for FSS (63.6%) imply a denominator other than 49 (63.6% not a multiple of 1/49). Figures b and c contain only graphical versions of tabulated data. The paper has an apparent inconsistency: the abstract/methods state 15 patients excluded for missing baseline VAS, while Results state complete VAS at both time points was required. Time since infection (min 3 months per inclusion) not converted to weeks.

summary: In this single-center Taiwanese RCT, 120 adults with long COVID were randomized to a 12-week physical therapist-supported home telerehabilitation program (aerobic plus resistance training) or to exercise counseling with self-directed exercise. The telerehabilitation group had greater improvements in VO2peak (B=2.12), anaerobic threshold (B=1.83), O2 pulse, 2-min heart rate recovery, gait speed (B=0.07 m/s), cadence, lean mass, and lower odds of fatigue (OR 0.20), which remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction; sleep and quality-of-life findings did not. Interpretation is limited by an unblinded design, differential dropout (14.0% vs 31.7%), and baseline imbalances.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Tables 2-4 (baseline characteristics, per-arm means/SDs, GEE results with CIs) are in supplementary files and not in the supplied text, so per-arm means, SDs, event counts, demographics, and CIs could not be extracted. Between-group B values and p-values come from the Results narrative; the reported p-values are unadjusted GEE values, with BH-adjusted p-values given in source_location. Fatigue OR direction (TG vs ACG) is as stated. Body fat/weight outcome has no numeric effect reported. Underscores in quotes (e.g. _p_) are from the source text.

summary: This pilot RCT randomised 21 adults with Long COVID (about one year post-infection, mostly non-hospitalised) to a 10-week twice-weekly supervised group videoconference exercise program (n=11) or usual care (n=10). The primary aim was feasibility: recruitment was 39%, adherence was high (18 ± 2 sessions; 100% of completers attended at least 16), 9 of 11 intervention participants completed follow-up, and there were no adverse events and two minor technical problems. Exploratory clinical outcomes showed wide variability and no between-group differences except a greater improvement in five-repetition sit-to-stand time favouring telerehabilitation (-1.4 s, 95% CI -2.6 to -0.2), which the authors interpret with caution given the baseline imbalances and small sample.

summary: In this open-label RCT, 100 Spanish primary-care adults with Long COVID (>12 weeks) were randomized to usual care plus the ReCOVery telerehabilitation app (with 3 motivational sessions) or usual care alone for 12 weeks. Per-protocol analysis (45 vs 42) found no significant between-group differences in SF-36 physical or mental health or any secondary outcome; adherence was poor (only ~25% significant app use). Exploratory regressions linked more app minutes with better physical function and community support.

summary: This double-blind RCT in Argentina randomized about 50 adults with Long COVID to 90 days of EchA Marine (sea urchin egg extract, 1.5 mg Echinochrome A/day) or placebo, with 46 analyzed. summary: This excerpt covers a two-group study of balneotherapy versus a control group in Long COVID, with questionnaire outcomes (SF-36, HADS, PCFS, mMRC, PSQI, MFE-30, VAS) assessed after balneotherapy and one month later. In BMI- and age-adjusted models, SF-36 role limitations (physical), energy/fatigue, social functioning and pain showed negative betas with CIs excluding zero at both timepoints, while general health and HADS depression were not clearly different; most FDR p-values are not legible. Adverse effects (mainly fatigue, weakness, dizziness, myalgia) were common among the 17 balneotherapy participants, and 2 withdrew for fatigue and dizziness.

summary: This method study in Uzbekistan used electroacupuncture according to Voll (EAV) medicament testing to determine individual daily ribavirin doses in patients aged 16-50 with long COVID (52 experimental, 49 placebo analysed after substantial dropout), with follow-up over about three years. Tested ribavirin doses rose over time on several meridians (e.g. Ne-3 232.8 to 607.8 mg) and correlated inversely with EAV pretest readings (Spearman rho about -0.77 to -0.92), and EAV readings differed between groups at p<0.001. No clinical outcomes or adverse events were reported, so the findings do not show clinical efficacy; the prognostic claim is unvalidated.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Output size limit: only Ne-3 and Kr-8b EAV pre/post readings and tested ribavirin doses were fully extracted. The other 10 meridians (3E-1b, He-8c, Le-1a, Pa/Mi(S)-1a, Pa/Mi(D)-1a, Ge-1b, Hau-1-3, Ni-1-3b, Bl-66, Pa/Mi-11) in Tables 2-4 and the Spearman correlations in Table 5 (e.g. Ne 2020-21 pre-test rho -0.766522, n=32; Kr rho -0.821824, n=41) were not extracted and can be added on request. Table 4 layout is garbled: the Placebo column has one value per meridian with no period, while the year columns appear identical to Table 3 (experimental), so the placebo period is unspecified and posttest placebo values are negative while experimental posttest values are about +6. Table 4 significance asterisks refer to comparison with the control group. SD vs SEM is not stated in the table text (figure captions mention SE). Per-outcome Ns not reported. The ratio, 96 vs 68 randomized, conflicts with the stated 1.06:1 ratio. Decimal commas converted to points in values. Allocation concealment, blinding details and primary outcome not reported. The paper is not a clinical efficacy trial.

summary: This single-center Egyptian RCT randomized 36 adults (30-45 years) with post-COVID-19 syndrome to computerized cognitive behavioral therapy plus physiotherapy or physiotherapy alone, 3 sessions/week for 12 weeks. The CBT group showed a 53.03% reduction in BDI and 56.14% improvement in Katz ADL, versus 0.39% (non-significant) and 10.71% in controls, with significant between-group differences post-treatment (both p=0.001). Per-arm means/SDs were not extractable, and the small unblinded trial with self-reported outcomes carries high risk of bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 (BDI) was unresolved and Table 3 (Katz) was empty in the source text, so per-arm means, SDs and Ns are not available; only percent changes and p-values from the results text were extracted. Percent reductions in BDI are coded as negative values. The between-group effect entry for the BDI percent-change outcome carries the within-arm p-value (study group) only. No participant flow, attrition, or adverse event data in the text (Figure 1 flowchart is an image). Methods say MANOVA was used. The 'alpha p > 0.05' statement appears to be a typo. The paper notes a sex count inconsistency: the text and table give 4 males and 14 females in group A, and 3 males and 15 females in group B (percentages in the table do not exactly match, e.g. 16.6%). Baseline-score p-values (0.39, 0.75) are included as baseline between-arm comparisons.

summary: This pilot RCT randomized adults with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 and fibromyalgia-like symptoms to 4 weeks of daily high-dose or low-dose (10%, placebo) wearable TENS, with 25 analyzed. High-dose TENS gave a greater reduction in pain interference (BPI-I mean difference 2.61, p=0.008) despite baseline imbalance, with no between-group differences in pain severity or fatigue, and within-group gait improvements in the high-dose arm. The device was feasible and acceptable with only mild adverse events, but the sample was small and results are exploratory.

FM subgroup text reports mean difference 1.39, p=0.125, d=2.257, conflicting with Table 3 (-1.397, p=0.08); text also gives GFI SE=10.61 vs Table 3 SE 2.188. summary: This mixed-methods sub-study of the UK TLC feasibility trial examined the views of non-hospitalised adults with Long COVID on three pacing interventions (app, book, video) using a Week 12 feasibility questionnaire (n=28) and 19 qualitative interviews. Uptake was 100% for video, 90% for book and 62.5% for app, and most participants tried pacing; participants reported benefits for activity planning and motivation, but also barriers such as time constraints, limited instructions and symptom burden. No efficacy outcomes or inferential between-arm comparisons were reported, so no statistical significance can be assessed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Descriptive feasibility study with no efficacy outcomes. The paper_id is the DOI supplied in the prompt, not one given in the paper text. Arm ids were reassigned so that usual care is arm 2, per instructions. Text says 18 (64.2%) participants agreed the intervention helped them understand pacing, but Table 6 strongly agree/agree counts sum to 16 (4+5+7); table values were used. The second Likert block in Table 6 has no row label and was not extracted. The text says 28 questionnaire completers were 43.7% of those randomised. Table 1 percentages are column-based and partly inconsistent; percent female was calculated from counts. Usual care arm did not complete the questionnaire. Per-arm completion numbers are the questionnaire completers (app 8, video 10, book 10). Number of sites, randomisation method and allocation concealment are only in the parent trial papers.

summary: In this Scottish multicenter open-label RCT of 233 adults within 12 months of COVID-19 infection (about 62% with symptoms >=90 days), a 3-month unsupervised personalized resistance exercise program was compared with usual care. ISWT distance improved more with exercise (adjusted mean difference 36.5 m, 95% CI 6.6-66.3, P=.02), with significant benefits also for EQ-5D-5L utility, PHQ-4 category and handgrip strength; fatigue, dyspnea, spirometry and frailty outcomes did not differ. No deaths occurred, and postexertional malaise was not increased.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: paper_id set to the paper's actual DOI rather than the template placeholder. Secondary outcomes are reported only as medians (IQR) of change, not means/SDs. Baseline BMI is reported only as median. PHQ-4 and other ordinal effect estimates (labelled as proportional-odds estimates) have direction that may favor the intervention when <1 for the deterioration category; the reference category is unclear, so interpret with caution. Table 1 shows identical serology values for both arms (likely a typo). The Results text says 'By 2 months' for secondary outcomes while the abstract says 3 months; 3 months used. Randomization, stratification and allocation concealment details are only in the supplement. Most per-outcome ns are taken from Table 4 'No. (No. missing)' rows. Per-arm withdrawals not reported (overall 26/233). Subgroup table n values for onset >=90 d rows contain mean (SD) in the change column and were not extracted.

summary: In a Belgian GP-based prospective Long COVID cohort (n=106), a small open-label, self-selected 15-day Paxlovid study (20 prescribed, 17 in the cohort comparison) was compared with dual antiplatelet therapy (n=73) and no treatment (n=16). Personalized symptom scores fell by about 24-31% on treatment, serum NFL/GFAP declined, and antiviral treatment independently predicted long-term improvement (e.g. strict improvement OR 18.46, 95%CI 3.26-136.90). Findings are non-randomized, open-label and confounded by treatment allocation, so causal inference is limited.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Preprint brief communication. Text and Fig 3 legend give conflicting p-values for the absolute symptom score (0.0074 vs 0.003) and the % change at day 15 (0.003 vs 0.0074); text values used. Table 1 antiplatelet sex counts (47F/16M=63) do not sum to n=73; percent female calculated from the stated counts. Table 1 n=17 for Paxlovid vs 20 prescribed in the open-label study (3 excluded per footnote); n_completed=16 is calculated from 20 minus 4 who did not complete. Per-outcome Ns for Table 1 means are not stated. Mean-change values for the paired COOP and SIMOA comparisons are in figures only. Logistic regression ORs compare antiviral vs all others, with the comparator arm unspecified. The Swedish PROLIFIC trial data are used for biomarker validation only and are not a study arm here. Methods describe a 0-6 symptom scale while the figure legend says 1-6.

summary: In this retrospective single-centre cohort of 163 non-asthmatic Long COVID adults, 75.5% had small airway dysfunction (SAD) by oscillometry; SAD patients were older, had higher BMI and more hypertension, with spirometry largely normal apart from lower FEV1. Among SAD patients, the 79 given ICS/LABA showed within-group improvements over 18 months in R5, R19, AX, X5, dyspnoea, fatigue, cough and C19-YRS symptom score, whereas the 44 untreated patients improved only in fatigue. No direct between-group test of treatment effect was reported and allocation was physician-decided, so findings are hypothesis-generating.

summary: Case series of three women with severe fatigue and cognitive dysfunction (two post-COVID-19, one during aromatase inhibitor therapy) given empiric metformin (500-1500 mg/day). All three reported rapid improvement within 48 hours to about 2 weeks, with symptom recurrence on withdrawal and improvement on re-challenge. Outcomes were unvalidated patient reports with no control group or statistical testing, so causality cannot be inferred.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No quantitative scale data, means, SDs, or p-values reported. Ages (50, 60, 50) were used to calculate mean and SD (53.3, 5.8). Only one of three patients had no COVID link, so the series is mixed (2 post-COVID, 1 aromatase-inhibitor-associated). Patient 1 had concurrent therapies and a partial recurrence on discontinuation. Patient 2 tapered off after about 18 months without relapse. Adverse events were reported only for Patient 1 (no GI effects or hypoglycemia). No countries stated; affiliation is Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center.

summary: This single-centre, double-blind phase 2a RCT randomised 41 adults with fatigue-predominant Long COVID to AXA1125 (amino acid/N-acetylcysteine metabolic modulator, 33.9 g BID, n=21) or placebo (n=20) for 4 weeks. summary: This open-label RCT in Egypt randomized 96 patients with anosmia persisting after COVID-19 viral clearance to ivermectin mucoadhesive nanosuspension nasal spray (n=49) or saline nasal spray (n=47). Recovery at 1 week was significantly higher with ivermectin (59.2% vs 27.7%, p=0.001) and median time to recovery was shorter (13 vs 50 days), but cumulative recovery over 3 months did not differ significantly (95.9% vs 89.4%, p=0.2). No side effects were reported in ivermectin-treated patients.

summary: This retrospective single-clinic case series of 195 patients (80.5% female, mean age 38.6) with post-COVID parosmia/dysgeusia/fatigue evaluated ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block with lidocaine and dexamethasone. summary: In this multicenter double-blind trial in Italy, 185 adults with post-COVID olfactory dysfunction lasting at least 6 months were randomized 2:1 to 90 days of PEA-LUT (700 mg/70 mg daily) or placebo, both with olfactory training. TDI rose from 20.6 to 29.8 with PEA-LUT versus 18.3 to 19.5 with placebo (between-group p<0.00001), and 56% vs 10% reached normal TDI. No adverse effects were reported, but the control arm was assessed only at 90 days and its placebo may not be inert.

summary: In this single-center, waitlist-controlled mixed-methods RCT (188 randomized adults with long COVID), a 3-week web-based yogic breathing and meditation program (Simha Kriya, Nadi Shuddhi, Isha Kriya) was tested for feasibility. Among 58 participants with complete adherence data, 55% met the adherence threshold, but retention was poor (36% had week-6 data). Compared with waitlist, the intervention significantly improved POMS total mood disturbance, fatigue, MDP dyspnea domains and SSS-8 at week 3, with no significant change in PSS or SF-12; these are exploratory secondary outcomes from unblinded self-report with heavy attrition.

NRS scores for fatigue (5.46 to 2.04), cough (2.32 to 0.43) and dyspnea (3.43 to 0.96) fell significantly over 30 days (repeated-measures ANOVA, all p<0.001). risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: randomization:some_concerns, deviations:some_concerns, missing_data:low, measurement:high, reporting:some_concerns
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Outcome assessors were not blinded and outcomes were subjective or examiner-dependent (self-reported QoL, monofilament, LP-ART), with a possible mismatch between the registered primary outcome and the multiple secondary outcomes reported in a split publication.

summary: In a single-center Egyptian RCT of 40 adults aged 30-40 with post-COVID-19 polyneuropathy, adding a sensory re-education paradigm to traditional physiotherapy for 6 weeks (3 sessions/week) was compared with physiotherapy alone. Post-treatment WHOQOL-BREF was higher with sensory re-education (75.77 vs 63.61; MD 12.16, p=0.001) and wrist proprioception errors (LP-ART) were lower in both hands, whereas monofilament tactile sensation did not differ between groups. Assessors were not blinded, the sample was small, no multiplicity adjustment was applied, and the sensory outcomes were exploratory.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Medians for SWM and LP-ART are reported with a single IQR value (interquartile range width) rather than quartile bounds, so iqr_low/iqr_high are null. Within-group pre/post MDs for WHOQOL-BREF (A 39.02, CI 43.56-34.48; B 29.37, CI 33.15-25.59; within-group d 4.43 and 3.07) were not extracted as between-group effects. Group-level eta-squared effect sizes are noted in source_location. Per-arm N analyzed is inferred from the statement that no data were missing and ITT analysis was used; flowchart is a figure. The WHOQOL-BREF table gives a single score per timepoint (domain scores not separately reported). Hand-grip outcomes were published separately and are not included.

summary: In a nested 12-month follow-up of an RCT of 4-week pulmonary telerehabilitation versus usual care in people with respiratory PASC, 29 of 50 participants (pooled across original arms, including crossovers) were reassessed and compared with baseline. There was no significant change in the primary 1-minSTST (+1.5 repetitions, p=0.277), but 5STST, CAT, several C19-YRS items and SF-36 physical functioning and emotional well-being improved significantly. With no control group and substantial attrition, the improvements cannot be attributed to rehabilitation and likely reflect natural recovery; higher BMI was associated with less fatigue improvement.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single pooled arm (PTR, crossover and non-crossover control); n=29 per Table II though Table IV lists n=27/25/27/27 for MCID analyses. Timepoint 2 weeks (65) calculated from 15±1 months. Table inconsistencies kept as printed: SF-36 social functioning CI (1.3 to 4.4) excludes mean difference 7.0; SF-36 energy/fatigue baseline SD 7.5 and difference -8.4 vs means 45.2→36.9; C19-YRS depression CI (-5.1 to -1.0) incompatible with p=0.124; CAT Q5 mean difference -0.7 inconsistent with 3.0→1.6; typos '0.10' and '3.00'; FSS MCID given as 0.45 in text and 4.05 in Table IV. The 1-minSTST baseline-to-follow-up difference (1.5) differs from the rounded means difference (1.4). Table cell quotes are single cell text since cells are separated by markup; locations given in source_location. Work-status distribution only in Figure 2 (not extractable). Normative values not extracted as outcomes.

summary: Small, non-randomized-appearing study of Pycnogenol plus Centellicum supplementation versus standard management in 19 patients with idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (8 months) and, preliminarily, 18 patients with post-COVID-19 lung disease (4 weeks). In IIP the echogenic fibrotic lung ultrasound fraction fell from 19.4% to 16.2% with supplementation versus no change in controls (18.5% to 18.9%; P<0.05). In the post-COVID cohort, symptoms, oxidative stress and Karnofsky index were reported as significantly better with supplementation (P<0.05), but only as p-values without group data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Only the abstract and journal page boilerplate were supplied; no full text or tables. Post-COVID cohort has p-values only (no means/SDs). Dispersion for ultrasound values (±) is unstated, so SD was not assigned. Per-outcome analyzed Ns are not reported. Combined treatment duration is 8 months (IIP) and 4 weeks (post-COVID); follow_up fields reflect the post-COVID cohort. 8 months converted to about 35 weeks. Study design and allocation method not described. Honeycombing outcome Ns use enrolled counts as denominators.

summary: This parallel RCT enrolled adults with persistent respiratory dysfunction after hospitalization for COVID-19 pneumonia and compared a 12-week fully remote pulmonary telerehabilitation program with a hybrid remote/in-person program. summary: Single-center Ukrainian case series of 15 patients with new-onset thrombocytopenia (platelets 2–95·10^9/L) diagnosed on average 69 days after COVID-19, selected from 25 patients with thrombocytopenia; 11 were women and mean age was 56.9 years. One-third were asymptomatic, the others had bruising or bleeding, and treatment was glucocorticoids with eltrombopag or platelet transfusion in severe cases. Most responded initially, but 2 relapsed, 1 developed chronic ITP and 1 developed Evans syndrome; there was no control group and no statistical testing.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Ukrainian; quotes copied verbatim from the Ukrainian text. Table 3 cells are garbled (merged/split row labels), so table-derived values (e.g. days to onset by severity) are given in subgroup_analyses rather than as per-arm outcomes. The text reports 6 patients treated with GCS plus 4 needing transfusion, while Table 3 lists 10 treated patients (5 untreated) and the text says '5 hospitalized-free asymptomatic' among 'surveyed'; counts were interpreted against the 15-patient cohort. Relapse count is ambiguous (one relapse after GCS withdrawal at 3 months plus two relapses at 4 and 9 months); the 2 relapses at 4 and 9 months were extracted. No SDs for platelet counts or overall age; no follow-up duration or adverse event data reported. Max time since infection (9 months) converted to ~39 weeks.

summary: This single-site, single-blind RCT randomised 114 adults with non-hospitalised post-COVID fatigue to 8 weeks of self-administered active tragus taVNS, sham tragus stimulation, or active earlobe stimulation, followed by crossover to taVNS. Baseline-adjusted F-VAS at week 8 did not differ between taVNS and sham (MD 2.6, 95% CI −7 to 12, p=0.59) or earlobe stimulation (MD 1.2, 95% CI −9 to 11, p=0.81), and CACE and duration analyses were also null. Secondary outcomes were mostly null; total FIS was lower with taVNS than earlobe stimulation (p=0.03, unadjusted for multiplicity). Adherence was low and analyses were of completers.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Sign convention: Table 3 labels contrasts as 'X vs taVNS'; regression and mixed-model estimates are positive (control higher F-VAS than taVNS) but CACE estimates are negative, so sign direction is inconsistent/unclear; effect values recorded as printed. All secondary effects are from linear mixed models at week 8; per-arm raw secondary data are in Figshare only. Neurophysiological regression results (Table 4, within taVNS arm only, estimates vs F-VAS at weeks 8/16) not extracted as between-group outcomes. Table 2 baseline N for sham is 27 (header says 28). Per-arm withdrawals computed as randomized minus completed (include lost to follow-up). Time since infection converted from days (/30.4375). Per-protocol 59-participant analysis cited from another reference; no data. Several effect_quote values are table cell values only. No placebo/sham pairwise comparison of sham vs placebo reported.

summary: Single-center prospective cohort of 61 critically ill COVID-19 survivors (mean ICU stay 57 days, 93.4% ventilated, 91.8% ICU-acquired weakness) undergoing inpatient neurorehabilitation, assessed at study inclusion and at discharge (mean 36 days apart). Mobility, disability (mRS), independence (Barthel), grip strength, EQ-5D-5L and dyspnea improved significantly, while fatigue and anxiety did not change significantly; all patients remained substantially impaired relative to their preclinical state. There was no control group, so the effect of rehabilitation cannot be separated from natural recovery, and regression models found no predictors of disability, fatigue or hospitalization length.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post; arm 1 pooled cohort. Ordinal scale values in Table 3 are median (IQR) with a single IQR width given, so iqr_low/high left null. Stacked multi-row cells (HADS, EQ-5D-5L, Sniffin, TUG) make p-value/statistic alignment partly ambiguous; HADS anxiety p and Z assignment is inconsistent in the table (text: anxiety not significant). Outcome-level Ns not given for ordinal scales/grip/TUG means. Weeks from enrollment derived from mean 36.3 days between visits. Treatment duration 8.2 weeks from mean 57.3 days inpatient rehabilitation. Time since infection months calculated from 84.6 days. BI also measured at hospital admission (median 17.5, IQR 30.0) and preclinical (median 100, IQR 0) but not included as arm results. Preclinical vs discharge comparisons (FAC Z=-3.862, CFS Z=-6.570, mRS Z=-6.885) not extracted as arm results. Cognitive impairment (76.6% of 47), restrictive lung disease (72.1% of 43) reported once only.

summary: Case series of 7 adolescents with prolonged sleep (>=2 h above baseline) after COVID-19 infection, treated with low-dose aripiprazole (mean final dose 1.4 mg) over several months or longer. Mean total sleep time fell from 13.2 to 9.4 h (p=0.01) and wake-up time advanced from 11.3 to 8.2 h (p=0.03), with no significant change in sleep onset (p=0.23). The design is uncontrolled and unblinded, so spontaneous recovery cannot be excluded.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Substantial post-randomization exclusions (35 of 177), under-powered sample (142 vs planned 160), spirometry in only a small subset, and subjective semi-quantitative CT scoring.

summary: In this multicenter double-blind RCT in China, 142 convalescent COVID-19 patients with CT-evident pulmonary fibrosis received Fuzheng Huayu tablets or placebo for 24 weeks alongside rehabilitation training. The fibrosis regression rate was higher with FZHY (66.7% vs 47.1% in the FAS, p=0.019; 71.2% vs 49.2% in the PPS, p=0.011), as was the HRCT score reduction (-1.25 vs -0.45, p=0.005) and lung inflammation regression (83.8% vs 68.8%, p=0.041). Symptoms, QOL, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 did not differ, spirometry was available only for a small subset, and no serious adverse events occurred.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Number randomized per arm not reported (177 'enrolled eligible', 35 excluded before the 142 FAS). FVC and FEV1 results and 6MWT time-course are figure-only (Figures 3, 4A); FVC/FEV1 outcomes omitted. HRCT score change n not stated. Table 4 fatigue FZHY entry 19 (63.3%) with n=33 is internally inconsistent (19/30=63.3%). Table 2 and 3 FAS n differ (72/70 vs 68/64). subgroup_analyses.variable: Elevated FSMC (>=53), n=255; post-rehabilitation self-initiated therapy (ANCOVA, adjusted for baseline WAI)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Beta (reference=intervention received; negative favors intervention): exercise -0.98 (SE 0.42, p=0.02, p_adj=0.30); sports -0.88 (SE 0.36, p=0.02, p_adj=0.27); cognitive therapy 0.96 (SE 0.39, p=0.02, p_adj=0.27); physiotherapy 0.37 (p=0.31); psychotherapy 0.43 (p=0.29). WAI1 rose from M=2.55 to 3.73.
Exercise beta -1.37 (SE 0.51, p=0.01, p_adj=0.17); sports -1.06 (SE 0.49, p=0.03, p_adj=0.43); others non-significant. WAI1 M 2.26 to 2.86 to 3.50.
Psychotherapy beta 0.79 (SE 0.69, p=0.25); sports -1.14 (p=0.08); no significant differences. WAI1 M 1.66 to 2.61 to 3.08.

Cognitive therapy beta 1.00 (SE 0.39, p=0.01, p_adj=0.19), greater improvement without it; exercise -1.02 (p=0.02, p_adj=0.29); sports -0.87 (p=0.02, p_adj=0.33). WAI1 M 2.61 to 3.94. None significant after Holm correction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm, no comparator. Text and Table 2 differ slightly in rounding (e.g. FSMC 78.5 vs 78.54; WAI1 baseline 2.73 here vs 2.67 in Table 1 which uses n=319). Table 2 N is per outcome. Pairwise post-hoc Wilcoxon p_adj/r values (not all captured as structured fields) are given in text, e.g. PHQ-9 1v2 r=0.699, 1v3 r=0.255, 1v4 r=0.311; FSMC 1v2 r=0.278, 2v3 r=0.291, 3v4 r=0.219 (p_adj=0.002); LK-18 1v2 r=0.446, 2v3 r=0.329, 2v4 r=0.286; WAI1 1v3 r=0.290, 1v4 r=0.394, 3v4 r=0.259. Timepoint weeks are approximations (discharge ~ median 34-day stay; 6 and 12 months after discharge). Percent female 69.6% uses denominator 319 including 10 missing sex. WAI 2 direction ambiguous (scale described 1=very good but text interprets decrease as improvement). Several quotes are short fragments because the source text has irregular spacing. Table 3 (20 ANCOVA contrasts) only partly transcribed in subgroup summaries.

summary: In this single-center Norwegian RCT of 60 adults with post COVID-19 condition, tailored individual CBT-based follow-up (4 consultations over 6-8 weeks) was compared with a one-day group course, both with an optional app. No significant between-group difference was found in the primary outcome EQ-5D-5L index at 6 months (one-sided p=.11; adjusted p=.48), nor in most secondary or neuropsychological outcomes. Both groups improved over time in fatigue, EQ-VAS, symptom count and some cognitive tests, so the one-day course appeared similarly effective, though the trial was small, open-label and lacked an untreated control.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 reports mean (95% CI) with a single total N per row (not per arm), so per-arm n_analyzed is null; primary N=58 total. Table 3 column order is Standard treatment first, Intervention second (mapped to arm 2 and arm 1). Primary outcome text reports 'score difference = 0.07; 95% CI [−0.18, .04]' which is internally inconsistent in sign/range with Table 3 (standard 0.75 vs intervention 0.68); extracted verbatim. Footnote for breathlessness mislabeled as 'feeling more depressed'. Within-group changes, MCID responder percentages (EQ-VAS 58% vs 45%; CFS 32% intervention vs 48% standard) and app use (3 months 39% standard vs 63% intervention; 6 months 28% vs 46%) are reported only in text/figures and not extracted as arm results. CFS GEE used multiple imputation; Table 3 means may or may not be imputed. Raw SDs not reported anywhere. Trial registration/allocation concealment not described. Adverse events: 'No harms or unintended events were reported' (summary only; per-arm zeros inferred from this statement).

summary: In this pilot randomized trial of 66 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Padova, Italy, a 5-week outpatient Health Resort program (thermal water, aquatic and land exercise, cognitive training) was compared with a similar home-based program. Both groups improved on quality of life, dyspnea, physical performance, pain and cognition. For the primary outcome (SF-12 PCS-12), the between-group difference was not significant at end of treatment (1.09, 95% CI -3.27 to 5.44) but favored the Health Resort group at 6 months (7.72, 2.59 to 12.86), and handgrip, anxiety and depression also favored it at some time points. Group B had substantial attrition (25 of 33 analyzed), baseline imbalances and no multiplicity adjustment, so the findings are exploratory.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm raw means/SDs are not reported (only medians in Figure 2); per-arm results are model-based estimated change from baseline (T0-T1) from Table 4 with 95% CIs, and between-group effects are the time x group interaction coefficients from Table 3 (difference in change from baseline, Group A minus Group B, adjusted for age and hospitalization). Table 4 T1-T2 and T1-T3 contrasts (changes from T1) were not extracted. Table 3 mixed-model N: Group A 33/33/33/31, Group B 25/25/15/15 at T0/T1/T2/T3 (per footnote), so n_analyzed for T2/T3 differs from T1. Timepoint weeks for T2 and T3 are calculated from 3 and 6 months post-treatment. n_completed for arm 1 is inferred from 33 analyzed. The satisfaction scale is described as 0-100 in methods but reported values are about 30-40; the scale range is unclear. Discussion text on baseline anxiety/depression direction conflicts with Table 3 group coefficients. Table 4 sign convention header says T0-T1 but footnote says change is later minus earlier. Some results exist only in figures (medians over time in Figure 2). Quotes for Table 4 per-arm cells are single-number cells because the cells contain line breaks.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Substantial attrition (12-month completion 50.5% intervention vs 60.4% control) with available-case analysis, patient-reported phone-collected outcomes, non-randomized patient assignment to clinicians, and low clinician attendance.

subgroup_analyses.variable: Number of referrals / completed encounters (below vs above median) within intervention arm
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Intervention patients with fewer than median referrals: T-score 59 (SD 10) baseline to 54 (SD 11) at 12 months; those with more referrals: 63 (SD 9) to 60 (SD 10). Exploratory.

summary: In a cluster-randomized pragmatic trial in a US federally qualified health center, 20 primary care clinicians were randomized to a weekly Project ECHO case-based virtual community of practice (plus webinars and short courses) or to webinars and short courses alone; 587 patients with long COVID/ME/CFS/IACC were followed for 12 months. Both arms improved on most PROMIS measures; the primary outcome (physical function) did not differ significantly between arms (adjusted difference 1.49, 95% CI -0.04 to 3.02, p=0.06), while pain interference was modestly better in the intervention arm (-1.95, p=0.04), below the minimal important change, with fewer referrals and encounters.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Patients were not randomized (clinicians were); no cluster-adjusted variance (random intercept per patient only), so design_adjusted is null. Per-arm randomized Ns not stated; 298/289 are baseline completers (590 enrolled). n_screened 1577 comes from CONSORT figure alt text (987 excluded). Table 2 SD values are rounded integers; table quotes are single cell values with location in source_location. Table 3 estimates are 12-month baseline-adjusted LME interaction terms. ME/CFS symptom screener results (muscle pain severity 12M: control 7.8 (5.5) vs intervention 5.8 (4.9), p=0.01; joint pain 7.6 (5.4) vs 6.1 (4.8), p=0.06) not extracted as outcomes because the values are split by markup. UW cohort comparison and Supplementary Tables S1-S9 are not in the text.

title: Effectiveness of an Extension for Community Health Outcomes case-based virtual community of practice model on patient outcomes for the management of long COVID and other fatiguing illnesses: a randomized control trial
authors: Sydney P. Sharp; Tianmai M. Zhang; Douglas Taren; Alexandra Zuber; Jane C. Samaniego; Elizabeth R. Unger; Jeanne Bertolli; Jin-Mann S. Lin; Joanna J. Regan; Amy J. Armistad; John D. Scott; Bruce B. Struminger; Job G. Godino; Christian B. Ramers
release_limitations: AI-screened and AI-extracted; eligibility and numerical values have not been independently adjudicated.

study_design.design_type_detail: single-center, single-blinded, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial (1:1), nested in the multicentric Recovery Trial

arms.label: Supervised multicomponent training (IG)
arms.dose: ~70 min/session; Phase 1: balance 15 min, resistance 15-20 min, aerobic 25 min; Phase 2: resistance 20-25 min, aerobic 25 min
co_interventions: one 1-h physical activity guidance meeting was given to the control group only

arms.label: Control: physical activity recommendations (CG)
arms.intervention_name: Physical activity and sedentary behavior guidance
arms.dose: single ~1 h face-to-face meeting plus two chapters of the Brazilian Guide to Physical Activity

study_design.randomization_method: www.randomizer.org, permuted blocks of 4-6, stratified by sex, 1:1; computer-generated sequence created by an independent researcher
study_design.setting: single-center university rehabilitation center (UFSC)

participants.long_covid_definition: Post-COVID-19 condition: previously hospitalized with moderate to critical COVID-19, or non-hospitalized with chronic postinfection fatigue (Chalder score >4); at least 6 weeks after discharge/acute phase
key_inclusion_criteria: admitted to UFSC University Hospital with moderate to critical COVID-19, or non-hospitalized with Chalder score >4
discharge or end of acute phase at least 6 weeks prior
general respiratory, functional and cognitive stability
key_exclusion_criteria: previous participation in a rehabilitation or physical exercise program

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: randomization:low, deviations:some_concerns, missing_data:some_concerns, measurement:low, reporting:some_concerns
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Participants could not be blinded, adherence was low (only 9 of 21 IG participants met the 70% attendance threshold), 20% of participants were lost with maximum-likelihood imputation, and the favorable conclusions rest on small per-protocol subsets.

summary: In this single-center Brazilian RCT (n=40), a 24-week supervised multicomponent exercise program (balance, resistance, aerobic) was compared with a single session of physical activity guidance in adults with post-COVID-19 condition. In the ITT analysis, the primary outcome (6MWT) improved similarly in both groups (IG +35 m, CG +32 m) with no significant group-by-time differences for most outcomes, whereas fatigue (Chalder mental and general domains) improved only in the exercise group. Per-protocol results (n=9 exercise, 10-12 control) favored exercise for the 6MWT (ES 0.61), TUG-m and some body composition outcomes, but these rest on small, self-selected high-adherence subsets and are at risk of bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table values are mean ± SE (per methods) from GEE models; recorded in se field with mean_type unknown. The 'Mean difference (95% CI)' columns are within-arm changes and were not extracted as between-group effects. 6MWT arm-level means and Chalder arm-level values appear only in figures (not extracted); 6MWT mean changes are from the Discussion. ES is the Morris-type difference of changes (IG minus CG) divided by pooled baseline SD, so negative values favor IG for lower-is-better outcomes; the p values attached to ES are group x time interaction p values. The PP 6MWT CI (50.6-124.4) appears to be the within-IG change CI and was not recorded as a between-group CI; Chalder p values (0.005, 0.017, 0.026, 0.047) are ambiguous in scope and were omitted. Chalder physical ES (-0.74 ITT, -0.89 PP) is from the Discussion. Text inconsistencies: '21 male and 18 female' vs Table 1 (21 M, 19 F); CG losses are 5 in the text but 7 in the flow diagram; text says 3 IG withdrawals but the flow diagram lists 1 dropout plus 2 additional losses; PP n varies by table (CG 10, 12 or 11; IG 9). Phase 2 TUG-m PP ES is -0.50 in the table but -0.51 in the Discussion. One myocardial infarction occurred in an unspecified arm and was not related to training. BMI/time-since-infection per-arm values: BMI mean is from Table 5 (SE only); time since infection converted from days to months (/30.44). Pulmonary PP analysis not performed; physical activity n not stated.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Difference in 6MWT distance before and after rehabilitation
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Age R=-0.31984 (p<0.001); BMI R=-0.26962 (p<0.001); hospitalization length R=0.12359 (p=0.218); rehabilitation length R=0.04552 (p=0.589); time to start R=-0.16260 (p=0.052). Multivariable logistic regression for improvement >=30 m (MCID) found no significant predictors.

summary: This single-center, single-arm study in Poland assessed a 2-6 week inpatient comprehensive rehabilitation program (breathing, aerobic, strength/endurance training) in 146 patients after COVID-19, with pre-post assessment on admission and discharge. 6MWT distance rose from 370.03 to 490.47 m (about +120 m, p<0.001), with significant improvements in %predicted distance, walking speed, SpO2, Borg fatigue, and mMRC dyspnea. With no control group, spontaneous recovery cannot be excluded; older age, higher BMI, diabetes and hypertension were associated with smaller gains/lower performance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post; no between-group effects. Within-group changes calculated from Table 2 means (p-values from paired tests as reported; SD of change not reported). n screened (171) taken from 'study involved 171 participants'; 146 analyzed. Discharge timing varied (2-6 weeks), so weeks_from_enrollment for timepoint 2 is null. Table 3 subgroup results captured in subgroup_analyses text only. Table 5 logistic regression ORs not tied to a specific outcome comparison and not extracted as effects. Time since infection capped at 12 months (52 weeks).

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Retrospective medical-file study with unclear allocation procedure, no blinding or concealment, tiny sample (n=16), no prespecified primary outcome, and baseline imbalances (e.g., 6MWT, SBP).

summary: A retrospective, small (n=16 analyzed, 8 per group) study of young adult university students in Quito, Ecuador with post-COVID condition compared a 4-week asynchronous web-based pulmonary telerehabilitation program (breathing plus aerobic exercises, 12 sessions) against no treatment. The intervention group showed significant group x time interactions for the labeled heart and respiratory rates, 6MWT distance, sit-to-stand repetitions and Borg exertion after the sit-to-stand test, but not SpO2, blood pressure or Borg after the 6MWT. The non-randomized/unclear allocation and tiny sample mean the findings are hypothesis-generating only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 labels appear inconsistent with the Methods: the HR row has values ~20 and the RR row has values ~70 (physiologically reversed), and the 6MWT is placed under 'Physical capacity' and sit-to-stand under 'Cardiorespiratory capacity' whereas Methods say the opposite; values extracted as labeled in the table. Text refers to 'heart' and 'respiratory' interaction results in that order, so the HR/RR mapping of interaction p-values follows the text labels and may be swapped. Per-arm randomized Ns not reported (18 eligible randomized, 16 analyzed, 8/8; text mentions only one discontinuation). Within-group Table 3 p-values (Pre vs Post): CG/EG SpO2 0.401/0.042; RR 0.779/0.012; HR 0.401/0.012; SBP 0.746/0.122; DBP 0.484/0.208; 6MWT 0.084/0.028; Borg(6MWT) 0.969/0.051; Sit-to-stand 0.059/0.012; Borg(STS) 0.006/0.001. Eta-squared effect sizes (0.08, 0.02, 0.08, 0.28, 0.03, 0.27, 0.13, 0.11) and F values reported but no between-group mean differences or CIs; the same F(1,14)=15.121 is reported for two different outcomes. Percent female per arm calculated from counts (Table 3 percentages are row percentages). Control arm described as receiving no treatment. Borg scale values from 6MWT and STS blocks identified by position in table. Figure 2 data not available in text.

summary: This retrospective single-center study in Romania compared 160 patients with mild-to-moderate post-COVID-19 conditions who received a stage-based inpatient plus outpatient rehabilitation program for up to 12 months with 33 patients given standard follow-up. In the rehabilitation group, TUG normal mobility rose from 30.6% to 60.6% and 10MWT category C from 1.3% to 25.6%, with significantly larger shifts than controls (Cramér's V 0.468 for TUG, 0.500 for 10MWT; p<0.001), though the binary TUG within-group change was not significant (p=0.118). Non-randomized design, small unbalanced control group, no adjustment, and some text/table inconsistencies limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No continuous TUG time (s) or gait speed (m/s) means/SDs reported; only categorical distributions. Overall mean age differs between text (59.79) and Table 2 (58.79). Table 2 age-group rows show mean±SD ages rather than n(%). Control-group TUG table shows Pre B=25, Pre C=8 and Post C=21, i.e. apparent worsening, contradicting text implying stable status; control 10MWT p<0.001 in table contradicts 'limited changes' in text; 10MWT category A (<0.4 m/s) rose in controls (5 to 13), implying worsening. 10MWT category labels in text (A <0.4, B 0.4-0.8, C 0.8-1.2, D>1.2) differ from methods' 'functional' dichotomy wording. Text r for TUG McNemar is 0.12 (results) vs 0.11 (discussion). Control follow-up timing not stated; assumed same 12 months. Binary functional outcomes (ids 4, 8) calculated by summing categories. Cramér's V values are reported for category shift analyses (N=187), not as standardized mean differences; effect_measure 'smd' used as nearest placeholder with null value. Control group n=33 yet some prose p-value differs from table.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Non-randomized allocation by clinical pathway/logistics with unequal groups (160 vs 33), no adjustment for confounders (comorbidity, BMI, severity), exclusion of non-completers from the rehabilitation group, and unblinded retrospective MRC assessment.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Women vs men ΔMRC did not differ in study group (p=0.561) or control group (p=0.435); within-group improvement significant in study women (p<0.001) but not study men (p=0.079); in control, significant in men (p=0.024) but not women (p=0.084).
In study group, >=60 improved more than <60 (mean ΔMRC 4.03 vs 1.44; p=0.025); in control, difference borderline (p=0.05). Study vs control ΔMRC in age-stratified analysis p=0.016.
Age correlated weakly positively with ΔMRC: whole cohort r=0.170 (p=0.020); study group r=0.172 (p=0.033); control r=0.287 (p=0.106).

summary: This retrospective single-center Romanian cohort compared 160 adults with mild/moderate COVID-19 who completed a structured rehabilitation program (10-day inpatient plus outpatient phase) with 33 who received standard follow-up, measuring change in total MRC muscle strength over about 2 weeks. MRC improved in both groups (mean ΔMRC 2.76 vs 1.00), but the between-group difference was not statistically significant (p=0.278); age-stratified analyses suggested greater gains with rehabilitation in those >=60 years (p=0.016). Non-randomized design, small control group and lack of confounder adjustment limit inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table values extracted from cell text; table quotes are single-cell values with source_location giving row/column. Internal inconsistencies noted: control-group women mean MRC fell (49.83 to 49.47) yet reported ΔMRC +0.53; control overall median final 52 vs mean 49.82; study SDs of ΔMRC are large relative to means. The paper's sex-stratified study-vs-control p (0.278) merely repeats the overall p. The Table 5 study-vs-control p=0.016 is described only as 'within age strata' so the specific stratum is unclear. Mean differences are calculated from reported ΔMRC means without CIs. Time since infection, vaccination, BMI, hospitalization and adverse events not reported. Figures contain no additional extractable numbers.

summary: Single-arm observational study of 127 patients (124 analyzed) with work-related COVID-19 (mean ~409 days post-infection) undergoing a ~29-day inpatient multidisciplinary post-COVID rehabilitation program in Germany. Physical performance (6MWD median +64 m, 1MSTST, quadriceps strength), cognition (MoCA, DSST), anxiety, depression and fatigue improved significantly (handgrip did not), but total work ability did not change and 72.5% remained unable to work. No control group, so natural recovery cannot be excluded.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: 1-min STST repetitions, SF-36 total and other outcomes
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: All outcomes improved in both groups except fatigue in non-hospitalized (p=0.065) and general health in hospitalized (p=0.154). Post-intervention between-group p: repetitions 0.008, %predicted 0.021, SF-36 total 0.038, mMRC 0.031, fatigue 0.448; non-hospitalized had better post values.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: 1-min STST repetitions, SF-36 total and other outcomes
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: All outcomes improved except four SF-36 domains in ICU patients (bodily pain, general health, emotional role, mental health). Post-intervention between-group p: repetitions 0.271, SF-36 total 0.019, bodily pain 0.013, emotional role 0.032, mMRC 0.648, fatigue 0.473.

summary: In a prospective multicentre single-arm study in Chilean primary care, 115 adults with persistent dyspnea after COVID-19 (half previously hospitalized) completed a 9-week home-based telerehabilitation programme of 24 sessions. 1-min sit-to-stand repetitions rose from 20.5 to 29.4, SF-36 total from 39.6 to 58.9, and dyspnea and fatigue scores fell, all p<0.001, with smaller gains in hospitalized and ICU patients. With no control group and 23% dropout, improvements cannot be attributed to the intervention.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm study; subgroups (hospitalized, ICU) are not separate arms and are extracted as subgroup outcomes under arm 1. Text reports 55.4% female, but Table 1 gender 49/66 implies 57.4%; the text value was used. Table 3 footnote mislabels the intergroup comparison as non-hospitalized vs hospitalized (it is ICU vs non-ICU). Table 3 ICU n=36 but text reports 35 requiring MV. Table 1 hospitalized BMI SD (46.5) and height values look erroneous. Time from discharge to rehab start was 30 (27-35) days; no long COVID definition was stated. Dispersion for mean ± values assumed SD per methods. Within-group changes were only calculated where source values were in prose. No adverse event reporting. Table cell quotes are short single cells because table text cannot be joined across markup.

summary: In this retrospective single-centre study of 50 long COVID patients undergoing NASA lean testing, 31 with dyspnoea and supine/orthostatic hypocapnia were referred for Papworth breathing retraining (5 sessions), and 13 completed it. Among completers, Malmö POTS score (59.3 to 42.3, p=0.0033), BPAT (5.7 to 2.1, p<0.0001) and mean arterial pressure improved significantly, while end-tidal CO2, heart rate, HADS, Nijmegen, fatigue and diastolic BP did not change significantly. The uncontrolled design, small sample and attrition limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Systolic BP, end-tidal CO2 and heart rate values are only in Figure 1 (not in supplied text). Non-significant outcomes have no numeric values; p-values set to 0.05 with operator >= as placeholders for 'not significant' (exact p unreported). Timing of post-rehab assessment not stated. Total n_enrolled set to 13 (analysed completers); 31 were referred. n_lost_to_followup refers to the 2 who started but did not complete.

summary: In this multicenter retrospective single-arm study from Japan, 42 patients with Long COVID (CPTH/mTBI-like and orthostatic-autonomic phenotype) received a single epidural injection of 100% oxygen, mostly via the sacral hiatus. Eight patients had minor transient adverse events (subcutaneous emphysema 5, dyspnea 2, back pain 1), all resolving within 1 week, with no serious events. Among 35 patients with paired SF-36v2 data about 1 month later, median scores rose in all eight domains (median change +5.0 to +25.0, largest for vitality), all significant after Bonferroni correction. Without a control group these findings are hypothesis-generating and cannot be separated from placebo or expectancy effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Only medians/IQRs reported (no means/SDs). Table 4 cells are separated in the XML, so pre/post result_quote uses the table caption and source_location identifies the row/column. Post-treatment timepoint set to 4.6 weeks from the median 32-day interval between SF-36 assessments. Per-domain p-values are Bonferroni-adjusted. Individual-level data are in Figure 3 only (box plots).

summary: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of 200 Indian adults with post-COVID fatigue enrolled a median of about 3 weeks after a negative COVID test, 14 days of oral ImmunoSEB (systemic enzymes) plus ProbioSEB CSC3 (Bacillus probiotics) was compared with placebo. By day 14, 91% of the supplement arm versus 15% of the placebo arm were fatigue-free by CFQ-11 bimodal scoring, and mean total CFQ-11 Likert scores were 8.54 versus 19.91 (p<0.001). No adverse events were reported; follow-up was short, SDs were not reported, and the sponsor's employees were authors.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm SDs not reported for CFQ-11 means (Figure 3 shows box plots; Figure 4 shows mean ± SEM for individual items). Eleven per-item CFQ-11 means at day 0 and day 14 (Q1-Q11) were not extracted as outcomes: day 14 values are listed in an order that conflicts with the stated 'test vs. control' ordering and no SEMs are given in text. Baseline day-0 median total/physical/mental reported only for test arm. Primary outcomes in methods are proportions improved on physical and mental CFQ-11 at day 14; results report fatigue-free proportion (total) instead. Fatigue-free percentages converted to events using n=100 per arm. Event counts at baseline not entered (all patients fatigued). Number completing the trial and CONSORT flow data are only in Figure 1.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:serious, classification:low, deviations:moderate, missing_data:serious, measurement:moderate, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: No longitudinal control group, complete-case analysis with substantial attrition, and unmeasured confounders (medication, iron supplementation, menopausal status) preclude causal attribution of changes to the diet.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Baseline ferritin higher with higher meat consumption (140.9 ± 114.0 vs 106.1 ± 89.6 ng/mL; p = 0.026); ferritin change did not differ (5.7 ± 31.3 vs 1.3 ± 56.4 ng/mL; p = 0.555). Group Ns not reported.

summary: This exploratory prospective cohort study gave an approximately 32-week, 30% energy-restricted Mediterranean-style diet to adults with overweight/obesity who were healthy (n=49 analyzed), had long COVID (n=108), or had metabolic syndrome (n=33), with a baseline-only normal-weight comparison group (n=61). Weight, body composition, metabolic markers, fatigue (FACIT), and quality of life changes did not differ significantly between groups. Only MEDAS change (p=0.045) and ferritin change differed, with ferritin falling in the MS group (−22.0 ± 58.8 ng/mL) relative to the other two. There was no untreated longitudinal control, so changes cannot be attributed to the diet.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 contains duplicated/unclear Men/Women rows that were not used. Table 2 ΔHbA1c in healthy overweight (−0.9 ± 0.2) looks inconsistent with other groups, likely a typo; extracted as printed. Table 1 baseline values other than demographics and inflammatory markers were not extracted. Arm ordering: arm 1 = long COVID, 2 = healthy overweight, 3 = MS, 4 = normal-weight baseline only. Per-outcome n assumed from table header n (49/108/33); the paper does not state per-outcome n. Between-group p-values are omnibus tests (one-way ANOVA for Table 2; Kruskal-Wallis for ferritin); pairwise effects only for ferritin. Regression (Table 5) and MANOVA (Table 4) results not extracted as outcomes. Meat-consumption subgroup data have no group Ns.

summary: Fifteen patients with persistent anosmia/hyposmia 12-24 months after COVID-19 were randomized (stratified by gender) to five sessions of 0.5 mA frontal-anode/inion-cathode tDCS (n=8) or sham (n=7), with Sniffin' Sticks testing before and after. Mean TDI did not change in either arm (active 24.06 to 23.56; sham 27.68 to 27.68), and no stimulation × time interaction was significant. A non-significant improvement was seen only in the two anosmic participants, so the pilot is inconclusive because of its small sample.

Table 5 stimulation-group columns also include Anosmia (n=2)/Hyposmia/Total groupings, not extracted as arm results. ANOVA used 3 groups, so p-values are omnibus, not arm-specific. Allocation to stimulation was based on baseline score, and 25 recruited -> 20 allocated -> 15 completed. AEs not reported.

summary: In this single-center non-randomized prospective cohort, 93 patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19 pneumonia received either a 14-day prednisone taper (n=30), prednisone for about 3 months (n=44), or no additional corticosteroid (n=19) after discharge. At 3 months, CT patterns and most lung function measures and symptoms did not differ, but the control group had significantly higher DLCO (p=0.03) and less dyspnea (p=0.04); allocation was by physician choice, so confounding by indication is possible. The authors conclude there is no evidence of benefit from prolonged corticosteroids for post-COVID lung sequelae.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Three arms; arm_id 3 is control (usual care). Lung function reported as medians with IQR only; Ns per outcome not stated (null). CT2 Ns (21/38/11 of 70) taken from Table 2; reasons for loss to follow-up not given (lost counts calculated from enrolled minus HRCT n, assumed to apply to all outcomes only for CT). Symptom Ns assumed equal to enrolled group sizes (percentages match). Table 1 non-smoker control cell shows '0' and smoking percentages inconsistent. Decimal commas preserved in quotes. Within-group CT p-values reported jointly for groups I and II as p<0,001.

summary: Single case report of an 86-year-old woman with residual lung infiltrates/fibrosis and oxygen dependence after severe COVID-19, treated with azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly alongside a rapidly tapered prednisone course. No statistical testing was done, and the concurrent steroid and natural recovery confound attribution to azithromycin.

summary: Single-center retrospective study of 75 patients with persistent respiratory symptoms and abnormal chest CT after COVID-19; 30 received oral prednisone (20-80 mg/day, ~57-day taper) after clinic evaluation and 45 did not. The steroid group (who had lower baseline DLCO) showed significant within-group improvement in FEV1, FVC and DLCO% on follow-up in small subsets (n=16, n=12), and CT ground-glass opacities improved in both groups; no between-group differences in follow-up PFT were found and the nonsteroid group had only 6 follow-up spirometries, so steroid benefit relative to natural recovery cannot be established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 header lists steroid baseline n=69 and nonsteroid n=40, inconsistent with 30/45 group sizes and 69 total spirometry; steroid baseline n left null and nonsteroid baseline n=40 taken from header. Between-group follow-up mean differences are calculated from unpaired subsets (n=16 vs n=6). Table 1 nonsteroid GGO 37/45 does not equal printed 84%. Overall 22-patient paired PFT (FEV1 2.51±0.69 to 2.67±0.84, P=0.004; FVC 3.16±0.89 to 3.32±1.09, P=0.004; TLC 3.78±0.91 to 4.12±1.02, P=0.04; DLCO 14.74±4.91 to 18.21±7.05, P=0.01) is not arm-specific and was not entered. Baseline TLC by group and other CT findings at follow-up not given by arm. The DLCO mL/min/mmHg steroid change is described as significant in text but P=0.07.

summary: Retrospective single-arm study of a UK NHS multidisciplinary post-COVID rehabilitation service, using routinely collected EQ-5D-5L (n=21) and C-19 YRS (n=30) data at baseline and 12 weeks. C-19 YRS symptom severity and functional disability improved significantly, and the EQ-5D-5L usual activities dimension improved (p=0.049), while EQ VAS, C-19 YRS overall health and other EQ-5D-5L dimensions did not change significantly. With no control group, a small sample and unrecorded exclusions, improvements cannot be attributed to the service.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Two overlapping samples: EQ-5D-5L completers n=21 (age M 48.5, SD 13.29; 47.6% female) and C-19 YRS completers n=30 (age M 50.6, SD 13.31; 56.67% female); the demographics section reports the C-19 YRS sample. Anxiety/depression follow-up SD is 1.16 in Table 2 but 1.17 in text (table used). Text says anxiety/depression d range −0.052 to 0.218 while table gives 0.101; the Health today t=6.838 is inconsistent with p=0.874. Table 1 percentages are inconsistent (47.52% vs 47.62%). Within-group change means are calculated as follow-up minus baseline. Enrolled and screened numbers and exclusions were not recorded. Table 3 level data (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain, anxiety levels 1-3 collapsed categories) were not extracted as outcomes. Between-instrument correlations (r=-0.215 to 0.686) are not treatment effects. No primary outcome was stated.

summary: This single-center Egyptian RCT randomized 60 adults aged 40-50 with post-COVID respiratory symptoms to 12 weeks of traditional chest physiotherapy alone (Group A) or the same program plus the active cycle of breathing technique (Group B). Group B showed larger improvements in fatigue (FAS 38.66 to 15.06 vs 39.06 to 25.03), 6MWT (487.03 to 592.3 m vs 478 to 531.03 m), SaO2, PaO2 and PaCO2, with between-group p=0.001 at follow-up. Methodological reporting is poor (no flow data, unclear randomization and concealment), so the findings should be interpreted cautiously.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm mapping: arm_id 1 = paper's Group B (ACBT + traditional), arm_id 2 = Group A (traditional only). Table MD rows are Group A minus Group B, so between_group_effects use comparison arm2_vs_arm1 with the paper's sign retained. Per-outcome analyzed Ns are not stated (n=30/arm is the randomized number only), so n_analyzed is null. Text/table inconsistencies: Table 1 lists 18+17=35 females while text states 31 women and 29 men; text gives Group A fatigue decline 34.92% vs Table 2 35.92%; SaO2 Group A 2.75 (text) vs 2.70 (Table 3) vs 2.7 (abstract); text states within-group p>0.001 (likely typo for <0.001). Table values were used. Percent changes for PaCO2 are reductions reported as positive magnitudes. Methods mention a modified dyspnea scale (Mann-Whitney) but no results are reported. Table 3 PaCO2 p-value row is split into a separate table in the source; p-values 0.14 baseline and 0.001 post were taken from it. Main time/treatment/interaction MANOVA F statistics (interaction F=78.04, treatment F=25.41, time F=500.18) are reported only as omnibus across outcomes. Between-group p-values apply to unadjusted group comparisons at each timepoint (Bonferroni post hoc stated in methods).

summary: This quasi-experimental study in Russian university students compared a 9-month program of neuro-stimulating exercises combined with volleyball (n=25, post-COVID symptoms) against standard physical training (n=25 first-year students). The experimental group showed larger improvements in STAI anxiety, HADS anxiety and depression, tapping, ruler reaction, balance, Schulte attention time and volleyball skills (reported p<0.01), but allocation, control-group comparability, blinding and dispersion measures were poorly reported, so the evidence is at critical risk of bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Tables report 'M±m'; m is undefined in captions (conventionally SEM), so values were put in se with uncertainty_type unknown. Within-group changes were calculated from table values and match the text. Percentage-change outcomes in the text and abstract were not extracted as separate outcomes. No age, sex, vaccination or time-since-infection data reported. Null range/CI/median fields were omitted from arm_results for compactness.

summary: This single-center trial in India randomized 58 adults (18-45 years) with post-COVID-19 condition and balance/gait impairment to six weeks of Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization exercises or conventional physiotherapy (isometric strengthening plus TENS), with 29 per group. Tinetti balance improved more with DNS (9.97 to 14.14 vs 11.00 to 13.07; time x group interaction p<.001) and gait showed a significant interaction (p=0.006), although the gait gain (2.55 vs 1.69 points) did not reach the 3-point MDC. No follow-up after treatment and no adverse event reporting; methodological reporting has several inconsistencies.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Week 3 means for the Tinetti balance score appear only in a figure. Week 3 gait means (approx. 10.1 and 9.7) are from approximate text values with no SD. The overall age text is garbled ('31:83 _ 2:33') so overall age was not extracted. Post hoc tables (Tables 3 and 6) pool both groups and are not between-arm contrasts. The gait baseline is labelled 'Week 1' in Table 7 and 'Day 1' elsewhere; both were treated as baseline. The paper states that all outcomes were assessed as primary outcome measures, so is_primary was set to true for both. No between-arm mean difference or CI was reported; only omnibus interaction statistics.

summary: In 48 young, non-smoking women with mild-to-moderate post-COVID-19 symptoms, a 6-week, 3x/week supervised home telerehabilitation program (breathing, aerobic and resistance exercise) was compared with education-only control. The telerehabilitation group improved significantly more on 6-minute walk distance (between-group MD 55.83 m, p=0.001) and on all eight SF-36 domains (MD 11.87-17.68 points, p=0.001), while FVC and FEV1 did not differ between groups (p=0.12 and p=0.19). Adherence was high (94.21%) and no significant adverse events were reported, but participants and treating therapists were unblinded and no dropout data were given.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Outcome 12 is a bundle: percent changes were reported only in the intervention group, in prose (SF-36 subscales in Results; FEV1 7.66% and FVC 7.75% in Discussion); only the first value (25.88%) is entered as the arm mean and the remaining values are listed in the outcome name and quote. Baseline between-group MD/p values are in Tables 2-3 but omitted from between_group_effects; the 'Social role' and 'Emotional role' rows are mapped to the SF-36 social functioning and role-emotional scales. Percent female (100%) is inferred from recruitment of females only; blinding is inferred as assessor-blinded only. No CI, dropout, or adverse-event counts were reported. Mixed MANOVA omnibus: interaction F=413.09, time F=942.28, intervention F=32.78 (all p=0.001). n_screened (98) calculated as 48 participants plus 50 excluded.

risk_of_bias.domain_judgments: confounding:serious, selection:serious, classification:low, deviations:moderate, missing_data:moderate, measurement:serious, reporting:moderate
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Non-randomized self-selected allocation (controls were those unable to attend), with significant baseline imbalances in several outcomes (e.g., 6MWT, anxiety, SF-36 subscales), no confounder adjustment, unblinded self-reported outcomes, and 27% attrition handled by complete-case analysis.

summary: In this single-center, non-randomized controlled study of 41 healthcare professionals recovering from COVID-19 (26 yoga, 15 non-intervention), an 8-week supervised yoga-based exercise program (2 x 60 min/week) improved within-group 6MWT, physical activity (IPAQ), dyspnea (mMRC), flexibility, grip strength and several SF-36 domains. Between-group differences were significant for IPAQ, Beck anxiety and pain/social functioning but not for 6MWT, depression or most other measures, and baseline imbalances plus self-selected allocation limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Flowchart (Figure 1) not available as text; analyzed Ns (26/15) taken from Table 2 and dropout counts in text. Table 4 uses '+' instead of '±' and labels PSQI as 'PSQL'. Reported Beck anxiety change SD (±0.46 in YBEG) appears inconsistent with the other SDs and may be a typo. Table 4 and 6 report omnibus time/group p values, not arm-specific within-group p. Text says PSQI time effect nonsignificant (p=0.054) but group effect significant (p=0.049); text claims significant pain between-group difference although the interaction p=0.067 (group main-effect p=0.028). Between-group MDs are calculated (yoga minus control) from post-treatment means, not baseline-adjusted. Text describes the 6MWT change difference as nonsignificant without a p value. Hospitalization percent for control group in Table 2 (14.3%) is inconsistent with 1/15; overall hospitalized calculated as 7/41. Median-based outcomes include no means/SDs. No adverse events reported.

summary: Retrospective single-arm case series of 27 critically ill, post-ICU COVID-19 survivors in Sao Paulo who received intensive multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation (mean 22.7 days). Muscle strength (MRC 43.81 to 50.67), functional independence (FIM 72.63 to 100.67) and ambulation (FAC) improved significantly (p<0.01, p<0.0001 and p<0.01), with 13 patients (48.15%) walking independently at discharge. There was no control group, so improvement cannot be attributed to the program, and several measures had substantial missing data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post; discharge timepoint set at 3.2 weeks (mean 22.70 days of rehabilitation). Participants are post-hospital COVID-19 survivors, not formally defined Long COVID. Spearman correlations reported but not extracted as outcomes: FIM-Delta vs treatment duration r=0.71 (n=27); FFBM-Delta vs duration r=0.79 (n=18). Within-group change means for MRC and FIM are calculated from group means. Table 1 row MV/eP appears to have median/IQR/max values duplicating the later table pattern; reported as printed. Table 2 MoCA 'Abnormal' 1 (3.70%) conflicts with Discussion stating cognition was altered in almost all patients. Baseline-only variables (length of stay, CRP 253.37 mg/L, DASS-21 stress/depression, IES-R, pressure ulcer 70.37%) not extracted as outcomes beyond DASS anxiety/MoCA. Percentages of dysphagia, GLIM and DASS events are calculated sums of reported category counts.

summary: This neuroimaging substudy of a pilot RCT tested whether a 12-week cognitive rehabilitation program (virtual sessions plus computerized training) altered resting-state connectivity in the central executive, default-mode and salience networks, versus an attention-matched control, in adults with long COVID and cognitive impairment (39 analyzed: 19 intervention, 20 control). No significant group, time or group-by-time effects were found on within- or between-network connectivity (e.g., overall mean interaction b = 0.003, p = 0.66). Exploratory brain-behavior associations (notably salience-DMN connectivity with worse cognition) were nominal only and did not survive multiple-comparison correction; the study was underpowered.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Per-arm connectivity means/SDs are not reported in text (boxplots in supplemental figures; Supplemental Table 1 not provided). Only the overall network mean interaction has full statistics; other networks reported only as p>0.25 (abstract says all P>0.22). Randomization, blinding, allocation concealment and per-arm randomized Ns are deferred to the parent trial (Becker et al. [18]). Exploratory change-score regressions (8 nominal associations, e.g., DKEFS Word Reading vs CEN b=9.64, p=0.028; WCST perseverative errors vs Salience-DMN b=-5.97, p=0.007) pool participants and are not between-arm treatment effects, so they were not extracted as outcomes. Timepoint and Intervention main effects (e.g., overall mean Timepoint b=-0.005, p=0.36; Intervention b=-0.011, p=0.11) are not treatment-effect contrasts and were omitted. Figure 1 flow diagram text is not available beyond 58 enrolled and 39 imaged.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Baseline severity and D0-to-D28 change in CAT, CFQ-11, BSRS-5
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Logistic regression (Table 3) found no statistically significant associations for any predictor with baseline severity or D0-D28 change; all ORs had CIs spanning 1 (lowest p=0.0535 for non-vegetarian vs vegetarian, CFQ-11 on D0).

summary: This single-center retrospective, single-arm cohort of 47 Taiwanese outpatients with COVID-19 sequelae evaluated personalized traditional Chinese herbal medicine over 14 and 28 days. Median CAT (respiratory) and CFQ-11 (fatigue) scores fell significantly from D0 to D14 and D28 among patients with higher baseline symptoms, and the proportions with moderate-to-high respiratory and fatigue symptoms decreased significantly; emotional distress improved significantly only in patients with baseline BSRS-5 of 6 or more, and the proportion with distress did not change significantly. With no control group, a small sample, and no adverse event reporting, the improvements cannot be attributed to the intervention.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Only medians/IQRs reported (no means/SDs); within-group p-values given only as significance statements or stars in figures (exact values not in text), so p_value is null for Friedman comparisons. Per-group counts at D14/D28 in proportion outcomes were calculated from reported percentages of N=47. Figure-only content (Figs 2-4) not available. Text states CFQ-11 'score >16' and 'scores >=16' inconsistently (n=30 high group, n=17 low, consistent with >=16 cut-off); BSRS-5 '>6' likewise treated as >=6 (n=22). Table 1 baseline lab values were not extracted as outcomes since they are baseline-only. Table 3 logistic regression ORs (ORs per predictor for baseline severity and change) not extracted into structured fields; summarized in subgroup_analyses. Table 3 results not itemised. Combined co-occurrence proportions (3 symptom types 34.04%/17.02%/21.28%; 2 types 31.91%/17.89%/17.02%; 1 type 27.66%/40.43%/19.15%) not captured as separate outcomes.

summary: Single-center Saudi case series of 21 patients (mean age 34.4, 90.5% female) with persistent parosmia after PCR-confirmed COVID-19. Mean MA-SNOT score at presentation was 18.14 ± 10.99; 3 of 9 patients given intranasal/oral steroids and 2 of 12 untreated patients reported improvement. There was no comparison group or inferential testing, so no treatment efficacy conclusion can be drawn.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 caption says n=19 but counts sum to 21 and the row labels are garbled; the 11/10 split is read as <=3 vs >3 months. Figures 1 and 2 are images, so only the text values were used. Treatment improvement counts come from text only. Discussion figures (four treated with no improvement, two just started) were not extracted. Intervention arm details are non-standardized because treatments were not assigned by the study.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Improvement in TIBSIT scores at 3 and 6 months
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Univariate Fisher's exact analyses found no statistically significant associations with TIBSIT improvement at 3 or 6 months (all p > 0.05).

summary: This small single-center Malaysian RCT (n=31) compared olfactory training alone, olfactory training plus mometasone furoate nasal spray, and no intervention in adults with persistent post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction over 6 months. TIBSIT and eODQ scores improved within all groups, with the combination group significantly better than control at 3 months (p=0.036) but not 6 months (p=0.085), and olfactory training alone not different from control. The authors conclude that no intervention showed superiority over control, suggesting spontaneous recovery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Arm mapping: arm_id 1 = paper Group 2 (mometasone + training), arm_id 2 = paper Group 3 (control), arm_id 3 = paper Group 1 (olfactory training alone). Only medians/IQRs reported (no means/SDs). Between-arm effect sizes not reported, only p-values (Mann-Whitney U); within-arm Wilcoxon p-values are recorded with p_value_scope within_arm. Per-arm age, sex and BMI not reported (overall only: age mean 35.9 ± 9.7, 67.7% female). Control-group intervention not described. Stated sample size calculation of 30 vs 31 randomized; the text says 31 recruited while Table 1 percentages use n=31. Spearman correlation between TIBSIT and eODQ reported identically at 3 and 6 months (rs = -0.454, p = 0.010), likely a reporting error, so not extracted as an outcome. Blinding: only 'the research team was kept blinded'; participant blinding not possible/stated. n_screened/n_eligible derived from recruitment flow (53 attended, 13 ineligible, 9 declined, 31 recruited). Comparison of Group 1 vs Group 2 not reported. Per-arm vaccination status is in Table 1 but not extracted as percent_vaccinated.
